articles/audio/channels/Binaural-Audio.h.title: Binaural Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/Binaural-Audio.h.keywords: Binaural Audio Binaural audio is designed around the signals reaching two ears. Differences in arrival time, level, and frequency response help the listener perceive where a sound is coming from, including directions that ordinary left/right balance does not fully describe. It can be recorded with microphones positioned like ears, or generated by filtering sound for a modeled listener. The filtering uses head-related transfer functions , or HRTFs: descriptions of how the head, torso, and outer ears alter sound arriving from a direction. Qualitative illustration of unequal paths to the ears. Timing, level, and spectral cues depend on direction and the listener; the diagram contains no measured delay or filter response. Two channels can carry a spatial presentation A finished binaural render usually has one channel for each ear. Its file can therefore be labeled stereo even when it was created from many spatial sound components. Two-channel presentation What its signals are intended to represent Conventional stereo mix Left and right sides of a soundstage Binaural render Sound reaching the left and right ears Headphones deliver those signals to the ears with relatively little acoustic mixing between sides. Speakers send each signal to both ears and add the room's response, so a headphone-oriented binaural render does not necessarily produce the same spatial result over speakers. Individual anatomy matters. An HRTF that works convincingly for one listener may make elevation or front/back distinctions less clear for another. Head tracking can update generated cues as the listener moves, but a stored two-channel binaural recording does not automatically contain such a capability. In Emby, the channel count alone cannot identify whether a track is binaural. Track descriptions or the release's documentation may provide that context. If the signals already contain binaural cues, another virtual-surround processor can alter the intended presentation rather than simply adding more spatial detail. See Also Stereo Audio Virtual Surround Object-Based Audio References W3C Web Audio API: Channel interpretation and HRTF panning Microsoft: Virtualized surround sound over headphones Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/channels/layouts/Mono-Aud.title: Mono Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/layouts/Mono-Aud.keywords: Mono Audio Mono audio uses one channel for the complete presentation. It can contain dialogue, music, and effects together, but it does not assign separate left and right positions to them. That one signal can be reproduced by one speaker, both stereo speakers, or an appropriate route in a larger system. Hearing it from two speakers does not turn the source into stereo. Stored presentation What the channels contain One-channel mono One complete signal Two channels with identical audio The same mono presentation in both channels Two different independent mono programmes Two selections or signals; not necessarily a stereo mix Older television material, archival recordings, and some spoken-word content naturally use mono. Its usefulness does not depend on having fewer musical instruments or on using a low bitrate: a complex mix can still be mono. Mono and a center channel are different A mono track is the entire soundtrack. The center channel is one part of a multichannel soundtrack, commonly used for screen-centered dialogue and other front sounds. Selecting a mono track should not mean discarding all the other parts of a surround mix. Conversely, converting a stereo mix to mono requires combining left and right. Opposing signal components can partially cancel when summed, so a stereo mix with an unusual phase relationship may change noticeably in mono. Merely taking one side can lose material that exists on the other side. In Emby, a mono label helps identify the track's layout. It does not indicate an incomplete delivery or require audio conversion by itself. If an old programme sounds equally strong from both sides of a stereo system, that can be exactly the intended playback of its mono source. See Also Stereo Audio Multichannel Audio The Audio Center Channel References Microsoft WAVEFORMATEX: Sample rate, channels, and data rate W3C Web Audio API: Channel interpretation and HRTF panning

articles/audio/channels/layouts/Stereo-A.title: Stereo Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/layouts/Stereo-A.keywords: Stereo Audio Stereo audio carries left and right channels. Differences in their signals allow a mix to place voices and instruments across a soundstage, instead of presenting everything through one mono signal. Stereo does not require every sound to appear on only one side. A voice sent equally to both channels can seem centered between correctly arranged speakers. This is a phantom center : the apparent source exists between the speakers without a physical center speaker carrying its own channel. Relationship between the channels Typical impression with suitable playback Equal, matching signal on both sides Centered image More level on one side Image moves toward that side Different ambience or timing information Width and spatial character change These are basic examples, not universal rules for every mix or room. The phantom center is strongest near the intended listening position; moving close to one speaker changes the balance and arrival times. Two channels do not settle every question Duplicating mono audio into left and right produces two channels but no new stereo information. Two independent language programmes can also occupy two channels without being intended as one stereo soundstage. Binaural audio is commonly stored in two channels as well. Its signals are designed around the cues reaching each ear, usually for headphones. It shares the channel count with stereo while using a different spatial presentation. An Emby track described as stereo tells you that left and right signals are present. It does not specify the codec, recording method, or spatial processing applied by the output system. If a six-channel source is converted to stereo, the resulting two channels can include contributions from the center and surround channels; they are not simply the original front pair. See Also Mono Audio Binaural Audio The Audio Center Channel References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system W3C Web Audio API: Channel interpretation and HRTF panning Microsoft: Virtualized surround sound over headphones

articles/audio/channels/layouts/Surround.title: 5.1 Surround Sound | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/layouts/Surround.keywords: 5.1 Surround Sound 5.1 surround sound carries five main channels plus a low-frequency-effects channel. The conventional layout places three channels at the front and two around the sides or rear of the listener. Schematic top view of the conventional 5.1 layout. Speaker positions are illustrative; the LFE label identifies a signal, not a prescribed subwoofer location. Channel Role in the layout Left and right Front soundstage and panned front sounds Center Stable front-center position, often used for dialogue Left surround and right surround Side/rear effects and ambience LFE Separate low-frequency effects signal The “.1” describes the LFE's limited frequency range, not one tenth of a normal channel's loudness. There are six signals altogether. The main channels can contain bass too; LFE is not the complete bass content of the soundtrack. ITU-R BS.775 gives a reference arrangement with the front left and right at ±30 degrees and surrounds in sectors 100–120 degrees from front center. Actual installations should follow the system's placement guidance and the room's constraints. What the label leaves open 5.1 describes a layout, not a codec. Compressed and uncompressed formats can carry it. It also does not promise that the output system will reproduce six independent signals: a stereo destination needs an appropriate combined presentation. When playing a 5.1 track through Emby, distinguish the source channel layout from the player's final output. A subwoofer can receive redirected bass even from a stereo source, while a 5.1 source can play without a physical subwoofer if the system routes bass appropriately. The number of physical bass speakers is therefore not a reliable way to identify the source track. See Also Multichannel Audio 7.1 Surround Sound The Audio Center Channel Low-Frequency Effects (LFE) References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/channels/layouts/Surround.title: 7.1 Surround Sound | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/layouts/Surround.keywords: 7.1 Surround Sound In the common home-theater layout, 7.1 adds a rear surround pair to the five main-channel roles familiar from 5.1 . Separate side and rear channels give a mix more control over sounds around and behind the listener. Schematic top view: three front channels, two side surrounds, and two rear surrounds. The separate LFE signal is shown without fixing a subwoofer position. This illustrates the common layout, not every possible eight-channel arrangement. Main-channel group Number of channels Front left, center, and front right 3 Left and right side surround 2 Left and right rear surround 2 With LFE included, the track has eight channels. Those extra surrounds are still around the listener's plane; 7.1 alone does not describe height channels . A speaker arrangement such as 7.1.4 explicitly adds four height positions, and belongs to a different description of the playback system. Extra positions need the complete path A 7.1 source does not require every listener to own eight speakers. It can be reduced for another layout. The intended conversion combines the additional positions; dropping channels arbitrarily can lose sounds. Likewise, playing a 5.1 soundtrack through a receiver with seven main speakers does not give the file new discrete rear channels. The receiver may derive outputs through spatial processing, but that is a different source of information. For an Emby session, the channel label identifies what the selected track contains. The codec, client, and output connection determine how that presentation reaches the audio system. If eight channels appear in a report, check the actual layout and order , because channel count alone cannot distinguish rear surrounds from other possible positions. See Also 5.1 Surround Sound Multichannel Audio Audio Channel Order Object-Based Audio References Dolby: 7.1.2 speaker placement, including side and rear surrounds Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/channels/Matrix-Surround..title: Matrix Surround | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/Matrix-Surround..keywords: Matrix Surround Matrix surround carries information for a surround presentation within fewer transmitted channels. The classic example is a two-channel signal designed to be decoded into front and surround outputs. The encoder combines channel contributions using chosen level and phase relationships. A matching decoder analyzes those relationships and steers sound toward the intended positions. Unlike discrete multichannel audio, the transmitted signal does not contain a separate, independently recoverable waveform for every output speaker. Label What it describes Lt/Rt: left total/right total Two channels prepared for matrix-surround decoding Lo/Ro: left only/right only A conventional stereo downmix without that matrix encoding Discrete multichannel Separate encoded signals for the defined channel roles Lt/Rt can be listened to as ordinary stereo. A compatible matrix decoder can then use its encoded relationships to produce a surround presentation. The chosen system matters: classic Dolby Surround and later Pro Logic II do not describe identical output arrangements. Two stored channels can be intentional An Emby media report showing two channels does not rule out matrix encoding. The spatial instructions are in the relationship between those channels rather than in six discrete channel streams. Preserving both channels and their relationship matters; taking one side or altering their phase independently can impair decoding. There is also a distinction between decoding an intentionally encoded matrix and applying an upmixer to an arbitrary stereo recording. The latter derives extra outputs from the available content, but cannot establish that the producer placed a particular sound in a separate source surround channel. Matrix decoding and virtual surround address different stages. A matrix decoder determines signals for surround positions; a virtualizer can try to reproduce those positions over headphones or a smaller speaker arrangement. Both can be involved in one session, but neither changes the file's original channel count. See Also Stereo Audio Multichannel Audio Virtual Surround References Dolby DP563 Pro Logic II and Surround Encoder: Quick start guide Dolby: A Guide to Dolby Metadata

articles/audio/channels/Multichannel-Aud.title: Multichannel Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/Multichannel-Aud.keywords: Multichannel Audio Multichannel audio carries several sound channels within one audio presentation. A film's left, center, right, and surround signals can therefore remain separate until the playback system decides how to reproduce them. Channels are not the same as selectable tracks. A single 5.1 English track normally contains six channels. A second 5.1 French track contains another complete presentation; it is not one of the first track's six channels. Information What it answers Channel count How many signals the presentation carries Channel layout Which roles those signals have Channel order Where each role appears in the data Output arrangement Which speakers or headphone rendering will reproduce it The layout matters as much as the count. Four signals intended for front and rear positions are different from four unrelated recording stems. Software needs their meaning, not just the number four. A source layout is not a speaker inventory A six-channel soundtrack can be played on a stereo television by combining its channels appropriately. A receiver can also redirect bass from main channels to a subwoofer. Neither operation changes how many channels the original soundtrack contains. When Emby reports a source as 5.1 , that identifies the track, not a guarantee of six independent output paths all the way to the room. The client, connection, and audio system must support the presentation, or a conversion is needed. Likewise, object-based audio can carry spatial instructions beyond the channels visible in a basic media report. A plain channel count cannot establish whether those instructions survive playback. If dialogue comes from an unexpected speaker or effects appear in front instead of behind, check channel mapping . More channels cannot compensate for channels sent to the wrong places. See Also 5.1 Surround Sound 7.1 Surround Sound Audio Channel Order Object-Based Audio References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/channels/object-based/Dol.title: Dolby Atmos | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/object-based/Dol.keywords: Dolby Atmos Dolby Atmos carries spatial information beyond a conventional fixed surround mix. A renderer uses that information to place sounds around and above the listener, according to the supported speaker or headphone arrangement. Atmos is not one fixed channel count or one storage bitrate. A basic media report can show 5.1 or 7.1 for a track whose encoded data also contains Atmos information. That number alone cannot confirm or rule out immersive rendering. The delivery form matters Common form Role in the playback path Dolby Digital Plus with Atmos Compressed delivery using audio and additional object information; lossy Dolby TrueHD with Atmos Lossless delivery of the encoded audio presentation with Atmos information Dolby MAT with Atmos Metadata-bearing transport used to carry decoded audio and Atmos information to a compatible system Dolby Digital Plus object carriage is specified in ETSI TS 103 420. It uses a compatible channel mix together with information for recovering and rendering objects. A decoder that supports the conventional presentation can play that presentation without reproducing the full Atmos experience. Dolby MAT is especially relevant to interpreting a receiver's input. Decoding an Atmos track does not necessarily destroy its spatial information: an object-aware path can carry the decoded audio and metadata onward. Ordinary channel PCM without that metadata is a different result. Source format and final rendering are separate A speaker description such as 5.1.4 describes the listening arrangement, not the number of objects in the file. The renderer distributes the spatial presentation over its supported outputs. A headphone render uses ear cues instead of separate physical height speakers. For Emby playback, check the selected track, the server's delivery method , and what the player sends to the audio system. Support for one Atmos delivery form does not establish support for every other one. A receiver can also apply an immersive listening mode to ordinary audio, so its processing-mode name and its detected input format answer different questions. See Also Object-Based Audio 7.1 Surround Sound Binaural Audio References Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Technology and delivery Dolby Atmos Renderer guide ETSI TS 103 420 V1.2.1: Backwards-compatible object audio carriage using Enhanced AC-3

articles/audio/channels/object-based/DTS.title: DTS:X | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/object-based/DTS.keywords: DTS:X DTS:X is an immersive audio technology that uses spatial information to place sound for the playback arrangement. Its description can include objects and channels, rather than requiring every sound to be tied to one fixed speaker position. A moving effect can therefore be rendered across the outputs the system supports. That flexibility is still bounded by the decoder, device, and its supported layouts; the DTS:X name does not promise an unlimited speaker configuration. A disc track can have a compatible presentation DTS:X Master Audio delivery used on Blu-ray and UHD Blu-ray builds on the DTS-HD family. The encoder provides compatibility with legacy DTS-HD and DTS Digital Surround playback. An older compatible decoder can reproduce a conventional presentation while missing the additional immersive rendering. Observation What it establishes A track contains DTS:X information Spatial information is present in the encoded source Playback falls back to compatible channel audio A soundtrack can remain audible without full DTS:X rendering The audio system renders DTS:X Its input path and renderer have accepted the required information The label also needs delivery context. ETSI TS 103 491 specifies DTS-UHD for channels, objects, and sound fields in streaming and broadcast applications. Compatibility with a disc-based DTS:X Master Audio track should not be assumed to cover every other DTS:X delivery form. What to inspect during Emby playback The source's channel count can describe its compatible presentation; it need not describe every spatial component. If a client or conversion produces ordinary channel PCM, the original object instructions are not conveyed by those samples alone. Compare the source label with the detected input at the audio system. Also distinguish DTS:X content from DTS Headphone:X , which is a headphone rendering technology. It can process ordinary stereo or multichannel sources. Hearing spatial processing through headphones does not by itself establish that the selected file contains a DTS:X soundtrack. See Also Object-Based Audio Dolby Atmos 7.1 Surround Sound Virtual Surround References DTS: Object-based audio and DTS:X backward compatibility DTS:X Encoder Suite: Production tools and compatibility ETSI TS 103 491 V1.2.1: DTS-UHD delivery of channels, objects, and sound fields DTS Headphone:X

articles/audio/channels/object-based/Obj.title: Object-Based Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/object-based/Obj.keywords: Object-Based Audio A conventional surround mix assigns signals to fixed channel positions. Object-based audio describes sound components with spatial metadata , allowing a renderer to decide how to reproduce them on the available system. A helicopter can be described as moving above the listener rather than simply being assigned to one named surround channel. Its audio and its position through time are separate parts of the description. The renderer turns that description into speaker or headphone signals. Conceptual rendering path. Delivery codecs can combine and reconstruct components in different ways; the diagram does not imply a separate file or transmitted channel for every object. An object-based production can also include beds : channel-based elements used alongside objects. The format is not required to turn every instrument, voice, or background sound into a separate object. Why the metadata matters Information kept in the playback path What remains possible Sound plus object metadata Rendering for a supported spatial arrangement A conventional channel render only Playback of that fixed presentation A stereo render only Playback of its two-channel presentation Once a mix is flattened to ordinary channel PCM, those samples alone do not preserve the original objects and their movement instructions. An object-aware transport can carry metadata alongside audio, but that is additional information beyond plain channel PCM. This explains why an Emby source may display a familiar channel count while also containing immersive information. The count can describe a compatible channel presentation rather than the complete spatial description. Dolby Atmos and DTS:X are examples readers will encounter. Their rendering flexibility still depends on the exact encoding, player, and output path. Object-based audio adapts a mix to supported arrangements; it does not make missing hardware, metadata, or decoder capabilities appear automatically. See Also Dolby Atmos DTS:X Multichannel Audio Binaural Audio References ITU-R BS.2076-3: Audio Definition Model Dolby Atmos Renderer guide Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.title: The Audio Center Channel | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.keywords: The Audio Center Channel The center channel is a separate signal assigned to the front-center position in a multichannel layout. It is commonly used for dialogue anchored to the screen, but can also carry music, effects, or other front sounds. A dedicated center helps keep that position stable for listeners who are not seated exactly between the front left and right speakers. Stereo can create a phantom center by sending matching signals to both sides, but its apparent position changes more with the listening position. Presentation How a centered voice can be carried Stereo Shared between left and right Conventional 5.1 or 7.1 Often in the separate center channel Stereo conversion of surround Center contribution combined into left and right These are common mixing choices, not a guarantee that all spoken words occupy one channel. A character speaking from elsewhere in the scene may be deliberately panned, and ambience can accompany dialogue across several positions. Why voices can disappear while effects remain If a surround track's center is sent to an unavailable output or omitted during an incorrect conversion, much of its dialogue may be lost while music and effects remain audible. Taking only front left and right from a 5.1 track is not the same operation as making a proper stereo presentation. The opposite is also possible: a center speaker can be present but level, placement, or room acoustics can make voices difficult to understand. Channel routing and dialogue intelligibility are related checks, not interchangeable diagnoses. When playing through Emby, inspect the selected track and the actual output arrangement before concluding that the source mix is defective. A stereo version of the same material, if available, can provide a useful comparison. Increasing overall volume cannot restore a channel that never reaches the output. See Also Stereo Audio 5.1 Surround Sound Audio Channel Order References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.title: Audio Channel Order | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.keywords: Audio Channel Order Channel order is the assignment of signal positions in the data to their intended roles. The decoder and output system must agree about which values belong to left, right, center, surrounds, and LFE. Count alone is insufficient. Six correctly decoded waveforms sent to the wrong positions can still put dialogue in a surround speaker or ordinary sound into an LFE path. For interleaved PCM, one frame stores a value for each channel before the next frame begins. A channel mask or layout tells the reader how to interpret that sequence. WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE example Interleaved order defined by its mask Stereo, mask 0x3 Front left, front right 5.1 with side surrounds, mask 0x60F Front left, front right, front center, LFE, side left, side right Common 7.1, mask 0x63F Front left, front right, front center, LFE, back left, back right, side left, side right These examples use Microsoft's WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE convention. They are not a universal byte order for every codec or file format. A 5.1 mask using back positions instead of side positions also exists. Distinguishing those labels is useful when inspecting files, even when an installation's two surround speakers are physically similar. Decode first, then map by meaning Compressed formats can have their own internal ordering. A decoder may expose its output using a different working convention. Correct software maps roles across those conventions; manually rearranging channels based on a guessed codec order can break an already correct decode. Planar and interleaved are separate storage arrangements. Planar audio still needs channel roles even though each channel occupies its own buffer. If an Emby session has consistently misplaced sound, compare the source layout, the decoder's output layout, and the destination's configuration. A “six channels” label proves neither their order nor their final routing. Silence in a particular scene, however, can simply be the mix: not every channel must carry sound continuously. See Also Multichannel Audio PCM Sample Formats 7.1 Surround Sound References Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks FFmpeg: Audio sample formats

articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.title: Low-Frequency Effects (LFE) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/roles-and-orderi.keywords: Low-Frequency Effects (LFE) Low-frequency effects , or LFE, is a separate signal used for additional low-frequency energy. It is the “.1” in a conventional 5.1 or 7.1 soundtrack. The main channels can already contain low frequencies. LFE therefore does not mean “all the bass,” and a subwoofer's output is not necessarily a direct copy of the LFE channel. Signal reaching a subwoofer Where it comes from LFE content The soundtrack's separate effects channel Redirected bass Low-frequency content removed from main channels by bass management A combination Both paths summed by the playback system ITU-R BS.775 specifies an LFE band extending up to 120 Hz. The crossover used to redirect bass from small speakers is a separate setting. A system's 80 Hz crossover, for example, does not redefine the source LFE channel as an 80 Hz channel. The “.1” describes the source signal One LFE signal can feed more than one physical subwoofer. Conversely, a stereo source with no LFE channel can produce substantial subwoofer output through bass management. Counting subwoofers does not establish the source layout. LFE also has reproduction-level conventions handled by the decoding and calibrated playback system. It should not be treated as another full-range channel or boosted arbitrarily to make its meter look like the others. In an Emby session, the track's LFE flag identifies a source channel. The receiver or other output system determines how LFE and redirected bass reach the room. A stereo conversion may omit LFE while retaining bass from the main channels, so a different bass impression does not prove that all low-frequency audio has been lost. Correct diagnosis needs the source layout and the final output routing. See Also 5.1 Surround Sound The Audio Center Channel Multichannel Audio References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/channels/Virtual-Surround.title: Virtual Surround | Emby Learn
articles/audio/channels/Virtual-Surround.keywords: Virtual Surround Virtual surround uses signal processing to suggest sound positions beyond the available physical outputs. A headset marked “7.1,” for example, usually still has one main driver for each ear. The additional positions are represented by processed signals, not seven separate speakers around the listener. A headphone renderer can take a multichannel mix and filter each position into a binaural presentation . A speaker-based virtualizer works through a different acoustic arrangement, and can depend strongly on seating and the room. Input presentation What a virtualizer can use Discrete multichannel audio The existing channel positions Object-based audio with supported metadata The spatial descriptions provided by the source Ordinary stereo The information in two channels, possibly with derived spatial processing Virtualizing known surround positions and deriving new positions from stereo are different operations. A processor can make stereo feel wider or more enveloping without recovering separate surround recordings that never existed in the source. Convincing space depends on the listener Headphone spatialization uses timing and spectral cues associated with a head and ears. The model's fit, the headphones, and any head-tracking behavior affect the impression. “Virtual” describes the method, not a guarantee that every listener hears the same convincing external soundstage. For Emby playback, the processing may live in the operating system, headset software, television, soundbar, or receiver. The source track and the server's delivery method do not identify which of those effects is active. A stored binaural track already has ear-specific cues. Passing it through another spatializer may alter them. Likewise, a stereo-only path can leave a virtualizer with fewer source positions than a preserved multichannel path. To compare listening modes meaningfully, use the same track and level, and distinguish the detected input format from the system's selected effect. See Also Binaural Audio Multichannel Audio Matrix Surround References Microsoft: Virtualized surround sound over headphones Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering DTS Headphone:X

articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Des.title: Audio-Description Tracks | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Des.keywords: Audio-Description Tracks Audio description adds narration of important visual information , such as actions, scene changes, expressions, or text that the main soundtrack does not explain. It helps people who are blind or have low vision follow the programme. The narration is usually fitted around dialogue and other important sound. It is a different presentation of the programme, not simply a clearer recording of its existing speech. Track description Intended role English — Main The ordinary English soundtrack English — Audio Description English soundtrack with visual description English — Commentary A discussion of the programme, often by its creators These are illustrative titles. Real files use varied labels, and a language code alone cannot distinguish the roles. Complete mix or supplementary audio A stored movie can provide a complete alternative mix with the narration already combined with the programme. Selecting that audio track is enough to hear the described presentation. Broadcast systems can instead carry supplementary description that a capable receiver combines with the main audio. The supplementary component is not necessarily a complete soundtrack by itself. Its signaling and intended mixing arrangement matter when preserving or converting a recording. In an Emby library, keep track titles and language metadata informative so that a described track can be recognized among several audio choices. If the track contains a complete described mix, selecting it should be understood as choosing that presentation, regardless of its stereo or surround layout. Audio description must be supplied or created as content. A codec conversion, a louder center channel, or automatic dialogue transcription does not add explanations of visual events. Losing an alternate track during file conversion can therefore remove an accessibility option even when the main soundtrack still plays normally. See Also Streams and Tracks Track Language Metadata Audio Codecs Explained Dolby AC-4 Audio References W3C: Description of visual information W3C WCAG 2.2: Audio description of prerecorded video ETSI EN 300 468 V1.17.1: DVB service information and audio description signaling

articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Pla.title: The Audio Playback Path | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Pla.keywords: The Audio Playback Path The soundtrack in a file and the format arriving at an amplifier are two different observations . Following the stages between them helps explain why a TrueHD source can correctly reach a receiver labeled “PCM,” or why a multichannel source ends up as stereo. Original schematic: these are logical stages. A television, soundbar, or integrated player may combine several in one device. Delivery comes before output Emby's playback method describes what the server sends. Direct Play can deliver the stored track unchanged. Direct Stream can repackage compatible media, and may convert audio while retaining the video. Transcoding creates a new encoded presentation where required. After delivery, the player can decode the audio to PCM or send a supported encoded format onward using passthrough . The operating system and physical output then impose their own format and channel requirements. Finally, a receiver or DAC turns the delivered presentation into sound. Speaker routing, bass management, headphone rendering, and an optional listening mode can affect this stage. Inspect the labels in context Start with the selected track's codec and layout. Then check the server session, the player's output choice, and the receiver's detected input , in that order. The receiver's surround-processing mode may be a separate label. If a 7.1 source becomes 2.0 PCM, locate where the channel count changed. It could be server conversion, player downmixing, or the output configuration. If the output is 7.1 PCM, the absence of the compressed codec's name on the receiver is not itself a fault. This approach is more informative than treating a single “Direct Play,” “PCM,” or “Atmos” label as a description of the entire session. See Also Audio Bitstream Passthrough Decoded PCM Output Audio Transcoding References Microsoft: Choosing an audio codec Microsoft: Representing formats for IEC 61937 transmissions Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE

articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Vid.title: Audio/Video Synchronization | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Audio-Vid.keywords: Audio/Video Synchronization Audio/video synchronization means presenting related sound and picture at the right time. A clap or a clearly spoken consonant makes an offset easy to notice because the visual event and its sound belong together. The streams have different units: video is organized into frames, while audio is organized into samples and coded audio frames. Timestamps relate those units to a playback timeline. Equal packet arrival times are not the goal. Constant offset or growing drift? Observation What it suggests The same mismatch throughout the programme A fixed timing offset or processing delay Alignment starts well, then gradually worsens A rate, clock, or timeline mismatch A sudden change after a seek or discontinuity Re-establishment of timing may be involved Only one audio output route is affected Delay in that route is worth checking These are diagnostic clues, not complete fault diagnoses. A fixed offset can often be addressed by delaying the earlier presentation. For example, if sound arrives 80 ms before its matching picture, adding 80 ms of audio delay aligns that particular route. Interfaces use different signs for their adjustment controls, so verify the result rather than assuming what “positive” means. A single offset cannot fix continuing drift. A hypothetical clock-rate difference of 50 parts per million accumulates 0.18 seconds in one hour: 3,600 × 50 / 1,000,000. Changing the starting delay leaves that rate difference intact. In an Emby session, compare the same passage through another client or output route and note whether the mismatch is constant or grows. Display processing, decoded-audio buffering, and wireless output can add different delays. Keeping those observations separate from the file's timestamps narrows where to investigate. See Also Packet Timestamps Time Bases Video Frame Rate The Audio Playback Path References ITU-R BT.1359: Relative timing of sound and vision RFC 3550: RTP timestamps and synchronization FFmpeg: Audio filters, mixing, and delay

articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.title: Audio Downmixing | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.keywords: Audio Downmixing Downmixing combines audio channels for a smaller output layout , such as turning a 5.1 film soundtrack into stereo for a television or headphones. It should preserve useful content from the source presentation. Simply retaining front left and front right can omit much of the dialogue carried by the center channel. A stereo fold-down Source role Typical treatment in a stereo downmix Front left and right Contribute to the corresponding output side Center Contributes to both output sides Surrounds Contribute according to the selected mixing matrix LFE Treatment depends on the downmix design and playback system This is a routing overview, not a universal coefficient recipe. Ordinary stereo and matrix-compatible stereo can use different relationships and phase treatment. Combining channels also raises a numerical problem. If two channels each contain a simultaneous sample of +0.8, adding them at full gain produces +1.6, beyond the usual normalized full-scale limit. Mixing coefficients, gain adjustment, or other overload handling provide headroom. Channel reduction can change level without involving another lossy codec. Where the layout changed An Emby session may downmix during server conversion, client decoding, or output processing. If dialogue becomes weak, compare the source's center content with the resulting stereo channels and verify that the source layout was interpreted correctly. The LFE channel is not the same as all bass in the soundtrack. Bass management can redirect low frequencies from ordinary channels to a subwoofer separately from the LFE mix. A downmix preserves a useful smaller presentation, but it cannot keep every original channel independently available. Later upmixing cannot reverse that combination into the original discrete tracks. See Also The Audio Center Channel Low-Frequency Effects (LFE) Audio Clipping Audio Upmixing References ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system W3C: Web Audio API channel interpretation FFmpeg: Audio resampler and rematrixing options

articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.title: Audio Transcoding | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.keywords: Audio Transcoding Audio transcoding makes a new encoded audio stream from a decoded source. It can change the codec, bitrate, channel layout, or sample rate to suit the playback device and delivery conditions. In Emby, incompatible audio does not necessarily require re-encoding compatible video. A Direct Stream session can copy video while converting the soundtrack. Audio operation What happens to the samples Compatible lossless-to-lossless conversion Can preserve them when the formats and processing allow it Lossless to lossy Introduces the destination codec's approximation Lossy to lossy Encodes an already reconstructed signal again Downmixing or resampling during conversion Changes the presentation even before the final encoder By contrast, copying encoded packets into different packaging is remuxing . It does not make a new audio encoding. Why the target bitrate is not a restoration tool Giving an encoder a larger data budget can reduce new compression damage. It cannot restore detail discarded by an earlier lossy codec. A high-bitrate AAC delivery made from a low-bitrate MP3 remains limited by that input. Transcoding can also change more than fidelity. A multichannel track may become stereo, and an ordinary channel encoder may omit the object information of an immersive source. Producing another E-AC-3 stream, for example, does not automatically recreate an original Atmos presentation. For diagnosis, compare the source track with the delivered audio: codec, channel layout, bitrate, and relevant spatial information. The server's activity label tells you that conversion occurred; those details explain what changed. A converted stream can be the appropriate compatible result for a client. Keeping the original library file preserves the option to use its original presentation on another supported playback path. See Also Lossy Audio Compression Audio Downmixing Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata References FFmpeg: Stream copy and transcoding FFmpeg: Audio resampler and rematrixing options Xiph.Org: Vorbis FAQ

articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.title: Audio Upmixing | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.keywords: Audio Upmixing Upmixing uses more output channels than the source provides. A receiver can spread stereo music across surround speakers, or derive height activity from a conventional movie soundtrack. This is processing applied to an existing presentation. It does not prove that the source contains an immersive mix. Listening result What the processing can do The same signal from several speakers Duplicate or redistribute channels A stronger central image Derive center activity from relationships between channels Surround ambience Analyze and redistribute less central or less correlated material Height-speaker activity Derive output for an expanded speaker layout Methods differ. Matrix decoding can recover cues deliberately encoded into a stereo signal. An adaptive upmixer can also infer useful spatial behavior from ordinary material, but cannot guarantee the original separate studio channels. The receiver's mode is not its input Dolby Surround and DTS Neural:X are examples of processing used to expand compatible channel-based content. A receiver may show one of these mode names while its input is only 2.0 or 5.1. In an Emby movie session, check the receiver's detected input separately from the listening mode. Sound coming from height speakers may be the result of upmixing a conventional track. Native object rendering uses spatial information carried by an appropriate source and supported path. Whether an upmix sounds helpful depends on the material and listening arrangement. Comparing the same passage with the processing enabled and disabled can reveal changes to dialogue placement and ambience. A downmixed stereo version followed by upmixing is also not equivalent to preserving the original multichannel soundtrack. Once channels were combined, the upmixer has fewer independent signals to work with. See Also Matrix Surround Object-Based Audio Audio Downmixing Virtual Surround References Dolby: Atmos installation guidelines, Dolby Surround upmixer miniDSP: Surround decoding and upmixing FFmpeg: Audio filters, mixing, and delay

articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.title: Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/conversio.keywords: Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core An embedded core is an existing compatible part of an audio stream that a less capable decoder can use. Falling back to it can keep sound playing without re-encoding the full presentation. The common example is a DTS-HD disc soundtrack containing a DTS core . A core-only decoder uses the lossy compatible presentation; a full decoder can also use extension information. Operation Where the fallback audio comes from Embedded core fallback An already encoded component inside the stream Selecting another audio track A separately stored presentation Audio transcoding A new encoding made from decoded audio These operations can produce similar receiver labels while having different origins. A core does not preserve every enhancement A DTS core from a Master Audio track is not the lossless Master Audio result. It can also lack additional channels or immersive information available through the full presentation. The benefit is compatibility without another encoding generation, not preservation of all source features. Do not assume that every DTS-HD stream has a core: the format also allows extension-only arrangements. The Dolby case is different. TrueHD may be accompanied by an AC-3 fallback in disc packaging, but TrueHD itself does not contain a DTS-style lossy AC-3 core. E-AC-3 independent substreams are also not automatically AC-3 components. In an Emby session, confirm what the file actually contains and what was delivered. If a core is selected or extracted, compare that result with the full source presentation. If the server creates another codec, that is transcoding , even if the new track happens to use the same familiar codec name as a typical fallback. See Also DTS Core Audio DTS-HD Master Audio Dolby TrueHD Audio Audio Transcoding References ETSI TS 102 114 V1.6.1: DTS Coherent Acoustics core and extensions DTS: Production tools and backwards compatibility Dolby: TrueHD lossless audio Dolby: Dolby Digital Plus audio coding

articles/audio/decoding-output/Immersive.title: Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/Immersive.keywords: Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata An immersive soundtrack includes information about how sound should be rendered , as well as audio. Object positions and related metadata let a renderer adapt the presentation to a supported speaker or headphone arrangement. Keeping the audio audible is therefore a smaller requirement than keeping all the spatial information available for later rendering. Three different results Playback path Spatial information at the next stage Supported encoded passthrough Relevant information remains in the delivered bitstream Object-aware decoding and suitable metadata-bearing output Audio and required spatial information continue together Ordinary channel PCM output A channel presentation remains; original object metadata is not carried as such The middle route is why decoding does not automatically destroy Atmos. A suitable MAT path can carry decoded audio and metadata onward. This requires an object-aware implementation, not merely an ordinary multichannel PCM decoder. A player can also render an immersive source into its final output channels or a binaural signal. The listener can benefit from that render even though the receiver no longer gets the original objects to render again. Find the stage that changed the presentation Check the source's actual delivery form, the server's audio delivery , and the player's output. A metadata-bearing Dolby Digital Plus presentation and a TrueHD presentation ask different decoding and transport capabilities of the system. Transcoding with an ordinary channel encoder does not preserve object information merely by choosing the same codec family. Likewise, extracting a compatible audio core can leave the immersive extension behind. A basic “5.1” or “7.1” source report cannot confirm or rule out additional object information. A receiver's height-speaker activity also cannot settle the question, because an upmixer can derive height output from conventional channels. The useful evidence is which presentation and metadata actually reached the active renderer. See Also Dolby Atmos DTS:X Dolby MAT Audio Transport Audio Transcoding References ETSI TS 103 420 V1.2.1: Backwards-compatible object audio carriage using Enhanced AC-3 Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering Dolby: Atmos Renderer guide Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Audio Bitstream Passthrough | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Audio Bitstream Passthrough Bitstream passthrough leaves audio decoding to a downstream device , such as an AV receiver. The player sends an encoded presentation through a compatible output path instead of turning it into ordinary PCM channels first. That is separate from Emby's server-side Direct Play decision. A client can receive an unchanged file and still decode its soundtrack locally. Several capabilities have to agree Part of the route Required capability Player Recognize and output the specific encoded format Operating system and driver Expose a suitable encoded-audio output path Connection and intervening devices Carry that format through the selected route Receiver or soundbar Decode the delivered presentation Support at the final receiver does not remove a limitation earlier in the chain. A television forwarding audio can be a separate compatibility step even when it does not decode the soundtrack itself. IEC 61937 defines carriage of encoded audio over interfaces based on the digital audio framework. Different codec types have different transport requirements; the presence of an HDMI connector alone does not prove that a particular app can pass every format. Processing changes the question Mixing system sounds into a soundtrack or applying ordinary sample-based volume control generally requires decoded audio or a specially supported processing path. A passthrough option may therefore change which local controls are available. The receiver's detected input helps confirm what was delivered. Its chosen listening mode can add processing after decoding, so a surround-mode label is not proof of the original bitstream. For an Emby movie with immersive audio, passthrough can preserve suitable encoded spatial information when every stage supports it. An object-aware MAT output is another possible route; plain channel PCM and metadata-bearing transport should be distinguished. See Also Decoded PCM Output Dolby MAT Audio Transport The Audio Playback Path Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata References IEC 61937-1:2021: Non-linear PCM encoded audio bitstreams Microsoft: Representing formats for IEC 61937 transmissions Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Decoded PCM Output | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Decoded PCM Output When a receiver displays PCM , it is receiving sample values rather than being asked to decode the file's original compressed codec. The player or an earlier component has already reconstructed the audio. This can be the normal result of playing a lossless soundtrack. Decoding FLAC or a supported TrueHD presentation to PCM does not itself introduce lossy compression. What to check Why it matters Output channel count and layout Confirm whether the intended speaker presentation survived Output sample rate Identify any rate conversion Valid sample precision Separate audio precision from storage-word size Volume, mixing, and effects Identify processing applied after decoding A 24-bit signal can travel in a 32-bit storage word, so those two numbers need not match. Similarly, a high-rate PCM output can contain resampled lower-rate content rather than a high-rate original recording. PCM does not identify the source Both lossy and lossless decoders produce PCM. A receiver's PCM label therefore cannot tell you whether the library file was MP3, FLAC, or another codec. Ordinary channel PCM also does not carry the original object-position metadata of an immersive bitstream. A supported player can first render an immersive mix into output channels, or use a metadata-bearing path such as Dolby MAT . Those are different results. In an Emby session, compare the selected source, server delivery , and actual PCM output. A change from 7.1 to 2.0 needs investigation; a change from a compressed format's name to PCM can simply show that decoding happened in the player. See Also Linear PCM (LPCM) Audio Bitstream Passthrough Dolby MAT Audio Transport Audio Downmixing References Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEX Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.title: Dolby MAT Audio Transport | Emby Learn
articles/audio/decoding-output/output-tr.keywords: Dolby MAT Audio Transport The library file says Dolby Digital Plus with Atmos . The receiver says Dolby MAT . Follow one playback session, and those two labels can fit together: Point in the session What is present Job performed here Library file Dolby Digital Plus with an Atmos presentation Stores the compressed soundtrack Emby Server delivery The selected audio track, supplied without conversion Delivers the source presentation to the app Player processing Decoded audio with the required spatial information retained Decodes the compressed presentation Supported HDMI output A PCM-based Dolby MAT presentation Transports audio and associated Atmos information Receiver The received presentation and the configured speaker layout Renders the audio for those speakers This example assumes a player with the appropriate decoder and a supported PCM-based Atmos output route. Dolby MAT , Metadata-enhanced Audio Transmission, is the transport in the fourth row. The receiver names what arrived there; the file names what was stored in the first row. Read the chain at each boundary 1. Server to player. Supplying the selected compressed track unchanged leaves decoding to the player. A receiver indication farther downstream cannot establish whether the server changed the audio; check the actual server delivery path for that part of the chain. 2. Decoder to output. Decoding reconstructs audio, while rendering determines how a channel or object presentation becomes signals for speakers. An object-aware player can decode a compressed Atmos presentation and retain the information needed for downstream rendering. These are separate jobs, which is what makes a decoded Atmos transport useful. 3. HDMI to receiver. In the PCM-based MAT 2.0 use, the link carries audio together with the associated Atmos metadata. The receiver can use that presentation with its speaker arrangement. It receives more information than an ordinary set of completed 5.1 or 7.1 channel samples. 4. Receiver to speakers. Detected input information and the selected listening mode answer different questions. The former describes what arrived; an upmixer or other listening mode describes processing after receipt. Read the input-format report when tracing the source-to-receiver path. Change one part of the session Keep the same source track and server delivery, but select ordinary channel PCM output in the player. The receiver might now receive a completed 7.1 presentation: eight channels that it can play or further process. Those channels describe that particular rendering. They do not carry the original object presentation simply because the connection has room for multichannel PCM. Select encoded passthrough instead, where the whole path supports it. The downstream device then performs decoding as well as rendering. The placement of the decoder has changed, while the selected source may stay the same. Now change server delivery to an ordinary audio transcode. The app may receive a new channel-based presentation before it makes any output decision. A later MAT-capable output cannot reconstruct spatial information that the earlier conversion omitted. These changes explain why “where was it decoded?” is only part of the investigation. Follow what information survived each boundary , and the audible result becomes easier to account for. The audio playback path describes the surrounding stages. Why TrueHD playback also uses the MAT name MAT originally provided carriage for a variable-rate TrueHD bitstream over the HDMI audio transport arrangement. In that use, the source packs encoded TrueHD data into the transport and the receiving device unpacks and decodes it. PCM-based MAT 2.0 extends the possible route by carrying a decoded Atmos presentation with its metadata. The shared MAT name consequently does not locate the decoder by itself: identify the actual use and the source and output information. A media inspector examines the stored track. It can correctly identify TrueHD in an MKV even though the receiver describes its transport using MAT. There need not be a stored MAT track in the library file. Record the session in terms that can be compared For an Emby playback investigation, collect the selected source track, server delivery mode, player output choice, receiver input report, and speaker/rendering configuration. Together they describe a path. Reading just the file label or just the receiver's listening mode leaves several operations unexplained. Transport also preserves the compression history of the audio it carries. A decoded lossy source already contains the reconstruction from that lossy encode. Sending it onward without another lossy encoding step preserves that result; it does not turn the source into a lossless recording. A lossless TrueHD source can retain its recovered samples through a supported output path that preserves them. The file and receiver labels then have precise roles in the record: one identifies the retained source, and the other identifies the presentation delivered across the audio connection. See Also Dolby TrueHD Audio Dolby Atmos Decoded PCM Output Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata References IEC 61937-1:2021: Non-linear PCM encoded audio bitstreams Microsoft: Representing formats for IEC 61937 transmissions Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/formats/Audio-Codecs.html.title: Audio Codecs Explained | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/Audio-Codecs.html.keywords: Audio Codecs Explained A codec answers a practical question: what must the player understand to turn this track into sound? A media file can contain perfectly usable video while its soundtrack needs a decoder the client does not have. The name can refer to an encoded format or to software that implements it. Two AAC encoders may make different quality choices while producing tracks that the same AAC decoder can play. Three descriptions to keep separate Description Example What it identifies Container M4A or Matroska How tracks, timing, and tags are stored Audio codec AAC or FLAC How the audio data is represented Decoder implementation A player or system decoder The component that reconstructs sound A container extension alone cannot settle codec compatibility. An M4A file, for example, can contain AAC or Apple Lossless . The same extension can therefore describe two quite different audio streams. Compression and playback are different decisions Lossy codecs reduce data by allowing changes to the reconstructed signal. Lossless codecs preserve the encoded source samples exactly. Linear PCM stores sample values without audio compression. That distinction says little about which component decodes the track. A player can decode locally and send PCM to an amplifier, or pass a compatible encoded bitstream onward. When checking an Emby session, look at the codec, channel layout, and delivery method together. A client may accept a codec in stereo but require conversion for a multichannel presentation. A successful Direct Play session also does not establish that the receiver is receiving the original compressed format. See Also Containers and Codecs Audio Bitrate The Audio Playback Path References Microsoft: Choosing an audio codec Xiph.Org: Vorbis FAQ

articles/audio/formats/DSD.html.title: Direct Stream Digital (DSD) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/DSD.html.keywords: Direct Stream Digital (DSD) DSD represents sound as a very fast stream of one-bit values . It is associated with Super Audio CD and downloadable music, and uses a different sample representation from ordinary multibit linear PCM . Its large sample-rate number needs context. DSD64 uses 2,822,400 one-bit samples per second per channel: 64 times 44.1 kHz. That is not equivalent to PCM at the same numerical rate and a 16- or 24-bit word length. Common label One-bit sample rate per channel DSD64 2.8224 MHz DSD128 5.6448 MHz DSD256 11.2896 MHz These labels describe the usual 44.1 kHz family of rates. DSD encoding uses noise shaping to keep much of its quantization noise outside the audible band; playback and conversion require appropriate filtering. A higher DSD rate alone cannot establish that one release sounds better than another master. Representation, file, and output DSD is not a container. DSF and DSDIFF are file formats that can store it. WavPack can compress DSD losslessly, preserving the one-bit data for later restoration. A player may send DSD through a supported DSD output path or convert it to PCM. Conversion to PCM involves filtering and a change of representation; it is not the same operation as losslessly unpacking a compressed DSD file. For DSD music in an Emby library, distinguish the stored stream from the stream delivered to the client and the signal received by the DAC. The source's DSD label alone does not confirm native DSD output. Its unusual rate and bit depth are useful identifiers, not a direct quality score against PCM. See Also Linear PCM (LPCM) DSF: DSD Stream File DSDIFF: DFF Container WavPack Audio References Sony: DSF file format specification WavPack 5 porting guide: DSD compression and decoding Sony and Philips: Super Audio Compact Disc technical proposal

articles/audio/formats/lossless/ALAC.htm.title: Apple Lossless (ALAC) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/ALAC.htm.keywords: Apple Lossless (ALAC) Apple Lossless, or ALAC, compresses PCM audio reversibly. It is a distinct codec from AAC, even though both commonly appear in files ending in M4A. That shared extension is a frequent source of confusion: one M4A can be a lossy AAC music file, while another preserves its encoded PCM samples losslessly. Description ALAC meaning Codec identifier “alac” Identifies Apple Lossless content 16, 20, 24, or 32-bit Supported integer PCM sample precision One to eight channels Codec capability, subject to supported channel configurations M4A or CAF Possible file packaging, not the compression method Apple's published reference code and configuration description explain the format and channel mapping. Their included example conversion utility has narrower input support than the codec itself; limits of that tool should not be mistaken for limits of every ALAC implementation. Moving between lossless formats Converting supported PCM samples from FLAC to ALAC can preserve the audio exactly. The outer file, tags, artwork handling, and compressed bitrate can change. A larger ALAC copy is not automatically better or worse than the FLAC it came from. Similarly, converting an AAC file to ALAC preserves the decoded AAC result; it cannot undo the earlier lossy encoding. For an Emby music collection, identify the actual codec before diagnosing two M4A files that behave differently. The player's delivery compatibility and its supported sample format remain separate from ALAC's general format capabilities. See Also Lossless Audio Compression M4A and M4B File Conventions FLAC Audio CAF: Core Audio Format References Apple: ALAC reference implementation and format features Apple: ALAC configuration and container mapping

articles/audio/formats/lossless/Audio-Lo.title: Lossless Audio Compression | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/Audio-Lo.keywords: Lossless Audio Compression Lossless compression changes how audio is stored, not the sample values recovered by decoding. For supported source data, the decoder reconstructs exactly the values supplied to the encoder. Audio samples often have predictable relationships. An encoder can store a prediction and the remaining error more efficiently than a full value for every position. The error is retained completely, so even an imperfect prediction can be reversed. A small example Suppose the samples are 100, 104, 107, and 109. Predicting each value from the previous one gives: Stored item Value Reconstructed sample Starting sample 100 100 Difference +4 104 Difference +3 107 Difference +2 109 This is an illustration, not the complete algorithm of a particular codec. Real encoders use more sophisticated predictions and efficient integer coding. What “exact” applies to Converting the same supported PCM samples between FLAC and ALAC can preserve the audio. Tags, artwork, container headers, and file bytes may nevertheless change. Compare decoded samples when checking audio equality, rather than expecting the two files to have identical checksums. A compression setting normally trades encoding effort against file size. It does not make a lossless decoder restore a better or worse version of the samples. There are also two limits to the promise. A lossless copy of decoded MP3 audio cannot recover the pre-MP3 source. And a lossless file played through resampling, downmixing, or volume processing need not reach the output unchanged. In Emby, delivery conversion and the client's output are therefore worth checking separately from whether the stored codec is lossless. See Also Lossy Audio Compression FLAC Audio Apple Lossless (ALAC) Linear PCM (LPCM) References RFC 9639: Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC) Xiph.Org: FLAC format overview Monkey's Audio: Lossless compression theory

articles/audio/formats/lossless/Dolby-Tr.title: Dolby TrueHD Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/Dolby-Tr.keywords: Dolby TrueHD Audio Dolby TrueHD preserves the encoded audio without lossy compression. It is found in Blu-ray and Ultra HD Blu-ray movie soundtracks and may also carry Dolby Atmos information. Inspection tools can identify the stream using an MLP-related label, reflecting its Meridian Lossless Packing heritage. That does not make every MLP-based format interchangeable with TrueHD. Reading the format limits Blu-ray capability described by Dolby Supported configuration Up to eight full-range channels 96 kHz, 24-bit audio Up to six full-range channels 192 kHz, 24-bit audio Maximum encoded data rate Up to 18 Mbit/s These are capabilities, not the properties of every soundtrack. An actual track can use fewer channels, a lower sample rate, and a much lower average bitrate. Lossless compression also allows the encoded rate to vary with the content. Where decoding happens A capable player can decode TrueHD and send the resulting PCM channels to the audio system. If that output preserves the relevant sample values and channel presentation, local decoding does not itself introduce lossy compression. Alternatively, a supported bitstream output path lets a downstream device perform the decoding. TrueHD transport over HDMI uses Dolby MAT packaging; the details of that transport should not be confused with the codec stored in the file. For a TrueHD track with Atmos , ordinary channel PCM and metadata-bearing Atmos output are different results. Preserving lossless channel audio does not alone prove that the immersive information survived. An Emby movie may offer a separate AC-3 fallback, but TrueHD does not contain the same kind of embedded lossy core used by common DTS-HD disc streams. Confirm the available tracks rather than expecting an AC-3 mix to be extractable from any TrueHD file. See Also Dolby MAT Audio Transport Dolby Atmos Decoded PCM Output Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core References Dolby: TrueHD high-level bitstream description Dolby: TrueHD lossless audio Dolby Atmos for the Home Theater: Delivery and Dolby MAT

articles/audio/formats/lossless/DTS-HD-M.title: DTS-HD Master Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/DTS-HD-M.keywords: DTS-HD Master Audio DTS-HD Master Audio is a lossless audio format. In its common disc arrangement, a compatible lossy DTS core is combined with extension information that allows a full decoder to reconstruct the source audio exactly. The core's lossy nature does not make the complete Master Audio result lossy. The additional information corrects what the lossy representation alone cannot preserve. Data used by the decoder Result DTS core alone A compatible lossy presentation Core plus the required lossless extension The full lossless presentation A supported extension-only lossless stream Lossless decoding without a legacy core fallback The last arrangement matters: the DTS specification permits lossless streams without a backward-compatible lossy component. “DTS-HD” should not be treated as proof that an extractable core exists. Interpreting playback information A player that decodes the complete Master Audio presentation can output PCM . The receiver then identifies PCM rather than Master Audio because it receives decoded samples. That label does not imply an extra lossy conversion. A receiver showing ordinary DTS can indicate core-only delivery, but check its actual input information and the player's output before drawing that conclusion. A listening-mode name may describe processing applied after input detection. In Emby, the selected source track, server delivery, player decoding, and output transport form separate steps. A compatible video stream can reach the screen while the audio takes a fallback route. DTS:X can add immersive information in a compatible DTS-HD delivery form. Lossless reconstruction of a channel presentation and preservation of the immersive metadata are related but separate capabilities. DTS-HD High Resolution Audio is another distinct format and should not be substituted for Master Audio merely because both share “DTS-HD.” See Also DTS Core Audio DTS-HD High Resolution Audio DTS:X Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core Decoded PCM Output References ETSI TS 102 114 V1.6.1: DTS Coherent Acoustics core and extensions DTS: Digital Surround and DTS-HD Master Audio DTS: Production tools and backwards compatibility

articles/audio/formats/lossless/FLAC.htm.title: FLAC Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/FLAC.htm.keywords: FLAC Audio FLAC preserves integer PCM audio without compression loss. Its decoder reconstructs the encoded sample values exactly, making it useful for a music master that can later be copied into other listening formats. The format is defined in RFC 9639. It supports one to eight channels and sample precision from 4 to 32 bits, although a particular player may support a narrower practical subset. FLAC information Useful meaning Sample rate and bit depth Describe the preserved PCM audio Compression preset Trades encoding effort against file size Encoded bitrate Depends on both the source and compression efficiency Audio MD5, when present Helps verify the reconstructed sample data FLAC's usual compression presets, 0 through 8, do not change decoded quality. A smaller level-8 file and a larger level-0 file made from the same input can restore the same samples. Checking the right thing FLAC includes frame checks and can carry an MD5 signature for the decoded audio. The reference tool's test mode validates decoding without writing a new audio file. An integrity check establishes consistency with stored checks, not whether the original rip or recording was accurate. A native FLAC file can also contain tags and artwork. Repacking or retagging it can change the file checksum while leaving the audio unchanged. During Emby playback, FLAC is typically decoded before it reaches an amplifier as PCM . Seeing “PCM” therefore does not indicate that the server replaced the lossless source with a lossy one. Check any server conversion and client resampling separately; lossless storage alone does not guarantee an unchanged output path. See Also Lossless Audio Compression Linear PCM (LPCM) Apple Lossless (ALAC) Audio Resampling References RFC 9639: Free Lossless Audio Codec (FLAC) Xiph.Org: FLAC FAQ Xiph.Org: FLAC compression presets and verification

articles/audio/formats/lossless/Monkeys-.title: Monkey's Audio (APE) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/Monkeys-.keywords: Monkey's Audio (APE) Monkey's Audio compresses audio without losing the source data. Its familiar file extension is APE. Different compression levels change the balance between compression and processing effort; they do not select different decoded audio quality. Choice What changes Faster compression setting Usually less encoding effort and a larger result Stronger compression setting More processing effort to reduce size Verification mode Checks an APE file's integrity Conversion to another compatible lossless codec Changes the representation while preserving the audio The codec uses prediction and compact coding of the remaining information. The project's SDK and source code are the implementation reference for decoding, encoding, and related file handling. An album can still be one audio stream APE collections sometimes use a single album file with a CUE sheet describing track boundaries. The CUE sheet does not contain the music and is not part of the compression algorithm. Keeping it associated with the audio can matter when moving such a collection. APE tags are another separate detail: they describe metadata and can also occur outside Monkey's Audio files. A tag-format name is not sufficient to identify the soundtrack's codec. When an Emby client needs a converted version, a supported lossless conversion can preserve the decoded PCM, while a lossy delivery version introduces its own tradeoff. A smaller APE file than a FLAC made from the same samples does not imply better sound; successful lossless decoding returns the same audio. See Also Lossless Audio Compression FLAC Audio WavPack Audio CUE Sheets References Monkey's Audio: SDK and source code Monkey's Audio: Help and verification Monkey's Audio: Lossless compression theory

articles/audio/formats/lossless/WavPack..title: WavPack Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/WavPack..keywords: WavPack Audio WavPack is often found among lossless formats, but a WavPack file is not necessarily lossless . It supports lossless compression, lossy compression, and a hybrid arrangement that can provide both uses from related files. The filename ending in WV does not settle which mode was used. Three arrangements Files used for playback or decoding Result A WV made in lossless mode Original supported audio data can be restored A WV made in lossy or hybrid mode, alone A lossy reconstruction Hybrid WV plus its matching WVC correction file Original audio can be restored when both are used In hybrid mode, the WV file is independently playable. The correction file contains the additional information needed for lossless restoration. A decoder must support and actually use that matching correction file; merely placing it somewhere in a library does not establish that it participated in playback. More than ordinary integer PCM WavPack supports integer PCM, floating-point PCM, and lossless compression of DSD. Its DSD mode uses lossless storage rather than the PCM hybrid arrangement. That distinction is useful during conversion. A WavPack containing supported integer PCM can be converted to another suitable lossless PCM codec without changing the samples. A floating-point or DSD source cannot automatically be represented unchanged by a target designed for integer PCM. “Lossless” needs to apply to the particular data, not just appear in both codec names. For WavPack music in Emby, inspect the stream's mode and sample representation as well as the delivery method. If a hybrid file plays without its correction information, the fact that a lossless pair exists elsewhere does not make that session lossless. Retaining both parts together matters for a hybrid archive. The WV alone can remain useful, but losing the correction file removes the ability to reconstruct the original from that pair. See Also Lossless Audio Compression Direct Stream Digital (DSD) FLAC Audio Media File Extensions References WavPack: Audio compression modes WavPack 4 and 5: Binary file and block format WavPack: User documentation

articles/audio/formats/lossless/WMA-Loss.title: WMA Lossless Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossless/WMA-Loss.keywords: WMA Lossless Audio WMA Lossless preserves the original encoded audio data. It is a distinct Windows Media Audio variant; the ordinary WMA name or extension does not establish that a file is lossless. Microsoft identifies the Lossless variant separately from WMA Standard and Professional. This helps explain why support for a typical WMA music file does not guarantee support for an archival WMA Lossless file. Detail Useful interpretation Lossless codec identification Establishes the compression variant Sample rate and bit depth Describe the preserved source audio Variable encoded bitrate Reflects source complexity and compression WMA extension Describes a file convention, not proof of lossless coding A complex passage can require more compressed data than a simple one without changing sample fidelity. Comparing the bitrate to a lossy WMA therefore cannot directly rank audio quality. Using a lossless master When the source samples fit the destination format, converting WMA Lossless to another lossless codec can preserve the audio. Container bytes and metadata handling may change, so file checksums are not an audio-equality test. An Emby client may instead need a lossy delivery conversion . That session no longer preserves the source samples exactly, even though the library file remains lossless. Conversely, making a WMA Lossless file from an already lossy recording preserves only its decoded result. The codec can protect the input it receives; it cannot restore information removed before that input was created. See Also Windows Media Audio (WMA) Lossless Audio Compression FLAC Audio Audio Transcoding References Microsoft: Windows Media Audio encoder and format identifiers Microsoft: Configuring Standard, Professional, or Lossless audio encoding Microsoft: About the Windows Media codecs

articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.title: AAC-LC Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.keywords: AAC-LC Audio AAC-LC is Advanced Audio Coding, Low Complexity. It is the familiar AAC variant used for many music files and video soundtracks. “Low Complexity” names a coding design; it does not label a recording as low quality. In Emby media information, “AAC” may be an abbreviated codec label. The profile, channel layout, and sample rate give a more complete description of the selected track.
