AAC-LC characteristic Why it matters Lossy compression Decoded samples approximate the source Transform-based coding The encoder represents short sections in the frequency domain Mono, stereo, and multichannel capability AAC-LC is not restricted to two channels Separate stream packaging The codec can appear inside different file or transport formats The encoder spends bits on signal components and quantization accuracy rather than storing a PCM number for every sample. Shorter coding windows can help represent sudden attacks. Choosing a higher bitrate gives the encoder more room, but no one bitrate guarantees the same result for every source. LC support is a specific capability AAC-LC does not include the high-frequency reconstruction tool used by HE-AAC , or the parametric stereo tool used by HE-AAC v2 . A device advertising AAC playback does not automatically promise every newer AAC-family profile. The stored file may be an M4A , an MP4 movie, or a differently packaged stream. Packaging and decoding need to be compatible independently. If a client accepts the codec but not the container, remuxing can change the packaging while preserving encoded audio. If decoding is the issue, a different wrapper cannot fix it. A stereo AAC-LC file and a 5.1 AAC-LC movie track also ask different things of the audio output, despite sharing the codec name. See Also HE-AAC Audio AAC Stream Packaging M4A and M4B File Conventions Lossy Audio Compression References ISO/IEC 14496-3: MPEG-4 Audio Fraunhofer: AAC-LC Karlheinz Brandenburg: MP3 and AAC explained

articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.title: HE-AAC Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.keywords: HE-AAC Audio A recorded broadcast can produce a puzzling pair of reports: one inspector says AAC at 24 kHz, while another identifies HE-AAC and a 48 kHz output. Those fields can describe two stages of the same encoded track. HE-AAC , High Efficiency AAC, combines an AAC-LC core with Spectral Band Replication (SBR) . The core supplies directly coded audio; SBR reconstructs an upper-frequency region using additional information. In a common dual-rate configuration, the core runs at 24 kHz and the completed output runs at 48 kHz. Field in this example What it describes Core rate: 24 kHz The directly coded AAC-LC signal Output rate: 48 kHz The signal after SBR reconstruction HE-AAC profile The combination of core coding and SBR To interpret a report, identify which field the tool is showing. Neither rate field establishes the sample rate of the original studio recording; each describes a stage in this coded presentation. What was stored instead of the missing upper-frequency detail? An encoder with a small data budget has to decide where those bits do the most useful work. Independently coding a wide frequency range at very low bitrate can leave too little precision for important parts of the sound. HE-AAC devotes much of its data to the AAC-LC core and represents the upper region more compactly. At the decoder, SBR takes patterns from the decoded lower-frequency content and uses them to generate candidate higher-frequency content. Transmitted information then shapes that result across time and frequency: how much energy belongs in different regions, how noise-like the content should be, and other reconstruction parameters. The generated upper region therefore has both a source of structure and a description of how it should sound. It is not another independently coded copy of every original upper-band detail. This is where the data saving comes from. A 24 kHz core can represent frequencies below 12 kHz, but that theoretical limit does not specify the encoder's chosen crossover between directly coded and reconstructed regions. The configuration and encoder decisions determine the actual division. Why an equalizer cannot do the same job. An equalizer raises or lowers frequency content already present. SBR generates upper-band content and controls its behavior. Turning up treble on a core-only decode cannot provide the reconstruction information that an SBR-capable decoder uses. Why ordinary upsampling is also different. Upsampling creates more sample positions. It does not, by itself, recreate the intended missing upper-band sound. SBR combines the higher-rate output with additional content-generation and shaping operations. The result can retain a convincing sense of bandwidth with relatively few bits. Rapid changes and difficult sound textures can reveal the approximation more readily, because their upper-frequency behavior is harder to represent using the compact reconstruction description. Do twice as many output samples make the track play more slowly? The rates and sample counts change together. For the usual 1,024-sample AAC-LC core block in this dual-rate example: Core duration: 1,024 / 24,000 = about 42.67 ms . Completed output duration: 2,048 / 48,000 = about 42.67 ms . The output has twice as many samples for the same interval. It supplies a higher-rate representation of that interval rather than doubling its duration. This calculation uses one common configuration; MPEG-4 audio also defines other block lengths and SBR modes. What happens if the player understands AAC-LC but not SBR? Where the stream's signaling permits backward-compatible core decoding, an AAC-LC-only decoder can reconstruct the core. It lacks the intended upper-band reconstruction, so the sound can have a narrower bandwidth than a complete HE-AAC decode. An SBR-capable decoder can produce the completed presentation. The player must also identify the configuration and pass the right information to the decoder. ADTS , LATM , and an MP4 track carry or signal that information differently. A decoder capability and a usable packaged stream are both needed for the expected result. For an Emby broadcast recording that sounds unexpectedly dull, follow the selected track through playback. Check the identified profile and core/output fields, whether the server delivers the audio unchanged or converts it, and which decoder handles the delivered stream. Server conversion and local decoding place the reconstruction in different parts of that path. HE-AAC v2 adds Parametric Stereo for low-bitrate stereo delivery. If that is the detected profile, SBR explains its bandwidth reconstruction while Parametric Stereo accounts for an additional part of its spatial presentation. See Also AAC-LC Audio HE-AAC v2 Audio AAC Stream Packaging Audio Sample Rate References FFmpeg 8.1: SBR generation and envelope processing ISO/IEC 14496-3: MPEG-4 Audio Fraunhofer: HE-AAC and HE-AAC v2 Fraunhofer: The AAC audio coding family for broadcast and cable TV

articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.title: HE-AAC v2 Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.keywords: HE-AAC v2 Audio For stereo audio, HE-AAC v2 adds Parametric Stereo, or PS, to HE-AAC . Instead of spending bits on two complete audio channels, it encodes a mono downmix plus information describing the stereo image. The decoder reconstructs that image from the mono signal and the parameters. The output is stereo, but the process is lossy: it does not preserve the original left and right sample streams exactly. Decoder capability Result for a compatible stereo stream AAC-LC core only Core audio without the full high-frequency reconstruction HE-AAC with SBR The reconstructed audio bandwidth, without PS stereo reconstruction HE-AAC v2 with SBR and PS The intended bandwidth and stereo image The table describes the tools required, not a promise that every player will accept every signaling or packaging variant. Some applications reject a profile they do not support rather than offering partial playback. A practical low-bitrate tool PS is useful where the stereo data budget is particularly tight. For example, broadcast radio can retain a stereo impression without encoding two complete HE-AAC channels independently. Stereo imaging can become less faithful on difficult material, even when the result remains intelligible and pleasant. The v2 profile also permits multichannel configurations where PS is not used; there it uses the same relevant coding tools as HE-AAC. The v2 label therefore should not be interpreted as “every track is a mono signal expanded into stereo.” When investigating an Emby recording, check the profile and actual channel description together. A report of mono core audio does not by itself prove that a correctly decoded HE-AAC v2 stereo presentation is mono. For the relationship between the core rate and the output rate, see HE-AAC . See Also HE-AAC Audio Stereo Audio AAC Stream Packaging References ISO/IEC 14496-3: MPEG-4 Audio Fraunhofer: HE-AAC and HE-AAC v2 Fraunhofer: The AAC audio coding family for broadcast and cable TV

articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.title: xHE-AAC Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/aac-family/.keywords: xHE-AAC Audio xHE-AAC is Extended High Efficiency AAC , based on Unified Speech and Audio Coding ( USAC ) and paired with MPEG-D loudness and dynamic-range control. It is designed to handle speech, music, and mixtures of both across a broad bitrate range. That matters for material such as an audiobook with music, a radio programme, or a movie soundtrack. A codec optimized only for speech can struggle when the signal changes character. USAC combines coding tools suited to both speech and general audio. Feature Intended benefit Unified speech and audio coding Consistent handling of voices and music Wide bitrate range Adaptation to different data budgets Switching support Smooth transitions among suitably prepared bitrate versions MPEG-D loudness and dynamic-range control Controlled playback loudness and optional dynamics adjustment These features still require appropriate content preparation and a capable playback implementation. “Adaptive” does not mean that a stored file automatically changes its bitrate without separately encoded delivery versions. A new member with a different core Despite its AAC-family name, an xHE-AAC stream is not an AAC-LC stream with a few extra tags. An AAC-LC or HE-AAC decoder cannot be assumed to decode its USAC content. The xHE-AAC profile provides decoding capability for earlier AAC-family formats, but that relationship does not work in reverse. A broad “AAC supported” statement is consequently too vague for diagnosing a particular xHE-AAC track. For an Emby session, distinguish the selected source format from the format delivered to the app . A device's ability to handle ordinary AAC music says little about this newer profile, and a codec's technical capabilities are not a support guarantee for every app using that device. See Also AAC-LC Audio HE-AAC v2 Audio Speech Coding Audio Codecs Explained References ISO/IEC 23003-4:2025: Dynamic range control ISO/IEC 14496-3: MPEG-4 Audio ISO/IEC 23003-3: Unified speech and audio coding Fraunhofer: xHE-AAC Fraunhofer: xHE-AAC technical paper

articles/audio/formats/lossy/Audio-Lossy.title: Lossy Audio Compression | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/Audio-Lossy.keywords: Lossy Audio Compression Lossy audio compression makes a tradeoff: use fewer bits while keeping the audible result close to the source. The decoder reconstructs a signal that can sound convincing, but it cannot restore every original sample. Many codecs use knowledge of hearing. A loud sound can conceal a weaker sound nearby in frequency or time, so an encoder can spend fewer bits on information unlikely to be noticed. This is more nuanced than simply removing all high frequencies. Where the tradeoff becomes audible Material or constraint Possible effect at an insufficient bitrate Sharp attacks, such as percussion Smearing or a faint sound before the attack Cymbals, applause, or dense ambience Swirling, metallic, or watery texture Very restricted data rate Reduced bandwidth or less stable detail Repeated lossy conversions New artifacts added to an already altered signal These are possibilities, not a promise that every encoded track has audible damage. Codec design, encoder settings, source material, and listening conditions all influence the result. Equal bitrates also do not imply equal quality across different codecs. A higher-quality lossy version should normally be made from the original or a lossless master. Converting an existing low-bitrate file to a larger MP3 does not bring the discarded information back. Saving its decoded output as FLAC preserves that output, not the earlier source. During playback Emby may convert audio for a client's capabilities or available bandwidth. If both the source and delivery codec are lossy, this is another encoding generation. Keep that separate from ordinary decoding, which simply reconstructs the signal described by the existing bitstream. A compatible original track can avoid that extra conversion, but file size or a codec name alone cannot tell you whether a difference will be audible. See Also Lossless Audio Compression MP3 Audio AAC-LC Audio Opus Audio Audio Transcoding References Fraunhofer: Psychoacoustic models for perceptual audio coding Xiph.Org: Vorbis FAQ

articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.title: Dolby AC-4 Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.keywords: Dolby AC-4 Audio AC-4 is a separate Dolby audio format , used in newer broadcast and delivery systems. It is not an AC-3 or E-AC-3 track with a new filename. The format can describe several ways to present the same programme. A presentation selects and combines the necessary audio components, allowing language, accessibility, or immersive choices within the coded structure. AC-4 concept Practical meaning Audio component A coded part of the programme Presentation A selected combination of components and rendering information Channel-based audio A defined speaker-channel arrangement Object-based audio Sound and associated spatial information for rendering Not every AC-4 programme uses every feature. Dialogue enhancement or audio description depends on what the content provides and what the playback system exposes. Why the recording can be harder to interpret A conventional list of tracks may not capture every selectable presentation inside one AC-4 bitstream. Seeing one audio stream does not necessarily mean that only one language or listening arrangement is available. AC-4 is one of the audio systems specified for ATSC 3.0 broadcasts. A recording can therefore contain usable video while its audio requires a different decoder from older TV recordings. Changing the container or relabeling the audio cannot supply that decoder. When an Emby library encounters such a recording, identify the actual audio format and presentation before investigating the delivery path . Support for Dolby Digital Plus or Dolby Atmos in another delivery form does not establish AC-4 support. If conversion is available, the resulting ordinary channel track represents a chosen presentation. It should not be assumed to retain all of the original bitstream's alternate languages, accessibility choices, or object information. See Also Audio Codecs Explained Audio-Description Tracks Preserving Immersive Audio Metadata Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) References ETSI TS 103 190-1 V1.4.1: AC-4 channel-based coding ETSI TS 103 190-2 V1.3.1: AC-4 immersive and personalized audio ATSC A/342 Part 2: AC-4 system

articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.title: Dolby Digital (AC-3) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.keywords: Dolby Digital (AC-3) Dolby Digital and AC-3 name the same audio coding format. It is a lossy format found on DVDs, in television broadcasts, and in many stored movie soundtracks. AC-3 supports up to five full-bandwidth channels plus a low-frequency effects channel: the familiar 5.1 layout . An AC-3 track can also be mono or stereo. The codec name alone does not identify a surround presentation. Property AC-3 context Compression Lossy Common coded sample rates 32, 44.1, or 48 kHz Maximum standard encoded bitrate 640 kbit/s DVD-Video application limit 448 kbit/s Metadata Can describe dialogue level, dynamic-range control, and downmixing A format's maximum and an application's limit are different. A 640 kbit/s AC-3 track need not indicate damage merely because it exceeds the DVD-Video limit. Metadata influences playback AC-3 can carry instructions that help a decoder present the same programme on different systems. A stereo downmix can include the center and surround information instead of discarding those channels. Dynamic-range processing can reduce the distance between loud and quiet moments when the playback mode applies it. These instructions do not turn AC-3 into lossless audio, and a 5.1 track need not sound identical through every decoder configuration. An Emby client can decode AC-3 and output PCM, or use bitstream passthrough when its output path and receiver support that format. The latter moves decoding to the receiver; it is not synonymous with the server's Direct Play decision. Dolby Digital Plus is a related but different bitstream format. AC-3 support by itself does not establish native E-AC-3 decoding. See Also Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) Audio Bitstream Passthrough Audio Downmixing 5.1 Surround Sound References ETSI TS 102 366 V1.4.1: AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3 standard Dolby: Dolby Digital 5.1

articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.title: Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/dolby/Dolby.keywords: Dolby Digital Plus (E-AC-3) Dolby Digital Plus is E-AC-3, or Enhanced AC-3. It builds on AC-3 with additional coding tools and more flexible presentation structures. It remains lossy, even when a track uses a high bitrate or carries Dolby Atmos . A media report may show E-AC-3, EC-3, or Dolby Digital Plus. Those are useful clues about the encoded format; the selected track's actual channel layout still needs to be checked. Information What it describes Independent substream A presentation that can be decoded without dependent substreams Dependent substream Additional audio used with an associated independent substream Channel presentation Often stereo, 5.1, or 7.1 in consumer delivery Atmos extension information Spatial information beyond an ordinary fixed channel presentation An independent E-AC-3 substream is not automatically an AC-3 core . Its independence refers to other E-AC-3 substreams, not compatibility with an old AC-3-only decoder. What “backward compatible” can mean A playback system may provide AC-3 output by converting a Dolby Digital Plus presentation. Particular disc delivery arrangements can also include a compatible AC-3 component. Neither fact means that every E-AC-3 file contains an AC-3 track ready to extract. For an Emby recording or movie, distinguish that kind of fallback from passing the original E-AC-3 bitstream to a capable receiver. Plain PCM output is another possibility after decoding. Atmos carriage adds another capability requirement: a player may decode the compatible channel presentation without preserving the immersive rendering information. A successful 5.1 result therefore does not confirm that every feature of an Atmos-bearing E-AC-3 track survived the playback path. See Also Dolby Digital (AC-3) Dolby Atmos Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core Audio Bitstream Passthrough References ETSI TS 102 366 V1.4.1: AC-3 and Enhanced AC-3 standard Dolby: Dolby Digital Plus Dolby: Dolby Digital Plus audio coding

articles/audio/formats/lossy/DTS-Core.ht.title: DTS Core Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/DTS-Core.ht.keywords: DTS Core Audio The DTS core is an independently decodable lossy audio component. It provides the conventional DTS Digital Surround presentation and is also present in many DTS-HD movie soundtracks. “Core” describes its role in the stream. It is not necessarily a second selectable audio track beside the higher-quality presentation. Situation What the core provides A conventional DTS soundtrack The main encoded audio A compatible DTS-HD stream Audio an older core decoder can use Full DTS-HD decoding A foundation that can be combined with extension data Core-only fallback A lossy presentation without the full extension result DTS Digital Surround commonly delivers up to 5.1 discrete channels at an encoded rate up to about 1.5 Mbit/s. The media report still needs to identify the actual presentation; the name is not a promise that every file has six channels. Decoding less is different from re-encoding A core-aware player can select an existing compatible component without creating a new lossy encoding. The result still has the losses of that core's original encoding. In particular, a core extracted from DTS-HD Master Audio is not the lossless Master Audio result. For an Emby playback session, a receiver showing “DTS” may be receiving this fallback even though the selected source track is labeled DTS-HD. Check the delivered audio and receiver's detected input before assuming that the full extension was decoded. The DTS family also permits extension-only arrangements. An embedded core should consequently be confirmed from the actual stream rather than inferred from every filename containing “DTS-HD.” This distinction becomes useful when a player can decode one DTS variant but cannot extract a fallback from another. See Also DTS-HD High Resolution Audio DTS-HD Master Audio Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core Audio Bitstream Passthrough References ETSI TS 102 114 V1.6.1: DTS Coherent Acoustics core and extensions DTS: Digital Surround and DTS-HD Master Audio

articles/audio/formats/lossy/DTS-HD-High.title: DTS-HD High Resolution Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/DTS-HD-High.keywords: DTS-HD High Resolution Audio DTS-HD High Resolution Audio is lossy. Its name refers to an enhanced audio presentation, not to exact preservation of every original PCM sample. It is distinct from the lossless DTS-HD Master Audio format. In disc soundtracks, the High Resolution format can extend the conventional DTS core with additional audio information. Consumer presentations support up to 7.1 channels and 96 kHz sampling, according to the format description in Denon's receiver documentation. Playback result What has happened DTS-HD High Resolution decoding The supported enhanced presentation is reconstructed DTS core decoding Only the compatible lossy core presentation is used PCM received by the amplifier Decoding happened earlier in the path A PCM input label does not tell you which of the first two presentations was decoded. Channel count and the player's reported output can help distinguish them. Two easily confused quality labels A 24-bit or 96 kHz description concerns the audio sample representation supported by the format. It does not make lossy compression reversible. Likewise, a receiver that abbreviates its input as “DTS-HD” may not distinguish High Resolution from Master Audio on that particular display. An Emby movie can retain its High Resolution soundtrack while the player chooses a supported decoding or output route. The receiver's processing mode is another separate choice: upmixing a conventional input cannot recreate extension information that never reached it. When a setup plays DTS but not this DTS-HD variant, inspect the full source profile, available fallback component, and output path. Merely enabling a generic DTS option does not establish that every component understands the High Resolution extensions. See Also DTS Core Audio DTS-HD Master Audio Fallback to an Embedded Audio Core Decoded PCM Output References ETSI TS 102 114 V1.6.1: DTS Coherent Acoustics core and extensions Denon: DTS-HD High Resolution Audio format description

articles/audio/formats/lossy/MP2.html.title: MPEG Audio Layer II (MP2) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/MP2.html.keywords: MPEG Audio Layer II (MP2) MP2 is MPEG Audio Layer II , an audio codec often encountered in broadcast recordings. It is a different layer from MP3 ; its name does not mean “any audio accompanying MPEG-2 video.” Layer II divides the signal into frequency subbands and allocates bits among them. Its lossy coding preserves an approximation of the source rather than every original sample. Why it turns up in a library Encounter What MP2 tells you An older television recording The soundtrack may be Layer II even when the video is MPEG-2 Conventional DAB radio Layer II is part of the original DAB audio system DAB+ radio The audio system uses the AAC family instead An MP2 elementary stream It contains encoded audio, not the whole TV programme Broadcast recordings commonly package the soundtrack inside a transport stream with video and timing. A file extension such as TS does not identify the audio codec by itself. Two-channel Layer II audio can be stereo or dual-channel material, depending on its coding mode. A channel count alone therefore does not tell you whether those channels should be heard together as a stereo pair. Compatibility after recording Keeping a recording's video intact does not require keeping an unsupported soundtrack unchanged. In an Emby Direct Stream session , compatible video can be copied while audio is converted for the client. Conversion may make an MP2 recording easier to play on a particular device, but another lossy encoding cannot improve on the retained source. For diagnosis, inspect the actual track's codec and channel information; changing the extension or assuming that the video codec dictates the audio does not resolve a decoding mismatch. See Also MP3 Audio Lossy Audio Compression Streams and Tracks Audio Transcoding References ISO/IEC 11172-3: MPEG-1 Audio ISO/IEC 13818-3: MPEG-2 Audio Fraunhofer: DAB and DAB+ codec definitions Karlheinz Brandenburg: MP3 and AAC explained

articles/audio/formats/lossy/MP3.html.title: MP3 Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/MP3.html.keywords: MP3 Audio MP3 means MPEG Audio Layer III . It is a lossy audio format used for music, podcasts, and many older digital collections. The “3” is an audio layer number, not a reference to MPEG-3 video. An MP3 encoder reduces the data needed to describe sound, including by allocating precision according to what is likely to be audible. Decoding produces PCM, but not an exact restoration of the original recording's sample values. Reading an MP3 description Field Useful interpretation 128 or 320 kbit/s Encoded data rate, not sample precision CBR A selected bitrate used throughout the stream VBR Bitrate changes with the encoder's allocation decisions Joint stereo Stereo coding can share information between channels 44.1 kHz Audio sample rate, independent of encoded bitrate Joint stereo does not mean mono. For example, a mid/side representation describes what the channels share and how they differ, allowing the decoder to reconstruct left and right. At an average 192 kbit/s, four minutes of audio occupy about 5.76 MB before tags and other overhead. This is a storage example, not a universal quality recommendation. Audio and the file around it MP3 files usually store MPEG audio frames together with tags and, sometimes, information that helps seeking or accurate trimming. Album artwork and track titles do not belong to the compression mechanism itself. When playing an MP3 collection in Emby, separate the stored codec from any delivery conversion . Re-encoding an MP3 at a higher bitrate cannot recover details removed earlier. If another format is needed, retaining the original files avoids making the converted copy the only surviving version. See Also Lossy Audio Compression MP3 Files and MPEG Audio Frames Audio Bitrate Audio Transcoding References ISO/IEC 11172-3: MPEG-1 Audio ISO/IEC 13818-3: MPEG-2 Audio Karlheinz Brandenburg: MP3 and AAC explained

articles/audio/formats/lossy/Opus.html.title: Opus Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/Opus.html.keywords: Opus Audio Opus handles speech and music in one lossy audio codec. Its design spans voice communication and full-band audio, making it useful for both conversational sound and stored media. It combines two approaches: linear prediction suited to speech, and transform coding suited to music and higher-frequency content. The encoder can use either approach or a hybrid arrangement according to the operating mode. Description What it means for Opus Bitrate The amount of encoded audio data Audio bandwidth The frequency range the stream actually carries Frame duration The time represented by a coded audio frame Channel mapping How decoded channels are assigned to the presentation These are separate properties. A high output sample rate does not prove that the encoder retained a full-band signal; it may be reconstructing a narrower-band source. Why 48 kHz appears so often Ogg Opus timing uses a 48,000-sample-per-second clock , regardless of the original capture rate or the decoder's chosen output rate. The input-rate field in its header is information about the source, not an instruction to interpret timestamps using that rate. Opus can be stored in Ogg and other containers. Mono and stereo streams are straightforward; multichannel presentations require the appropriate stream and channel mapping. Renaming an Ogg file does not change its codec. For an Emby library, an Opus track's packaging and presentation matter alongside the name. The low-delay design does not itself guarantee low latency through the rest of the player, operating system, or wireless output. Likewise, transcoding to another lossy codec is an additional conversion, not simply another way to unpack the existing Opus packets. See Also Speech Coding Lossy Audio Compression What Is a Media Container? Audio Transcoding References RFC 6716: Definition of the Opus audio codec RFC 7845: Ogg encapsulation for the Opus audio codec Opus codec: Features and reference implementation

articles/audio/formats/lossy/Vorbis.html.title: Vorbis Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/Vorbis.html.keywords: Vorbis Audio Vorbis is a lossy, general-purpose audio codec developed by Xiph.Org. “Ogg Vorbis” names both the codec and a common container pairing: Ogg stores the packets; Vorbis describes how those packets represent sound. An Ogg extension alone cannot establish that the audio is Vorbis. Other codecs also use Ogg, including Opus . What the decoder needs Vorbis packet type Purpose Identification header Describes channels, sample rate, and basic stream information Comment header Carries textual metadata Setup header Provides the coding configuration needed for decoding Audio packets Carry the encoded sound The setup header is particularly important for seeking and extraction. Audio packets are not interchangeable with a completely self-contained file header. A player needs the correct setup information before decoding packets at a later position. Vorbis normally uses variable bitrate coding. A quality setting lets the encoder vary the number of bits according to the material. A “nominal bitrate” reported from a header can be a hint rather than a precise measurement of the whole track's average. Keeping audio and packaging apart A Vorbis soundtrack inside a movie is still Vorbis even if its container is not Ogg. Moving compatible packets into another supported wrapper can preserve the encoded sound, whereas changing the codec requires decoding and re-encoding. For a Vorbis collection in Emby, check whether the original track is delivered before attributing a difference to the stored format. The quality of a lossy master, a later conversion, and the output processing are separate influences. If exact source-sample preservation is required, Vorbis is not a substitute for a lossless master. See Also Lossy Audio Compression What Is a Media Container? Container Indexes and Seeking Audio Transcoding References Xiph.Org: Vorbis I specification Xiph.Org: Vorbis FAQ

articles/audio/formats/lossy/WMA.html.title: Windows Media Audio (WMA) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/lossy/WMA.html.keywords: Windows Media Audio (WMA) WMA is a family name, not one audio format with one capability set. A legacy music collection, a multichannel video, and a speech recording may use different Windows Media Audio variants. That distinction matters when one WMA file plays and another does not. A decoder for the familiar Standard format is not automatically a decoder for every other member. Variant Purpose WMA Standard General-purpose lossy audio compression WMA Professional Lossy audio including multichannel and higher-resolution configurations WMA Lossless Preserving original audio data without compression loss WMA Voice A separately implemented speech-focused format Microsoft's format identifiers distinguish Standard (0x0161), Professional (0x0162), and Lossless (0x0163). Inspection tools can show codec labels derived from these identifiers. The reported variant is more useful than the filename when investigating compatibility. Files and the encoded sound A file ending in WMA is commonly an audio-only ASF file. ASF can also store audio alongside video. The outer wrapper and the soundtrack's particular codec are separate requirements. The same WMA extension therefore does not guarantee the same compression type. Neither a high sample rate nor a large file is reliable evidence that a WMA track is lossless; the codec variant needs to identify that explicitly. For an Emby library containing older Windows Media files, inspect the source track before planning a conversion. Re-encoding a lossy WMA as FLAC preserves the decoded approximation, not the samples discarded when that WMA was made. If the client needs a different delivery codec , keep the original file available. This preserves the ability to use a different compatible playback path later without repeatedly encoding an already converted copy. See Also WMA Lossless Audio Audio Codecs Explained Media File Extensions Audio Transcoding References Microsoft: Windows Media Audio encoder and format identifiers Microsoft: Choosing an audio codec Microsoft: About the Windows Media codecs Microsoft: Windows Media file-name extensions

articles/audio/formats/LPCM.html.title: Linear PCM (LPCM) | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/LPCM.html.keywords: Linear PCM (LPCM) Linear PCM, or LPCM, is audio represented directly by sample values. “Linear” means that equal numerical steps correspond to equal amplitude steps, unlike the companded PCM used in some telephone systems. LPCM is the familiar basis of digital music and decoded audio output. A receiver showing “PCM” is describing the signal it receives; the original file might have contained a compressed soundtrack. What its data rate means For tightly packed integer LPCM, the audio data rate is sample rate × bit depth × channel count. Example Calculation Audio payload rate Stereo, 44.1 kHz, 16-bit 44,100 × 16 × 2 1.4112 Mbit/s 5.1, 48 kHz, 24-bit 48,000 × 24 × 6 6.912 Mbit/s 7.1, 96 kHz, 24-bit 96,000 × 24 × 8 18.432 Mbit/s These figures exclude container and transport overhead. Storage can also use a wider word than the valid sample precision: 24 valid bits in a 32-bit slot occupy more space than tightly packed 24-bit samples. The outer format still matters WAV , AIFF , and other containers can store LPCM with different byte order and channel descriptions. “PCM” alone does not specify those details or a particular sample rate. Decoding a FLAC file restores PCM values. Decoding a lossy track also produces PCM, but those values are the codec's reconstruction rather than an exact copy of the pre-encoding source. The output label cannot distinguish the two. In an Emby playback path, PCM output can therefore be the expected result of decoding a compatible soundtrack. Whether every original channel reaches the speakers depends on the player's output format and the connected system. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Bitrate Decoded PCM Output WAV and RIFF References ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEX Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE

articles/audio/formats/speech/AMR-NB.htm.title: AMR-NB Speech Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/speech/AMR-NB.htm.keywords: AMR-NB Speech Audio AMR-NB is narrowband Adaptive Multi-Rate speech coding. It is associated with mobile voice and can appear in older phone recordings and messaging files. The codec supports several speech bitrates so that a system can choose an appropriate mode. Adaptive does not mean that the same file can recover more detail simply by being played on a faster network. Codec property Value Sample rate 8 kHz Speech-frame duration 20 ms Samples per speech frame 160 Speech coding modes Eight rates, from 4.75 to 12.2 kbit/s Those are coded speech rates; file headers, framing, and silence-related data affect the overall file size. AMR-NB is designed for voices in a restricted bandwidth. A thin or telephone-like quality can therefore be an expected property of a valid recording, rather than an Emby playback fault. Preserve what is actually there An AMR file stores coded frames, while a 3GP file can package them alongside other media. The codec and its storage wrapper should be identified separately. Converting AMR-NB to 48 kHz PCM or to a high-bitrate music codec can make a compatible listening copy. It cannot recreate the original high-frequency detail or remove the earlier speech-coding approximation. AMR-WB is a different wideband codec, not an output setting that upgrades a narrowband source. For an Emby session, check whether the original speech track is delivered or converted for the client before comparing formats. See Also Speech Coding AMR-WB Speech Audio Audio Sample Rate Audio Transcoding References ETSI TS 126 090 V18.0.0: AMR transcoding functions RFC 4867: AMR and AMR-WB RTP payload and file storage

articles/audio/formats/speech/AMR-WB.htm.title: AMR-WB Speech Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/speech/AMR-WB.htm.keywords: AMR-WB Speech Audio AMR-WB is the wideband member of Adaptive Multi-Rate speech coding. It carries a broader voice spectrum than AMR-NB and is also standardized by ITU-T as G.722.2. The similar names G.722 and G.722.2 do not make them the same codec. A decoder must support the specific format. AMR-WB property Value Sample rate 16 kHz Speech-frame duration 20 ms Samples per frame 320 Speech coding modes Nine rates, from 6.60 to 23.85 kbit/s The codec uses algebraic code-excited linear prediction. In practical terms, it stores a compact voice model and the information needed to drive it, rather than an exact copy of every source sample. Wideband speech can retain more of the upper-frequency cues that make voices sound clear. It is still lossy speech coding, and does not automatically offer faithful music reproduction. Recognizing a stored recording AMR-WB frames can be stored using the RFC 4867 file format, conventionally ending in AWB, or inside a 3GP container. The header and codec identifier are better evidence than a renamed extension. An AMR-WB recording in an Emby library should be evaluated as the source actually encoded. A later high-rate output or conversion cannot make it an uncompressed studio recording, and a client's AMR-NB decoder should not be assumed to decode AMR-WB. If a file sounds unexpectedly narrow, inspect its codec and source properties before treating the amplifier's output sample rate as evidence of the recording's bandwidth. See Also AMR-NB Speech Audio Speech Coding Audio Sample Rate References ETSI TS 126 190 V18.0.0: AMR-WB transcoding functions ITU-T G.722.2: AMR-WB speech coding RFC 4867: AMR and AMR-WB RTP payload and file storage

articles/audio/formats/speech/Speech-Cod.title: Speech Coding | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/speech/Speech-Cod.keywords: Speech Coding Speech coding focuses on making voices intelligible and natural with a small data budget . Instead of describing every sample independently, a speech codec can model how a voice is produced and how its characteristics change. Many designs use linear prediction: a filter describes short-term spectral structure, while an excitation signal supplies the energy and pitch behavior needed to reconstruct speech. This is an approximation of the recorded waveform, not a transcript and not a perfect model of the speaker. Coding choice Why it is useful for speech Pitch-related prediction Describes repeating patterns efficiently Spectral-envelope modeling Represents the resonances that distinguish speech sounds Voice-activity detection Identifies active speech and quieter intervals Discontinuous transmission Can reduce data use during inactive intervals Not every codec uses all these mechanisms, and behavior during silence depends on the format and encoder configuration. Why music can reveal the compromise A speech-focused model has an easier task with a single voice than with applause, several instruments, or dense background noise. A recording can be perfectly understandable while sounding restricted or synthetic on non-speech material. The encoded bandwidth is another constraint. Replaying a narrowband voice recording through a high-rate PCM output does not recover frequencies the recording never retained. An Emby collection can encounter speech codecs in older phone videos, voice messages, or spoken recordings. The right question is often whether the stored sound is intelligible and whether the player can decode its specific format, rather than whether its bitrate matches a music file. Opus illustrates a broader approach: it includes speech-oriented and music-oriented coding tools. For a preserved original voice recording, keep the source while making any needed compatible listening copy. See Also AMR-NB Speech Audio AMR-WB Speech Audio Speex Speech Audio Opus Audio Lossy Audio Compression References Speex: Codec manual ETSI TS 126 090 V18.0.0: AMR transcoding functions RFC 6716: Definition of the Opus audio codec

articles/audio/formats/speech/Speex.html.title: Speex Speech Audio | Emby Learn
articles/audio/formats/speech/Speex.html.keywords: Speex Speech Audio Speex is an open codec designed for speech. It uses code-excited linear prediction, or CELP, to represent voices efficiently and includes tools useful for packet-based voice communication. Speex mode Nominal sample rate Narrowband 8 kHz Wideband 16 kHz Ultra-wideband 32 kHz The sample rate helps identify the mode; it is not the encoded bitrate. Each mode can use different quality and bitrate settings. Speex is lossy in all of them. Codec versus voice processing A Speex-based application may also apply noise suppression, automatic gain control, or echo cancellation. Those processing functions are separate from the coded audio format. A quiet background or a changing recording level does not establish which codec was used. Stored Speex can use Ogg packaging, while RFC 5574 defines its RTP payload for communication. The audio format and transport are different pieces of the playback problem. The project's current guidance directs new codec uses toward Opus . Existing Speex recordings still require a Speex decoder; they do not become Opus merely because a newer application uses that codec elsewhere. In an Emby collection, Speex is more likely to matter as an existing speech source than as a music master. Converting it can help compatibility, but cannot undo its original compression or recover frequencies absent from the selected mode. Check the stored format and any delivery conversion independently. See Also Speech Coding Opus Audio AMR-NB Speech Audio AMR-WB Speech Audio References Speex: Codec manual RFC 5574: RTP payload format for the Speex codec Speex: Project status and technology

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Bitrat.title: Audio Bitrate | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Bitrat.keywords: Audio Bitrate Audio bitrate measures how much audio data is needed per second. It is usually written in kbit/s or Mbit/s. These are bits, not bytes: divide by eight to estimate bytes per second. For tightly packed, uncompressed integer PCM, the calculation is straightforward: bitrate = sample rate × bits per sample × channel count PCM example Calculated audio payload bitrate 44.1 kHz, 16-bit, stereo 1.4112 Mbit/s 48 kHz, 24-bit, stereo 2.304 Mbit/s 48 kHz, 24-bit, six channels 6.912 Mbit/s Decimal units are used here: one Mbit/s is 1,000,000 bits per second. These values exclude file and transport overhead, and assume samples have no storage padding. A ten-minute stereo track at the second rate contains about 172.8 MB of sample data. If those 24-bit values occupy 32-bit slots instead, storage grows even though the useful sample precision can stay the same. Compressed audio follows different rules Compressed formats represent the signal more efficiently. Their encoded bitrate cannot be calculated from sample rate and bit depth alone. A variable-bitrate track can also spend more data on some passages than others, so a reported figure may be an average. For lossy coding, bitrate is one part of a trade-off involving the codec, channel count, signal complexity, and encoder. For lossless coding, changing the compression ratio changes the size, while successful decoding still restores the same samples. A larger lossless file is not inherently a better copy. An Emby session's total delivery rate includes video and other overhead as well as the selected audio. Use the audio figure when comparing soundtracks or estimating their contribution to network demand; use the overall media rate when estimating the complete stream. See Also Audio Sample Rate Audio Bit Depth Multichannel Audio References Microsoft WAVEFORMATEX: Sample rate, channels, and data rate ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Clippi.title: Audio Clipping | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Clippi.keywords: Audio Clipping Clipping occurs when a signal asks for more amplitude than a stage can represent or reproduce. Peaks are cut off instead of following their intended shape. This changes the waveform and can introduce audible distortion. Calculated example: a sine with peak amplitude 1.3 is hard-clipped to a normalized range of −1 to +1. The dashed line shows the requested signal; the solid line shows the clipped result. This is a mathematical example, not a measurement of Emby output. A signal already close to full scale can exceed the limit when gain is added or several channels are summed. Individual input channels can be valid while their combined output is too large. Where the limit applies Stage What its range means Integer PCM Values must fit the selected integer representation Floating-point processing Intermediate values may exceed nominal full scale Final output Values must fit the converter and playback chain's available range Floating point can preserve an over-range intermediate result so that gain can be reduced before output. It does not give a loudspeaker unlimited headroom. For FFmpeg floating-point audio, −1 to +1 is the nominal full-volume range. Turning the volume down after clipping makes the distorted waveform quieter. It cannot recover the cut-off shape. Reducing gain before the overloaded stage can prevent clipping, which is why the position of a volume or boost control matters. If an Emby soundtrack distorts only after a downmix, boost, or other level change, the original encoded bitrate is not the first explanation to reach for. Follow the level through the processing path. Also distinguish sample peaks from peaks of the reconstructed waveform: values between sample instants can matter at conversion and output. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Dynamic Range Audio Quantization Noise References FFmpeg: Audio sample formats FFmpeg: Audio resampler documentation

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Dither.title: Audio Dithering | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Dither.keywords: Audio Dithering Dither is a small noise signal added before audio is quantized. Adding noise can sound counterintuitive, but the purpose is to make rounding behave more predictably, especially for quiet material and fades. Without dither, a low-level signal can repeatedly land on the same few numerical levels. The resulting error follows the signal and can create distortion. Properly chosen dither prevents that pattern from dominating the result, at the cost of a little additional noise. Operation What happens at the quantizer Round without dither Error can depend on the signal Apply suitable dither, then round Signal-dependent rounding artifacts are replaced by controlled noise Use noise shaping The error spectrum is redistributed; the noise is not simply removed Triangular-probability-density dither is a common choice. The particular distribution and level matter; adding arbitrary background hiss is not equivalent to a properly designed dither process. When the choice matters Reducing a processed signal to a lower integer bit depth is a typical place to use dither. Gain changes or mixing can create fractional values even when the input started as integer PCM. A final conversion to 16-bit samples must decide how to round them. Merely copying samples without changing their values or precision does not require another rounding operation. Repeatedly adding dither to unchanged copies would only add noise. Dither also does not recreate a lost high-resolution recording. It allows low-level signal behavior to survive quantization statistically; an individual output sample still occupies one of the available levels. In Emby playback, precision conversion may occur in an audio decoder, processing stage, or output system. Do not assume that every conversion uses the same dither settings. The FFmpeg resampler exposes several choices, but their existence does not establish which a particular playback path uses. A smoothly decaying fade is the practical goal, not the appearance of a higher bit-depth label. See Also Audio Quantization Noise Audio Bit Depth PCM Sample Formats References Wannamaker: The Theory of Dithered Quantization University of Waterloo: Digital audio and dither research by Stan Lipshitz FFmpeg: Audio resampler documentation

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Dynami.title: Audio Dynamic Range | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Dynami.keywords: Audio Dynamic Range A whisper followed by an explosion can be difficult to hear comfortably at one volume setting. That is an example of a recording using a wide dynamic range : quiet and loud passages are far apart. The same term also describes a system's usable range, from its noise floor to the largest signal it can handle cleanly. A recording's level variation and a device's capacity are related, but they are different quantities. Use of “dynamic range” What is being compared A soundtrack's dynamics Quiet and loud parts of the programme A converter's usable range Noise floor and maximum clean signal Crest factor Peak amplitude and RMS amplitude over the same interval Crest factor is useful for describing peaks, but does not by itself measure the difference between a quiet scene and a loud one. Measurements also depend on the chosen interval and method; a single unlabeled “DR” number can be ambiguous. Decibels describe a ratio For comparable signal amplitudes, the level difference is 20 × log10(larger / smaller) . An amplitude ratio of 1,000 to 1 gives 60 dB. This is a calculated ratio, not an absolute listening volume. The sound pressure in the room also depends on the playback gain and the speakers. More integer bit depth can lower the quantization limit, but it does not force a soundtrack to use wider dynamics. A highly compressed mix can occupy 24-bit storage just as easily as an uncompressed musical performance. When watching through Emby at night, lowering the volume reduces loud and quiet parts together. Processing that narrows the level difference can make quiet passages easier to hear without increasing peaks as much. Its availability and behavior depend on the actual player, decoder, and output system. The source track's bitrate or channel count does not tell you whether that processing is active. See Also Audio Bit Depth Audio Clipping Audio Quantization Noise References Analog Devices MT-001: Quantization noise and ideal converter SNR ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Quanti.title: Audio Quantization Noise | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Quanti.keywords: Audio Quantization Noise Quantization rounds a value onto a set of available levels. The difference between the value you wanted and the level you stored is quantization error . That error exists even in an ideal numerical conversion with no microphone noise or analog electronics. It becomes especially interesting near the bottom of the available precision, where a small signal may cross very few levels. Follow a few values through rounding Use a deliberately coarse uniform step of 0.125, with no clipping. Rounding to the nearest level produces: Input amplitude Stored amplitude Error: stored minus input 0.10 0.125 +0.025 0.19 0.250 +0.060 0.31 0.250 −0.060 0.49 0.500 +0.010 An input can move while the stored level stays fixed. At the next boundary, the stored value jumps. Within the unclipped range, nearest-level rounding keeps the error within half a step: 0.0625 here. Calculated example: a sine with peak amplitude 0.6 and a quantizer step of 0.125. The exaggerated step makes rounding visible. The lower panel is the actual error, not an unrelated noise recording. More integer bits provide smaller steps across the same full-scale range. Each additional bit doubles the number of levels, which is why precision can improve without raising the maximum allowed signal. Why the error may repeat with the sound The rounding operation is deterministic. A periodic input that visits the same positions relative to the levels can produce a repeating error. For a sufficiently small signal, the quantized output may spend much of its time on only a few values. Its shape can then differ from the smooth waveform in a systematic way. Heard as audio, that error can contain distortion components related to the original signal, rather than behaving like a steady unrelated hiss. Calling all of it “quantization noise” can obscure this distinction. The waveform itself tells you why: when the input determines the rounding error, the error is correlated with the input. What dither changes Dither introduces a controlled random signal before the final rounding. Appropriate dither changes how the input crosses level boundaries, allowing the quantizer to behave more consistently for very small signals. It does not make the output numerically identical to the original. It exchanges unwanted signal-dependent behavior for a controlled noise contribution. For a low-level tone or a fade, that can be preferable to periodic distortion or an abrupt disappearance. This is why the order matters. Dither applied after the value has already been rounded cannot change which level that earlier rounding selected. Interpreting the familiar SNR estimate The ideal estimate 6.02 × N + 1.76 dB compares a full-scale sine with a particular model of uncorrelated uniform quantization error. For 16 bits, the result is about 98.08 dB. Reducing the sine's level reduces its signal-to-error ratio under that fixed noise model. Changing dither, noise shaping, or the assumptions about error changes the analysis too. The formula describes a model, not the whole noise performance of a recording. In playback and conversion, the useful place to apply this understanding is a precision-reduction step. If decoded audio is adjusted and then stored at a lower integer precision, values need rounding again. The source recording's noise and earlier compression remain separate parts of that signal. A higher-precision working format provides room for processing between conversions. The final rounding and its treatment determine what happens when the result must fit a lower-precision output. See Also Audio Bit Depth Audio Dithering Audio Dynamic Range References Analog Devices MT-001: Quantization noise and ideal converter SNR Wannamaker: The Theory of Dithered Quantization

articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Resamp.title: Audio Resampling | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/Audio-Resamp.keywords: Audio Resampling Resampling changes an audio signal's sample rate. It produces values on a new time grid while keeping the intended duration and pitch. It is more than changing the sample-rate number in the file header. For example, one second of 44.1 kHz audio contains 44,100 samples per channel. Converting that second to 48 kHz produces 48,000 samples per channel. The new positions generally fall between the old ones, so the converter calculates their values using interpolation and filtering. Treatment of a one-second 44.1 kHz signal Samples per channel Resulting duration Keep its original rate 44,100 1.000 seconds Resample to 48 kHz 48,000 1.000 seconds Only relabel it as 48 kHz 44,100 0.91875 seconds Calculated example without encoder padding or other timing adjustments. The relabeled case also raises pitch. Filtering is part of the conversion When reducing the rate, frequencies above the new Nyquist limit must be attenuated to avoid aliasing. When increasing it, the converter must avoid creating unwanted spectral images. The exact filter determines how close the result comes to the desired conversion, including its transition band and processing cost. Upsampling does not invent information above the original recording's frequency limit. A 48 kHz file converted to 96 kHz has more sample positions, but that alone does not make the recording more detailed. An Emby client, an operating-system mixer, or a server conversion may need a different rate for the destination. If playback is smooth and correctly timed, a rate change is not automatically a problem. The useful questions are whether conversion is required and whether it is performed well. If integer precision is reduced as part of the same processing, dithering is a separate decision. See Also Audio Sample Rate Digital Audio Sampling Audio Dithering References FFmpeg: Audio resampler documentation Analog Devices MT-002: Sampling and the Nyquist criterion

articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.title: Audio Bit Depth | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.keywords: Audio Bit Depth Bit depth is the precision available for a PCM sample's amplitude. With integer samples, more bits allow more numerical levels across the same full-scale range. They do not add sample positions in time or make the loudest permitted value louder. For an integer representation with N bits, there are 2^N possible bit patterns. Each extra bit doubles the number of levels and halves the size of a uniform quantization step. Integer bit depth Available levels 8-bit 256 16-bit 65,536 24-bit 16,777,216 Why the extra precision matters Rounding a signal onto those levels produces quantization error . Smaller steps allow quieter signal detail to sit farther above that error. Extra precision is also useful while mixing or adjusting levels, because processing introduces values between the original levels. A 24-bit recording can still contain microphone noise, a noisy room, or audio originally captured at lower precision. The file's capacity and the useful detail in its contents are different things. Converting a 16-bit recording to 24-bit storage does not recover information that was never captured. Bit depth also needs a qualifier. 32-bit floating-point audio uses a different numerical representation; it is not equivalent to 32-bit integer precision. And a 24-bit sample can occupy a 32-bit storage slot, with only 24 valid bits. PCM sample formats explains those labels. If Emby reports a bit depth, use it to describe the audio's representation, not as a quality score. Lossy compressed codecs do not generally have a PCM-style bit depth that explains their compression quality. Their decoded samples still need a working format, which may differ from how the source was recorded. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Quantization Noise Audio Dithering References Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks Analog Devices MT-001: Quantization noise and ideal converter SNR

articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.title: Audio Sample Rate | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.keywords: Audio Sample Rate Sample rate describes the spacing of audio samples in time. A 48 kHz track has 48,000 sample positions per second in every channel. It does not mean that the track contains a 48 kHz sound. For ordinary audio sampled around zero frequency, the highest representable frequency lies below half the sample rate. This boundary is the Nyquist frequency . Practical filters need some room before it, so the boundary is not a promise that every frequency up to that point is preserved equally well. Sample rate Nyquist frequency Time between samples 44.1 kHz 22.05 kHz 22.68 microseconds 48 kHz 24 kHz 20.83 microseconds 96 kHz 48 kHz 10.42 microseconds What goes wrong above the limit Calculated demonstration: at a deliberately low 1 kHz sample rate, a 700 Hz sine and an inverted 300 Hz sine have identical sample values. This illustrates ambiguity after aliasing; it is not a recommended recording setup. Once an out-of-band signal has aliased into the recording, increasing the rate afterward cannot identify and restore the original frequency. Resampling changes the time grid of the available signal. The file's rate and the output device's rate can differ. A player or the operating system may convert 44.1 kHz material to a 48 kHz output while keeping the same pitch and duration. Merely relabeling the samples would change both. In Emby media information, sample rate is useful for understanding compatibility and the source format. A higher number alone does not prove a better recording, and it does not describe compression quality or the number of channels. See Also Digital Audio Sampling Audio Resampling Audio Bitrate References Analog Devices MT-002: Sampling and the Nyquist criterion ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios Microsoft WAVEFORMATEX: Sample rate, channels, and data rate

articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.title: Digital Audio Sampling | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.keywords: Digital Audio Sampling A microphone produces a changing electrical signal. Sampling measures that signal at regular instants , turning its movement through time into a sequence of numbers. Sound created digitally can produce the same sort of sequence without a microphone. The time spacing is set by the sample rate . At 48,000 samples per second, neighboring samples in one channel are about 20.8 microseconds apart. The sample's numerical precision is a separate choice: bit depth . Calculated example: a 1 kHz sine wave sampled at 8 kHz, shown over two milliseconds. The continuous line is the original mathematical signal; the dots are its sample values. The reduced rate keeps the sample positions visible. The gaps are not missing pieces of sound Those dots do not instruct a loudspeaker to jump from one flat step to the next. Reconstruction uses the sequence to form a continuous waveform. For a signal limited to frequencies below half the sample rate, ideal reconstruction can recover the waveform from its samples. Real recording systems filter out frequencies that cannot be represented before sampling. Without that filtering, a high-frequency component can masquerade as a lower one: aliasing . Filters also matter when changing an existing digital signal's sample rate. A stereo sample frame contains one sample for the left channel and one for the right at the same time position. “48 kHz stereo” therefore means 48,000 such frames per second, not 24,000 for each side. When an Emby audio track shows a sample rate, it describes this time grid. Compressed audio may store blocks of coded information rather than a visible list of sample values, but decoding still produces audio on a sample timeline. See Also Audio Sample Rate Audio Bit Depth PCM Sample Formats References Analog Devices MT-002: Sampling and the Nyquist criterion ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios

articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.title: PCM Sample Formats | Emby Learn
articles/audio/fundamentals/sample-repre.keywords: PCM Sample Formats “PCM” tells you that audio is represented by sample values. A PCM sample format tells you how to interpret those values: integer or floating point, their storage size, and sometimes their byte order. This becomes useful when a log shows a name such as s16 or fltp . These are FFmpeg's names for working sample formats, not additional audio codecs. FFmpeg format Meaning s16 Signed 16-bit integer samples, interleaved s32 Signed 32-bit integer storage, interleaved flt 32-bit floating-point samples, interleaved fltp 32-bit floating-point samples, separate plane per channel Interleaved stereo stores successive frames as left, right, left, right. Planar stereo keeps the left samples in one plane and the right samples in another. Correct conversion between those arrangements changes where the values live, not what the listener hears. Storage size is not always signal precision A decoder can place 24-bit audio in 32-bit integer slots. The extra storage bits do not establish that the source contains 32 bits of useful precision. Similarly, an s32 line in a processing log does not by itself tell you the original bit depth . Floating-point processing commonly treats −1 to +1 as the nominal full-scale range. It can represent intermediate values beyond that range, but the eventual output still has limits. A later conversion or output stage can clip if those values are not brought back into range. For stored PCM, endianness describes the order of bytes within each multibyte sample; it is separate from channel order . Misreading either arrangement can produce severely wrong sound even though every byte arrived intact. Emby playback and transcoding logs may show a decoder's working format. A change from an encoded soundtrack to floating-point samples is a normal processing step, not evidence that the file itself was stored as floating-point PCM. See Also Audio Bit Depth Digital Audio Sampling Audio Channel Order References FFmpeg: Audio sample formats Microsoft WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE: Sample precision and channel masks

articles/audio/Understanding-Audio-in-Me.title: Understanding Audio in Media | Emby Learn
articles/audio/Understanding-Audio-in-Me.keywords: Understanding Audio in Media A film can have a surround soundtrack, a stereo commentary, and another language version inside the same file. Each is an audio track . Selecting a different track in Emby chooses a different presentation; it does not simply change the volume of the current one. An audio description such as “48 kHz, 5.1, 640 kbit/s” combines several independent facts. Understanding which number answers which question makes media information much easier to read. Part of the description What it tells you Codec How the sound is encoded and which decoder is needed Sample rate How many sample positions each channel has per second Bit depth, when applicable The numerical precision of PCM samples Channel layout Which sound positions the channels represent Bitrate How much encoded data is carried per second Language and track title Which presentation the track is intended to provide The container and codec are separate. A file extension describes the outer file; it does not tell you which soundtrack is inside. Likewise, six channels do not specify whether the audio is compressed, lossless, or object-based . Following the sound The player reads the selected track, decodes it or sends it to a compatible decoder, and arranges the result for the listening system. A stereo television, headphones, and a receiver with separate surround speakers can therefore present the same soundtrack differently. Emby's playback method describes how the server delivers the media. Direct Play can still involve decoding, volume adjustment, or spatial processing after delivery. If the audio needs conversion for the client, the server can change the soundtrack while leaving compatible video intact. Start with sampling for how sound becomes numbers, or multichannel audio for how those numbers become a soundstage. See Also Digital Audio Sampling Audio Bitrate Multichannel Audio References ITU-R BS.646-1: Source encoding for digital sound signals in broadcasting studios ITU-R BS.775-4: Multichannel stereophonic sound system Microsoft: Spatial sound and object rendering

articles/media-files/containers/ASF-Cont.title: ASF Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/ASF-Cont.keywords: ASF Container Files ending in .wmv and .wma often use Advanced Systems Format (ASF) as their container. WMV and WMA also name codec families, which is why these extensions can blur the distinction between packaging and encoding. ASF organizes the file into identified objects. Its design includes timed data packets and optional navigation indexes, supporting both file playback and streaming-oriented uses. Main ASF object What it provides Header Descriptions of streams and file properties Data Packets carrying the encoded content Index objects, when present Information for finding positions efficiently The codec carried by a stream is a separate property. An ASF reader can recognize the structure and still lack the decoder needed for the audio or video inside. Understanding an older Windows Media file For a file in an Emby collection, inspect the precise video and audio codec names before looking for a compatibility solution. Different members of the Windows Media families have different decoder requirements. The extension alone does not tell you which member is present. ASF also supports content-protection mechanisms. A structurally recognized file is not necessarily usable outside the software authorized to decrypt it. Repackaging does not remove that requirement. When investigating slow seeking, compare normal playback with jumps into the middle of the file. The presence and quality of index information can matter independently of decoding. A stream-copy remux can change the way timing and navigation are stored, but the destination must support the codecs, and metadata may not transfer unchanged. ASF remains worth recognizing when handling older collections. Its age is context, not a diagnosis: identify the actual streams, protection status, and symptom before attributing a failure to the container. See Also Containers and Codecs Packet Timestamps Container Indexes and Seeking References Microsoft: ASF file structure Microsoft ASF Specification 1.20.06: archived download catalogue

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: AIFF Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: AIFF Container AIFF , the Audio Interchange File Format, is a familiar home for uncompressed audio in recording and editing workflows. Files commonly end in .aif or .aiff. AIFF uses an IFF-style structure of chunks inside a FORM container. Its original PCM representation stores multibyte numbers and samples in big-endian order, a useful distinction when diagnosing raw sample interpretation. Important AIFF chunk Information it supplies COMM Channel count, sample count, precision, and sample rate SSND Audio sample data with positioning information MARK, when present Named marker positions Text or instrument chunks, when present Supporting descriptions or instrument information The AIFF-C variant extends the format with an encoding identifier, allowing compressed audio and additional representations. An inspection report saying AIFF-C therefore needs the actual encoding alongside it; the name is not a complete decoder requirement. Comparing it with WAV A WAV and an AIFF can hold the same decoded PCM samples without one having better sound. Their chunk layouts and storage conventions differ. Converting between those packages need not reduce precision, but a tool can also change sample rate, bit depth, or encoding if instructed to do so. For an Emby music collection, those audio properties are more informative than the file extension when comparing an imported master with a listening copy. Check duration, channels, and sample format after conversion, along with the tags the library actually receives. Metadata handling varies between writing and reading tools. The survival of a title or artwork should be checked separately from the preservation of the audio samples. A technically lossless audio conversion can still lose useful descriptive information. See Also WAV and RIFF PCM Sample Formats CAF: Core Audio Format References Apple Audio Interchange File Format 1.2: original specification mirror Apple: AIFF file type

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: CAF: Core Audio Format | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: CAF: Core Audio Format A long recording can run into the size conventions of classic WAV or AIFF before the recording software runs out of disk space. Core Audio Format (CAF) was designed to avoid that limitation while accommodating different audio encodings. CAF is Apple's chunk-based audio container. It uses 64-bit chunk sizes and can represent both uncompressed samples and packet-based compressed audio. The .caf extension therefore describes the package, not one particular sound format. CAF information Its purpose Audio description Defines encoding, sample rate, and other audio properties Audio data Contains the actual samples or encoded packets Packet table, where needed Describes variable packets and valid audio length Channel layout and metadata chunks Describe speaker roles and supporting information Some codecs produce packets of varying size or duration. A packet table lets the reader connect those packets to usable audio instead of guessing from the overall file size. An editing file is not automatically a delivery file CAF's flexibility is valuable in capture and production workflows, including recordings that grow while they are being written. It does not imply that every music player implements every CAF encoding or optional feature. If material from such a workflow is intended for an Emby collection, inspect the audio format first. The useful decision is which encoding and container the intended listening app can handle, while retaining the precision and channels that matter for that recording. WAV , AIFF , and CAF can all store uncompressed audio. Switching between them does not inherently improve its sound. A container change can preserve samples, but conversion settings may also resample or alter their precision, and metadata can need separate handling. Keep the original production file until the listening copy has been checked for complete duration, expected channels, and correct descriptive information. See Also WAV and RIFF AIFF Container PCM Sample Formats References Apple Core Audio Format Specification 1.0

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: DSDIFF: DFF Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: DSDIFF: DFF Container A file ending in .dff usually uses Philips' Direct Stream Digital Interchange File Format, or DSDIFF . It was designed for exchanging DSD material, including production and mastering information. Like DSF , DSDIFF is a package around an audio representation. The two containers organize their data differently, so changing the filename extension is insufficient to convert between them. DSDIFF information Why it is useful Format and sound properties Describe sample rate, channels, and encoding DSD sound data Store uncompressed DSD DST sound data, when used Store a losslessly compressed DSD representation Optional markers and comments Describe production or editing context DST , Direct Stream Transfer, is lossless compression of DSD. It is not another name for PCM, and a reader that handles raw DSD may need additional support to decode DST. The .dff extension does not settle which representation is inside. Why two DSD files can behave differently A DSF file may carry ID3v2 album information in the location specified by Sony. DSDIFF's own specification defines different descriptive and mastering structures. Some tools add further tagging conventions, whose handling should be checked rather than assumed universal. This distinction matters when a conversion preserves the sound but a music library loses artist, album, or artwork information. Audio preservation and metadata preservation are separate results. For playback through an Emby app, investigate the selected output path as well as the source. Reading DSDIFF, decoding DST if present, converting DSD to PCM when needed, and delivering native DSD are different capabilities. Inspect the file's audio representation, sample rate, channel layout, and duration before choosing a conversion. If the aim is a convenient listening copy, evaluate that copy on the actual app and output device. A package carrying the original DSD does not by itself establish what reaches the speakers. See Also DSF: DSD Stream File Lossy and Lossless Compression Media Probing Direct Stream Digital (DSD) References Philips DSDIFF Specification 1.5: original PDF mirror

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: DSF: DSD Stream File | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: DSF: DSD Stream File DSF means DSD Stream File. It is a container for Direct Stream Digital audio , a one-bit representation commonly described with sample rates in the megahertz range. DSD names the audio representation; DSF names one way to store it. A .dsf extension does not mean the audio output reaches a DAC as native DSD. DSF component What it contributes DSD header File size and optional metadata location Format chunk Channel layout, sample rate, and sample count Data chunk Raw DSD in blocks for each channel Optional metadata ID3v2 tags stored at the end of the file Sony's published specification describes 4,096-byte blocks per channel. Padding can occupy the final block, so the stored sample count matters when determining the actual audio duration. Storage and output are separate questions DSF can store album and track descriptions through ID3v2. That makes it useful for tagged DSD collections, but the particular reader still decides which tags it exposes. Preserve and check the tags separately when changing packaging. For an Emby playback investigation, distinguish the source file from the output path. A pipeline may read DSD and convert it to PCM for the selected app or device. That conversion concerns sample representation, not merely the DSF container. Native output needs compatible handling throughout the path. DSDIFF, usually .dff , is another container used for DSD. Its data arrangement and metadata conventions differ. Renaming DSF to DFF does not translate those structures. Likewise, repackaging raw DSD is different from decoding it to PCM. Before comparing two copies, inspect their sample rates , channels, audio representation, and full duration. A new extension alone says little about whether the original signal or useful tags were preserved. See Also DSDIFF: DFF Container Audio Sample Rate Media Probing Direct Stream Digital (DSD) References Sony DSF File Format Specification 1.01: original PDF mirror ID3v2.4.0: main structure

articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.title: WAV and RIFF | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/audio-or.keywords: WAV and RIFF A .wav is often uncompressed PCM, but WAV is a file format , not a promise about the encoding.
