The format description inside the file tells a reader how to interpret the audio data. The familiar structure uses RIFF , a system of identified chunks, with WAVE as its file type. RIFF also underlies other formats such as AVI; that does not make an AVI an audio file. WAV component What it contains RIFF/WAVE header Identifies the overall file structure fmt chunk Audio format, channels, sample rate, and related parameters data chunk Encoded or uncompressed audio data Additional chunks Optional metadata or other supporting information A reader should follow the chunk structure instead of assuming all WAV headers have one fixed length. Metadata or an extended format description can move the start of the audio. PCM needs more than a sample rate For linear PCM , sample precision, integer versus floating-point representation, and byte layout matter. Multichannel WAV commonly uses WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE, which can describe speaker positions and distinguish valid bits from the space occupied by each sample. That makes a channel count insufficient to establish channel order . Six channels need the correct roles as well as six sets of numbers. When checking a WAV for an Emby music library, inspect those properties and the actual encoding. Two files at the same sample rate can differ in precision, channel layout, and decoder requirements. Classic RIFF uses 32-bit chunk sizes, creating a practical size limit near 4 GiB. Large-file variants such as RF64 use additional conventions; renaming a large file .wav does not teach an older reader to understand them. CAF is another format designed to avoid that classic size constraint. See Also PCM Sample Formats Audio Channel Order AIFF Container CAF: Core Audio Format Linear PCM (LPCM) References Microsoft: RIFF and WAVE file structure Microsoft: WAVEFORMATEX Microsoft: extensible wave format descriptors

articles/media-files/containers/AVI-Cont.title: AVI Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/AVI-Cont.keywords: AVI Container AVI , short for Audio Video Interleave, is a longstanding container for audio and video. Its RIFF-based structure divides the file into chunks, with stream descriptions near the beginning and encoded media in a media-data list. An old AVI may contain MPEG-4 Part 2 video and MP3 audio; a capture AVI may contain DV or uncompressed media. None of those codecs is defined by the .avi extension itself. AVI component Purpose Header list, hdrl Describes the file and its streams Media list, movi Holds interleaved stream chunks Indexes, such as idx1 or OpenDML indexes Locate media chunks for navigation OpenDML extensions allow AVI to handle larger files and provide extended indexing. That is different from assuming every legacy AVI reader understands every extension. Why the index is worth noticing A file can sometimes play sequentially while seeking badly because its index is absent or damaged. Rebuilding an index may improve navigation, but it cannot restore missing media or repair the encoded contents of a broken chunk. AVI also predates many modern delivery conventions. It is a less natural fit for some combinations of advanced codecs, per-sample timing, and subtitle features than newer containers. A successful mux is not proof that every target player will interpret the result as intended. For an AVI in Emby, start with stream inspection . If the app can decode the video but needs a different package, a remux may be enough. If the selected codec itself is unsuitable, changing AVI to MP4 or MKV while copying the stream will leave that limitation in place. Check synchronization and seeking as well as the first few seconds of playback. See Also Container Indexes and Seeking Codec Identifiers and FourCC Damaged and Incomplete Media Files References Microsoft: AVI RIFF File Reference FFmpeg: format documentation

articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.title: MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.keywords: MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format You drag the playback position forward in an Emby movie. The player now needs pictures and sound for a new time, but an MP4 file is a sequence of bytes. How does it get from that time request to the right encoded data? An MP4 carries the media together with descriptions of its tracks, timing, and data locations. Following a seek makes the purpose of those descriptions visible. The example below uses a conventional nonfragmented layout. Logical layout of a simple conventional file. The boxes contain descriptions and data; their drawn widths do not represent actual byte sizes. 1. Identify the selected track and its decoder configuration The reader first needs to know which video and audio tracks are selected, how they are encoded, and how to configure their decoders. The movie description in the moov box contains the track information. Within each track, a sample-description table such as stsd identifies the coding arrangement and its configuration. H.264 video and AAC audio are common in MP4, but the filename extension does not select a codec for every track. The actual sample entry supplies that identification. A sample here is a coded media unit in the file-format sense. A coded audio sample can represent many decoded PCM amplitude samples. The reader needs the encoded unit's size and timing, then the audio decoder expands it into the corresponding sound. 2. Relate the requested time to a usable starting sample The track has timing information for its samples. A conventional stts table describes their durations on the decoding timeline; ctts , when required, supplies offsets for the presentation timeline. These can differ because predicted pictures may need to be decoded in a different order from the order in which they appear on screen. The reader uses that information to relate the requested time to the track's samples. For video with reference dependencies, it also needs a suitable starting point. A sync-sample table such as stss , where present, provides information about access points, while the codec's rules determine the required reconstruction path. If that starting point is earlier than the requested picture, the decoder reconstructs the necessary intervening pictures. The player can then begin presentation at the intended position. Audio is located on its corresponding timeline so that both tracks reach the same presentation time. This is why a seek does more than multiply the movie's average bitrate by the number of elapsed seconds. Encoded sample sizes vary, several tracks can be interleaved, and a requested picture may depend on data from an earlier point. 3. Turn the selected sample into a byte location Sample-to-chunk information such as stsc describes how the track's samples are grouped into chunks. A chunk-offset table, stco or co64 , gives the chunks' locations in the file. Sample-size information such as stsz supplies the size of each coded unit. Consider a small constructed example. The reader has chosen sample 15 as its starting sample. The tables establish that chunk 5 begins at byte offset 40,000 and contains samples 13 through 16: Sample in chunk 5 Encoded size Calculated start offset 13 1,000 bytes 40,000 14 1,500 bytes 41,000 15 900 bytes 42,500 16 1,100 bytes 43,400 To locate sample 15, add the lengths of the preceding samples in that chunk: 40,000 + 1,000 + 1,500 = 42,500 The reader can now obtain 900 bytes beginning at that offset. It did not need to decode samples 13 and 14 merely to discover where sample 15 was stored. Their lengths and the chunk location supplied the navigation information. That byte lookup is separate from the decoder's reference requirements established in step 2. Locating a coded picture does not make it independently decodable. The tables get the right data to the right decoder; the codec determines how that data reconstructs a picture. 4. Decode the data and restore the presentation order The selected samples are passed to the configured decoder in the necessary order. Decoded pictures are presented using their presentation times, and decoded audio is placed on the same presentation timeline. For the user, the result is a new playback position. Underneath, the reader has connected four pieces of information: track configuration → timing and access point → byte locations → decoded presentation . A damaged table can break that chain even when much of the encoded media remains intact. A wrong offset directs the reader to the wrong bytes; missing configuration can prevent decoding; incorrect timing can affect duration, ordering, or synchronization. Each failure concerns a different relationship in the file. A small dictionary for the file structure MP4 organizes information into boxes , each with a size and type. Some boxes contain others, producing a hierarchy. The ISO base media file format defines the shared structure on which MP4 is built. Box or table What to look for ftyp Brands declaring file-format conventions moov Movie and track descriptions mdat Stored media data stsd Sample coding descriptions and configuration stts / ctts Decode durations and presentation offsets stsc / stsz Sample grouping and sizes stco / co64 Chunk locations stss, where present Sync-sample information The shared ancestry with QuickTime explains many familiar structures in MOV and MP4. The specific file conventions and supported coding arrangements still determine how a reader uses them. What changes when the layout changes? In a conventional file, the main description can be placed after the bulk media data. A sequential reader then needs access to that later description before it can interpret the presentation. Fast start moves the description earlier and updates affected offsets. It makes navigation information available sooner. Fragmented MP4 supplies initialization data followed by descriptions and media for successive fragments. The lookup information for later samples arrives with those fragments, which suits segmented delivery and media still being produced. The conventional table walkthrough above therefore does not describe every fragmented-file lookup. For an Emby item, inspect the packaging actually delivered to the app as well as the stored file. A server-prepared stream may organize the same encoded media differently. If the playback problem concerns duration or seeking, follow the timing and location descriptions. If the descriptions lead to the correct data but decoding fails, inspect the selected codec and its configuration. That follows the same chain the reader uses to reach the requested playback position. See Also Containers and Codecs Codec Identifiers and FourCC MP4 Fast Start Fragmented MP4 H.264 / AVC Video AAC-LC Audio References Apple: chunk offsets Apple: decode and presentation timing Apple: sample-table relationships W3C: ISO BMFF initialization and media-segment structure ISO/IEC 14496-12:2026: ISO base media file format ISO/IEC 14496-14:2020: MP4 file format MP4 Registration Authority: codec sample entries

articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.title: QuickTime: MOV Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/iso-base.keywords: QuickTime: MOV Container A MOV from a phone and a MOV from a video editor can ask very different things of a player. QuickTime describes the package, not a fixed choice of codec, resolution, or bitrate. QuickTime files are organized into atoms , including movie descriptions and media data. Their structure was the basis for the ISO base media file format , but MOV and MP4 remain distinct file types. Changing the extension is not a format conversion. Information a MOV can contain Why a reader needs it Track descriptions Identify the media and codec configuration Sample timing and locations Find and schedule encoded samples Edit information Relate track media time to presentation time Display transformations Present a track at its intended orientation The container can describe several kinds of timed media. Practical support depends on which of those features the file uses and which the reader implements. A production file can be a heavy playback source MOV is common in capture and editing workflows, where preserving quality and supporting further work can matter more than small files. A production codec at a high bitrate may be expensive to send over a home or remote connection, even though a compact phone MOV plays easily. When adding such material to an Emby library, inspect its streams and bitrate before deciding that the extension is the problem. A supported codec may only need repackaging; a different codec or an unsuitable data rate can require re-encoding. Also check rotation metadata when a phone recording appears sideways after conversion. A tool that copies the compressed video but drops its display transformation can change the visible result without changing a single encoded frame. See Also MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format Streams and Tracks Video Rotation Metadata References Apple: QuickTime File Format

articles/media-files/containers/matroska.title: Matroska: MKV and MKA | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/matroska.keywords: Matroska: MKV and MKA An MKV can hold a film, its original soundtrack, a commentary track, and several subtitle languages in one file. Matroska organizes those components; the codecs inside still determine how much decoding work playback requires. The usual extension is .mkv for video and .mka for audio-only files. Both use the same container family. A different extension does not turn one codec into another. Part of a Matroska file What it contributes Tracks Codec descriptions and properties of each stream Clusters Timed blocks of encoded media Cues Locations useful for seeking Chapters and attachments Navigation points and embedded supporting files Matroska is built on EBML , a binary structure of identified elements. That allows readers to skip optional elements they do not understand. It does not make missing support for a required codec harmless. One file, several playback choices For an Emby library, the useful question is often which tracks the viewer selects. The same MKV can behave differently with a stereo soundtrack, a surround soundtrack, or a subtitle track that needs rendering. Inspect the track list rather than treating the extension as a support verdict. Matroska has mappings for many codecs , which makes it a flexible home for media collections. A remux can preserve encoded picture and sound while changing their packaging. Check that alternate tracks, chapter information, and attachments survive the operation: these are separate parts of the container, not baked into the video. Ordinary chapter markers identify positions. Ordered chapters are a more demanding feature that can alter the playback sequence, so their presence deserves a separate compatibility check. See Also Streams and Tracks Codec Support in Containers Matroska Attachments Matroska Ordered Chapters How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References RFC 9559: Matroska Media Container Format Specification RFC 8794: Extensible Binary Meta Language Matroska codec mappings

articles/media-files/containers/matroska.title: WebM Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/matroska.keywords: WebM Container A WebM download may resemble an MKV internally because WebM is based on Matroska . Its more constrained format and web-oriented guidelines give producers a clearer target for browser playback. That relationship does not make the extensions interchangeable. Renaming an MKV containing H.264 video to .webm leaves the H.264 data and container declarations untouched; it does not create a conforming WebM file. Common WebM component Role VP8, VP9, or AV1 Encoded video Vorbis or Opus Encoded audio Matroska elements with the WebM document type Structure and timing The published project guidelines describe VP8/VP9 with Vorbis/Opus. Modern implementations also write AV1: FFmpeg n8.1 explicitly includes it in its WebM codec mappings. That establishes a valid writing path, not support in every browser or device. Why browser playback still needs a check A browser receives both a media type and the encoded content. A codec parameter can make a MIME type more precise than video/webm alone. Decoding requirements such as profile, resolution, and bit depth still apply; recognizing the container is only the first step. For a WebM file in an Emby collection, inspect its actual video and audio streams. A client may accept the original file, need different packaging, or need one of the streams converted. The result depends on that app and platform, as described in Emby's playback methods . WebM is useful when the encoded streams and the intended web player agree. It is less suitable as a general archive wrapper for every track type found in a movie collection. Matroska can accommodate a broader set of components without pretending they all fit the WebM delivery conventions. See Also Matroska: MKV and MKA Media MIME Types Codec Support in Containers AV1 Video Opus Audio References WebM Project: container guidelines Matroska codec mappings FFmpeg n8.1: WebM codec mappings

articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.title: MPEG Program Stream | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.keywords: MPEG Program Stream An older .mpg movie or a DVD's VOB data may use MPEG program stream (PS) . This systems format combines encoded streams into a presentation with timing information for coordinated playback. PS uses variable-size packs containing packetized elementary streams. Its original design suits storage or delivery environments where errors are less prominent than in broadcast reception. Transport stream instead divides delivery into small fixed-size packets and provides programme-discovery tables. Item encountered in PS Meaning Pack header Systems timing and delivery information PES packet Payload belonging to an encoded stream Presentation timestamps When decoded media should be presented Stream identifiers Distinguish components within the multiplex Program stream is a container structure, not the name of the video compression. It is commonly associated with MPEG video, but identifying PS still leaves the individual codecs and their properties to inspect. A VOB is part of a larger presentation DVD-Video uses a constrained, extended form of program-stream packaging for its video objects. A VOB can contain audio and subtitle data as well as video. Its surrounding DVD navigation files describe title order and other playback choices. Opening an isolated VOB therefore differs from opening the complete disc presentation. The visible file boundary may divide a longer title, and normal sequential playback need not reproduce the intended navigation. For an .mpg or VOB in an Emby collection, check the whole source and selected streams. Repackaging into a suitable modern container may preserve the encoded content, but simply joining VOBs by filename can select the wrong sequence or retain unrelated material. A reliable conversion follows the intended title and carries its timing into the new package. See Also MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS DVD-Video File Structure Packet Timestamps References ITU-T H.222.0 (04/2025): MPEG systems FFmpeg: format documentation

articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.title: MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/mpeg-sys.keywords: MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS A television multiplex needs to keep delivering media even when receivers join halfway through. MPEG transport stream (TS) packages content in repeated, identifiable packets so a receiver can discover programmes and recover packet boundaries. A basic TS packet is 188 bytes , including its header. Its packet identifier, or PID , tells the reader which stream or signalling data the packet belongs to. One transport stream can carry several programmes, each with its own video, audio, and other components. Original schematic of stored packet framing. Header and payload are simplified; widths are not byte-accurate. PAT and PMT tables describe that programme structure. They are distinct from the codecs used to compress picture and sound. TS therefore does not mean that the video must be MPEG-2 Video. Why M2TS is slightly different Blu-ray stream files commonly use .m2ts. They wrap each 188-byte TS packet with an additional four-byte prefix, producing 192-byte stored units . The underlying transport packets retain their normal structure. A .ts recording and a Blu-ray .m2ts can consequently require different input handling even when they contain similar encoded video. Renaming one to the other does not add or remove the prefix. For an Emby recording or imported stream file, inspect the programme and track selection as well as the codecs. A large broadcast transport stream may contain components unrelated to the programme you want. Timing discontinuities or missing packets can also affect playback without changing the codec name. A remux into a file-oriented container can build more convenient navigation information , while copying suitable streams. It cannot recreate broadcast packets that were never received. Preserve the recording and check where a repeatable glitch occurs before treating it as a decoding issue. See Also MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT Packet Timestamps MPEG Program Stream Blu-ray File Structure References ITU-T H.222.0 (04/2025): MPEG systems Blu-ray Disc Association: BD-ROM audiovisual application white paper, March 2005 (original PDF mirror)

articles/media-files/containers/Ogg-Cont.title: Ogg Container | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/containers/Ogg-Cont.keywords: Ogg Container Ogg is a container, while Vorbis and Opus are audio codecs that can use it. When someone says an .ogg file is Vorbis, they are describing a common combination rather than defining every Ogg file. Ogg groups codec packets into pages . A packet may fit inside one page or continue across pages. Each logical stream has its own serial number, allowing the reader to keep its packets together. Ogg field or structure Why it matters Page capture pattern Helps identify page boundaries Stream serial number Identifies the logical stream Page checksum Detects changes in that page's data Granule position Supplies position information interpreted by the codec mapping The granule position is not a universal millisecond timestamp. Its meaning comes from the mapping for the codec carried by the stream. For example, Opus has specific rules for start trimming, seeking, and the final sample position. The same container can carry different audio A music file using Vorbis and an .opus file using Ogg Opus require different decoders even though both use Ogg pages. Inspect the codec when comparing their behaviour in an Emby app. Packaging recognition is only part of the playback decision. Ogg also permits chaining : one logical stream can finish and another begin within the same physical file. That is useful for concatenated or continuous material, but software may differ in how it presents the resulting duration, track changes, or seeking. A page checksum can reveal a damaged page; it does not correct the damage or establish that all audio decodes successfully. If a file reports an odd duration or fails after a particular point, compare its probe information with actual playback through that transition. Keep the container, codec, and stream layout together in a report. The .ogg extension by itself leaves all three questions partly unanswered. See Also Streams and Tracks Container Indexes and Seeking Containers and Codecs Vorbis Audio Opus Audio References RFC 3533: Ogg encapsulation format RFC 7845: Ogg encapsulation for Opus

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Codec Identifiers and FourCC | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Codec Identifiers and FourCC A media report may describe a video codec as HEVC while showing a codec ID of hvc1 . Those fields are related, but they are not interchangeable. The readable codec name identifies the coding system. The container's identifier tells its reader which track representation it has encountered, sometimes including important packaging requirements. Where the identifier appears Example Meaning MP4 sample entry avc1 An AVC video sample-entry type MP4 sample entry hvc1 or hev1 HEVC types with different parameter-set placement rules Matroska CodecID V_MPEG4/ISO/AVC Matroska's mapping for AVC video A FourCC is a four-character code. It appears in several media systems, but not every codec identifier is four characters long, as the Matroska example shows. Why changing a tag can be misleading The distinction between hvc1 and hev1 includes where HEVC parameter sets are permitted. Replacing one label with another is only valid if the track meets the target label's requirements. A decoder also needs details beyond a short identifier: profile , level , dimensions, bit depth, and codec configuration can affect compatibility. A familiar code does not prove that every stream bearing it fits a device's capabilities. When troubleshooting through Emby, include the codec name and codec ID in the media report if packaging seems relevant. An incorrect or unusual tag can explain disagreement between players, but retagging blindly can conceal the actual problem rather than repair the stream. See Also Containers and Codecs Codec Support in Containers Media Probing Video Codec Profiles Video Codec Levels and Tiers References MP4 Registration Authority: codec sample-entry codes Matroska codec mappings Microsoft: video FOURCC identifiers

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: What Is a Media Container? | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: What Is a Media Container? A container gives encoded picture and sound a usable file structure. It identifies the tracks, describes their formats, and provides timing so the player can put the right sound alongside the right picture. It can also carry navigation and descriptive material, such as chapters, language tags, titles, and attachments. Those features vary by format. Conceptual components; their order and byte layout depend on the container. A container does not necessarily compress anything itself. Its video and audio tracks may already be compressed by their codecs , or may contain uncompressed samples. Why packaging affects playback The app needs a container reader as well as decoders for the selected streams. Reading a familiar video codec out of an unfamiliar package is still a compatibility problem. Some containers concentrate navigation information in a central set of tables. Others distribute it among packets or fragments. This affects startup, seeking, and how useful an unfinished file may be. It does not establish picture quality. For Emby, a packaging problem can sometimes be solved by remuxing compatible tracks into a different container. That can preserve the encoded picture while making the delivered stream easier for the app to read. When checking a file, look beyond the extension: verify its container, track descriptions, and seeking information . A valid package and a supported decoder are separate parts of a successful playback path. See Also Containers and Codecs Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Container Indexes and Seeking References RFC 9559: Matroska media container format

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Codec Support in Containers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Codec Support in Containers A container is not an unrestricted box into which any codec can be placed. The format needs a defined way to identify that codec, store its configuration, and represent its encoded units. Matroska supports a broad collection of mappings. WebM uses a more restricted set of video and audio formats. Those different design choices affect whether a file can be repackaged without changing its codecs. Compatibility question What must be checked Can the format describe this codec? Its specification and codec mapping Can the writing tool create that combination? The muxer's implementation Can the target app open and decode it? Its container reader and decoder capabilities These checks can have different answers. A recognized codec registration is not proof that every muxer, browser, television, or app implements it. Why a remux can fail A video track may fit the destination while an audio or subtitle track does not. A conversion tool must then omit that track, convert it, or choose a different output format. A successful output file does not prove that all original components were preserved. For Emby, the relevant combination is the one delivered to the selected app. If the picture codec is suitable but its packaging is unsuitable, remuxing may help. If the decoder cannot handle the codec's properties, changing the container alone is insufficient. Inspect the full track list before and after a packaging change. This is especially useful for alternate audio, subtitles, and metadata that might otherwise disappear unnoticed. See Also Codec Identifiers and FourCC Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Containers and Codecs References Matroska codec mappings WebM container guidelines MP4 Registration Authority: codec sample-entry registrations

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Container Overhead | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Container Overhead The size of a media file is not simply the sum of its video and audio payloads. The container also needs headers, track descriptions, timestamps, and navigation structures. Those bytes are container overhead . Some costs occur once, such as a track description. Others repeat for each packet, group of samples, or fragment. Added bytes Purpose Track headers and codec configuration Tell the reader what each track contains Timing and indexes Synchronize playback and locate seek positions Repeated packet headers Identify and delimit media in the stored sequence Padding or reserved space Maintain an output layout or allow later changes For scale, a standard MPEG-TS packet occupies 188 bytes and has at least a four-byte header. That minimum header alone is about 2.1% of the packet. Adaptation fields, tables, and padding can add more, so 2.1% is not a general total-overhead estimate. Why remuxed files differ in size Copying the same encoded tracks into another container can produce a different file length without changing their decoded picture or sound. Different indexing, packetization, metadata, and padding account for some of the difference. Removing an audio track or an attachment changes the size too, but that is removed content, not improved container efficiency. Compare the track list when assessing a remux. For Emby network estimates, distinguish container overhead from HTTP, TCP, IP, and other delivery overhead. The file's overall bitrate includes its container bytes; a network transfer includes additional protocol costs. Neither is a direct measure of compression quality. See Also File Size and Duration MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT Multiplexing and Demultiplexing References ITU-T H.222.0 / ISO/IEC 13818-1: MPEG systems RFC 9559: Matroska data structure

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Types of Media Containers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Types of Media Containers Containers make different tradeoffs depending on how media will be stored and delivered. A file that can be opened at any byte position has different needs from a broadcast that a receiver joins halfway through. Structural approach Why it is useful Familiar example Indexed file Describes stored tracks and their locations for navigation A conventional MP4 file Repeating transport packets Allows receivers to find stream descriptions in an ongoing transmission MPEG transport stream Clustered or fragmented media Carries media in successive groups instead of depending entirely on one complete final index Matroska clusters or fragmented MP4 These are structural approaches, not exclusive product categories. A format may support both ordinary file playback and streaming arrangements. “A streaming format” needs context An ordinary media file can be served over HTTP, especially when the client can request byte ranges. That does not make it the same thing as a live broadcast or an adaptive-streaming presentation. Conversely, transport packets can be recorded into a file. Their broadcast-oriented structure remains even though the programme is now on disk. When Emby delivers media, the server may use packaging that suits the receiving app rather than send the original file structure unchanged. The playback method tells you more about that session than a label such as “streaming container.” For a container choice, consider the actual question: can the target read its tracks, begin promptly, and seek reliably? A format's ability to store a codec or survive an interrupted recording is useful, but neither guarantees compatibility with every player. See Also What Is a Media Container? Container Overhead Damaged and Incomplete Media Files References Apple: QuickTime file structure ITU-T H.222.0 / ISO/IEC 13818-1: MPEG systems Matroska streaming specification

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Damaged and Incomplete Media Files | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Damaged and Incomplete Media Files A file can contain gigabytes of picture data and still fail to open if essential structure is missing. An interrupted recording may never have written its final index or track tables. Corruption in the encoded media is a different kind of damage. What is missing or damaged? Typical consequence Navigation index Playback may work, while seeking becomes slow or unreliable Essential track configuration or sample tables The reader may be unable to interpret otherwise present media Encoded packets Visible artifacts, silence, decode errors, or gaps at particular moments These are clues, not diagnoses from a single error message. Why unfinished files behave differently Some recording arrangements carry enough information in successive fragments or packets to leave earlier portions readable after an interruption. Others depend heavily on structures completed at the end. Recoverability depends on both the container and how it was written. A remux can rebuild some structure when a reader can still recover the streams. It cannot recreate pictures or sound whose bytes were never recorded. A missing MP4 moov box may require recovery information that ordinary remuxing cannot supply. When an Emby item fails, first check that the file is complete and readable from the server's storage. Then compare probe results and errors near the failing position. An unsupported codec can produce a playback failure even when the file is intact. Preserve the original and attempt repairs on a copy. If the source is still available, a clean replacement is often more reliable than a partial recovery whose duration, tracks, or seeking behavior remain uncertain. See Also Media Probing Container Indexes and Seeking Multiplexing and Demultiplexing References FFmpeg formats: fragmentation and interrupted output Matroska: streaming and incomplete-length segments

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Elementary Streams | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Elementary Streams An elementary stream is one encoded component, such as a sequence of H.264 video data or AAC audio data. It is the material a container packages, rather than the complete movie presentation. The word elementary does not mean simple to decode. The stream can contain sophisticated compression, reference pictures, and codec-specific headers. What can be missing outside the container A raw video stream can describe the pictures without carrying the same presentation timeline, chapter list, language tags, or track-selection information as a container file. Some timing and configuration may be available inside the codec data, but the available information depends on the format. That distinction matters when an extracted video stream plays too quickly or loses synchronization after being combined with audio. The original container may have supplied timing that extraction did not preserve. A packetized elementary stream (PES) adds a systems-layer wrapper around elementary-stream data in MPEG systems. That wrapper can carry timestamps; it is still a different layer from the smaller transport-stream packets that deliver it. For an Emby library, keeping a suitable container is usually the more useful arrangement because it carries the presentation as a whole. Extracting a raw stream can be helpful for technical diagnosis, but it is not a general compatibility fix. Even copying encoded data between containers can require framing changes . For example, H.264 units can be represented with start codes or with lengths, depending on their packaging. Changing that framing is not the same as recompressing the picture. See Also Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Packet Timestamps Streams and Tracks References ITU-T H.222.0 / ISO/IEC 13818-1: MPEG systems FFmpeg: bitstream filters and framing conversions

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Multiplexing and Demultiplexing | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Picture, sound, and subtitles are separate sequences of data. Multiplexing , usually shortened to muxing , combines them into a container with track descriptions and timing. Demultiplexing , or demuxing , reads that structure and routes each component to the appropriate decoder or renderer. The packet sequence is illustrative. Container packets are not network packets, and track timing need not be evenly spaced. Interleaving places portions of related tracks near one another. A player can then obtain upcoming picture and sound without jumping across large sections of a file. It does not change how either stream was compressed. What a remux preserves A remux demultiplexes one source and multiplexes selected encoded streams into another output. It can change track order, container headers, indexing, and metadata while preserving encoded media. That is why a remux can finish much faster than re-encoding and can preserve picture quality. However, the destination needs a valid mapping for each codec . Some formats require different headers or bitstream framing, and some metadata may not have an equivalent destination field. Emby can use this kind of repackaging in a Direct Stream session. If the video is copied but the audio is converted, the overall job combines remuxing with audio transcoding. When comparing before and after, inspect track count, languages, and duration as well as codecs. Preserving the main video alone does not prove that every soundtrack, subtitle, chapter, or attachment survived. See Also Streams and Tracks Elementary Streams Codec Support in Containers References FFmpeg: processing flow and stream copy

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Chapter Markers | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Chapter Markers A chapter marker is a bookmark on the media timeline. It can label the opening, a scene, or a song within a concert recording, letting the player jump to that position. Ordinary chapters do not divide the movie into separate video streams or require separate files. A chapter normally has a start time and may also have a title or an end time. Example marker What the player can offer 00:00 — Opening A named starting point 12:40 — The journey A jump into the existing timeline 48:15 — Finale Another named destination These times are an illustrative chapter list, not prescribed intervals. Markers and previews are separate The text and timestamp of a chapter are different from a preview image. A thumbnail may be generated from the picture at a chapter position; adding chapter metadata alone does not embed that image. For an Emby file investigation, inspect the chapter list to establish whether named markers are actually present. A player can also provide navigation aids derived separately from the file. A chapter destination does not make the picture at that moment a keyframe. The player still uses the normal seeking and decoding process to reach it. Some formats support more elaborate chapter systems, including alternative editions or ordered segments. Those are additional features. A simple list of timestamps should be understood as bookmarks unless the file explicitly describes a different presentation. See Also Container Indexes and Seeking Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe References Matroska chapter specification

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Container Indexes and Seeking | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Container Indexes and Seeking Moving a playback slider to 10 minutes asks a time question. The file is stored as bytes. A container index helps the player translate between those two views. Without useful navigation information, the reader may have to scan data to find a suitable position. An index can shorten that search, especially for large files or remote storage. Simplified timeline. Exact seeking behavior depends on the codec, index, and player. Finding bytes is only the first step Compressed video often needs earlier reference pictures. The player therefore commonly seeks to a suitable random access point , then decodes forward to the requested moment. The index cannot make every picture independently decodable. In Matroska, Cues provide timestamp-to-cluster references, and the specification recommends referencing video keyframes. Other containers use their own tables or indexes. An Emby seek can involve several delays: locating data, reading it from storage, obtaining network bytes, and restarting decoding or a server conversion. A slow jump is not enough by itself to identify which stage is responsible. Compare a file that starts normally but seeks poorly with one that is slow in both cases. Missing indexes can be rebuilt by a suitable remux when the media remains readable; damaged encoded pictures require a different response. Chapter markers give named destinations on the timeline. They are navigation labels, not a substitute for the container's means of locating and decoding the requested media. See Also Packet Timestamps Chapter Markers Damaged and Incomplete Media Files References Matroska: cues and seeking recommendations Matroska: random access points

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Packet Timestamps | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Packet Timestamps The order in which compressed video is read is not always the order in which pictures appear. A picture may depend on a later displayed picture, so the decoder needs that reference first. Two timestamps keep those jobs separate: DTS , the decoding timestamp, places data on the decode timeline. PTS , the presentation timestamp, places the decoded result on the display or sound timeline. Packet in decode order DTS PTS Picture A 0.00 s 0.04 s Picture C, a reference for B 0.04 s 0.12 s Picture B 0.08 s 0.08 s Simplified reordered-video example. The decoder receives A, C, B; the viewer sees A, B, C. The timestamps are often stored as integer ticks. Their time base tells you how to convert those ticks to seconds. A container or inspection tool may represent one timeline through durations and offsets rather than store both values explicitly for every packet. Why a warning needs interpretation A non-monotonic presentation timestamp in decode order can be normal for reordered video. A DTS that moves backward in a stream expecting ordered decode timestamps is a different problem. Gaps, incorrect offsets, or discontinuities can affect audio synchronization and seeking through Emby. A media packet is also not necessarily a single displayed frame, and it is not an IP network packet. Do not “fix” timestamps by making every number consecutive without understanding the source. That can destroy legitimate reordering or variable timing. Compare the actual times, the selected tracks, and the reported symptom first. See Also Time Bases Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Container Indexes and Seeking References FFmpeg: AVPacket timestamp definitions Apple: QuickTime time-to-sample and composition timing

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Time Bases | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Time Bases A timestamp value of 45,000 does not mean 45,000 seconds. It needs a scale. If the stream's time base is 1/90000 , each tick lasts one ninety-thousandth of a second, and 45,000 ticks means half a second. time in seconds = timestamp × time base 45,000 × (1/90,000) = 0.5 seconds Different tracks can use different scales while referring to the same moment: Time base Timestamp Time in seconds 1/90000 45,000 0.5 1/48000 24,000 0.5 1/1000 500 0.5 These are illustrative scales, not a rule that every audio or video track must use one of them. A time base is not a frame rate A stream at 25 frames per second might advance by 3,600 ticks per frame on a 90,000-tick scale. Its time base is still 1/90000 , not 1/25 . Variable-frame-rate video can advance by different amounts while keeping one time base. When remuxing, software may rescale timestamps into the destination container's units. Larger integer values after the operation do not mean the movie became slower. For an Emby synchronization investigation, compare timestamps converted to seconds. ffprobe reports values such as pts_time and dts_time for this purpose. The raw integers from two tracks are not directly comparable until their scales have been applied. A nonzero starting timestamp is not automatically an error either. The relative alignment of the tracks and the presentation's start handling determine what the listener sees and hears. See Also Packet Timestamps Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe References FFmpeg: stream time-base definitions

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Default Track Flags | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Default Track Flags A file's default audio flag is a hint about which track should be considered for automatic playback. It is not a command that every player must follow. The distinction matters when a film starts with a different soundtrack in two apps. Language preferences, accessibility choices, and remembered selections can affect the result as well as the file's flags. File property What it expresses Default audio flag Eligibility or preference for automatic selection Track language Which language the track represents Forced subtitle flag A subtitle selection hint for content such as foreign dialogue or signs Commentary or accessibility flags The track's intended service, where the format supports them The precise semantics depend on the container. In Matroska, more than one track can be eligible as default, including different languages. A player may override the default hint to meet user preferences. Default subtitles are not forced subtitles A default subtitle track might contain the full dialogue. A forced subtitle track commonly contains only the text needed alongside an otherwise understood soundtrack. Setting a forced flag on full subtitles can therefore produce an unwanted result. For an Emby selection problem, inspect the language and flags of the actual tracks, then compare the user's audio and subtitle preferences. A title containing the word “default” is merely text unless the relevant field is also set. Correcting these container fields usually does not require recompressing the picture or sound. It does require understanding the intended track: an English commentary track should not become the main soundtrack simply because its language matches the user. See Also Track Language Metadata Streams and Tracks References RFC 9559: Matroska track flags and default selection Matroska element specification: track flags

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT An MPEG transport stream can carry several television services in the same packet sequence. Each packet has a PID , a packet identifier, so a receiver can distinguish the pieces. It also needs a map showing which pieces belong together. The Program Association Table (PAT) identifies programmes and the PIDs of their Program Map Tables (PMTs) . A PMT then describes the elementary streams in one programme and identifies the PID used for its programme clock reference. Illustrative programme and stream PIDs. The PAT uses PID 0; the other values are examples. A programme is a grouping One programme can contain video, several audio tracks, subtitles, and other data. “Programme” in this systems-layer sense is not the film or episode title shown in a library. A recorded broadcast can preserve more than one programme if the recording process does not select a single service. The tables repeat during transmission so a receiver joining later can learn the structure. They can also change when a service's stream arrangement changes. This explains why inspecting a television recording needs more than the first visible video track. ffprobe's programme output can show which streams are grouped together, while language and descriptors help distinguish audio choices. For Emby, missing or inconsistent tables in a source can complicate stream discovery or playback. They are separate from the encoded picture quality. A receiver must first find the intended programme before it can decode the right media. See Also Streams and Tracks Multiplexing and Demultiplexing Media Probing References ITU-T H.222.0 / ISO/IEC 13818-1: MPEG systems

articles/media-files/container-structure.title: Track Language Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/container-structure.keywords: Track Language Metadata An audio track can contain English dialogue but appear as “Unknown” because its language field is missing or unhelpful. Software generally reads the tag; it does not establish the language by listening to the dialogue. Language metadata helps Emby identify choices and apply playback preferences. The same mechanism is useful for subtitles, but the language describes the subtitle text, which may differ from the soundtrack. Language value What it indicates eng English, using an ISO 639-2 code deu / ger German; terminology and bibliographic ISO codes pt-BR Portuguese with a Brazil region subtag in BCP 47 und Undetermined language Containers differ in the code systems they use. Matroska includes a legacy language field and a BCP 47 field; when both are present, the BCP 47 field takes precedence under its specification. A track title is another field “English 5.1” in a title is useful for a person, but it is not the same as a machine-readable English language tag. Likewise, setting the language to English does not identify a track as commentary or mark its subtitles as forced. If the wrong language is chosen, check the file's actual fields alongside the user's preferences. Correcting a container language tag can often be done without re-encoding the audio or video. The movie's original language in library metadata is a separate property. It describes the work, while track language describes one particular audio or subtitle component. A multilingual film can legitimately contain several differently tagged tracks. See Also Streams and Tracks Default Track Flags Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo References Library of Congress: ISO 639-2 language codes RFC 5646: language tags Matroska: language-code fields and precedence

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: Bitrate | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: Bitrate A bitrate of 10 Mb/s means ten million bits for each second of media, averaged over the interval being measured. It describes the amount of data, not the resolution or a guaranteed level of quality. That rate is about 1.25 megabytes per second. The factor of eight matters because network speeds are usually shown in bits per second, while file sizes and copy speeds often use bytes. What a reported rate covers What is included Video bitrate The encoded picture stream Audio bitrate One encoded soundtrack Overall file bitrate The whole file's bytes divided by its duration Network transfer rate Bytes delivered over the connection, which may arrive in bursts A film's overall rate can include several soundtracks even though only one plays at a time. Direct delivery of the complete file and delivery of selected tracks can therefore move different amounts of data. How to use the number For storage, average bitrate and duration give a useful file-size estimate . For streaming, the variation over time and the available buffer also matter. A connection that just matches the reported average can struggle during demanding scenes. When comparing quality, keep the codec, source, and encoding settings in mind. A more efficient codec can use fewer bits for a similar picture. Raising the rate of an already compressed source cannot restore detail that was discarded. In an Emby playback session, distinguish the source bitrate from the delivered bitrate. A quality limit may cause conversion, and the resulting stream can have different characteristics from the library file. See Also Bitrate Variation File Size and Duration Digital Media Data Units References FFmpeg: overall bitrate and stream information NIST: metric prefixes

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: Bitrate Variation | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: Bitrate Variation A quiet conversation is usually easier to compress than a crowd moving through rain. A variable-bitrate encode can spend fewer bits on the conversation and more on the difficult scene. The rate printed in a media report is often an average across both. Illustrative four-second intervals. These are encoded media rates, not measurements of network traffic. This example averages 12 Mb/s, but its busiest interval needs twice that rate. Over four seconds, the 24 Mb/s interval contains 96 megabits, or 12 MB. Why buffers help A player can receive data ahead of the play position and keep it in memory. If a connection delivers 18 Mb/s during that demanding interval, it falls 24 megabits behind over four seconds. About 3 MB of already buffered media can bridge that simplified gap. Protocol overhead and changes in connection speed require additional allowance. The same average rate can hide very different demands: a short spike is easier to absorb than a long scene that stays above the connection's capacity. Measured peaks also depend on the interval used; a frame-level peak and a ten-second average are different statistics. In Emby, repeated buffering around the same busy scenes can suggest a sustained throughput or buffer limitation. The source rate is a useful clue, but the active playback method and delivered stream determine what actually crosses the network. A file need not use variable-bitrate encoding to arrive in bursts. Even constant-rate media can be fetched faster than playback speed, followed by pauses while the player consumes its buffer. See Also Bitrate File Size and Duration References FFmpeg: encoder bitrate and rate-control options

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: Digital Media Data Units | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: Digital Media Data Units Symbol Meaning Typical media use b bit Network and media bitrate B byte: eight bits File size and transfer amount /s per second A rate rather than an amount To convert bits per second to bytes per second, divide by eight. 100 Mb/s ÷ 8 = 12.5 MB/s , before transmission overhead. Look up the prefix Unit Number of bytes MB, megabyte 1,000,000 MiB, mebibyte 1,048,576 GB, gigabyte 1,000,000,000 GiB, gibibyte 1,073,741,824 Decimal prefixes use powers of 1,000; binary prefixes use powers of 1,024. One billion bytes is 1 GB , or approximately 0.931 GiB . Both describe the same file length. Convert a streaming rate into an amount At an average of 8 Mb/s , the stream uses approximately 1 MB each second , or 60 MB each minute . For a longer interval, multiply the byte rate by the number of seconds. Bitrate and file size versus duration develop that calculation. See Also Bitrate File Size and Duration References NIST: prefixes for binary multiples NIST: SI prefixes and their use

articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.title: File Size and Duration | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/bitrat.keywords: File Size and Duration A two-hour movie at an average video bitrate of 10 Mb/s needs about 9 GB for the video stream. The calculation is straightforward: size in bytes = average bitrate in bits/second × duration in seconds ÷ 8 10,000,000 × 7,200 ÷ 8 = 9,000,000,000 bytes That estimate uses decimal GB. It is not yet the size of the complete file if the rate describes video alone. Component in this example Average rate Size over two hours Video 10 Mb/s 9.00 GB One audio track 384 kb/s 0.346 GB Second audio track 384 kb/s Another 0.346 GB Container structures and other content Depends on the file Additional bytes Use the overall average bitrate to estimate the whole file. Use individual stream rates when deciding what contributes most to its size. Cover images, attachments, and metadata can add bytes without representing any extra running time. What size cannot tell you A large file can contain a long programme, a high bitrate, several soundtracks, or a codec that compresses less efficiently. Its size alone cannot identify quality or predict whether an Emby app will play it directly. Two equal-size movies with different durations have different average rates. Even two equal-duration files can distribute their data differently across scenes, so an estimate does not describe streaming peaks . If an inspection tool derives overall bitrate from file size and duration, those three fields are not independent checks. An incorrect duration can produce an incorrect bitrate too. Investigate suspicious values through probing instead of using the arithmetic to “confirm” them. See Also Bitrate Digital Media Data Units Container Overhead References FFmpeg: duration and total bitrate fields

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Contai.title: Containers and Codecs | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Contai.keywords: Containers and Codecs Two files ending in .mp4 can have very different playback requirements. One might contain H.264 video and AAC audio; another might contain HEVC video and a different audio format. MP4 identifies the container, while H.264, HEVC, and AAC identify codecs. The distinction explains why changing a file extension cannot make a movie compatible. The player still has to open the package and decode the streams inside it. Layer Its job Example Container Stores tracks, timing, and descriptions MP4 or Matroska Video codec Represents the moving picture H.264 or HEVC Audio codec Represents the soundtrack AAC or FLAC These examples explain the layers; they are not a device support list. Repackaging versus re-encoding A remux copies encoded streams into a new container. The packaging changes, but the picture and sound need not be decoded or compressed again. A tool may adjust headers and metadata to meet the new container's requirements. Transcoding decodes and re-encodes one or more streams. That can change codec, bitrate, resolution, or other properties and requires more processing. In Emby's playback methods , a container mismatch can sometimes be handled through Direct Stream. A video codec mismatch may require video transcoding. Audio can be converted while the video is copied, so the processing cost is not always all-or-nothing. To understand a specific file, inspect both its container/codec combination and the streams selected for playback. Knowing only the container leaves the most important compatibility questions unanswered. See Also What Is a Media Container? Media File Extensions Multiplexing and Demultiplexing References FFmpeg: processing flow and stream copy

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: What Is a Media File? | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: What Is a Media File? A movie file is more than a row of pictures. It usually contains compressed video , one or more soundtracks, timing information, and descriptions that tell a player how those pieces fit together. Subtitles and chapter markers may be included too. Most of that is organized by a container . The codecs describe how the picture and sound data are represented. A file can use a familiar container while carrying a codec that a particular player cannot decode. An illustrative file layout, not a byte-level map of a particular format. What Emby needs to find out When Emby examines a file, the useful questions include which streams exist, their formats, and how long they run. Those details help describe the item and determine how to deliver it to an app. The filename alone cannot answer them. The information also has two different purposes. Technical metadata such as resolution and audio language helps playback. A library title, synopsis, or poster describes the work. A movie can have correct library information while its underlying file has an incorrect language tag or damaged timestamps. For a playback question, begin with the file's media information and the selected audio and subtitle tracks. “It is an MKV” describes its packaging; it does not yet describe what the app must play. See Also Containers and Codecs Streams and Tracks Media Probing How Digital Video Represents Moving Pictures References Matroska: basic container concepts

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: Media File Extensions | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: Media File Extensions The ending of a filename helps an operating system choose an application and helps media software decide which files to examine. It is a useful clue, but it is not a technical report. A container extension such as .mkv normally tells you how tracks are packaged. It does not tell you the video codec, audio languages, resolution, or HDR format. Other endings, such as .mp3 , are more closely associated with a particular encoded audio format. Renaming does not convert Renaming Movie.mkv to Movie.mp4 leaves every byte inside the file unchanged. A player that recognizes the contents may still open it; another may reject the mismatch. Neither outcome means conversion took place. Changing containers requires remultiplexing . Changing a codec requires re-encoding the relevant stream. Emby library discovery and naming rules also depend on filenames and folder structure. Keep the expected extension for the actual file format, then use media inspection to identify its contents. If a download or recording has a misleading ending, find out what it contains before renaming it. A small practical trap is hidden extensions: a file shown as Movie.strm may actually be Movie.strm.txt . Showing the full filename is often enough to explain why software does not recognize a newly created pointer file. See Also Containers and Codecs Media MIME Types Media Probing References Apple: QuickTime file format introduction

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: Lossy and Lossless Compression | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: Lossy and Lossless Compression A lossless codec reconstructs exactly the digital samples supplied to its encoder. A lossy codec allows differences in the decoded result in exchange for a smaller representation, often concentrating its effort on changes people are less likely to notice. Both can make files smaller than uncompressed media. “Lossless” does not mean “uncompressed,” and “lossy” does not necessarily mean an obvious defect. Operation What is preserved? Lossless encode and decode The encoder's input samples Lossy encode and decode An approximation of those samples Copy encoded tracks into another container The copied encoded media, without another compression pass The source still matters Converting an MP3 recording to a lossless format preserves the samples decoded from that MP3. It cannot recover the information discarded when the MP3 was created. A lossless label describes the new compression step, not the history of the recording. The same principle applies to video compression . A lossless encode of a previously compressed film preserves that decoded picture, including any existing artifacts. Pixel-format conversions, scaling, or resampling before encoding may also change the material independently of the codec's lossless mode. For Emby, the source's compression type and the playback method answer separate questions. Direct Play can deliver a lossy source unchanged. A lossless source may need conversion for a particular app or output route. Repeated lossy re-encoding can introduce additional changes. If only the container needs changing, remuxing can often avoid that extra generation. Whether the tracks fit the destination container is a separate compatibility check. See Also Containers and Codecs Bitrate How Video Compression Works References RFC 9639: FLAC format and compression definitions

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: Media MIME Types | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: Media MIME Types An HTTP response can announce Content-Type: video/mp4 . That label is a media type , commonly called a MIME type. It helps the receiving software interpret the content before examining the bytes. The type has two parts: video is the top-level category and mp4 is the subtype. Some types also define parameters that describe the contents more precisely. Label What it communicates video/mp4 MP4-family content containing video audio/mp4 MP4-family content containing audio without video audio/mpeg MPEG audio content application/vnd.apple.mpegurl An HLS playlist, not the encoded movie itself The registered meanings come from IANA and the relevant format specifications. Labels used in older software can differ. A label is only part of compatibility A generic container type does not establish which codecs the client can decode. The standardized codecs parameter can provide more detail, but the actual media must still match what the sender declares. For Emby playback through a browser or another HTTP-based app, the delivered response type concerns what the server sends. It can differ from the original library file when the server repackages or converts the media. An incorrect Content-Type can affect how a browser handles a resource even when the file is valid. Changing the label, however, does not convert the data. Investigate it alongside the actual container and codecs , rather than treating it as a replacement for inspection. See Also Media File Extensions Containers and Codecs References RFC 6838: media type specifications and registration RFC 6381: codecs and profiles parameters IANA media types registry

articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.title: Streams and Tracks | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/fundamentals/Media-.keywords: Streams and Tracks A film with two audio languages usually stores two audio tracks alongside one video track. Selecting another language changes which audio sequence is played; it does not require a second copy of the film's picture. In file discussions, stream and track often refer to the same component. Track emphasizes its place in the container; stream emphasizes the sequence of media data read from it. A network stream is a broader use of the word and may deliver an entire container with several tracks. Example file component What selecting it changes Main video The moving picture Original-language audio The dialogue and soundtrack Commentary audio An alternative soundtrack Subtitle track Text or images displayed over the picture One audio track can contain several audio channels , such as a 5.1 soundtrack. Six channels are not six selectable audio tracks. Why the track list matters An Emby playback decision depends on the selected components. A compatible video track may play directly with one audio choice but need audio conversion with another. Choosing an image-based subtitle track can also change the work required to display it. Track numbers help inspection tools distinguish components, but they are not durable identities across editing. A remux that adds or removes tracks may reorder them. Language, codec, channel layout, and track title make a more useful comparison. A title such as “English commentary” is descriptive metadata. The actual language tag and any selection flags are separate fields. Checking all three helps explain why a player offers or chooses a particular track. See Also What Is a Media File? Track Language Metadata Default Track Flags Understanding Audio in Media References FFmpeg: stream descriptions

articles/media-files/inspection/Media-In.title: Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/inspection/Media-In.keywords: Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe ffprobe is FFmpeg's inspection tool. It reads media information and reports it as text or structured data; it does not re-encode the input. With ffprobe installed and available on the command path, this produces a JSON report: ffprobe -v error -show_format -show_streams -show_chapters -of json "Movie.mkv" The three requested sections separate whole-file information, individual tracks, and chapters. Missing fields mean the tool did not report a value, not necessarily that the underlying property is zero. Output field How to read it format_name The detected demuxer or format family; it can list related formats codec_name / codec_type A track's codec and whether it is video, audio, or another type time_base The scale used for that track's integer timestamps tags / disposition Reported metadata and selection flags duration / bit_rate Reported or estimated values at the relevant scope Examine the part that matches the problem For a transport-stream recording, add -show_programs to see programme groupings. For timing, request packets from a short interval: ffprobe -v error -select_streams v:0 -read_intervals "%+5" -show_packets -show_entries packet=pts_time,dts_time,duration_time,flags -of json "Movie.mkv" This selects the first video stream and examines an interval of approximately five seconds from the initial read position. Packet durations and reordering mean the result need not correspond to exactly five seconds of displayed pictures. For Emby troubleshooting, use the same source file and record the selected tracks. Compare timestamp values in seconds and avoid mistaking a demuxer family name for a precise file subtype. A summary probe does not decode every frame. Packet inspection can reveal timing clues, but a full integrity investigation may need decoding as a separate step. See Also Media Probing Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo Packet Timestamps MPEG-TS Program Tables: PAT and PMT References ffprobe documentation

articles/media-files/inspection/Media-In.title: Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/inspection/Media-In.keywords: Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo MediaInfo is useful when “this file will not play” needs to become a more precise description. Open the file and use a detailed view, such as Tree or Text , to see the container and each media track separately. Read the report from the outside inward: Report section Useful questions General Which container is it, how long is it, and what is the overall bitrate? Video Which codec, profile, dimensions, bit depth, and color signaling are present? Audio Which codec, language, channel arrangement, and sample rate belong to each track? Text Which subtitle format and language does each track use? Menu, when present Which chapters or navigation entries were detected? Field availability depends on the file and the version of the tool. Bring the right details to a playback question For Emby troubleshooting, a text report is more useful than a screenshot showing only the extension and resolution. Keep the sections for the selected audio and subtitle tracks, because another track can change the playback requirements. MediaInfo's Format and Codec ID fields serve different purposes. “HEVC” names a coding system; hvc1 identifies a particular container representation. Both can matter when players disagree about compatibility. Color and HDR metadata fields describe information detected in the source. They do not show the display's active output mode or prove that the entire playback route preserved that information. MediaInfo is an inspector, not a decoder test or repair tool. If a film fails at one scene, a normal-looking summary does not rule out damage there. Include the failing time and playback method alongside the report, and use ffprobe when packet or timing details are needed. See Also Media Probing Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe Codec Identifiers and FourCC HDR Metadata References MediaInfo: features and report contents MediaInfo: analysis and display questions

articles/media-files/inspection/Media-Pr.title: Media Probing | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/inspection/Media-Pr.keywords: Media Probing Before a player can choose a decoder, it needs to know what it has received. Probing reads a source's structure and, where necessary, samples some encoded data to identify its streams and properties. For Emby, that technical information contributes to the media details and playback decisions. It is different from finding posters, episode names, or descriptions for the library. Conceptual workflow. A particular property can come from a header, direct examination, or an estimate. A successful probe is not a full integrity check A report showing codec, resolution, and duration establishes that the tool identified useful information. It does not prove that every frame in a two-hour film can be decoded. Some properties are explicitly stored. Others are inferred from limited data, or calculated from size and duration. A missing bitrate field does not mean that the stream contains no data; the tool may lack a reliable value to report. Live or irregular sources can also need more data before all streams appear. Inspection tools expose analysis limits because there is a tradeoff between fast discovery and a fuller examination. When a report looks suspicious, compare MediaInfo with ffprobe , including the file path, selected tracks, and tool versions. Different field names or estimates do not necessarily indicate file damage. For a repeatable Emby failure, note whether it happens at startup, on seeking, or at the same scene. That symptom helps decide whether a short probe is enough or whether the relevant part of the media needs a deeper decode check. See Also Media Stream Inspection with MediaInfo Media Stream Inspection with ffprobe Damaged and Incomplete Media Files References FFmpeg format options: probing limits MediaInfo: technical information displayed

articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-A.title: AAC: Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-A.keywords: AAC: Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) A file ending in .aac often uses Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) framing. ADTS puts a header before encoded AAC data, letting a reader find frame boundaries and discover important audio properties as it reads. It is an audio framing format. It is not the same thing as MPEG transport stream , although ADTS-framed AAC can be carried within TS. ADTS header information What it helps the reader do Synchronization pattern Locate a candidate frame boundary Frame length Determine how many bytes belong to the frame Core profile and sampling-frequency fields Establish basic decoder information Channel configuration Describe the core channel arrangement or signal further configuration A common single-block ADTS frame has a seven-byte header without CRC protection, or nine bytes with it. The header's synchronization pattern is a clue for parsing; validating lengths and successive frames is more reliable than treating one matching byte pattern as proof of a valid file. A header is not a complete codec description in every case More advanced AAC tools can require additional signalling in the audio data. With HE-AAC , for example, the final decoder output properties can differ from those described for the core. Read the complete probe result rather than inferring every property from one header field. For an Emby import, an ADTS AAC file and an AAC track in M4A may ask the same audio decoder to handle the sound, while using different readers to supply it. Moving between those packages can be possible without recompression. Such a move must translate the configuration and remove or add the appropriate framing. Renaming .aac to .m4a does neither. A general MP4 also supplies track timing and metadata structures that a bare ADTS stream does not provide in the same way. See Also AAC Stream Packaging AAC: Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS HE-AAC Audio References ISO/IEC 13818-7:2006: MPEG-2 AAC ISO/IEC 14496-3:2019: MPEG-4 Audio FFmpeg: aac_adtstoasc bitstream filter

articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-L.title: AAC: Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-L.keywords: AAC: Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) A broadcast recording may report AAC with LATM rather than the familiar ADTS packaging. That extra name identifies an input structure the player must understand before it can decode the sound. Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) carries MPEG-4 audio data with multiplex and configuration information. Configuration can be supplied in-band and reused, avoiding the need to repeat a full independent description around every audio unit. Layer Its job AAC coding tools Represent the compressed sound LATM Organize audio payloads and the information needed to interpret them LOAS, when used Add synchronization and length framing around LATM data Outer delivery, such as TS or RTP Carry the packaged audio to the receiver LOAS , Low Overhead Audio Stream, is a related framing layer, not a synonym for the multiplex itself. RFC 6416 also defines carriage of LATM audio elements in RTP, illustrating why LATM need not always arrive with the same outer wrapper. The receiver needs both parsing and decoding A device can support an AAC variant yet lack the input path for LATM in a particular container. Conversely, recognizing LATM does not establish support for every MPEG-4 audio coding tool its configuration can describe. For an Emby recording with sound problems, inspect the transport and the audio profile together. A successful probe on the server does not by itself establish that the selected app can consume the original packaging directly. The delivered stream and its handling on that platform matter. Changing LATM to ADTS or MP4 is not a filename operation. A converter must interpret the configuration and translate the framing, and some combinations may need more than a simple header rewrite. Retain the original when investigating such a conversion. Check channel layout, output sample rate, timing, and playback through the affected programme transition, where a fresh configuration can become important. See Also AAC Stream Packaging AAC: Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS References ISO/IEC 14496-3:2019: MPEG-4 Audio RFC 6416: MPEG-4 Audio transport and LATM
