articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-S.title: AAC Stream Packaging | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/aac/AAC-S.keywords: AAC Stream Packaging Two files can contain the same AAC-encoded sound and still require different input handling. AAC is the compression family ; its packaging tells a reader where encoded units begin and how to configure the decoder. The decoder needs information such as the audio object type, sample rate, and channel configuration. That information can be carried in transport headers or in a containing file's track description. Packaging Where a reader finds structure and configuration ADTS Repeated transport headers around encoded audio MP4/M4A Container sample descriptions, timing, and stored decoder configuration LATM A multiplex structure carrying audio and configuration information Those choices do not establish whether the audio is AAC-LC , HE-AAC , or another member of the family. Some coding tools and configurations need signalling beyond the basic fields in a particular wrapper. Copying the sound can still change bytes Moving AAC from ADTS into MP4 commonly removes the repeated ADTS headers and creates an AudioSpecificConfig in the container. This is a bitstream-packaging adjustment that can preserve the encoded audio without decoding and recompressing it. The resulting files will not be byte-for-byte identical, and their total sizes may differ. That difference is not by itself evidence of a quality change. Compare the encoded audio and configuration rather than treating container overhead as extra sound information. For an Emby source that is identified as AAC but behaves differently from another AAC source, check both the coding variant and the wrapper. A suitable decoder is insufficient if the input stage cannot understand the framing or discover the required configuration. Use inspection information that includes the container and profile, not only the word AAC. This avoids confusing a transport problem with a need to re-encode the soundtrack. See Also AAC: Audio Data Transport Stream (ADTS) AAC: Low Overhead Audio Transport Multiplex (LATM) M4A and M4B File Conventions Elementary Streams AAC-LC Audio HE-AAC Audio References ISO/IEC 14496-3:2019: MPEG-4 Audio ISO/IEC 13818-7:2006: MPEG-2 AAC FFmpeg: aac_adtstoasc bitstream filter

articles/media-files/packaging/disc/Blu-.title: Blu-ray File Structure | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/disc/Blu-.keywords: Blu-ray File Structure A Blu-ray film does not have to live in one enormous .m2ts file. Its BDMV structure can define a feature through a playlist that selects ranges from several clips. That separation lets different presentations reuse media. It also explains why copying the largest stream file may omit parts of a movie, choose the wrong version, or lose chapter navigation. Original simplified BDMV schematic. It shows the main relationships, not every directory or optional feature. PLAYLIST holds .mpls files describing the clip sequence and playback ranges. CLIPINF holds .clpi files describing clips and access information. STREAM contains the actual .m2ts media, using transport-stream packaging. The index and movie-object information provide entry and navigation logic. Interactive BD-J material can add further application behaviour, which is separate from simply decoding a stream file. The playlist establishes what to play Several playlists can reuse the same clips in different orders or ranges. Similar durations and sizes therefore do not always identify the version a viewer expects. Selecting a stream file bypasses the playlist's presentation decisions. For an Emby collection, distinguish the disc presentation from a remuxed movie in MKV or MP4. Playing the encoded feature and reproducing the disc's full menu or application behaviour are different capabilities. The result depends on the app, platform, and source layout; see the movie organization guidance . When making a self-contained copy of the feature, verify its scene order, full duration, audio, subtitles, and chapters . Preserving the codecs is valuable, but it is not enough if the wrong playlist was selected. Keep the complete source until those presentation details have been checked. See Also MPEG Transport Stream: TS and M2TS Disc Images: ISO Files Chapter Markers References Blu-ray Disc License Office: format specifications Blu-ray Disc Association: BD-ROM audiovisual application white paper, March 2005 (original PDF mirror)

articles/media-files/packaging/disc/Disc.title: Disc Images: ISO Files | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/disc/Disc.keywords: Disc Images: ISO Files An ISO file is usually a disc image: a file containing the logical sectors of a disc volume, including its filesystem and the files within it. It packages the disc as a whole rather than combining its movie tracks into a new media container. The extension does not guarantee ISO 9660. Images can contain UDF or a bridge of filesystem conventions, depending on the source disc. A DVD or Blu-ray image also retains application structures above that filesystem layer. Layer inside a movie-disc image Example Volume and filesystem Directory entries and file locations Disc presentation VIDEO_TS or BDMV navigation structures Media files VOB or M2TS encoded streams Codecs within those streams The actual picture and sound representations Mounting an image exposes its contained files as a volume. It does not convert those files to MP4 or MKV, decode the video, or remove content protection. A disc copy and a movie copy answer different needs Preserving a disc image can retain menus, extras, multiple presentations, and their relationships. A self-contained movie remux instead selects a presentation and packages its chosen tracks for ordinary file playback. It may omit menus or extras by design while preserving the encoded feature. For an Emby library, the image adds a disc-reading requirement before the usual container and codec checks. Playback depends on the app and platform; a device that accepts an MKV movie need not accept the equivalent disc image. Use the movie organization guidance to keep those sources recognizable. Inspect the contained DVD or Blu-ray structure when a title or duration is unexpected. Renaming the image .mp4 cannot bypass its filesystem or select the feature. An image is also a copy, not an integrity guarantee. Unreadable source sectors or incomplete copying can leave damaged content inside an otherwise recognized volume. See Also DVD-Video File Structure Blu-ray File Structure Types of Media Containers References ECMA-119, 6th edition: ISO 9660 volume and file structure ECMA-167, 3rd edition: volume and file structure ECMA TR/71: DVD read-only disk file system specifications Blu-ray Disc License Office: format specifications

articles/media-files/packaging/disc/DVD-.title: DVD-Video File Structure | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/disc/DVD-.keywords: DVD-Video File Structure A DVD-Video folder is a presentation made from several related files, rather than a directory of independent movies. Its VIDEO_TS structure keeps encoded media and the navigation needed to interpret it. The filesystem and the DVD-Video application rules are different layers. A correctly copied directory preserves file relationships; the player still needs to interpret the disc's title and navigation information. File type in VIDEO_TS Role .VOB Video objects containing multiplexed picture, sound, subtitles, and navigation data .IFO Descriptions of title sets, programme chains, chapters, and playback choices .BUP Backup copies of IFO information A title's media is often split across numbered VOB files. Those boundaries are storage divisions, not necessarily chapter or scene boundaries. Follow the title, not just the filenames DVD navigation can select and order cells within the video objects. Menus, alternative angles, or different cuts can make the intended sequence more complicated than playing every VOB in directory order. An isolated VOB uses program-stream packaging and may open in a general media reader. That does not establish that it represents the complete feature or follows the same path as a DVD-aware reader. For a collection used with Emby, distinguish a complete DVD folder or image from a single movie file. Disc navigation support and the available playback path depend on the app and platform; follow the movie organization guidance for the library layout. If creating one self-contained movie from a disc presentation, choose the intended title and verify its full sequence, selected audio, subtitles, and chapters. Repackaging its encoded streams can avoid recompression, but it still requires resolving the disc structure correctly. The largest file or the first numbered title is only a clue, not proof of the main feature. See Also MPEG Program Stream Disc Images: ISO Files Chapter Markers References ECMA TR/71: DVD read-only disk file system specifications DVD Format/Logo Licensing Corporation: DVD format book catalogue FFmpeg: format documentation

articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.title: Matroska Attachments | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.keywords: Matroska Attachments Styled subtitles can look different even when their text is identical. One reason is that the original file supplied a font that the new playback path never receives. Matroska attachments provide a way to bundle supporting files with the media. An attachment has a filename, media type, and file contents. It is separate from the timed video, audio, and subtitle tracks: a font file does not have a sequence of presentation timestamps. Common attachment Possible use TrueType or OpenType font Supplies a typeface requested by styled subtitles Cover image Provides artwork associated with the file Other supporting resource Stores a file the receiving software may choose to use The container can carry a resource without forcing a player to interpret it. A reader may ignore attachments or support only particular uses. A font can matter to more than appearance A different font changes letter widths and line breaks. That can shift text, alter signs, or make a carefully positioned subtitle harder to read. Having the font attached helps only if the subtitle renderer can use it in the selected playback path. When troubleshooting an Emby subtitle difference, check both the subtitle track and the attachment list. A direct playback renderer and a server rendering subtitles into video may receive and handle supporting resources differently. Their results need to be compared on the actual app and server configuration. Remuxing can copy picture and sound while dropping attachments. That is a metadata/resource preservation issue rather than loss of the encoded movie. Inspect the output package before concluding that a conversion preserved everything. Cover attachments also differ from separately stored library artwork. Their presence does not establish that a library will display them in every artwork role. The source file and the library's metadata choices are distinct layers. See Also Matroska: MKV and MKA Streams and Tracks Multiplexing and Demultiplexing References RFC 9559: Matroska Media Container Format Specification MKVToolNix: mkvmerge manual

articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.title: Matroska Ordered Chapters | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/matroska/.keywords: Matroska Ordered Chapters Ordinary chapter markers help you jump to a scene in a movie whose sequence is already fixed. Ordered chapters can define the sequence itself, by listing the ranges a Matroska presentation should play. An ordered edition can refer to different portions of the current segment or to linked segments identified by their unique identifiers. A shared opening could therefore be stored once and referenced by several episode presentations. Original conceptual example using linked segments. It illustrates the sequence, not a claim about support in a particular player. A chapter list can be a playback recipe A reader that follows the ordered edition plays the declared ranges in their specified order. A reader that only plays the physical media linearly may produce a different duration or omit the linked material. Recognizing basic MKV tracks is insufficient to establish support for this feature. This is useful context for an Emby item that plays a body of content but misses an opening, repeats scenes, or differs from a desktop player. Inspect the edition and segment references as well as the audio and video codecs. A codec conversion alone does not reconstruct the intended sequence. All referenced media must remain available to a reader that resolves the links. Copying only one file from a collection can leave a presentation incomplete even though that file's encoded data is intact. A conversion to one self-contained movie needs to resolve the edition and assemble its intended ranges with correct timing. Merely copying the current file's streams ignores that extra presentation logic. Use ordinary chapter markers when all you need is navigation within a conventional fixed sequence. Ordered chapters introduce another compatibility and dependency question that should be checked on the intended playback path. See Also Matroska: MKV and MKA Chapter Markers Packet Timestamps References RFC 9559: Matroska Media Container Format Specification MKVToolNix: mkvmerge manual

articles/media-files/packaging/MP3-Files.title: MP3 Files and MPEG Audio Frames | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/MP3-Files.keywords: MP3 Files and MPEG Audio Frames An MP3 file is usually a sequence of MPEG audio frames rather than a general container holding many tracks. Each frame has a small header that helps the reader identify its encoding and boundaries. This file framing is distinct from the MP3 codec's compression method . The codec determines how the sound is represented; the file also needs a way to carry the resulting frames and useful descriptive information. MP3 file information What it contributes MPEG audio frame header Version, layer, bitrate, sample rate, and channel mode Encoded frame data Compressed audio information ID3 tags, when present Track descriptions and optional artwork Optional Xing or VBRI information Frame counts or navigation information useful for variable-bitrate files ID3 also calls its metadata items frames . An ID3 title frame is not an MPEG audio frame and contains no block of decoded music samples. Variable bitrate complicates simple estimates Estimating duration from file size and one observed bitrate can give a misleading duration for a variable-bitrate MP3. The reader can use frame counts, optional navigation information, or a fuller examination of the stream instead. MP3 Layer III also uses a bit reservoir , allowing encoded data associated with a frame to draw on bytes carried earlier. Cutting at an apparent frame boundary does not guarantee clean independent decoding from that point. In an Emby music collection, missing or unusual tags can affect identification while the audio plays normally. Incorrect duration or seeking can point to a different problem with frame information or navigation. Keep those symptoms separate. When a file is rewritten, verify the tags and seek behaviour along with the sound. Copying the compressed audio is a different preservation task from retaining album information, artwork, or accurate navigation. See Also Containers and Codecs Container Indexes and Seeking Bitrate Variation MP3 Audio References ISO/IEC 11172-3:1993: MPEG-1 Audio RFC 5219: MP3 frame structure and bit reservoir ID3v2.4.0: main structure

articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/Fragm.title: Fragmented MP4 | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/Fragm.keywords: Fragmented MP4 A live presentation cannot wait until its final frame exists before describing the entire movie. Fragmented MP4 , often shortened to fMP4, solves that packaging problem by describing successive portions of the media as they become available. The initial information identifies tracks and codec configuration. Each movie fragment then describes samples associated with its media data. Original schematic of a common streaming layout. Optional boxes are omitted; fragments need not have equal durations. The key boxes are moof , the movie-fragment description, and mdat , its encoded media. For browser Media Source Extensions, the W3C byte-stream note defines initialization and media-segment rules built on these structures. HLS also defines an fMP4 segment format. A fragment is not automatically a standalone movie A media fragment can depend on the initialization information for its codec description. Decoding can also depend on earlier pictures unless the fragment begins at a suitable random access point . Copying one downloaded fragment into a new file therefore does not necessarily produce something independently playable. Fragmentation describes the internal structure. It does not require one physical file per fragment: a fragmented presentation can be stored in a single file or delivered through separate segments. For an Emby playback investigation, distinguish the original library file from the package delivered to the app. A streaming path may use segmented media even when the source is a conventional MP4 or another container. The source extension alone cannot reveal that delivery structure. Unlike fast start , fragmentation repeatedly supplies sample information. Neither method changes the codec or encoded picture quality. Compatibility still depends on the chosen codecs and the player's support for the particular streaming conventions. See Also MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format MP4 Fast Start Container Indexes and Seeking References ISO/IEC 14496-12:2026: ISO base media file format W3C ISO BMFF byte stream format: 23 July 2024 Group Note RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming, media segment formats

articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/M4A-M.title: M4A and M4B File Conventions | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/M4A-M.keywords: M4A and M4B File Conventions M4A and M4B usually describe audio-oriented members of the MP4 container family . The extensions help software recognize the intended use; they do not name an audio codec. M4A is common for music. M4B is commonly used for audiobooks, often with chapters and applications that remember a listening position. Those behaviours are implemented by the player and library, rather than guaranteed solely by the final letter of the filename. Property What the extension tells you Intended content M4A usually suggests audio; M4B usually suggests a book Audio encoding Must be read from the track; AAC and ALAC are possible examples Chapters Must actually be present in a supported chapter representation Resume behaviour Depends on the library and playback app An M4A can contain lossy AAC or lossless ALAC . Treating all M4A files as the same audio quality therefore overlooks a more important property than the extension. Book structure is separate from sound encoding A long recording can be one continuous audio track with chapter markers . The chapter boundaries do not imply that the encoded sound is stored as separate files or separately compressed tracks. Several chapter conventions exist in the MP4/QuickTime family. A conversion can preserve audio but omit the particular chapter information an app understands. Inspect the resulting chapter list and listening position behaviour separately from the audio properties. For Emby, use the appropriate library context and audiobook organization guidance . Renaming an audio file to .m4b does not add chapter titles, repair album metadata, or ensure that every client treats it as a book. When comparing a source with its converted copy, check encoding, complete duration, chapters, and descriptive tags. Those four facts explain much more than the filename convention. See Also MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format Chapter Markers Media File Extensions Apple Lossless (ALAC) AAC-LC Audio References ISO/IEC 14496-14:2020: MP4 file format Apple AVFoundation: M4A file type Apple Audio Toolbox: M4B file type Apple: QuickTime File Format

articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/MP4-F.title: MP4 Fast Start | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/packaging/mp4/MP4-F.keywords: MP4 Fast Start An MP4 can contain perfectly good media while making a player fetch the end of the file before it knows how to play the beginning. Fast start changes the layout so that the movie description arrives early. In a conventional nonfragmented MP4, the moov box describes tracks, sample timing, and data locations. Writers commonly finish that information after writing the encoded media, leaving moov near the end. Fast-start processing moves it ahead of the bulk media data and updates locations that changed. Original simplified layouts. Box widths do not represent actual sizes. The benefit depends on how the file is read A reader downloading bytes sequentially can reach the description quickly and begin once enough media is available. A server and reader that support byte-range requests can instead fetch a trailing moov directly; they need not download the entire file first. For an Emby library, this means fast start can help some direct file-delivery paths, while a repackaged streaming path may have its own initialization structure. It is not a universal explanation for every startup delay. Network access, decoding, and server processing still matter. Moving moov is a packaging operation. It does not reduce bitrate, improve sound, or make an unsupported codec decodable. The bulk picture and sound samples can remain unchanged, although the file's overall bytes and offsets differ. Fast start is also distinct from fragmented MP4 . A conventional fast-start file places its overall sample description early; a fragmented file describes successive groups of samples. Choose the layout the intended reader expects, and check both startup and seeking after a packaging change. See Also MP4 and the ISO Base Media File Format Fragmented MP4 Container Indexes and Seeking References ISO/IEC 14496-12:2026: ISO base media file format FFmpeg: format documentation

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: CUE Sheets | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: CUE Sheets A CUE sheet can describe several songs inside one long audio file. It records where tracks begin and can provide titles, performers, and disc-oriented information. The sound stays in the referenced file. FILE "Concert.wav" WAVE TRACK 01 AUDIO TITLE "Opening" INDEX 01 00:00:00 TRACK 02 AUDIO TITLE "Second song" INDEX 01 04:30:00 Illustrative two-track description of one recording. The final number in a CUE timestamp is not milliseconds. Its format is minutes:seconds:frames , using 75 CD frames per second. CUE timestamp Position 00:00:00 Start of the referenced file 04:30:00 4 minutes, 30 seconds 04:30:30 4 minutes, 30.4 seconds Boundaries are not separate soundtracks INDEX 01 marks a track's main start. A CUE sheet can also describe pregaps and other indexes, so a more elaborate file may express disc layout beyond a simple song list. This “track” is a region of an audio recording, unlike a separately selectable audio track in a movie container . The distinction helps when organizing a concert or album for an Emby music library. A CUE sheet does not physically split or convert the referenced sound. For software that does not interpret the sheet, the audio remains one long file. An export into separate songs needs to use the boundaries and preserve the appropriate metadata. Changing the audio filename without updating the FILE reference can break that connection. Changing the recording's timing can make the boundaries inaccurate even though the text file still parses. See Also Chapter Markers M3U Playlists References libcue: CUE parser grammar libcue: minutes, seconds, and frame conversion

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: M3U Playlists | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: M3U Playlists An M3U file lists where media can be found. It does not contain the picture or sound itself. A plain list can name local files; an extended playlist adds lines describing the entries. #EXTM3U #EXTINF:180,Opening song Music/Opening.flac #EXTINF:240,Second song Music/Second.flac Illustrative local playlist. Durations are in seconds; the media paths supply the actual content. The path after each description is the important part for opening the media. A relative path is generally resolved against the playlist's location, so moving the playlist without its referenced files can break it. The same family serves different jobs Use What its entries point to Music playlist Individual songs or recordings IPTV channel list Sources for television channels HLS playlist Media segments or other playlists in a streaming presentation HLS defines its own tags and behavior in RFC 8216. A file ending in .m3u8 usually indicates UTF-8 text, but the extension alone does not prove that it is an HLS presentation. Emby's M3U tuner setup uses a channel list and its associated source information. That is different from a listening queue of songs. If a list loads but an entry fails, check the destination itself: a working text file cannot guarantee that a media URL is reachable, current, or suitable for the receiving app. Titles and channel tags help organize entries; they do not change the codecs carried by the referenced source. See Also PLS Playlists Media Pointer Files: STRM References VideoLAN: M3U playlist reader implementation RFC 8216: HTTP Live Streaming playlists

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: PLS Playlists | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: PLS Playlists A PLS file is a playlist written as key/value pairs. It is often encountered when a radio station provides a small download that opens its stream in a media player. A simple version looks like this: [playlist] File1=Music/Opening.mp3 Title1=Opening song Length1=180 File2=Music/Second.mp3 Title2=Second song Length2=240 NumberOfEntries=2 Version=2 The matching numbers associate each location with its title and duration. Length values are conventionally seconds; a value of -1 is commonly used when the duration is unknown, as with a live stream. The playlist is not the recording The PLS file can be tiny because it stores only references and descriptions. Downloading it does not save the radio audio for offline playback. If a referenced URL changes or a relative file moves, the entry can stop working while the playlist remains readable. Inspect the FileN values rather than treating the displayed title as the source address. For an Emby user collecting media references, distinguish this playlist syntax from STRM pointer files and from the M3U channel lists used by Live TV. They may all point to media, but their readers expect different text structures. There is no universal rule that renaming a PLS file to another playlist extension converts it. Conversion needs to preserve the media locations in the destination syntax. Player-specific handling can also affect which optional fields are used. See Also M3U Playlists Media Pointer Files: STRM References VideoLAN: PLS playlist reader implementation

articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.title: Media Pointer Files: STRM | Emby Learn
articles/media-files/playlists-and-refer.keywords: Media Pointer Files: STRM A STRM file supplies a location for media rather than storing the media itself. Emby can use it to present an externally located video as a library item, provided the referenced source uses a supported format and delivery method. The STRM documentation describes a plain text file containing a direct media URL or a path to a local or shared file. Name the pointer according to the library's content naming rules and give it the .strm extension. A pointer supplies an address. The referenced source still determines the playback requirements. A direct media address matters A webpage with a video player is not necessarily the media address that player opens. A pointer to the webpage can therefore return HTML instead of playable media. Likewise, a location that works on an administrator's desktop may not be accessible from the server. The relevant path, permissions, and network access need to work where the source is opened. The pointer's small size says nothing about the bitrate or size of the movie. Downloading or backing up the STRM file preserves the reference, not the referenced recording. A changed or expired source address can stop playback while the library item remains. When troubleshooting in Emby, verify the text contents and the destination separately. If the address is correct and reachable, inspect the actual media and selected tracks just as you would for a local file. Changing the pointer filename cannot alter an unsupported codec or repair damaged content. See Also What Is a Media File? M3U Playlists References RFC 3986: URI syntax

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.264 / AVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.264 / AVC Video H.264 and AVC are names for the same video coding standard. AVC means Advanced Video Coding ; its corresponding MPEG specification is MPEG-4 Part 10. It is different from the older MPEG-4 Part 2 format. H.264 is familiar in disc-derived media, camera recordings, and streaming files. Its encoded pictures may live in different containers, so an MP4, MKV, or transport stream is not a separate kind of H.264. Label you may encounter What it identifies H.264 / AVC The coding standard and bitstream format x264 A software encoder that creates H.264 Baseline, Main, High, High 10 Different H.264 profiles AVC1 or a similar container identifier How the container identifies its H.264 track An encoder chooses how to use the standard's tools. Different software or hardware encoders can therefore produce compatible H.264 streams with different bitrates, quality, and encoding effort. “Encoded with x264” does not require an x264 decoder. Which H.264 file? The profile matters. Ordinary 8-bit H.264 and High 10 H.264 place different requirements on a decoder. A device can provide hardware decoding for one while relying on software, or lacking an app playback path, for the other. The level adds limits such as picture size, processing rate, and buffering. Resolution alone leaves out frame rate and other resource demands. In Emby, H.264 can be the original library format or the output of video transcoding. An H.264 source still needs conversion if other stream characteristics or delivery requirements are incompatible. Compare the source and delivered stream information when troubleshooting: seeing “H.264” in both places does not mean the video was copied unchanged. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Profiles H.265 / HEVC Video Video Encoder Presets References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.265 / HEVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.265 / HEVC Video H.265 and HEVC identify the same coding standard. HEVC stands for High Efficiency Video Coding . It is frequently encountered in UHD films and recordings, including files carrying HDR video. The format offers more flexible ways to divide and predict pictures than H.264 . The practical aim is to preserve useful picture quality with less data. There is no fixed file-size saving that applies to every source or encoder: texture, grain, settings, and the quality being compared all affect the result. Common HEVC profile Sample depth Color sampling Main 8-bit 4:2:0 Main 10 8-bit or 10-bit 4:2:0 Selected profiles only. Other HEVC profiles cover additional formats and tools. A Main 10 label does not establish that the pictures are HDR. HDR10 uses HEVC in common delivery workflows, but HDR also involves transfer characteristics, color information, metadata, and the display path. An SDR file can use 10-bit HEVC. Check decoding separately from encoding x265 is one software encoder that creates HEVC. It is not another name for the format, and a player does not need x265 to decode the result. For an Emby playback session, check the app's decoder, profile, level, resolution, and frame rate. The server's ability to decode a source for transcoding is a separate capability from the app's ability to play it directly. Hardware decoding and hardware encoding are separate capabilities too. A supported HEVC source can still be transcoded because of a bitrate limit, subtitle processing, or another playback requirement. Conversely, a smaller HEVC file is not necessarily easier for an older device to decode than a larger H.264 file. See Also H.264 / AVC Video Video Codec Profiles HDR10 How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: MPEG-2 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: MPEG-2 Video MPEG-2 Video is the picture-compression format standardized as ITU-T H.262 and ISO/IEC 13818-2. It appears in many older disc transfers and television recordings. The name “MPEG-2” can also refer to the broader standards family. In a file's media information, distinguish the video codec from an MPEG systems container: a transport stream can carry codecs other than MPEG-2 Video. Name in a media discussion What it describes MPEG-2 Video / H.262 Compression of the moving pictures MPEG Program Stream A container combining streams MPEG Transport Stream A packet-based container MPEG Audio A separate family of audio coding formats MPEG-2 Video uses independently coded pictures and pictures predicted from others. Its groups of pictures affect random access and the amount of preceding video needed to reconstruct a chosen point. That explains why seeking is more involved than reading a single image. Preserve the recording's timing MPEG-2 Video can carry progressive or interlaced material. Converting a television recording is not just a decision about its codec: field timing , aspect ratio, and source cadence also matter. A careless conversion can discard motion detail or stretch the picture even when the new file is smaller. In Emby, an app with a suitable MPEG-2 decoder may play the source directly; another playback path may need video transcoding. Inspect the session's reason before assuming the format is damaged. Converting to H.264 or HEVC can make a derivative easier to deliver, but it cannot recreate detail the MPEG-2 source already discarded. The original recording remains the best reference when checking a conversion. See Also H.264 / AVC Video Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Interlaced Video Containers and Codecs References ITU-T H.262: MPEG-2 Video

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: MPEG-4 Part 2: DivX and Xvid | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: MPEG-4 Part 2: DivX and Xvid MPEG-4 Part 2 , also called MPEG-4 Visual , is an older video coding standard commonly associated with Xvid and classic MPEG-4-based DivX encoders. It often appears in AVI files from earlier video collections. Part 2 is important: H.264 / AVC belongs to MPEG-4 Part 10 and uses a different bitstream. The word “MPEG-4” alone does not distinguish them. Term What it means here MPEG-4 Part 2 The visual coding standard Xvid An implementation that encodes MPEG-4 Part 2 video Classic MPEG-4-based DivX A branded implementation of this format AVI A possible container, not the video codec The DivX brand also covers products and formats beyond Part 2. DivX Plus, for example, uses H.264. Use the probed stream's codec information rather than treating every “DivX” label as interchangeable. Why an old file can behave differently Part 2 profiles and optional coding tools affect decoder requirements. Support for a straightforward stream does not prove support for every tool combination encountered in a historical collection. FourCC identifiers such as XVID and DX50 can help identify a stream's origin or intended decoder. They are labels within a container; changing one does not convert the underlying video. For Emby, repackaging can address a container problem when the encoded streams already suit the app. A codec or coding-tool mismatch instead requires video conversion, provided the server can decode the source. Keep those two cases separate when a file plays on one device but needs transcoding on another. Renaming an AVI file to MP4 addresses neither case. See Also H.264 / AVC Video Containers and Codecs Codec Identifiers and FourCC How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References ISO/IEC 14496-2: MPEG-4 Visual Xvid: MPEG-4 video codec implementation DivX: DivX Plus and H.264 at a glance

articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.title: H.266 / VVC Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/mpeg-itu/Video-Cod.keywords: H.266 / VVC Video H.266 is the standard also known as VVC , or Versatile Video Coding . It continues the development of block-based video compression beyond HEVC , with additional prediction, partitioning, and coding tools. The goal is improved compression for a range of video uses. A smaller stream can reduce storage and delivery needs, but a codec's efficiency potential does not establish a particular saving for your files. That requires a comparison using the same source and an appropriate quality target. VVC is a distinct bitstream format. A decoder that understands H.264 or HEVC cannot decode VVC merely because all three belong to the same standards family. Capability to establish Question it answers VVC input decoding on the server Can this server build reconstruct the source for conversion? VVC decoding in the receiving app Can the app play the video without changing its codec? Compatible container handling Can the playback framework identify and extract the VVC track? Required profile and resource limits Can the selected decoder handle this particular stream? A format name is not a playback promise For an Emby library, verify the actual server and app versions and their available decoders before relying on a VVC file. Software availability, hardware capabilities, and integration into a playback framework are different pieces of the path. If the server can decode the source, conversion into a format the app accepts may be possible. If source decoding is unavailable, changing the output codec or renaming the file cannot solve that missing first step. A successful test on one computer also does not establish compatibility on a TV or phone. Keep the original source while testing the intended playback devices, and use stream-level compatibility information to explain any differences. See Also H.265 / HEVC Video How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.266: Versatile video coding

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Avid DNxHD Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Avid DNxHD Video Avid DNxHD is the familiar name for HD production workflows in the VC-3 video coding family. It encodes pictures independently, making it useful for editing, exchange, and retained production copies. Traditional DNxHD modes use defined HD raster and coding combinations. A label such as “DNxHD 145” belongs to a particular picture format and rate; the number should not be treated as a quality score that transfers unchanged to every frame rate. Detail to record Why it matters Raster and frame rate Select the applicable legacy coding mode Quality or bitrate label Distinguishes representations within that mode Bit depth and sample format Establish decoder and processing requirements Container Describes how the coded pictures and audio are packaged DNxHD is compressed and lossy. Its suitability for production does not mean the reconstructed pictures are mathematically identical to the input. Retaining a good master can limit further generation loss during later delivery conversions. The naming has changed Avid now uses Avid DNx as the unified name, dropping the HD, HR, and GX suffixes from its newer naming scheme. That does not change what an older file contains. Read historical DNxHD modes in their original context rather than applying every capability of the newer unified codec to them. DNxHR is the related name associated with resolution-independent production workflows. Neither suffix, nor the newer unified name, is enough to establish direct playback compatibility. For Emby, a DNxHD production file may need conversion into a format suitable for the app and available bandwidth. Preserve it as the source when creating that derivative. Encoding an already reduced consumer copy as DNxHD can make it easier to edit, but cannot restore lost texture or detail. See Also Avid DNxHR Video Apple ProRes Video Intra-Frame Video Compression Video Generation Loss References SMPTE ST 2019-1: VC-3 picture compression and data stream format (2016) Avid: DNx naming scheme and data rates Avid: DNx SDK and specification overview

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Avid DNxHR Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Avid DNxHR Video Avid DNxHR is the established name for resolution-independent production workflows in the VC-3 coding family. It extends the practical use of DNxHD -style picture coding to a wider range of picture sizes, including UHD and larger production rasters. The codec encodes pictures independently. Its quality levels serve different production purposes, from lightweight editing proxies to copies intended to retain more picture information. Familiar level Intended distinction LB Low-bandwidth production or proxy representation SQ Standard quality HQ High quality HQX High quality extended 444 Higher-fidelity color representation Level names identify codec choices, not universal quality scores or direct-play guarantees. Their permitted sample formats depend on the codec generation and implementation. A level does not specify one fixed bitrate for every file. Picture size and frame rate matter, and Avid's newer unified DNx implementation also offers customizable rates. Consult the applicable mode's specification when estimating storage. Legacy labels remain useful Avid now calls the family Avid DNx , with the HD, HR, and GX suffixes removed from the newer naming scheme. The old DNxHR label remains relevant when inspecting existing files and older software exports. Historical mode restrictions should not be assumed to describe every capability of the newer codec. DNxHR is a lossy production codec. High quality and independence between pictures make it suitable for editing; neither property proves exact reconstruction of the original samples. For Emby, keep the production copy when creating a smaller playback version. A server input decoder and a receiving app's direct-play decoder are separate requirements. If video conversion is needed, start from the retained master and verify the actual delivered stream. A smaller derivative is a convenience copy, not a substitute for the source's preserved information. See Also Avid DNxHD Video Apple ProRes Video Video Generation Loss How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References SMPTE ST 2019-1: VC-3 picture compression and data stream format (2016) Avid: DNx naming scheme and data rates Avid: DNx SDK and specification overview

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: DV Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: DV Video DV video is the compressed video found in many digital tape recordings and their file transfers. Common consumer standard-definition DV uses roughly 25 Mb/s for the coded video. The complete DV data stream also carries audio and other information, so that figure is not its total file rate. DV compresses pictures independently. A transfer that copies the digital DV data from a tape preserves that existing compressed video; creating H.264 instead introduces a separate decoding and encoding step. Common SD recording system Stored picture size Frame rate 525/60 consumer DV 720 × 480 30000/1001, approximately 29.97 fps 625/50 consumer DV 720 × 576 25 fps Common consumer recording formats, not the complete DV family. A system's line count includes lines outside the active stored picture. What matters in a tape transfer? DV's stored pixels are commonly non-square. The same stored dimensions can represent different display aspect ratios, so resizing according to width and height alone can stretch a transfer. Follow its aspect information when creating a playback version. Interlaced recordings also preserve motion across two field instants. Check the actual field order and decide how the progressive output should retain that motion. Deinterlacing and changing the codec answer different questions. For Emby, keep a copied DV transfer as a source and assess a separate delivery version on the intended apps. DV decoding, container handling, and interlacing support determine whether a particular source can play directly or needs conversion. DV is already compressed and normally lossy. Copying its bytes preserves the tape's digital representation, but does not make the original camera recording lossless. Re-encoding at a higher bitrate cannot recover detail discarded during capture. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression Video Pixel Aspect Ratio Video Field Order Deinterlacing References SMPTE ST 314: DV-based audio, data, and video at 25 and 50 Mb/s IEC 61834-2: Consumer DV standard-definition recording format

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: FFV1 Lossless Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: FFV1 Lossless Video FFV1 is a lossless video coding format. After correct decoding, the stored sample values match the values supplied to its encoder. This makes it useful when preserving video samples is more important than minimizing a delivery file's bitrate. FFV1 compresses spatial relationships within pictures without the lossy approximation used in ordinary delivery encodes. Its compression ratio depends on the input: noisy or grainy pictures generally leave less predictable information to compress. Conceptual lossless round trip. The comparison applies at the codec's input and output, using the same sample format. Define what is being preserved Encoding into FFV1 cannot undo an earlier conversion. If a process first reduces bit depth, changes color sampling, or applies a lossy filter, FFV1 preserves the resulting samples. It does not preserve the discarded input information. Property What it does and does not establish Lossless sample coding Exact reconstruction of the encoder's input samples Version 3 slice CRCs, when enabled Detection of damaged slice data, not automatic repair A container such as Matroska Packaging for video, audio, and metadata A preserved file Still requires storage checks and separate backups RFC 9043 describes FFV1 versions 0, 1, and 3. Version 3 includes configuration and slice structures that can support error checking and parallel processing. These features do not guarantee that a consumer app has an appropriate decoder. For Emby, an FFV1 preservation file may serve as a source for a separate playback version, provided the server can decode it. Direct decoding in the app and the bitrate needed for delivery remain independent questions. Keep the preservation copy when creating a lossy derivative: that derivative no longer carries the same exact sample guarantee. See Also Lossless Video Compression Video Generation Loss Lossy and Lossless Compression How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References RFC 9043: FFV1 video coding format versions 0, 1, and 3

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Motion JPEG Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Motion JPEG Video Motion JPEG , often shortened to MJPEG , represents moving video using JPEG-compressed images. Pictures are compressed independently rather than predicted from earlier or later pictures. Some implementations encode interlaced fields separately. This makes an individual picture straightforward to access once its container location and required JPEG tables are known. It also means that unchanged scenery is encoded again for successive pictures, rather than being reused through inter-frame prediction. Conceptual diagram of frame-based MJPEG. Field-based variants can store two separately compressed fields for one video frame. One label, several implementations JPEG's underlying image coding is standardized, but “Motion JPEG” is not a single universal video packaging specification. Container conventions, field handling, and storage of compression tables can differ. Apple's QuickTime documentation, for example, distinguishes Motion-JPEG A and B representations. Characteristic Consequence Independent picture compression No temporal prediction chain to reconstruct Usual lossy JPEG coding Picture independence does not mean lossless storage Repeated backgrounds Compression may be less economical than inter-frame coding Different packaging conventions The decoder and container reader must agree For Emby, MJPEG can appear in older camera clips or captured video. An app needs to understand the specific stream and its packaging; the general codec name alone cannot guarantee direct playback. If a conversion is necessary, preserve the source's dimensions, timing, and field interpretation while checking the result. A modern delivery codec can reduce the data needed for an acceptable picture, but it cannot undo JPEG artifacts already present in the original. Keep the source for future conversions instead of repeatedly converting the latest derivative. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Compression Artifacts Apple ProRes Video References ITU-T T.81: JPEG compression and coding Apple: QuickTime video sample data and Motion-JPEG variants

articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.title: Apple ProRes Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/production-preserv.keywords: Apple ProRes Video Apple ProRes is a family of codecs aimed at production and editing. Its ordinary video variants encode each picture independently, allowing editors to work without reconstructing a long chain of predicted pictures. That convenience and the retained picture information often come with a higher data rate than a delivery encode. A large ProRes export can therefore be useful as a production source while being inconvenient to stream to ordinary playback devices. ProRes group Main distinction 422 variants: Proxy, LT, 422, HQ Different quality and data-rate targets for 4:2:2 video 4444 and 4444 XQ Higher-fidelity color workflows and optional alpha ProRes RAW and RAW HQ A separate RAW sensor-data workflow The 422 and 4444 picture coding is lossy, even when its output is visually very close to the input. Alpha in the 4444 variants is encoded losslessly; that does not make their color-picture coding lossless. ProRes RAW should not be treated as another ordinary 422 playback profile. Production source and playback version A ProRes file's name does not establish its exact variant, color interpretation, or decoder requirements. Inspect the profile and stream details. A MOV extension only identifies packaging, and MOV can carry other codecs. For Emby, a ProRes master can be the input to a more suitable playback version when the server has the necessary decoder. Direct playback depends on the receiving app and its selected framework, rather than the codec's usefulness in an editing program. Transcoding a heavily compressed source into ProRes does not recreate camera detail. It can provide a convenient intermediate for further work, but the source's earlier losses remain. When possible, create delivery versions from the best retained master rather than from an already reduced streaming copy. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression Avid DNxHR Video Video Generation Loss How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References SMPTE RDD 36: Apple ProRes bitstream syntax and decoding process Apple: ProRes white paper Apple: About ProRes

articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-Compat.title: How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-Compat.keywords: How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Two files can have the same extension and resolution but take different playback paths. The video codec tells the player how to reconstruct the pictures; the container tells it how to find and deliver that encoded stream. For Emby, a useful starting question is whether the receiving app can decode this particular stream. A codec name is only the beginning of that check. Part of the stream description Why it matters Codec, such as H.264 or AV1 The decoder must understand that format Profile and sample format The supported tools, bit depth, and color sampling can differ Level, resolution, and frame rate The required processing and buffering may exceed a decoder's limits Container and codec signaling The app must recognize and extract the stream correctly A decoder implemented in software and a hardware video decoder can support different subsets. The app also needs a usable route to that decoder through its operating system or playback framework. A chip's capability list alone does not establish support in every app using the device. What changes when playback needs conversion? Direct Play delivers supported media without converting the streams. A container mismatch can sometimes be addressed by repackaging the video, while an unsupported video codec requires decoding and encoding into a suitable format. Audio and subtitles can impose additional requirements even when the video is compatible. For example, successful playback of an 8-bit file does not prove that a 10-bit file using the same codec will follow the same path. Inspect the profile and level before treating the second result as inconsistent. Changing an extension or codec label cannot add missing decoder support. The practical evidence is the file's media information, the app's capabilities, and the playback session's reported conversion reason. See Also Containers and Codecs Video Codec Profiles Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification

articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-VC1.ht.title: VC-1 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/Video-Codec-VC1.ht.keywords: VC-1 Video VC-1 is a compressed video format standardized in SMPTE ST 421. It is associated with the Windows Media video ecosystem and appears in older media collections. It is a distinct codec from H.264 and MPEG-2 Video. The standard defines Simple, Main, and Advanced profiles. The stream's profile is more informative than a generic “Windows Media” label, which can refer to several generations of video formats. VC-1 characteristic Practical meaning 8-bit, 4:2:0 samples The decoded sample format specified by ST 421 Profiles Different permitted tools and stream structures Advanced-profile interlaced coding Field handling may be part of decoding Metadata for display Aspect ratio and color information still matter after decoding VC-1 combines spatial prediction, transformed differences, and prediction from reference pictures. The standard defines the required decoding process; an encoder can choose among the permitted tools to meet a bitrate or quality goal. Decoder availability can differ by route A playback app can have a usable decoder for one VC-1 stream but not another profile or interlaced form. Software decoding and a hardware media engine also need not offer the same capabilities. Check the complete path before attributing failure to the file itself. For Emby, successful server decoding for video transcoding does not imply direct decoding in every app. Likewise, support for the container does not supply a missing VC-1 decoder. Repackaging changes the container while retaining that requirement. When a VC-1 source is interlaced, conversion should account for its field timing as well as the target codec. A file that opens successfully can still show incorrect motion if the fields are handled incorrectly. Preserve the source while assessing a conversion's picture and timing. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Video Codec Profiles Interlaced Video Containers and Codecs References SMPTE ST 421: VC-1 bitstream format and decoding process

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: AV1 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: AV1 Video AV1 is a video coding format defined by the Alliance for Open Media. It specifies the bitstream and how a decoder reconstructs pictures. Software such as libaom or SVT-AV1 and hardware encoders are implementations that can produce this format. An encoder's compression efficiency and speed are separate from a player's decoding capabilities. AV1 is therefore neither a promise of a particular file-size reduction nor proof that a device can play the result in hardware. AV1 detail What it tells you Main profile, sequence profile 0 8-bit or 10-bit, 4:2:0 or monochrome Higher profiles Additional sample formats are permitted Level and tier Resource and bitrate constraints Film-grain parameters, when present Grain is synthesized as part of output processing Selected distinctions; a profile's permitted formats are not a device support list. The complete playback path still matters For an Emby app, AV1 decoding must be available through the playback framework it uses. A software decoder can be an option, but real-time performance depends on the particular source and device. Hardware capability also needs suitable app and operating-system integration. The server needs its own input decoder when converting AV1 into another codec. That capability does not establish that it can encode AV1, or that a receiving app can play AV1 directly. Some streams use film-grain synthesis . The encoder can carry a cleaner coded picture plus parameters for generating grain during output, rather than preserving every source grain sample. This is part of reconstructing the intended appearance and should be considered when comparing decoded output. A 10-bit AV1 file can carry SDR or HDR. Use its color and transfer information alongside the codec details, and inspect the delivered stream when transcoding changes the playback path. See Also How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility VP9 Video Film Grain in Compressed Video Video Codec Levels and Tiers References AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: VP8 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: VP8 Video VP8 is a compressed video format associated with WebM files and web communication. Its coded pictures use 8-bit samples with 4:2:0 color sampling. The audio, timing, and container are separate parts of a complete media file. VP8 uses keyframes and pictures predicted from previously reconstructed content. It can retain selected reference pictures for later predictions. Those dependencies reduce repeated information, but a player still needs the relevant reference state to reconstruct a predicted picture. Part of a VP8 file Role VP8 video stream Reconstructs the moving pictures Container, often WebM Carries streams and timestamps Separate audio track Reconstructs the sound Keyframes Provide restart points for video decoding RFC 6386 documents the format and decoding process. It is an informational publication, and explicitly makes the supplied reference decoder authoritative where its narrative differs from the code. It should not be described as an IETF Internet Standard. A WebM extension does not identify the codec A WebM file can contain VP9 or another permitted video format. VP8 and VP9 need different decoders; support for one is not evidence of support for the other. For Emby, inspect the stream information when an older web recording behaves differently across apps. If the video is compatible but its packaging is not, repackaging may preserve the video. When a different video codec is required, the server has to decode and encode it. Neither repackaging nor increasing the output bitrate restores fine detail that a lossy VP8 source has already discarded. Keep the source when creating a more convenient playback version. See Also VP9 Video How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility Inter-Frame Video Prediction Containers and Codecs References RFC 6386: VP8 data format and decoding guide

articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.title: VP9 Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/codecs/vpx-av1/Video-Code.keywords: VP9 Video VP9 is a video coding format developed by the WebM Project. It is often encountered in web-origin video, including high-resolution content, but the codec is separate from its container. Compared with VP8 , VP9 provides additional coding tools and supports higher sample depths in selected profiles. Its profile number is especially useful when one VP9 file plays directly and another needs a different path. VP9 profile Sample depth Color sampling 0 8-bit 4:2:0 1 8-bit 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 2 10-bit or 12-bit 4:2:0 3 10-bit or 12-bit 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 Format permissions, not a claim that a particular device supports every combination. A decoder that handles Profile 0 may lack the required support for Profile 2. Even within Profile 2, do not infer 12-bit support from successful playback of a 10-bit stream. The selected decoder and its integration into the app determine the actual usable capabilities. Read HDR information separately A higher bit depth can help represent HDR pictures, but a VP9 profile alone does not identify HDR . Transfer characteristics, color information, and the display path still need to agree. In Emby, the source codec and profile describe the library file. If video transcoding is required, the delivered stream may use a different format. Repackaging without video conversion keeps the VP9 stream and its decoding requirements. The WebM Project links its bitstream description as a draft specification. Its published profile page and the implementation provide useful references; the draft's status should remain visible when using it as a technical source. There is no need to infer a universal bitrate or quality advantage from the codec name. See Also VP8 Video AV1 Video Video Codec Profiles What HDR Video Adds to SDR References WebM Project: VP9 bitstream and decoding specification (draft) WebM Project: VP9 coding profiles

articles/video/color-standards/Color-Gam.title: Color Gamut | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/Color-Gam.keywords: Color Gamut A bright red flower may look vivid on one screen and less saturated on another even when both show the same number of pixels. One possible limit is color gamut : the range of colors the display can produce. A video color space also has a gamut. Its red, green, and blue primaries define which colors can be represented by mixing those primaries with nonnegative amounts. A display receiving that signal still has its own physical limits. Primary coordinates plotted in CIE 1931 xy. Line colors identify the standards; they do not reproduce the extreme colors. This two-dimensional plot omits luminance and is not perceptually uniform. The outer boundary is useful, but it does not tell us how many distinct shades a file stores. That also depends on bit depth. Nor does the triangle indicate how bright those colors can become; that needs color volume . What a wider gamut changes Question What to look at Can a signal describe a more saturated green? Its color primaries Can the screen actually show that green? The display's measured gamut Are gradients smooth? Bit depth, compression, and processing Can the green remain saturated at high brightness? Color volume Imagine a file containing a green outside the screen's gamut. Sending the original file with Emby Direct Play preserves its encoded values, but does not expand the screen's capabilities. The playback chain must choose a reproducible color. Gamut mapping describes that adaptation. Likewise, changing a file's color-primary label does not create richer colors. The label tells the player how to interpret the existing numbers; a real color conversion changes those numbers to preserve their intended appearance. See Also Color Volume ITU-R BT.2020 P3 Color Gamuts References ITU-R BT.2407: Color gamut conversion ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters ICC color encoding registry: DCI P3

articles/video/color-standards/Color-Vol.title: Color Volume | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/Color-Vol.keywords: Color Volume Color volume adds light level to color gamut. It asks which colors a display can reproduce from its darkest output to its brightest, rather than describing only the reach of its red, green, and blue primaries. Consider two imaginary screens that can produce the same saturated red at a moderate light level. One can keep that red saturated as it becomes brighter; the other must reduce its brightness or move it toward white. Their gamut coverage at the tested level can look similar, while their handling of bright colored objects differs. Picture detail What matters A deep red costume in a dim room Low-light color and shadow separation A red traffic signal at night Saturation at a higher luminance A white reflection on chrome Peak white and highlight handling A bright orange flame Color and luminance together This is why a peak-brightness number alone cannot describe HDR picture quality. A white patch and a saturated color ask different things of a display. Test-window size and duration also matter when interpreting brightness measurements; one brief small highlight does not describe a whole bright scene. From the mastering display to yours HDR mastering-display metadata records a display's primaries, white point, and luminance limits. It describes the mastering reference, not every color actually used in the film and not the capability of your television. During Emby playback, the file can therefore describe a larger volume than the output display can reproduce. Tone mapping and gamut mapping address related parts of this problem. Preserving highlight brightness while ignoring saturation can still change the appearance of a flame or neon sign. For comparisons, look for measured performance across brightness and color, with a stated test method. A single percentage without its reference volume and measurement conditions is hard to interpret. See Also Color Gamut Why Tone Mapping Is Needed ITU-R BT.2100 References SMPTE study group report: HDR ecosystem ITU-T H.274: Supplemental enhancement information

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.2020 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.2020 BT.2020 , also called Rec. 2020, defines UHD television parameters, including a color gamut wider than BT.709 . In media information, it is especially familiar as the color-primary label attached to HDR video. That label describes the encoding space. It does not promise that every scene uses extremely saturated colors or that a connected television can reproduce the entire gamut. Parameter BT.2020 definition Red primary, CIE xy 0.708, 0.292 Green primary, CIE xy 0.170, 0.797 Blue primary, CIE xy 0.131, 0.046 Reference white D65 UHD image sizes 3840 × 2160 and 7680 × 4320 Signal precision 10 or 12 bits per component The gamut diagram shows how its primaries compare with P3 and BT.709. The coordinate values identify colors; they are not percentages of saturation. BT.2020 and HDR are separate clues BT.2020 itself includes a conventional transfer characteristic. HDR systems specified by BT.2100 use the same primaries with PQ or HLG. Consequently, “BT.2020” in the primaries field is insufficient to identify the brightness encoding. Matrix information matters too. BT.2020 defines both constant-luminance and non-constant-luminance representations. A report that says “BT.2020 non-constant” is describing the matrix, not a different gamut. Imagine importing two 4K files into Emby: one SDR and one HDR. Matching resolution and BT.2020 primaries would not make them interchangeable. Their transfer characteristics can require different rendering, and an SDR output may need tone mapping for the HDR file. Likewise, a film graded within a smaller gamut can be encoded using BT.2020 primaries. Think of the encoding space as the available coordinates, not evidence that the picture visits every corner. See Also ITU-R BT.2100 P3 Color Gamuts Color Gamut References ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.2100 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.2100 BT.2100 , or Rec. 2100, specifies the image parameters for HDR television. It brings wide color and HDR transfer functions into a defined system for producing and exchanging television pictures. Its two transfer-function systems are PQ and HLG . A playback chain must know which one it is receiving: the same numeric signal value has a different meaning in each system. Part of the system BT.2100 specifies Color primaries The same wide-gamut primaries as BT.2020 HDR systems Perceptual Quantizer (PQ) and Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) Image sizes 1920 × 1080, 3840 × 2160, and 7680 × 4320 Scanning Progressive Signal precision 10 or 12 bits per component The current recommendation is BT.2100-3, approved in February 2025. It also defines reference viewing conditions and explains the relationship between the capture, display, and overall transfer functions. What it tells you about a file A file does not need to show a single “BT.2100” badge. Its metadata may instead describe BT.2020 primaries together with PQ or HLG transfer characteristics and a suitable matrix. Those separate fields describe the signal more precisely than a filename containing “HDR.” Consider a 1080p HDR recording. It has fewer pixels than a 4K recording, but can still require HDR-aware playback. Shrinking it to 720p would reduce spatial detail without automatically changing the light-level interpretation. For the same reason, an Emby playback conversion must account for output capability as well as resolution. Sending an HDR signal to an SDR output with a different label is insufficient; HDR-to-SDR conversion needs to adapt the picture. BT.2100 is a television-system specification, not a video codec. A device's ability to decode a compressed stream and its ability to render that stream's HDR signal are separate requirements. See Also ITU-R BT.2020 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.601 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.601 BT.601 , also called Rec. 601, is a foundation of digital standard-definition television. It defines how component video is sampled and represented, including the relationship between red, green, blue, and luma/color-difference signals. For a media library, its most useful connection is older SD material. An archived television recording can need BT.601 color interpretation even when it is being shown on a modern 4K screen. BT.601 detail Why it is useful 4:2:2 studio representation Describes horizontal sampling of luma and color differences 13.5 MHz luma sampling for the standard 4:2:2 family Supports both 525-line and 625-line television systems Luma weights of 0.299 red, 0.587 green, 0.114 blue Identify the familiar BT.601 matrix Nominal 8-bit luma range 16–235 Black and white are not necessarily code values 0 and 255 The luma weights apply to nonlinear R′G′B′ signals. Luma is not a direct measurement of light emitted by the screen. Why upscaling does not settle the color question Suppose an SD recording is enlarged to 1920 × 1080. Adding pixels does not by itself convert its color representation to BT.709 . A converter must either retain the existing interpretation correctly or perform the appropriate color conversion and update the signal information. If one stage assumes BT.601 and another interprets the same color-difference values as BT.709, colored objects can shift while neutral grays still appear plausible. Increasing the bitrate cannot fix that disagreement. BT.601 is also not a complete shorthand for every SD source's color characteristics. Primaries, transfer characteristics, matrix coefficients, and range are separate descriptions. Old files may omit some of them. When comparing an Emby Direct Play and transcoded session , preserve the original file and compare the actual signal information before assuming the display needs a saturation adjustment. See Also ITU-R BT.709 Color Gamut References ITU-R BT.601-7: Digital television studio encoding ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: ITU-R BT.709 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: ITU-R BT.709 BT.709 , or Rec. 709, is the standard most closely associated with conventional SDR high-definition video. It specifies more than a color gamut: its parameters also cover the image format and the way picture signals are formed. When a media inspector shows “BT.709,” check which field contains it. The same short name can describe different parts of the signal. Field What BT.709 identifies there Color primaries Red, green, blue, and the D65 reference white Transfer characteristics The nonlinear relationship used at the source Matrix coefficients The RGB-to-luma/color-difference relationship For its nonlinear luma signal, the familiar weights are 0.2126 for red, 0.7152 for green, and 0.0722 for blue. These differ from BT.601 . The difference matters when reconstructing color from Y′CbCr. “Rec. 709” does not mean “no processing” A display with a wider native gamut must still reproduce the intended BT.709 colors. Simply stretching all colors to the display's most saturated primaries can make faces or foliage look unnaturally vivid. A wider-gamut panel is useful when its color management also handles smaller gamuts correctly. The source transfer characteristic is also distinct from the display response. BT.1886 specifies a reference SDR display EOTF; it does not rename the file's transfer-characteristic tag to “BT.1886.” For an Emby library, resolution is only a clue. A 4K file can contain SDR BT.709 video, and an HD file can contain HDR. Read the signal descriptions together rather than deciding from “1080p” or “2160p.” When HDR is converted for SDR playback, producing a coherent BT.709 output requires both suitable picture values and matching signal labels. See Also ITU-R BT.601 ITU-R BT.1886 Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) References ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters ITU-T H.273: Video signal identification ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/color-standards/standards.title: P3 Color Gamuts | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/standards.keywords: P3 Color Gamuts P3 identifies red, green, and blue primaries originally associated with digital cinema. Those primaries cover a wider gamut than BT.709, particularly toward saturated reds and greens. The name alone does not fully specify how picture values should be interpreted. The same primaries can be combined with different white points and transfer functions. These distinctions explain why “P3” on a display specification, an image file, and a mastering report need not describe identical encodings. Name or context What else matters Cinema DCI-P3 Cinema white point and a 2.6 display gamma P3-D65 P3 primaries with D65 white; the transfer function still needs specifying Display P3 D65 white and the sRGB transfer curve P3 colors in a BT.2020 video signal The video's declared encoding remains BT.2020 Display P3 is explicitly defined in the W3C color specification. It is not a synonym for a PQ-encoded HDR signal. A wide-gamut photograph can be SDR. Reading a “P3” claim A television advertised as covering a percentage of P3 is describing a measured color capability, subject to the stated measurement method. It does not follow that its video input should be forced into a P3 mode for every film. For example, a movie can be mastered using a display with approximately P3 capabilities and delivered in a BT.2020 signal. The mastering display and the signal's primaries describe different things. Reinterpreting the encoded numbers as P3 would change their meaning. During Emby playback, use the file's declared color information and the actual output path together. A display's marketing gamut is not a replacement for those signal descriptions. For bright colored highlights, color volume adds another question: how much of that gamut remains available as luminance rises? See Also Color Gamut ITU-R BT.2020 Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) References SMPTE EG 432-1: Color processing for digital cinema ICC color encoding registry: DCI P3 W3C CSS Color 4: Display P3 ITU-R BT.2020-2: UHD television parameters

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: ITU-R BT.1886 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: ITU-R BT.1886 BT.1886 specifies a reference display EOTF for HDTV production. It provides a consistent SDR target for displays that do not naturally behave like the CRT monitors used in earlier television workflows. Its exponent is 2.4, but the complete curve also depends on the display's black and white luminance. With a zero black level, it reduces to a pure 2.4 power curve. With a nonzero black level, the lower part of the response changes. Calculated reference curves. Both examples reach 100-nit white; the second has a 0.1-nit black floor. These are illustrative display parameters. The equation is L = a × max(V + b, 0)^2.4 . The parameters a and b are calculated from measured black and white so that signal values 0 and 1 reach those endpoints. The graph's shadow panel makes the difference easier to see than the full-range panel. What it does not change BT.1886 describes the display response. It does not change BT.709's encoded signal parameters, and a BT.709 file does not need to be relabeled “BT.1886” for ordinary SDR playback. Consider a dark jacket with several almost-black folds. The amount of separation that reaches your eyes depends on the display response and its black floor, as well as the source picture. A gamma label by itself cannot tell you whether those folds remain visible. If the same SDR file looks different between an Emby app and another player, compare the output and display modes as well as the server's playback method. A difference near black can arise after decoding. Applying HDR tone mapping to an SDR signal would address a different problem and is not a substitute for correct SDR rendering. See Also ITU-R BT.709 Video Gamma Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) References ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) An electro-optical transfer function , or EOTF, answers a practical question: how much light should the screen produce for this signal value? A pixel value halfway between black and white does not usually request half the light of white. Video uses nonlinear encoding, so equal steps in the signal do not produce equal steps in emitted light.
