For an idealized SDR display with zero black, 100-nit white, and a 2.4 power response, the relationship is L = 100 × V^2.4 . Here V is the normalized signal, and L is luminance in nits for neutral gray. Normalized signal V Calculated light output 0.25 3.6 nits 0.50 18.9 nits 0.75 50.1 nits 1.00 100 nits These values are an example of BT.1886's zero-black case , not universal settings for every television. PQ uses a different curve and an absolute light-level scale. Why the correct curve matters Imagine passing the value 0.50 to two renderers with different assumptions about the EOTF. They can agree on the pixel number and still produce different light. That is why a transfer-function mismatch can make an otherwise intact file look too dark or wrong in contrast. The EOTF is also separate from numerical range. A limited-range signal must first be interpreted with the correct black and white code values before applying the transfer function. When Emby reports Direct Play , it describes delivery from the server. The player and display still have to interpret the video and render it. For HDR-to-SDR playback, the rendering path may need to recover light values using the source EOTF, adapt them through tone mapping, and encode a suitable output signal. None of that is determined by bitrate alone. See Also Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) ITU-R BT.1886 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 References SMPTE ST 2084: HDR reference display transfer function ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) An opto-electronic transfer function , or OETF, converts scene-light values into a picture signal. It is associated with the capture side of the imaging chain: light measured by a camera is represented using nonlinear values suitable for a video system. The graph shows the reference BT.709 OETF. It rises steeply near black, allocating more signal space to low light levels than a straight linear encoding would. The axes show normalized scene light and signal values, not nits or raw camera sensor readings. The dashed line is a linear reference. For scene-light value E , the specified curve is 4.5 × E below 0.018 and 1.099 × E^0.45 − 0.099 at or above that point. At E = 0.18 , the resulting signal is about 0.409. The change from a straight lower segment to a power curve matters: “gamma 0.45” alone is only a shorthand. The inverse is not the whole viewing experience An OETF is not automatically the exact inverse of the display's EOTF . The complete camera-to-screen relationship also has to produce an appropriate image appearance. The OOTF describes that overall relationship. This distinction is useful when processing video. Suppose a filter needs to combine light contributions. Treating an encoded value of 0.4 as 40% of scene light would start from the wrong assumption. The processing stage needs the relevant inverse function before performing operations that require linear light. For an Emby library, camera footage may use a conventional video transfer characteristic, HDR, or a camera-specific log encoding. The filename and codec do not identify the curve. Correct signal interpretation must survive editing and export; merely adding a familiar transfer-function label does not convert footage to that representation. See Also Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) ITU-R BT.709 References ITU-R BT.709-6: HDTV parameters Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Opto-Optical Transfer Function (OOTF) The opto-optical transfer function , or OOTF, describes the overall change from light in a scene to light on the screen. It connects the two ends of an imaging system, including the combined effect of capture and display transfer functions. Conceptual reference chain. Exposure, grading, tone mapping, and viewing adjustments can also affect a real production and playback path. Why should this overall relationship do anything other than reproduce the original light exactly? A film viewed on a screen is not the same visual environment as the scene in front of the camera. The reproduced image occupies a limited field of view and is watched with a particular surround and adaptation level. A useful rendering accounts for that difference. A small mathematical example Suppose a simplified system encodes a relative light value using a power of 0.5 and its display applies a power of 2.4. The combined power is 0.5 × 2.4 = 1.2 . An input light value of 0.25 becomes approximately 0.189, relative to white, after both stages. That is an illustration of function composition, not the specified BT.709 chain and not an Emby preset. Real transfer functions can include offsets, linear segments, and luminance-dependent operations, so multiplying two advertised gamma numbers is not generally sufficient. The distinction helps explain why removing a camera's encoding and applying a display curve are not necessarily redundant operations. They may be implementing an intended overall rendering. An Emby playback session normally starts with an already produced picture. It should not blindly add a camera-to-display rendering transform that was already incorporated during production. The correct processing depends on whether the incoming representation describes scene light or an intended display image, and on which stages have already been applied. See Also Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) ITU-R BT.2100 References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 Perceptual Quantizer (PQ) is the HDR transfer function standardized in SMPTE ST 2084. It gives encoded values an absolute display-light meaning, with a reference range extending to 10,000 nits. Its nonlinear shape distributes signal precision with human visual sensitivity in mind. That upper limit describes what the encoding can represent. It does not mean a film uses 10,000-nit highlights or that an HDR television must reach that brightness. ST 2084 reference EOTF for neutral gray. The left axis shows actual luminance; the right uses a logarithmic scale to reveal shadows. Zero luminance cannot appear on the logarithmic axis. Light level Normalized PQ signal, rounded 1 nit 0.150 100 nits 0.508 1,000 nits 0.752 10,000 nits 1.000 The table is calculated from the inverse of the standard's EOTF. These normalized values are not raw 10-bit code values; numerical range must also be accounted for when storing them. Why PQ needs appropriate playback Imagine a highlight encoded for 1,000 nits and an output that can reproduce only 400. Correctly understanding PQ identifies the requested light level, but cannot make the display produce it. A subsequent tone-mapping decision determines how to fit that highlight alongside the rest of the image. Treating PQ values as an ordinary SDR gamma signal changes their meaning. Relabeling the stream or turning up saturation cannot perform the required conversion. For Emby playback, distinguish the source signal from the output signal. The server may convert HDR during transcoding, or a capable playback renderer may adapt it locally. The Emby Windows documentation describes rendering-stage tone mapping. PQ specifies the signal's light-level interpretation; it does not prescribe a single tone-mapping curve for every output screen. See Also Electro-Optical Transfer Function (EOTF) ITU-R BT.2100 Why Tone Mapping Is Needed References SMPTE ST 2084: HDR reference display transfer function ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television parameters

articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.title: Video Gamma | Emby Learn
articles/video/color-standards/transfer-.keywords: Video Gamma Gamma is the exponent in a power relationship between picture values and light. In a simplified display model, output = input^gamma , with input and output normalized between black and white. The curve matters most between the endpoints. Both of the example display curves below reach the same black and white, but the higher exponent produces less light at intermediate signal values. Idealized display curves with zero black and the same white level. The dotted diagonal is a linear reference; these are not tone-mapping presets. At a signal value of 0.5, gamma 2.2 produces about 0.218 of white, while gamma 2.4 produces about 0.189. On a hypothetical 100-nit display, that is roughly 21.8 versus 18.9 nits. The change can be visible without changing the maximum brightness at all. Why the direction needs stating A camera encoding curve often has an exponent below one; a display curve often has an exponent above one. Both can be called “gamma” in informal discussion. Always ask whether the number describes encoding, display output, or an adjustment made on top of an existing image. Real standards need more than a bare exponent. BT.709's OETF includes a linear segment near black. BT.1886 accounts for display black and white. PQ is not a single power curve at all. For playback troubleshooting, do not use a gamma adjustment to disguise a transfer-function or signal-range mismatch. It can make one scene look more acceptable while moving other tones farther from the intended result. In an Emby comparison, keep the file, output mode, and display settings consistent before judging whether two playback paths render the same picture. See Also ITU-R BT.1886 Opto-Electronic Transfer Function (OETF) Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 References Khronos Data Format Specification: Transfer functions ITU-R BT.1886: Reference display transfer function

articles/video/compression/Lossless-Vide.title: Lossless Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Lossless-Vide.keywords: Lossless Video Compression Lossless video compression allows a decoder to reproduce exactly the picture samples supplied to the encoder. It still saves space by representing repetition, prediction errors, and other patterns more efficiently. For example, a sequence of sample values can be represented by a starting value and exact differences: Representation Values Input samples 40, 42, 43, 43 Starting sample 40 Following differences +2, +1, 0 Reconstructed samples 40, 42, 43, 43 Original arithmetic example. Compact coding of the differences can save bits, but the saving depends on the data and coding method. A real lossless codec uses more elaborate predictors and coding rules. FFV1, for example, is a lossless format documented in RFC 9043 and used for preservation and intermediate workflows. Lossless relative to which input? The guarantee begins at the encoder's input. If a lossy film is decoded and then encoded losslessly, the new file preserves those already decoded samples. It cannot reconstruct detail discarded by the original lossy encoding. Likewise, a workflow can change the samples before the lossless stage: resizing, color conversion, reduced bit depth, or chroma subsampling may already have altered the picture. “Lossless video codec” does not certify every operation that preceded it. For an Emby library, lossless masters can be useful when preserving home recordings or avoiding repeated encoding damage during editing. They often need substantially more storage and delivery bandwidth than a viewing copy. Compression savings depend strongly on the picture: noise and fine random texture are difficult to represent compactly without approximation. Client support also matters. A format well suited to preservation may need server transcoding for a particular app. Keeping a lossless master and a compatible playback version can serve different purposes without treating the smaller viewing copy as the preservation original. See Also Lossy Video Compression How Video Compression Works Intra-Frame Video Compression References RFC 9043: FFV1 lossless video format ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/Lossy-Video-C.title: Lossy Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Lossy-Video-C.keywords: Lossy Video Compression Lossy video compression permits the decoded picture to differ from the picture supplied to the encoder. The aim is to reduce data while keeping the differences acceptable for the intended viewing conditions. In many modern codecs, an encoder predicts part of the picture, transforms the remaining difference, and quantizes the resulting values. Quantization approximates values using a chosen set of representable steps. Small differences can become zero, leaving less information to encode. Value before approximation Rounded to the nearest multiple of eight Difference 17 16 −1 −3 0 +3 39 40 +1 Original scalar example illustrating irreversible rounding. These are not pixel measurements or the quantization equations of a particular codec. The decoder cannot know whether a decoded zero originally came from −3, +2, or exactly zero. That information has been discarded. The file can still look indistinguishable in ordinary viewing: “lossy” describes mathematical reconstruction, not a guarantee of visible damage. What becomes noticeable first? Fine texture, grain, gradients, and fast movement can expose compromises differently. Too little data may soften detail, break up moving regions, or make smooth shading appear stepped. A bitrate that suits a quiet dialogue scene may be insufficient for dense grain or rapid action. Most films in an Emby library already use lossy video compression. Direct Play preserves that encoded video stream during delivery. Video transcoding creates another encoded representation; when that encoding is lossy, it can add differences on top of the original ones. Increasing the output bitrate cannot restore detail lost earlier. It can help the new encoding avoid further visible damage, but a larger converted file is not evidence that the picture became closer to the camera original. A good comparison therefore considers the actual pictures, playback conditions, and delivery requirements alongside the file size. See Also How Video Compression Works Lossless Video Compression Intra-Frame Video Compression References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Inter-Frame Video Prediction | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Inter-Frame Video Prediction Inter-frame prediction uses other decoded pictures to predict parts of the current picture. The bitstream describes where to find the reference samples and how to correct the prediction. If a camera pans across a wall, the wall may appear shifted between pictures. A motion vector can describe that shift. The encoder then represents the remaining difference, called the residual . New objects, changing light, and exposed areas still require appropriate information. Original qualitative schematic. Motion prediction plus a residual reconstructs an encoded picture; the drawing is not a measured codec output. Information What the decoder needs it for Reference selection Chooses an available decoded picture Motion information Locates the region used for prediction Residual Corrects the estimate to reconstruct the coded result Some regions can be predicted so well that little or no residual is needed. Others may be coded using intra prediction instead. An inter-predicted picture need not use one method everywhere. Pictures can arrive in a different order A reference picture can appear later in display order but be decoded earlier. The decoder buffers pictures so it can satisfy the prediction dependencies and then present the result at the correct times. GOP structure helps describe those relationships. For Emby playback, efficient prediction can reduce delivery bitrate, while dependencies affect random access and buffering. To show a picture reached by seeking, the decoder may need to begin at an earlier keyframe and reconstruct the intervening references first. This process does not invent extra moments of motion. It reconstructs the pictures already represented by the encoded stream. Motion interpolation has a different goal: estimating additional pictures for new presentation times. See Also Intra-Frame Video Compression Video Reference Frames Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Motion Interpolation References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Intra-Frame Video Compression | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Intra-Frame Video Compression Intra-frame compression encodes a picture without predicting its samples from other pictures. It can still exploit patterns inside the current picture, such as neighbouring samples with similar values or edges continuing through adjacent blocks. “Intra” therefore does not mean uncompressed. A picture can contain substantial compression and still be independent of earlier picture samples. Tool within a picture Example role Spatial prediction Estimates a region from already reconstructed neighbours Transform coding, where used Represents patterns in a block more compactly Entropy coding Uses short representations for common values or events The exact tools depend on the codec. Intra-frame compression can be lossy or lossless ; the absence of temporal prediction does not establish either property. Why production workflows like it An all-intra stream avoids chains of picture-to-picture dependencies. That can simplify editing, scrubbing, and distributing frames to separate processing tasks. At comparable quality within a suitable codec, the cost is often more data than an efficient inter-predicted representation of the same scene. A largely static shot makes the tradeoff easy to understand: all-intra compression finds patterns separately in each picture, while temporal prediction can reuse information about the scene across time. Difficult or rapidly changing footage can reduce that advantage. For Emby, an all-intra source still needs a supported codec, profile, resolution, and bitrate. Easy frame independence does not guarantee Direct Play or low bandwidth. An intra-coded picture is also not automatically a fully self-contained file. The decoder may still require stream configuration and other coded information. In a stream that also contains temporal prediction, the rules around a particular intra picture determine whether it is a clean random-access point . This distinction explains why “I-picture” and “keyframe” are useful related terms, but should not be assumed to mean exactly the same thing in every codec and container. See Also Inter-Frame Video Prediction Video Keyframes and Random Access How Video Compression Works References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding RFC 9043: FFV1 lossless video format

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Video Reference Frames | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Video Reference Frames A reference frame is a decoded picture kept available for predicting another picture. The decoder stores these pictures in a decoded picture buffer rather than immediately discarding every frame after display. Multiple references let an encoder choose useful earlier pictures or combine prediction information. For example, a region briefly hidden behind a moving person may be easier to predict from an older view in which it was visible. Whether extra choices improve compression depends on the content and encoder. The buffer contains pictures, not compressed packets The memory needed for references grows with resolution and sample precision. For a tightly packed 8-bit 4:2:0 picture with even dimensions, the sample payload is width × height × 1.5 bytes: Picture grid Payload for one decoded picture Payload for four 1920 × 1080 3.11 MB 12.44 MB 3840 × 2160 12.44 MB 49.77 MB Calculated examples using decimal MB. Actual decoder memory can be larger because of alignment, additional working surfaces, display reordering, and different pixel layouts. These are not compressed file sizes. A higher bit depth can increase storage further, especially when samples occupy wider memory containers. The number of pictures needed for reordering can also differ from the number actively used as prediction references. For Emby playback, a decoder must meet the stream's buffer and prediction requirements as well as recognize the codec. Codec levels place limits on relevant resources, and device support can have additional constraints. Reference count is not a quality score. A media inspector may report a maximum or an encoder setting rather than the references used for every picture. A stream with fewer references can still look better if other encoding decisions suit the content. Nor are all B-pictures excluded from the buffer. Modern codecs allow structures where B-pictures become references for other pictures. To interpret a dependency chain, examine the actual picture structure rather than treating each letter as a fixed lifetime rule. See Also Inter-Frame Video Prediction Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Groups of Pictures (GOPs) | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Groups of Pictures (GOPs) A group of pictures (GOP) describes a run of coded pictures and the relationships between them. A common structure combines intra-coded pictures with pictures predicted from one or more references. The familiar letters are I for intra-coded, P for predictive, and B for bi-predictive picture types. Their precise rules vary by codec. In particular, modern B-pictures can themselves be used as references; “B” does not always mean disposable. Original dependency example. B-pictures here are not references: B1/B2 use I0 and P3, and B4/B5 use P3 and P6. The shown decode order is one valid choice for this schematic, not a universal codec sequence. Length is a tradeoff At a constant 24 fps, 48 pictures span two seconds. If clean access points are placed every 48 pictures, that creates two-second spacing. Scene changes and encoder decisions can introduce shorter intervals. Structure choice Practical effect More frequent access points Less decoding from an earlier point may be needed after seeking Longer prediction runs Can improve compression, depending on content and encoder choices Closed GOP The group can be decoded without picture references from an earlier group Open GOP Prediction relationships can cross the nominal group boundary An open GOP is not inherently damaged. It needs correct access-point handling so the decoder knows which pictures are valid when starting partway through the stream. In an Emby session, GOP structure can influence seeking, the beginning of a transcode, and how quickly decoding recovers after damaged source data. It does not set the programme's frame rate, and a longer GOP does not necessarily require a longer startup delay in every playback route. File size and visible quality alone do not reveal this structure. Picture-level inspection is useful when diagnosing irregular access points or a file that seeks poorly despite playing normally from the beginning. See Also Video Keyframes and Random Access Inter-Frame Video Prediction Video Reference Frames References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Profiles, levels, and tiers

articles/video/compression/picture-predi.title: Video Keyframes and Random Access | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/picture-predi.keywords: Video Keyframes and Random Access When you seek into a film, the next picture you want may depend on earlier decoded pictures. A random-access point gives the decoder a suitable place to begin reconstructing the stream. Containers and tools commonly mark these entry points as keyframes . The player can start before your requested time, decode the necessary pictures, and suppress them until the requested picture is ready. That is why an exact seek and the physical start of decoding need not be the same position. Example with entry points every two seconds What decoding may need Seek to 10.0 seconds Start at the entry point at 10.0 seconds Seek to 11.3 seconds Start at 10.0 seconds and decode forward Seek to 12.0 seconds Start at the next entry point at 12.0 seconds Illustrative timeline. Real files can have irregular entry points, preroll rules, and container-specific seeking behaviour. An I-picture is only part of the story An intra-coded picture does not predict its own samples from other pictures. However, following pictures or pictures reordered around it may still depend on earlier references. A clean entry point must satisfy the codec's dependency rules, not merely have an “I” label. H.264's IDR pictures establish a reference reset. HEVC also defines several kinds of random-access pictures, with rules for pictures that lead the access point in display order. The decoder still needs suitable stream configuration. For Emby, the spacing and validity of these points can affect seeking responsiveness and the start of transcoded output. A longer gap can mean more source pictures must be decoded before reaching the chosen time. Network delivery, storage speed, and decoder performance also contribute. Changing a packet's keyframe flag cannot remove prediction dependencies. A damaged index or incorrectly marked entry point can therefore cause seeking failures even when uninterrupted playback seems fine. Groups of pictures describe the surrounding structure; shorter groups can provide more frequent entry points at a potential compression cost. See Also Groups of Pictures (GOPs) Intra-Frame Video Compression Inter-Frame Video Prediction References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding FFmpeg command-line documentation

articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-L.title: Video Codec Levels and Tiers | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-L.keywords: Video Codec Levels and Tiers A codec level describes limits on the workload and buffering required by a coded stream. A tier , in codecs that define one, distinguishes further limits within a level, particularly bitrate and coded-buffer requirements. A profile tells the decoder which kinds of tools and sample formats it may encounter. Level and tier address how much of that work it must handle. Constraint Why it matters Picture size A decoder must reconstruct and store the complete picture Samples or coding units per second Larger pictures and higher frame rates multiply throughput Decoded picture buffer References and reordered pictures consume memory Bitrate and coded buffering The compressed data must be accepted at the allowed rate A level is not one resolution A stream with smaller pictures at a high frame rate can reach a throughput limit that a larger, slower stream does not. Picture dimensions alone therefore do not establish conformance. Bitrate and buffer requirements can matter even when the resolution is familiar. The numbers are also codec-specific. H.264 Level 4.1 and HEVC Level 4.1 do not describe the same limits, and the profile can affect limits within a codec. Avoid universal tables that assign one maximum resolution or bitrate to every codec's level number. HEVC defines Main and High tiers. High tier permits larger bitrate and coded-buffer limits where that tier is defined; it does not automatically improve the encoded picture. A string such as “Main 10, Level 5.1, Main tier” combines three separate properties. For an Emby app to decode a stream, its playback path must meet the actual requirements. A device advertised for a particular resolution may also limit frame rate, profile, tier, or concurrent decoder workload. Lowering a level flag cannot make an oversized or excessive-throughput stream conform. Conversely, a stream may be tagged with a higher level than its pictures actually require. Establishing that the label can safely change requires checking the full bitstream requirements, rather than guessing from resolution. See Also Video Codec Profiles Video Reference Frames Video Resolution Video Frame Rate References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Profiles, levels, and tiers Android decoder video capabilities

articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-P.title: Video Codec Profiles | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Codec-P.keywords: Video Codec Profiles A codec profile describes a permitted set of tools and sample formats within one codec. It helps establish what a decoder must understand. It is a compatibility description, rather than a picture-quality setting. For example, “H.264 support” does not establish support for every H.264 profile. An app's decoder can handle ordinary 8-bit H.264 while lacking a path for a 10-bit variant. Profile example Bit-depth support Color sampling in this example H.264 Baseline 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264 Main 8-bit 4:2:0 H.264 High 8-bit 4:2:0, also monochrome permitted H.264 High 10 Up to 10-bit 4:2:0, also monochrome permitted HEVC Main 8-bit 4:2:0 HEVC Main 10 Up to 10-bit 4:2:0 Selected profile constraints, not the entire feature list or a decoder support guarantee. A permitted maximum does not mean every stream uses it. Baseline, Main, and High differ even though their common color depth and sampling can match. For instance, H.264 Main permits coding tools excluded from Baseline, while High adds further tools. The codec specifications define the full restrictions. Read the whole description A profile belongs to its codec. H.264 High and HEVC Main cannot be ranked by comparing the words “High” and “Main.” HEVC Main 10 also does not mean HDR: a 10-bit stream can carry SDR content. Levels and tiers describe another part of compatibility: resource limits such as picture size, throughput, buffering, and bitrate. They should be checked alongside the profile. For Emby, a profile mismatch can make video transcoding necessary for a particular app even when another file using the same codec plays directly. Changing the profile label alone does not convert the stream's tools or sample format. The encoded content must actually satisfy the target profile. Support depends on the complete playback path, including the app's selected decoder, operating system, and hardware. Treat the media information and the device's documented capabilities as complementary evidence. See Also Video Codec Levels and Tiers How Video Compression Works References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T H.265: High efficiency video coding x265: Profiles, levels, and tiers x264 source: Profile restrictions

articles/video/compression/Video-Compres.title: How Video Compression Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/compression/Video-Compres.keywords: How Video Compression Works A camera following a person across a plain wall records much of the same scene again and again. Storing every picture as a fresh list of sample values would spend a large amount of data describing that repetition. Video compression finds a cheaper description from which a decoder can reconstruct the pictures: where to get a useful prediction, how to correct it, and which small differences to retain. That description is what Emby stores and delivers as a compressed video stream. The player reconstructs full pictures for display. To understand the savings—and why quality, encoding speed, and seeking behave as they do—it helps to follow one region through this process. How much data is being replaced? For a 1920 × 1080 picture stored as 8-bit 4:2:0 video, four picture locations use four luma samples and two chroma samples. Luma carries the brightness-related signal; the two chroma components carry color differences. The lower chroma sampling density gives an average of 1.5 bytes per picture location. Ignoring padding and headers: One picture occupies 1920 × 1080 × 1.5 = 3,110,400 bytes . At 24 pictures per second, that is 74,649,600 bytes per second , about 74.65 MB/s or 597 Mb/s . One minute would occupy about 4.48 GB in decimal units. A hypothetical compressed video stream averaging 6 Mb/s would use about 45 MB for that minute, before audio and container overhead. The raw-to-compressed ratio in this example is roughly 100:1. That calculation describes the data reduction, not a guarantee of what any particular source will look like at 6 Mb/s. The raw baseline already has a defined sample format. Comparing it with full-resolution RGB or with samples of a different bit depth would give a different ratio. Compression operates on the picture representation supplied to the encoder; scaling, reducing bit depth, and changing chroma sampling are additional ways a workflow can change that input. Find a prediction worth describing The encoder divides a picture into regions and looks for useful ways to predict their samples. Region sizes and available prediction tools depend on the codec. A large region can describe a smooth wall efficiently. Around a moving hand or a detailed edge, smaller regions may provide better matches. There is a cost to that flexibility. Dividing a region means describing the divisions and their individual choices. The smallest possible regions do not automatically make the smallest file. The encoder has to weigh improved predictions against the extra instructions. Predict from the same picture With intra-frame prediction , a region can be predicted from neighboring samples that have already been reconstructed. If nearby samples have similar values, extending those values into the new region can be a good starting point. A directional prediction can continue an edge across the region. Both encoder and decoder know those reconstructed neighbors and the selected prediction rule. The encoder sends the choice of rule and a correction, rather than a completely independent value for every sample. “Intra” therefore does not mean “uncompressed.” Even a picture that has no dependencies on other pictures can exploit a great deal of repetition within itself. A broad, evenly lit wall is much easier to describe this way than a field of unrelated random values. Predict from other pictures With inter-frame prediction , the encoder can obtain samples from reconstructed reference pictures. When the person moves to the right, a region at the person's new position may resemble a region farther left in a reference picture. A motion vector tells the decoder where to obtain the selected prediction. The decoder does not need to recognize a person or understand the motion of an arm. It follows sample-location instructions. The encoder does the search; the decoder uses the result. Depending on the codec, predictions can use several reference pictures, interpolated sample positions, or combinations of predictions. Motion prediction is especially useful when a camera pans across a scene. Many sample positions change, but large areas still resemble shifted versions of an earlier picture. Conversely, a small newly revealed strip behind a moving object may have no useful match. The encoder can choose another prediction or code that region using intra prediction. The prediction is often imperfect: illumination changes, an edge moves by a fraction of a sample, or a surface deforms. The remaining difference is the residual . A useful prediction makes that correction easier to describe. Follow the correction through an encode Take four illustrative luma samples. The prediction is close to the source: Stage Four sample values Prediction 100, 102, 104, 106 Source 102, 101, 108, 107 Residual: source minus prediction 2, −1, 4, 1 If the decoder receives that exact residual, adding it to the prediction recovers the source exactly. This subtraction is reversible. Lossy compression enters when the encoder chooses to describe an approximation of the correction. Change the representation before rounding A transform expresses a region as a mixture of patterns. One pattern might represent a constant offset; others describe variations across the region. The resulting numbers are coefficients : how much of each pattern is present. A constant residual of 2, 2, 2, 2 illustrates the attraction. Instead of treating the four equal corrections as unrelated numbers, a suitable transform represents their common component and leaves the variation components at zero. Real picture regions often contain smooth areas and gradual changes that concentrate much of their information in relatively few coefficients. For a transparent numerical example, use a small reversible add-and-subtract transform. This is a teaching example, not the transform prescribed by H.264 or H.265. Given residual samples a, b, c, and d, calculate: c0 = (a + b + c + d) / 2 c1 = (a + b − c − d) / 2 c2 = (a − b + c − d) / 2 c3 = (a − b − c + d) / 2 For 2, −1, 4, 1, the coefficients are 3, −2, 3, 0 . For the constant residual 2, 2, 2, 2, they would be 4, 0, 0, 0 : all the correction is in the common component. The transform has not thrown away information. Applying the corresponding inverse to the unrounded coefficients recovers the original residual. It has put the information into a form that is often cheaper to approximate and code. Quantize the coefficients Quantization reduces the number of coefficient values that need distinct representations. For this example, round to the nearest multiple of two, with halfway cases rounded away from zero: Coefficient values Before rounding 3, −2, 3, 0 After rounding 4, −2, 4, 0 Levels, expressed in units of the step size 2, −1, 2, 0 A decoder given the levels and step size reconstructs 4, −2, 4, 0. It cannot determine whether an original coefficient of 3 or 4 led to the reconstructed value 4. Those distinctions have been merged. Larger quantization steps merge more distinctions and often make more coefficients zero. That can reduce the number of bits substantially, while changing the reconstructed picture more. Actual codecs define their own scaling and quantization rules, and encoders can adjust choices across a picture. The simple step of two here is not a codec QP setting. Code the remaining symbols compactly The bitstream must describe more than coefficients. It also contains prediction choices, region divisions, reference information, motion data, and other syntax. Entropy coding represents those symbols using their statistical patterns. For example, a long region of zero coefficients does not need a separate full-sized integer for every zero. Contexts in which one outcome is very likely can also be represented more economically than contexts with many equally likely outcomes. The exact method depends on the codec. This stage preserves the symbols it is given. It does not decide that a coefficient should become zero; quantization and the encoder's coding decisions have already established what will be represented. A decoded coefficient sequence can be an exact copy of the coded sequence even while the resulting picture differs from the original. Reconstruct the picture the player will get Applying the inverse toy transform to the rounded coefficients produces a residual of 3, −1, 5, 1 . Adding that correction to the same prediction gives: Four sample values Original source 102, 101, 108, 107 Decoded reconstruction 103, 101, 109, 107 Reconstruction minus source 1, 0, 1, 0 Two sample values changed by one. The decoder has done its job correctly: this is the picture specified by the compressed description. It has no access to the discarded distinctions needed to restore the two original values. The example also shows why a compression error need not look like a single missing pixel. Changing a transform coefficient changes a pattern spread over several samples. In real pictures, stronger approximation can soften texture, alter an edge, or produce visible patterns around it. Compression artifacts are the visible consequences of those decisions. The encoder keeps a local reconstruction so later predictions use pictures that the decoder can also obtain. The codec defines the actual transforms, syntax, and reconstruction rules. Why the encoder needs its own reconstruction For later pictures, the encoder must predict using the samples the decoder will have. After the example above, a reference region contains 103, 101, 109, 107, even though the original source contained 102, 101, 108, 107. Suppose the next source picture has a sample value of 104 at the corresponding position. Predicting from the reconstructed value 103 leaves a correction of 1. The decoder can make that same prediction and obtain 104. Predicting instead from the pristine source value 102 would leave a correction of 2; adding it to the decoder's reference value 103 would produce 105. That disagreement is why the encoder reconstructs its chosen approximation and uses the result for future references. Both sides must operate from matching information. A lossy reference does not inevitably make all following pictures worse: later corrections can account for differences, provided the encoder uses the correct reconstructed reference. Reconstruction can also include codec-defined processing such as in-loop filtering. In block-based coding, this processing can reduce some discontinuities or adjust reconstructed samples. When those filtered pictures serve as references, the encoder must account for the same processing. A filter used only for display has a different role because it does not redefine the samples used for subsequent predictions. Lossless video compression retains the information needed to recover the input samples exactly. It can still exploit prediction and statistical coding. It does not have to use this lossy transform-and-rounding path; FFV1, for example, codes sample differences without discarding them. Lossless applies to the samples supplied to that encoder. Any earlier scaling or color conversion remains part of how those samples were produced. Picture dependencies explain decoding order and seeking A reference picture must be reconstructed before a picture that uses it. The order in which pictures are decoded can therefore differ from the order in which they appear on screen. Consider a simplified sequence displayed as A, B, C. Suppose C is predicted from A, and B is predicted using both A and C. The decoder needs this order: Decode A. Decode C using A. Decode B using the two available references. Present A, B, C at their intended times. The player holds the necessary pictures and uses their timing information to restore presentation order. “A later picture” in a prediction description can mean later in display order; it is already available when the dependent picture is decoded. The same dependencies matter when seeking. Jumping directly into a dependent picture may omit references needed to reconstruct it. A player typically starts at a suitable random-access point , then decodes the necessary path to the requested time. Merely having a picture coded without inter prediction does not, for every codec structure, guarantee that all subsequent dependencies have been reset. More frequent independent access points can make entry into the stream easier, but give the encoder fewer opportunities to reuse earlier pictures. This is one reason a seek-friendly or low-latency stream can have different compression characteristics from a stream designed mainly for efficient sequential playback. The encoder chooses between competing descriptions For one region, an encoder may have several plausible descriptions: one large prediction, several smaller predictions, a different reference picture, or an intra prediction. Each produces a different residual and requires a different amount of syntax. A prediction with the smallest raw residual is not necessarily the best final choice. It might require many extra motion instructions. Conversely, accepting a slightly less accurate prediction can be worthwhile if its coded description is much smaller. Rate-distortion optimization expresses this tradeoff. “Rate” is the number of bits needed; “distortion” is a measure of the reconstructed picture's difference from the source. As a constructed example, consider two complete coding choices: Choice Bits for this region Distortion in illustrative units A 120 10 B 70 14 If the cost is distortion + 0.05 × bits, A costs 16 and B costs 17.5, so A wins. If bits are more expensive and the multiplier is 0.2, A costs 34 and B costs 28, so B wins. Nothing about the source changed; the available tradeoff changed. Real encoders use more involved calculations, and a simple sample-error score does not capture every aspect of perceived quality. The example explains why a coding decision can change when a bitrate budget changes. The x265 analysis options expose controls for how thoroughly such alternatives are evaluated. Scene complexity affects those alternatives. A static wall offers predictable samples and often small corrections. Film grain and sensor noise contain variations that are harder to predict. Leaves moving independently, splashing water, or newly revealed detail can require many corrections. Preserving that information costs bits; smoothing it makes the picture cheaper to describe. Rate control manages these choices over time. A quality-oriented encode can allow difficult sections to use more data. A constrained stream has to fit its delivery budget, potentially using stronger approximation in a difficult scene. A full movie's average bitrate hides those local differences. Resolution and frame rate describe the output grid and timing, while the coding decisions determine how faithfully that grid represents the source. Encoding effort and playback effort are different The decoder follows a selected description. The encoder may have tried many descriptions before choosing it. That search is why increasing encoder effort can improve compression without requiring the player to repeat the search. The x265 presets provide a concrete example: slower presets evaluate more possibilities, while faster presets take more shortcuts. Comparing encoders fairly means considering the resulting quality, bitrate, and time together. Identical codec names or nominal quality settings do not establish identical decisions. Playback still has work to do: entropy decoding, reference management, prediction, reconstruction, and any required filters. A device must support the particular codec features and sample format, and perform those operations fast enough for the picture rate. A compact stream can consequently be harder for a device to decode than a larger stream in a simpler supported format. For Emby, these distinctions separate three common paths. During Direct Play, the app decodes the stored compressed video. When the server copies that video into a different container, the compressed picture description remains intact. During a video transcode , the server decodes the source, performs any required processing, and creates a new compressed description for the destination. The new encoder sees the reconstructed source, including any texture or edge changes already present in it. More output bits can preserve that input better; they cannot identify discarded original detail. That is why keeping the original library file gives future playback and conversion paths the best available starting point. articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Video Compression Artifacts | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Video Compression Artifacts Compression artifacts are visible changes caused by the compromises in compressed video. They become noticeable when coding decisions fail to preserve an important feature of the picture, such as texture, a smooth gradient, or a sharp moving edge. Lossy compression does not always produce visible artifacts. Visibility depends on the source, settings, screen, and viewing distance. A clean dialogue scene can look convincing at a rate that damages a grainy action scene. Visible symptom Useful interpretation Block-shaped patches Neighboring coded regions differ noticeably Halos or ripples near edges Coding or processing struggles with abrupt detail Soft or smeared texture Fine information was simplified Texture that shimmers or changes Successive pictures preserve detail inconsistently Steps in a gradient Limited precision or coding compromises become visible These appearances are clues, not unique diagnoses. Banding can already be in the source, and ringing can come from scaling or sharpening. A file can contain both earlier processing defects and new compression artifacts. Compare the same picture at the same point For an Emby session, compare the original video with the delivered version when transcoding occurs. A visible defect that appears in both may originate in the library file. A new defect in the converted output points toward that conversion or its processing. Check difficult sections in motion as well as paused frames. A still picture can miss flickering grain, pulsing texture, or a defect that appears only around fast movement. Keep scale and display settings consistent. A higher bitrate or a more effective encoder can reduce additional coding damage when that is the cause. It cannot recover source detail already removed. Filters may conceal some artifacts, but can also remove legitimate detail; a smoother picture is not automatically a more faithful one. Use quantizer information and bitrate as context for the comparison, rather than as a diagnosis by themselves. See Also Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Bitrate Film Grain in Compressed Video Video Generation Loss References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding ITU-T T.81: JPEG compression and coding Zhou Wang: SSIM index and reference implementation

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Film Grain in Compressed Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Film Grain in Compressed Video Film grain is fine texture associated with photographic film. A digital video may retain that texture from a scan or add a grain effect deliberately. It can be part of the intended appearance rather than a defect to remove. Grain is difficult to compress because it changes across pictures and is less predictable than stable scenery. An encoder may need substantial data to retain it, or may simplify it when the budget is tight. Treatment What to look for Encode the visible grain directly The texture must fit the picture's data budget Filter it before encoding Smoother pictures, with a risk of removing real detail Use a grain-aware encoder tuning Different decisions about preserving the texture Encode a cleaner picture with grain parameters The decoder generates modeled grain for display Grain can change without the resolution changing A converted film can retain the same width and height yet lose its fine texture. Grain may become softer, form larger patches, or pulse between pictures. Inspect moving scenes: a paused frame does not show how consistently the texture behaves. Some encoders offer a grain tuning. This changes their priorities rather than restoring grain lost before the encode. The setting is implementation-specific, and its effect on bitrate should be assessed using the actual source. AV1 can signal film-grain parameters so grain is synthesized as part of output processing. This aims to reproduce the appearance of grain without coding every original grain sample in the picture. It is not exact preservation of the source's grain pattern. For Emby, grain differences between direct playback and a converted stream can explain why the same film looks smoother even when the delivered resolution matches. Check the source, rate-control constraints, and any filtering in the conversion path. If the original appearance matters, retain the source while evaluating smaller derivatives. A later encoder cannot reconstruct the original pattern from a copy that has already removed it. See Also AV1 Video Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Compression Artifacts Video Generation Loss References AOMedia: AV1 bitstream and decoding process specification x265: Presets and tunings

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Video Generation Loss | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Video Generation Loss Generation loss is the extra change introduced when lossy video is decoded and then encoded again. Each new encoder works from the pictures it receives, including compromises introduced by earlier encodes. A high-quality conversion can make those additional changes hard to see. It cannot know the detail discarded before its input was created. Conceptual workflows. The diagram shows where another lossy generation can occur, not the measured amount of visible loss. Operation on a video stream Another lossy video generation? Copy the original file No Repackage the same encoded video No Convert only the audio while copying video No Decode video and encode it with lossy settings Yes Losslessly encode decoded samples No new codec loss at that stage; earlier losses remain File size cannot reverse the process If fine texture disappeared in the first encode, the next encoder sees a smoother surface. Giving that surface more bits can preserve it accurately, but it does not recreate the original texture. Repeated conversions also need not add the same amount of damage each time. Codec, quantization, resizing, filtering, and source content all matter. There is no universal number of “safe generations.” For an Emby library, retain the best source when preparing versions for different devices. Make each derivative from that source rather than converting one small playback copy into another. A ProRes or lossless intermediate can be useful in an editing workflow, but converting an already lossy source into it does not remove previous losses. Direct Play and stream-copy delivery preserve the encoded video. Video transcoding can add another generation. If only the sound changes, do not attribute a picture-quality difference to video generation loss without checking what actually happened to the video stream. See Also Lossy Video Compression Apple ProRes Video FFV1 Lossless Video Video Bitrate References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding Apple: ProRes white paper

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) compares decoded samples against a reference. It measures numerical error on a logarithmic scale, usually in decibels. With the same sample format and peak convention, a higher value means smaller mean squared error. For one 8-bit plane using a peak sample value of 255: PSNR = 10 × log10(255² / MSE) MSE is the mean of the squared sample differences. Its square root is the root mean square, or RMS, error. Calculated curve for one 8-bit plane, peak 255, and positive RMS error. It is not an encoder test or a scale of guaranteed visible quality. RMS sample error PSNR in this example 1 48.13 dB 2 42.11 dB 4 36.09 dB 8 30.07 dB Doubling RMS error reduces PSNR by approximately 6.02 dB. With zero error, the mathematical result is infinite. That means the compared samples match exactly, not that the file's bytes, metadata, or source history are identical. Error is not the same as visibility Two pictures can have equal MSE and visibly different defects. PSNR gives a useful reconstruction measurement, but does not model all the ways people notice blur, grain changes, edges, or local artifacts. Keep geometry, corresponding frames, sample format, and the peak definition consistent. An offset of one picture or a different range conversion can dominate the result. Values reported for different planes or bit depths need their measurement conventions stated. For an Emby conversion, compare the delivered pictures with the retained source under the same preparation. PSNR can show how much additional numerical change occurred; it cannot tell whether the source already lost camera detail. Inspect the pictures too, and distinguish a PSNR calculated from pooled MSE from an arithmetic average of per-frame decibel values. See Also Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video VMAF Video Quality Metric Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Generation Loss References FFmpeg: PSNR filter Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, and Simoncelli: Image quality assessment from error visibility to structural similarity

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video Structural Similarity (SSIM) compares the local statistical structure of two pictures. It considers more than pixel-by-pixel error, aiming to reflect the importance of recognizable patterns and edges. In video evaluation, one sequence is the reference and the other is the test result. Corresponding decoded pictures are compared, often through small windows, before results are combined into an overall score. Part of the original SSIM comparison What it describes Luminance Local average sample value Contrast Variation around the local average Structure How the local variations correspond A blurred texture and a small uniform brightness change can have similar squared error but affect these relationships differently. SSIM can therefore distinguish cases that PSNR treats as equal. This does not make it a perfect predictor of what every viewer prefers. Read the implementation as well as the score A value of 1 represents identical compared content in the original formulation. SSIM is unitless, and negative values are possible; it is not universally confined to 0–1. A result such as 0.99 does not mean “99% picture quality.” Single-scale SSIM, multi-scale variants, and different implementations need not produce interchangeable numbers. Windowing, color handling, downsampling, and aggregation all matter. The reference implementation's suggested scaling is one reason tools can disagree even when using the same videos. For an Emby library conversion, compare candidate encodes against the same retained source with consistent timing, dimensions, and sample preparation. A different crop or one-frame offset can measure a mismatch rather than the effect of the encoder. Inspect difficult scenes in motion alongside the aggregate result. A whole-film score can hide a short bad section, and an image-similarity measurement does not describe network stalls or playback compatibility. SSIM helps evaluate the reconstruction; it does not prove the source was good or that the output retained every original sample. See Also Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video VMAF Video Quality Metric Video Compression Artifacts Video Generation Loss References Wang, Bovik, Sheikh, and Simoncelli: Image quality assessment from error visibility to structural similarity Zhou Wang: SSIM index and reference implementation Netflix: VMAF frequently asked questions

articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.title: VMAF Video Quality Metric | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/quality-.keywords: VMAF Video Quality Metric Suppose you are making smaller playback versions of the same retained movie source. Looking at every frame of every candidate is impractical, but file size alone says little about which version preserved the picture better. VMAF supplies one way to measure that comparison. VMAF, Video Multi-Method Assessment Fusion, is a full-reference video-quality metric. It receives decoded pictures from a reference and a test sequence, extracts comparison features, and uses a trained model to predict quality in a defined viewing context. What goes into the score The comparison begins with corresponding pictures, not with file extensions or compressed byte sizes. Features capture aspects of the relationship between the reference and test content, such as retained detail and motion-related behavior. A model combines the features using relationships learned from subjective-quality data. The published v0.6.1 model, for example, lists an ADM detail feature, a motion feature, and VIF features at four spatial scales. These give the model several measurements of the picture relationship rather than one overall sample-error value. The selected model defines which measurements it consumes. Training supplies examples for which comparison features and viewer assessments are both available. The fitting process learns a mapping from the feature combinations to those assessments. Evaluation then measures a new reference/test pair and applies the fitted mapping. The training happened before this evaluation; choosing a VMAF model does not train a new model on the movie being tested. That last stage is why the result differs from a direct error formula such as PSNR . VMAF's number is the output of a particular learned model. It is intended to be useful for perceptual comparison; it is not a count of retained bits, pixels, or original information. A score of 95 therefore needs context. Which model produced it? How were the inputs prepared? Is it a mean for a whole film, or the score of one scene? Prepare the comparison before interpreting it Corresponding input pictures must represent the same content at the intended comparison geometry. A frame offset can compare two different moments. A crop difference can compare different regions. A range or color conversion applied on only one side can become part of the measured difference. When comparing a lower-resolution playback version with a larger reference, scaling is an explicit part of the evaluation. Use a consistent preparation that represents the intended viewing situation. A different scaler can change what the metric sees. This is especially relevant to HDR-to-SDR material. A straightforward comparison of incompatible signal representations does not isolate compression quality. Establish which picture representation is being compared and whether the selected model is suitable for it. For repeatable results, keep a small record with each test: The reference source and the tested encode. Model/version and tool settings. Sample format, geometry, scaling, and timing preparation. How per-frame results were aggregated. Read the model's viewing assumptions Artifacts that are visible close to a large screen may be much less visible from farther away. Models calibrated for different viewing conditions can therefore assign different values to the same reconstruction. Netflix's familiar v0 models and the v1 models released in June 2026 have documented viewing assumptions. Common models use a 0–100 scale; the v1 4K model for viewing at three screen heights uses 0–110. These are model conventions, not a universal percentage scale. A score from one model should not be treated as the same quantity as an equal-looking score from another. Even within one model, changing clipping settings or input preparation can change the interpretation of the result. Look past the whole-film average Consider a hypothetical constant-frame-rate, one-minute test: fifty seconds score 95, and ten seconds score 50. The arithmetic mean is 87.5. That single number cannot tell you whether the lower-scoring section is an inconsequential transition or the scene the viewer most cares about. Per-frame and per-scene results help locate the weakness. A low-tail summary can be useful alongside the mean, and a targeted viewing check can show what happened: smeared grain, unstable texture, blurred fine detail, or another visible change. Enhancement processing can complicate the measurement. Sharpening may change measured features while introducing a look that a viewer dislikes. Grain handling can also affect a reference comparison even where a synthetic-grain presentation is intentional. The metric and a viewing check answer related questions, rather than replacing one another. For an Emby library conversion, use VMAF to narrow the candidate encodes and identify passages worth inspecting. After choosing a satisfactory picture reconstruction, test the intended playback path separately for decoding and delivery performance. That preserves a clear meaning for the score: how the tested pictures compare under the stated model and preparation. See Also Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) for Video Structural Similarity (SSIM) for Video Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Compression Artifacts References Netflix: published v0.6.1 model inputs Netflix: available comparison features Netflix: VMAF project Netflix: VMAF documentation Netflix: VMAF v0 models and viewing conditions Netflix: VMAF v1 model selection, viewing assumptions, and score ranges Netflix: VMAF frequently asked questions

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Bitrate | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Bitrate Video bitrate describes the amount of coded picture data per second. It excludes the soundtrack and container overhead. When choosing an encode, the number can be a target average, a local rate limit, or the measured result of a quality-based encode; those meanings should not be mixed. A bitrate is a data budget, not a picture-quality score. Its effect depends on the source, codec, resolution, frame rate, and the encoder's decisions. Illustrative video rate Data for one second Video-only size for two hours 4 Mb/s 0.5 MB 3.6 GB 8 Mb/s 1 MB 7.2 GB 16 Mb/s 2 MB 14.4 GB Decimal units and an exact average over 7,200 seconds. Audio and packaging are excluded; these are size calculations, not recommended quality settings. What must fit into that budget? At the same bitrate, doubling the frame rate halves the average number of bits available per picture. It does not follow that the rate must always double to preserve quality: neighboring pictures can share predictable information. Dense grain or complicated motion may be much harder to compress than a quiet scene. A slower preset can give an encoder more time to use its tools. That can improve the result within a fixed budget, but it does not add missing source detail or guarantee a particular quality. In Emby, compare the library video's bitrate with the delivered stream when video conversion occurs. The playback quality setting can constrain delivery; it is not a measurement of how faithfully every scene will survive that constraint. For storage, average bitrate is useful. For playback, short demanding periods and the available buffer matter too. Treat a video's reported average as one part of the delivery requirement, rather than assuming the connection needs exactly that rate at every instant. See Also Bitrate Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Encoder Presets References FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Bitrate Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Bitrate Video Encoding Constant bitrate (CBR) encoding tries to keep coded output near a specified data rate under the encoder's buffering rules. It is useful when predictable delivery demand is more important than allowing complex scenes an unrestricted amount of extra data. “Constant” does not mean every picture has the same byte count. A keyframe can be much larger than a predicted picture, and the buffer allows that variation while maintaining the required delivery behavior. Some strict CBR implementations can add filler or padding. Illustrative interval totals, not output from an encoder. Both examples contain 32 megabits over eight seconds. Actual CBR control is governed by its buffer model and need not produce identical one-second totals. The compromise moves into the picture If a fixed budget must cover both an easy scene and a difficult one, the encoder has less freedom to preserve the difficult scene. It can increase quantization or choose other coding compromises to meet the rate. CBR controls CBR does not guarantee A target delivery rate Equal bytes in every frame Rate behavior within a buffer model Uniform visible quality Predictability for a constrained channel Constant speed of network downloads The encoded output budget Recovery of detail missing from the source In Emby, do not diagnose rate control solely from a fluctuating transfer-speed graph. Players can request or receive data in bursts even when the encoded stream was made with CBR. When evaluating a converted stream, inspect its encoder settings and buffer constraints . A file's overall average being close to a round number is not enough to identify its rate-control method. See Also Video Bitrate Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Constant Quality Video Encoding References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Quality Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Quality Video Encoding Constant quality encoding starts with a quality target and lets the encoder use different amounts of data as the source changes. The target is defined by the encoder's method; it is not a guarantee that every scene looks equally good to every viewer. This is useful when creating a library copy whose acceptable appearance matters more than meeting an exact file size. A clean animation and a grainy live-action recording can produce very different sizes at the same setting. What you choose What is mostly allowed to vary An encoder-specific quality target The resulting bitrate and size A fixed quantizer mode The picture error and bitrate as content changes A quality target with a rate cap Bitrate, and potentially quality when the cap binds The methods are related but not interchangeable. CRF adapts encoding decisions around a rate factor. Constant QP holds a quantization setting according to its implementation. Some hardware encoders offer their own target-quality modes. A cap creates another constraint A quality target can be combined with a maximum rate and a buffer size. When the encoder cannot meet both the unconstrained quality target and the rate constraint, it must compromise. A difficult section may therefore look worse than the target would suggest. The numerical scales also differ. A quality value in one software encoder, hardware API, or codec should not be copied into another and assumed to represent the same result. For an Emby library, a quality-controlled source can still require conversion because its peaks, format, or profile exceed what the app can accept. Check the delivered stream before concluding that the library encode is responsible for a visible change. Use representative difficult scenes when assessing a setting: grain, dark gradients, fast movement, and fine texture reveal different compromises. The eventual file size is an outcome of that evaluation, not proof of quality on its own. See Also Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Variable Bitrate Video Encoding References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Constant rate factor (CRF) is a quality-control method used by encoders such as x264 and x265. It allows bitrate to vary while adjusting quantization and other decisions around an encoder-defined quality target. A lower CRF in these encoders generally means finer quantization and a larger result; a higher value generally means stronger compression. CRF does not specify a target bitrate or exact output size. Change within the same encoding setup Typical consequence Lower CRF More data to preserve the source Higher CRF Less data and greater compression compromises More demanding source at the same CRF A larger result Add a restrictive rate cap The quality target may no longer be maintained Directions, not measured results or a guarantee for every individual encode. The number belongs to the encoder CRF 20 in x264 and CRF 20 in x265 are not equivalent quality levels. An AV1 encoder's CRF-like control uses its own model and scale. Compare settings within the same encoder, version, preset, and sample format before drawing conclusions from the number. CRF is also different from constant QP . In CRF mode, the quantizers can change with the pictures and the encoder's analysis. The word “constant” refers to the chosen rate factor, not a fixed quantizer or identical visible quality. Do not interpret zero as a universal lossless switch. Encoders have different lossless conventions; x265, for example, documents an explicit lossless mode. A low CRF is not by itself proof of exact sample preservation. For an Emby source file, CRF explains how the file was encoded, not how it will be delivered to every app. A playback limit may still trigger conversion. A rate cap and buffer constraint can help control an encode's delivery demand, but they introduce a separate tradeoff when difficult scenes reach that cap. See Also Constant Quality Video Encoding Video Quantization Parameter (QP) Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) Video Encoder Presets References x265: Quality and rate-control options FFmpeg: Codec and encoder documentation

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Quantization Parameter (QP) | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Quantization Parameter (QP) A quantization parameter (QP) controls the strength of quantization in a codec's coding process. Quantization replaces precise values with coarser representable values, which can reduce the amount of information that needs encoding. Higher QP commonly means coarser quantization, but its numerical meaning belongs to the codec and implementation. In ordinary 8-bit H.264 luma coding, QP ranges from 0 to 51; increasing it by six doubles the quantization step size under otherwise unchanged scaling. Other formats and sample depths require their own interpretation. Generic scalar illustration: output = step × floor(input / step + 0.5), for input 0–32. Steps four and eight are arbitrary units, not a mapping from QP values to pixels or a particular codec's quantization equation. A fixed QP does not fix visible quality Property What it means Quantization step Spacing between reconstructed representable values A reported QP The codec's quantizer selection Constant QP mode A quantizer-control policy, possibly with separate picture-type settings CRF An adaptive quality-control method that can vary QP A detailed moving scene and a quiet flat scene can expose different errors at the same quantizer setting. Bits per frame also vary: fixed quantization does not make an encode CBR. Actual encoders can adjust quantizers between picture types and, in some modes, between regions. An average QP in a log summarizes those decisions and hides their distribution. It is not a perceptual score. For Emby transcoding, a QP reported by the output encoder describes part of that conversion. Comparing it with a source encoded using another codec or sample format does not establish which picture is better. Compare the decoded pictures under matching conditions, and use the quantizer information to explain the encoder's choices. See Also Lossy Video Compression Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Constant Quality Video Encoding Video Compression Artifacts References ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Two-Pass Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Two-Pass Video Encoding Two-pass encoding usually means analyzing the complete source in a first pass, then using those statistics to allocate data during the final encode. It is especially useful when an offline conversion must meet a target average bitrate or approximate size. The first pass can identify where the difficult scenes occur. The second pass can reserve more of the available budget for those sections instead of making every decision with only limited knowledge of what comes next. Conceptual whole-source workflow. The second pass reads the original source again; it does not encode the first pass's compressed pictures. Analysis is not an extra generation of picture loss The final encoder uses statistics from the first pass, rather than treating a lossy first-pass video as its new source. Two passes therefore do not automatically mean two successive lossy generations. Whole-source two-pass encoding What follows First pass observes the source Statistics describe its coding difficulty Second pass uses that information The overall budget can be allocated with hindsight Source is available twice Suits offline work more naturally than immediate playback A fixed target is still required The method cannot eliminate a too-small data budget This differs from hardware multipass frame encoding . For example, NVENC can analyze and encode a frame in multiple internal passes. That is not the same as scanning an entire film before encoding it again. An encoder's “two-pass” label needs its documented context. For Emby, whole-source two-pass processing is a useful concept when preparing a library derivative in advance. A playback transcode must normally begin delivering before the whole source could be analyzed, so its decisions operate under different timing constraints. If exact size is unnecessary, quality-based encoding can be a more direct way to choose acceptable pictures and let size vary. Neither method restores detail already missing from the source. See Also Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Encoder Presets Video Bitrate References x265: Quality and rate-control options NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Variable Bitrate Video Encoding | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Variable bitrate (VBR) encoding lets the amount of coded data change through a video. Simple pictures can use fewer bits, leaving more room for complicated motion, texture, or grain. The term covers more than one approach. An average-bitrate encode tries to meet an overall data budget while varying the rate locally. A quality-controlled encode can also produce VBR, with the final average determined mainly by the source and quality target. Each column represents one second. The VBR values are 2, 3, 6, 7, 2, 3, 5, and 4 Mb/s; their average is 4 Mb/s. This is a constructed allocation example, not a codec benchmark.
