Average and peak answer different questions Reported property What it helps establish Average bitrate Total data and approximate storage size Short-interval demand How much data a difficult section consumes Encoder rate and buffer limits How local variation is constrained Actual available delivery rate Whether playback can keep its buffer supplied An average of 4 Mb/s in the example does not mean a connection delivering exactly 4 Mb/s will handle every period without preparation. A buffer can accumulate data during easier periods and cover later demand, but starting or seeking near the demanding section changes that situation. In Emby, the source's rate variation remains relevant during direct delivery. Transcoding can create a new stream with different constraints; its rate-control settings and the selected quality limit determine that output. VBR does not automatically mean smaller files or better quality. Those depend on the target, encoder, and source. Use the actual pictures and delivery requirements when comparing results, and distinguish a maximum-rate constraint from a whole-file average. See Also Constant Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Two-Pass Video Encoding Bitrate Variation References NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.title: Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/rate-con.keywords: Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) A film can average 4 Mb/s and still contain a short section that needs data faster than a decoder can accept it. Video Buffering Verifier (VBV) constraints address that problem by asking whether the encoded pictures can pass through a defined rate-and-buffer model. The model has three essential ingredients: how data arrives, how much coded data can be stored, and when each picture removes its required data. An average for the whole film leaves the last two questions unanswered. Rate, capacity, and occupancy Suppose a simplified model accepts data at 4 Mb/s , has a capacity of 8 megabits , and starts with 4 megabits already available . The input rate describes how quickly the buffer can refill. Capacity is its maximum stored amount. Occupancy is how much it contains at a particular moment. A large picture can use data accumulated during easier pictures. It can require more than one frame interval's worth of arriving data without exceeding the model, provided that enough has arrived before its removal time. A picture fails the model if it needs bits that are not available when it must be decoded. The opposite limit matters too: arrivals and removals must follow rules that keep stored data within the permitted capacity. Codec models specify these details more precisely than this simplified illustration. Follow a burst through the buffer The following calculation groups picture removals into one-second intervals to make the arithmetic visible. Real bitstream conformance checks operate at the codec's specified removal times. Interval Starting occupancy Data arrives Pictures use Ending occupancy 1 4 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 2 Mb 2 2 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 0 Mb 3, same demand continues 0 Mb 4 Mb 6 Mb 2 Mb short The first two demanding intervals succeed because the buffer had a reserve. Continuing the burst exhausts it. An easier interval using 2 Mb could rebuild the reserve by 2 Mb under the same arrival rate. The film might still average 4 Mb/s overall. That would not repair the shortage in interval 3: data from a later easy scene cannot travel backward in time. Buffer capacity divided by arrival rate gives a useful scale. Here, 8 Mb / 4 Mb/s is two seconds. It is a description of the model's capacity relative to the rate, not an automatic two-second player startup setting. What the encoder changes An encoder enforcing VBV has to fit its choices to the available budget at each point. During a difficult scene it may increase quantization, simplifying the residual information and reducing the number of coded bits. The result can be a local loss of texture or visible artifacts even when a quality setting stays unchanged. In x265, vbv-maxrate supplies the rate constraint and vbv-bufsize supplies the capacity. Their documented units differ: kilobits per second for the former, kilobits for the latter. Initial fullness is another setting because starting with a larger reserve changes what an early burst can use. Combining CRF with these constraints lets the encoder pursue its quality target while the model permits it. When the two conflict, the delivery constraint can take priority. A smaller buffer or lower rate leaves less room to accommodate a difficult sequence at that quality. VBV is also not a synonym for CBR . A variable-rate encode can obey a bounded-buffer model. The buffer is exactly what allows some variation in picture sizes and short-term demand. Coding buffer versus playback buffer The coding model describes a constrained decoder's coded-data supply. An app's downloaded-data buffer deals with the actual network: requests, bandwidth variation, latency, and stalls. They are related in use but are different quantities. A player can accumulate data before starting, yet still have a decoder with limits on coded-picture size, timing, or buffering. Conversely, a conforming bitstream can stall over a connection that delivers less data than it needs. For an Emby transcode whose picture becomes softer during a busy scene, bitrate and buffering constraints provide a possible causal explanation: the encoder had to reduce that scene's data demand. For a stream whose picture is fine but playback pauses, examine delivery as well. The two observations lead to different parts of the playback path. See Also Constant Bitrate Video Encoding Variable Bitrate Video Encoding Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Codec Levels and Tiers References ITU-T H.262: MPEG-2 Video ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding x265: Quality and rate-control options

articles/video/encoding-quality/Video-En.title: Video Encoder Presets | Emby Learn
articles/video/encoding-quality/Video-En.keywords: Video Encoder Presets An encoder preset chooses a bundle of settings controlling how much work an encoder spends on its decisions. It can change searches for motion, picture partitioning, reference use, lookahead, and other analysis. A slower preset often gives the encoder more opportunities to use its bitrate efficiently. That can improve the picture at a fixed rate or reduce the data needed for a comparable picture. The result depends on the encoder and source; “slow” is not a fixed quality level. Choice What it controls Preset Encoding effort and tool choices Bitrate or quality target The rate-control objective Profile and level Bitstream compatibility constraints Tuning Priorities for a source type or use case These controls interact. Changing a preset while retaining the same CRF can change the size and picture, because the encoder makes different decisions. It is not safe to assume that the slower result must always be smaller. The labels are implementation-specific x265 names presets from ultrafast through placebo. A hardware encoder can use a different scale and different internal tools. A “medium” preset in two encoders does not establish equivalent speed, efficiency, or resource use. More encoding work also does not translate directly into more decoding work. The encoder's search can be expensive while producing a stream with similar decoder requirements. Check its actual profile and tool choices rather than judging playback compatibility from the preset name. For Emby video transcoding, the encoder has to supply pictures quickly enough for playback. Extra analysis is useful only within the available processing budget, including other sessions and required filters. For an offline library conversion, more time may be acceptable. Compare representative scenes and the resulting rate or size, and keep the source fixed. Moving from a fast to a slow preset cannot recover detail that the source's earlier compression has already removed. See Also Constant Rate Factor (CRF) for Video Video Bitrate Two-Pass Video Encoding How Video Codecs Affect Playback Compatibility References x265: Presets and tunings NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.1: Rate control and multipass encoding

articles/video/frame-timing/Frame-Rate-C.title: Frame-Rate Conversion | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/Frame-Rate-C.keywords: Frame-Rate Conversion Frame-rate conversion adapts video to a different picture rate. The result depends on how pictures are added, removed, or retimed; selecting a higher number does not automatically create more captured motion. Method What happens to the pictures Effect on programme duration Repeat or drop Existing pictures fill new time slots Can remain unchanged Blend Neighbouring pictures are mixed Can remain unchanged Motion interpolation Estimated intermediate pictures are created Can remain unchanged Speed change Existing pictures are played at a different pace Changes unless another operation compensates Repeating pictures is inexpensive, but uneven repetition can cause judder. Blending can leave ghost-like edges. Motion interpolation can look smoother while introducing errors in the estimated movement. Display cadence can change without a new file A 24 fps film fits a 120 Hz display evenly: each picture lasts five refreshes. On a 60 Hz display, a common presentation alternates two and three refreshes per picture. Original cadence schematic for exact 24 fps and 60 Hz. Ten refresh intervals present four film pictures. These are display holds, not interlaced fields or newly captured frames. Display mode selection can sometimes avoid the need to convert the encoded video. Support depends on the Emby app, operating system, and connected display. A server's output frame rate and the display's active refresh rate should therefore be checked separately. A speed change has a different purpose. Playing a 24 fps sequence at 25 fps makes it about 4.17% faster and shortens it. Audio and subtitles must follow the new timing; pitch handling is another processing decision. When comparing an original file with a converted Emby stream, ask whether the timeline stayed the same, whether the number of unique pictures changed, and where any repetition was introduced. Those questions explain the visible result more accurately than the output fps value alone. See Also Video Frame Rate Motion Interpolation Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown References FFmpeg command-line documentation FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters

articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.title: Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.keywords: Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 The familiar labels 23.976 , 29.97 , and 59.94 are rounded names for precise ratios. They are not irregular frame rates: a stream can run at one of them with perfectly constant picture spacing. Familiar label Exact rate Time per picture, approximately 23.976 fps 24000/1001 fps 41.7083 ms 29.97 fps 30000/1001 fps 33.3667 ms 59.94 fps 60000/1001 fps 16.6833 ms Each is the corresponding integer rate multiplied by 1000/1001. ITU-R BT.709 includes these fractional alternatives alongside the integer-rate systems. A small difference adds up Suppose a sequence contains exactly 86,400 pictures. At 24 fps it lasts 3,600 seconds. At 24000/1001 fps it lasts 3,603.6 seconds. The difference is only 0.1% in duration, but it becomes 3.6 seconds across this example. That helps explain a subtitle track that starts in sync and gradually drifts when it was timed against a version played at a slightly different speed. A constant subtitle offset moves everything together; it cannot correct a speed difference. For an Emby library, keep the file's original timestamps and exact rate consistent. Rounding a label for readability is harmless. Rewriting timing as if 23.976 were exactly 24 changes the presentation unless a proper conversion accompanies it. Audio timing also has to stay aligned. Telecine commonly connects 24000/1001 film pictures to 60000/1001 television fields. The ratios fit that repeating cadence exactly; using the rounded decimal values in long calculations introduces unnecessary error. Do not infer variable frame rate merely because the rate is fractional. “Fractional” describes the numerical rate. “Variable” describes whether the spacing between successive pictures changes. See Also Video Frame Rate Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown Variable Frame Rate References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg command-line documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.title: Variable Frame Rate | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.keywords: Variable Frame Rate Variable frame rate (VFR) means that the time between successive pictures can change within a video. The player follows each picture's presentation timestamp rather than assuming one fixed interval for the whole stream. Phones, screen recorders, and edited or combined sources can produce such files. A recording can use fewer pictures during a static period and more when the scene changes, although VFR does not require that particular strategy. Original numerical example. Constant-rate picture starts are 0, 40, 80, and 120 ms; variable-rate starts are 0, 40, 60, and 120 ms. It is not a measurement of a particular device. Variable-rate example Picture start Interval to next picture A 0 ms 40 ms B 40 ms 20 ms C 60 ms 60 ms An average frame rate summarizes a period; it cannot tell you every interval within it. A file described as approximately 30 fps may contain pictures with shorter and longer durations. Timing keeps the recording intact VFR is not inherently damaged video. When timestamps are correct and supported throughout playback, the pictures and audio can remain synchronized. Tools that assume every picture has the average duration can introduce timing errors during editing, conversion, or subtitle preparation. For an Emby video that behaves differently after conversion, compare the source timestamps with the converted output. Converting VFR to a constant rate can repeat or drop pictures while retaining the original timeline. Merely assigning a new fixed duration to every source picture can change the duration instead. Media inspection should include picture-level timestamps when stream-level summaries disagree. FFprobe can report individual frames; a single nominal or average rate is insufficient evidence for the full cadence. A constant fractional rate , such as 24000/1001 fps, is a separate case: its interval is precise and remains fixed. See Also Video Frame Rate Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 Frame-Rate Conversion References FFmpeg command-line documentation FFprobe media inspection documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.title: Video Frame Rate | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/frame-rates/.keywords: Video Frame Rate Frame rate describes how many complete video pictures are presented each second, usually written as frames per second or fps. At 24 fps, successive pictures are normally about 41.7 milliseconds apart; at 60 fps, they are about 16.7 milliseconds apart. Constant frame rate Time between pictures, approximately 24 fps 41.67 ms 25 fps 40.00 ms 30 fps 33.33 ms 50 fps 20.00 ms 60 fps 16.67 ms More captured pictures can describe motion more frequently. That is especially noticeable in sport, camera pans, or scrolling text. It does not automatically make each individual picture sharper: shutter exposure, motion blur, resolution, and compression still matter. The screen has a rate of its own A display's refresh rate is how often it updates, measured in hertz. A 120 Hz display can show a 24 fps film by holding each picture for five refreshes. Those extra refreshes do not contain additional recorded moments. If the rates do not divide evenly, some pictures may remain visible longer than others, producing an uneven cadence. Frame-rate conversion and display mode selection are different ways of dealing with rate mismatches. In Emby media information, the file's frame rate describes the source stream. An app or television can present it using a different refresh rate or additional motion processing. Check both when investigating judder; a smooth server delivery path does not establish a uniform display cadence. Also check whether the source is progressive or interlaced . A reported 25-frame/s interlaced recording can contain 50 field times per second. Treating it as 25 progressive motion samples loses an important part of its description. Finally, “24 fps” in a short label may actually mean 24000/1001 fps . The precise rate matters when matching timestamps and subtitles. See Also Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 Variable Frame Rate Frame-Rate Conversion References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg command-line documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Deinterlacing | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Deinterlacing Deinterlacing turns alternating fields into complete pictures suitable for progressive display. Its difficult case is motion: the two fields were captured at different times, so simply weaving their lines together can produce comb-like edges. Original reduced-line schematic. The reconstruction illustrates the principle of retaining one field's time and estimating its missing lines; it is not a measured output from a named filter. Approach Useful property Typical limitation Weave both fields Retains existing lines in a static area Moving edges can comb Reconstruct from each field Can retain every field's motion time Missing lines require estimation Blend fields Can soften combing Moving objects can leave double edges Motion-adaptive reconstruction Treats static and moving regions differently Accuracy depends on detecting motion correctly Algorithms can combine these ideas; the rows describe principles rather than four exclusive codec modes. The output rate matters A native 50-field/s source contains 50 motion times each second. Generating one complete picture per field produces 50p output and can preserve that motion cadence. Generating one picture per pair produces 25p output and generally retains fewer temporal samples. Corresponding fractional-rate examples are 59.94p and 29.97p. For Emby playback, deinterlacing can happen in the player or during server transcoding , depending on the route and capabilities. Check the delivered video's scan type and rate when a broadcast recording becomes less fluid after conversion. A “1080” height alone does not show whether its motion cadence survived. Correct field order is essential: reversing the temporal order can create backward steps. A progressive picture flagged as interlaced should not automatically be processed as native interlaced capture. For a clean film pulldown sequence, inverse telecine may recover original complete pictures more faithfully than estimating their missing lines. Mixed material needs processing that handles the changes between film and video sections. See Also Interlaced Video Video Field Order Inverse Telecine References FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Interlaced Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Interlaced Video Interlaced video alternates between two sets of picture lines, called fields . One field contains the top set of alternating lines; the other contains the bottom set. In native interlaced capture, they describe successive moments rather than one shared picture time. That is why weaving two moving fields together can reveal comb-like edges. An object has moved between captures, so its position differs on alternating lines. Original schematic with a reduced line count. Green lines belong to the earlier top field and blue lines to the later bottom field; their horizontal positions differ because the object moved. Interlaced timing Field times per second Pairs of fields per second 50-field/s system 50 25 60000/1001-field/s system About 59.94 About 29.97 A label such as “1080i50” commonly counts fields. A media inspector may instead report the pair rate as 25 fps. These can describe the same stream, so check the convention before deciding that half the motion is missing. Preserve the motion, not just the height Modern flat-panel presentation uses complete pictures. Deinterlacing reconstructs them from the fields. Producing one output picture per field can preserve the source's 50 or 59.94 motion samples per second; producing one per pair usually retains fewer temporal samples. For an Emby library containing broadcast recordings, the source scan type and field order help explain combing, jitter, or unexpectedly less fluid motion after processing. Correct delivery alone cannot repair an incorrect interpretation of the fields. Not every interlace-marked file contains native interlaced capture. Telecine can distribute progressive film pictures across fields, and progressive segmented frame transport is another distinct case. Choosing the right reconstruction depends on what the fields actually represent. See Also Video Field Order Deinterlacing Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown Progressive Video References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Inverse Telecine | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Inverse Telecine Inverse telecine (IVTC) recovers progressive film pictures from a telecined sequence. When a clean 3:2 cadence is present, it can turn a 29.97-frame-pair/s transfer back into the original 23.976 progressive pictures per second without changing the programme's duration. There are usually two jobs: join the fields that belong to the same film picture, then remove the redundant reconstructed picture in each five-picture cycle. Stage in an illustrative cycle Pictures or field pairs Stored telecined pairs AA, BB, BC, CD, DD Field matching using a suitable phase A, B, C, D, D Duplicate removal A, B, C, D Letters identify original film pictures. The matching phase can produce a different duplicate position while recovering the same four pictures. Recovery differs from interpolation When the fields match correctly, IVTC can reuse the original picture lines rather than estimating missing ones. That is an advantage over ordinary deinterlacing for a film transfer. The final encoding may still be lossy if the reconstructed pictures are compressed again. FFmpeg separates field matching from duplicate removal with filters such as fieldmatch and decimate. This also allows a deinterlacing fallback for portions that do not match cleanly. That implementation is an example, rather than a promise about the processing used in every Emby session. For a film in an Emby library, look for a regular repetition pattern and combed pairs before deciding that IVTC is appropriate. A generic 29.97 fps label is insufficient. Edits can interrupt the cadence, and an episode can combine film footage, video-shot inserts, and animated captions. Dropping every fifth picture without first matching fields can discard needed lines or leave combing. Applying the same operation to native interlaced video removes genuinely different capture times. A successful restoration should retain the programme's timing and audio synchronization, show complete pictures in moving scenes, and avoid introducing a repeated hitch at cadence changes. See Also Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown Deinterlacing Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 References FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Progressive Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Progressive Video Progressive video represents each picture as a complete frame. A 1080p frame contains the full 1080-line picture, rather than combining alternating lines captured at two successive field times. The letter p identifies progressive scanning. In “1080p24,” 1080 describes the picture height and 24 describes the frame rate. Neither value tells you the bitrate, color format, or quality of the compression. Progressive example Complete pictures per second Picture height 1080p24 24 1080 lines 1080p50 50 1080 lines 2160p60 60 2160 lines These examples use integer rates; corresponding fractional-rate formats also exist. Complete frames still sample time Progressive does not mean motion is continuous. Each captured picture comes from an exposure, and the next picture follows later. A low frame rate can produce visible steps during a pan; a long exposure can blur movement within one frame. Both effects can occur in entirely valid progressive video. For Emby playback, a progressive source can be decoded and scaled without reconstructing missing lines from alternate capture times. That simplifies the presentation path, but does not remove the need for compatible codecs, correct timing, or suitable display processing. There is one useful wrinkle in older studio material: progressive segmented frame (PsF) transport splits a progressive picture into two field-shaped segments. Both segments belong to the same captured picture. That differs from native interlaced video , whose alternating fields describe successive times. Consequently, the presence of field-like transport or an interlace flag does not by itself prove that the original scene was captured with interlaced motion. Inspect moving content and the source's signaling together. Unnecessary deinterlacing can alter an otherwise complete progressive image. See Also Interlaced Video Video Frame Rate Video Field Order References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-R BT.2020: Ultra-high-definition picture parameters

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Telecine and 3:2 Pulldown Telecine adapts film pictures to television timing. The familiar 3:2 pulldown cadence presents successive film pictures for alternating three-field and two-field intervals. Four source pictures occupy ten field intervals, fitting a 24-to-60 relationship. For the common fractional-rate version, 24000/1001 film pictures per second become 60000/1001 field intervals per second. Those fields are often stored or reported as 30000/1001 frame pairs per second. Original cadence schematic, starting at a two-field phase: A A B B B C C D D D. Top and bottom fields alternate. Adjacent pairs are AA, BB, BC, CD, and DD; a different starting phase shifts the pattern. More fields, the same film motion The repeated fields do not record new moments. They hold existing film pictures for different lengths of time. That uneven hold can create familiar film judder, especially during horizontal pans. Source within one cycle Television representation Four progressive film pictures Ten field intervals Equal source picture durations Alternating two- and three-field holds One picture time per film frame Some stored pairs combine different picture times In hard telecine , the repetitions are represented in the stored pictures or fields. In soft telecine , signaling can instruct presentation to repeat fields without storing all those repetitions as separate coded pictures. The handling depends on the codec and transport. For an Emby library of older film transfers or television recordings, a 29.97 fps interlaced description therefore does not necessarily mean the camera captured 59.94 distinct motion moments. The source may instead contain a recoverable 23.976 fps film sequence. Inverse telecine tries to recover that sequence. It is useful when this cadence is present; applying it to native interlaced sport can remove real motion samples. Mixed programmes may contain both kinds of material. See Also Inverse Telecine Interlaced Video Fractional Frame Rates: 23.976, 29.97, and 59.94 References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.title: Video Field Order | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/interlacing-.keywords: Video Field Order Field order tells a decoder or deinterlacer which field comes first in time. Top field first (TFF) presents the top field before the bottom field; bottom field first (BFF) does the reverse. “Top” and “bottom” identify alternating line sets. They do not mean the upper and lower halves of the image, and they do not determine which capture time is earlier without the field-order information. Correct 50-field/s example First pair Second pair TFF Top at 0 ms, bottom at 20 ms Top at 40 ms, bottom at 60 ms BFF Bottom at 0 ms, top at 20 ms Bottom at 40 ms, top at 60 ms Why reversed order looks like jitter For the TFF example, the intended motion order is 0 → 20 → 40 → 60 ms. Interpreting each pair backwards makes it 20 → 0 → 60 → 40 ms: the object repeatedly steps backward, then jumps forward. This can be more noticeable in a slow pan than in a still frame. Original numerical schematic using the field times from the table. Each dot is a temporal sample of steady movement; the arrows show presentation order. For Emby recordings, check field order when motion jitters despite an apparently adequate frame rate. A file's tag is evidence, but a wrongly tagged source can still need investigation. Inspect a moving section and compare the result under the two interpretations. Changing a field-order label and converting the actual field arrangement are different operations. Relabeling is appropriate when the samples are correct and only their description is wrong. A genuine conversion must handle the line sets and timing coherently. Progressive frames do not acquire new motion samples by adding a field-order flag. Telecined sources also need their cadence understood before field reconstruction is chosen. See Also Interlaced Video Deinterlacing Inverse Telecine References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/frame-timing/Motion-Inter.title: Motion Interpolation | Emby Learn
articles/video/frame-timing/Motion-Inter.keywords: Motion Interpolation Motion interpolation estimates pictures between existing frames. It tries to work out where objects move, then creates intermediate views for those extra presentation times. Original qualitative schematic. The middle position is estimated from the two recorded pictures; it was not captured by the camera. Repeating a frame holds the same object position. Blending two frames can show both positions at once. Motion-based interpolation instead tries to move the object to a plausible position between them. Situation Why estimation can be difficult An object passes behind another Hidden areas are unavailable in one picture A rapid cut changes the scene There may be no matching movement across the cut Thin wires, lettering, or a ball move quickly Small structures are easily matched incorrectly Strong blur or flashing light Picture differences do not describe movement alone Errors can appear as warped outlines, halos, or briefly broken objects. Even a technically clean result changes the look of motion, which is why interpolated film can resemble high-frame-rate video. It can happen after delivery Interpolation may be performed while making a new file, in a player, or by a television's motion processing. If a television applies it to an Emby app's output, the server can still report Direct Play : that delivery status does not describe every later display operation. When a film's motion looks unfamiliar, check the display's motion settings as well as the source frame rate. Different manufacturers use different names, and the settings can vary by input or picture mode. Interpolation cannot restore the actual camera exposures that were never recorded. It estimates plausible pictures from available evidence. Nor is it the same as inter-frame prediction , which helps a codec reconstruct already encoded source pictures rather than invent additional presentation times. See Also Frame-Rate Conversion Video Frame Rate Inter-Frame Video Prediction References FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/fundamentals/Digital-Vide.title: How Digital Video Represents Moving Pictures | Emby Learn
articles/video/fundamentals/Digital-Vide.keywords: How Digital Video Represents Moving Pictures A video is a sequence of pictures, called frames , together with information about when to show them. Each picture describes a grid of samples; displaying successive pictures at the intended times creates the appearance of motion. An original schematic: three pictures of one moving object, shown in time order. The drawing simplifies the pixel grid and does not represent a particular video codec. Three independent questions describe much of what you see in an Emby media information panel: Property The question it answers Example Resolution How many picture samples are there? 1920 × 1080 Frame rate How many pictures arrive each second? 24 frames/s Compression How are those pictures represented efficiently? A compressed H.264 bitstream Increasing resolution does not increase the number of moments recorded. Increasing frame rate does not reveal detail that the camera never captured. Both can increase the work required to decode and display the video, but neither alone measures picture quality. The file contains instructions, too Most library videos do not store every pixel of every frame independently. A decoder reconstructs pictures from compressed data, using predictions and corrections. It also needs the stream's dimensions, color description, and timing information. The media container keeps that video track alongside other tracks, such as audio. During Direct Play , the Emby app receives the original media and performs the required decoding. During video transcoding, Emby Server decodes the source and encodes a new video stream for the app. Either route must eventually produce pictures at the correct times. This is why a recognizable file extension is only the beginning of a compatibility check. The contents of the video track determine what the decoder must understand. See Also Video Resolution Video Frame Rate How Video Compression Works References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/An.title: Anamorphic Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/An.keywords: Anamorphic Video Anamorphic video uses a stored picture grid whose proportions differ from the intended displayed picture. In a common digital example, a 1440 × 1080 grid is presented as 16:9 by making its samples wider than square. This describes digital storage and presentation. It does not prove that a film was photographed through an anamorphic camera lens; a digitally anamorphic recording can come from an ordinary camera. Original proportional example: 1440 × 1080 samples with PAR 4:3 have the same display proportions as 1920 × 1080 square pixels. The drawing shows presentation, not newly captured detail. Property Example value Stored dimensions 1440 × 1080 Stored width-to-height ratio 4:3 Pixel aspect ratio 4:3 Intended display aspect ratio 16:9 The advantage is that the format can represent a wide image within a constrained sample grid. The tradeoff is fewer horizontal samples than an otherwise comparable 1920 × 1080 square-pixel recording. The actual quality also depends on the source and compression. A squeezed picture usually has an explanation If an Emby app or another player displays this example as 4:3, it has not applied the intended pixel aspect ratio , or the file lacks correct signaling. People look too thin and circles become narrow ovals. Stretching every file to 16:9 would fix this example while distorting a genuine 4:3 recording. A correctly handled anamorphic source can be displayed directly, or converted during processing to a square-pixel output. The output should retain the same intended shape. Letterboxing is a different technique: it adds bars around a picture instead of describing wider or taller pixels. For older disc and broadcast material, inspect the display ratio as well as the width and height. The dimensions alone do not tell you whether the file is anamorphic. See Also Video Pixel Aspect Ratio Video Display Aspect Ratio Video Resolution References ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/Vi.title: Video Display Aspect Ratio | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/Vi.keywords: Video Display Aspect Ratio Display aspect ratio (DAR) describes the intended shape of the video picture: its displayed width divided by its displayed height. A 16:9 picture is about 1.78 times as wide as it is tall, regardless of whether it fills a phone, a television, or a projector screen. Original proportional drawing. Both pictures have the same height; the wider outline is 16:9. The stored dimensions are only part of the calculation. For an unrotated rectangular picture with no additional display crop: DAR = (stored width ÷ stored height) × pixel aspect ratio Stored grid Pixel aspect ratio Intended display aspect ratio 1920 × 1080 1:1 16:9 1440 × 1080 4:3 16:9 720 × 576 16:15 4:3 The last row is a full-raster numerical example. Legacy capture and disc workflows can use different active-image conventions; follow the actual file's signaling. A screen ratio is a separate choice When a picture and screen have different proportions, fitting the whole picture produces letterboxing or pillarboxing . Filling the screen instead requires cropping or distortion. Making a 4:3 recording fit a 16:9 screen by stretching it sideways makes people wider, too. For an Emby library item that appears squeezed, compare the file's dimensions with its pixel aspect ratio and display ratio. A playback fit or zoom choice changes presentation; incorrect file metadata changes what the player considers the intended shape. Correcting one is not a substitute for checking the other. DAR usually describes the video frame. When black bars are baked into that frame, the film inside the bars can have a wider or narrower aspect ratio of its own. See Also Video Pixel Aspect Ratio Anamorphic Video Letterboxing and Pillarboxing References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/Vi.title: Video Pixel Aspect Ratio | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/aspect-ratios/Vi.keywords: Video Pixel Aspect Ratio A video sample does not always represent a square on the screen. Pixel aspect ratio (PAR) describes its intended width relative to its height. PAR 1:1 means square pixels; PAR 4:3 means that each sample is presented one-third wider than it is tall. FFmpeg calls this sample aspect ratio , often abbreviated SAR. Other contexts use SAR for the stored frame's width-to-height ratio, so check the tool's definition before comparing numbers. Original schematic. Both grids contain the same number of samples; their presentation widths differ. Pixel aspect ratio What it does to an unchanged grid 1:1 Preserves the grid's numerical width-to-height ratio 4:3 Makes the displayed picture one-third wider 16:15 Makes the displayed picture about 6.7% wider Why the metadata matters A 1440 × 1080 frame has a stored ratio of 4:3. With PAR 4:3, its display ratio becomes 16:9. Treating the samples as square squeezes the picture horizontally, even though every sample is still present. That makes PAR particularly useful when investigating older television recordings and anamorphic sources in an Emby library. Different files with identical stored dimensions can legitimately have different display shapes. Changing a PAR flag tells the player to interpret the existing samples differently. It does not resample the image or create additional detail. Converting the picture to an equivalent square-pixel grid is a separate processing operation. Be cautious with standard-definition rules copied from a format name. Whether a workflow describes the whole coded raster or a smaller active region can affect the expected ratio. The encoded signaling, container display information, and a recognizable object in the picture provide better evidence than dimensions alone. See Also Video Display Aspect Ratio Anamorphic Video ITU-R BT.601 References ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/geometry/Letterboxing-Pil.title: Letterboxing and Pillarboxing | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/Letterboxing-Pil.keywords: Letterboxing and Pillarboxing Black bars usually mean that the picture and the screen have different proportions. Letterboxing leaves space above and below a wider picture. Pillarboxing leaves space to the left and right of a narrower one. Original proportional examples on 16:9 screens: a 2.4:1 film at left and a 4:3 picture at right. Green marks the active image. The bars preserve the entire picture at its intended aspect ratio . Removing them by zooming requires part of the picture to leave the screen. Removing them by stretching changes the shapes inside it. Are the bars in the file? Where the bars come from What the file contains Consequence Added during display Only the narrower or wider picture Their size can change with the screen or player window Baked into the video Picture samples plus dark border samples The bars remain part of the decoded frame A 1920 × 800 film can gain bars when fitted to a 1920 × 1080 display. Another copy may already contain those bars in a 1920 × 1080 frame. Both can look identical on that display, yet behave differently when fitted to an ultrawide screen. For Emby playback, this distinction helps explain why selecting a fill or zoom mode sometimes still leaves bars. The player may be fitting the whole stored frame, including its baked-in borders. Cropping can remove those samples, but it should be based on the actual content. Films can change aspect ratio between scenes, and subtitles may occupy a border. A crop that looks right at the beginning can cut off material later. Empty space is often the correct way to preserve a composition, rather than evidence that playback quality is too low. See Also Video Display Aspect Ratio Cropping Video Video Resolution References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters FFmpeg video filters documentation

articles/video/geometry/Video-Cropping.h.title: Cropping Video | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/Video-Cropping.h.keywords: Cropping Video Cropping selects a smaller rectangular region of a video picture. It can remove baked-in black bars or unwanted edges, but it also discards whatever lies outside that rectangle. A crop is described by its output width and height and by where its upper-left corner begins. For example, suppose a 1920 × 1080 frame contains a 1920 × 800 film centered vertically: Crop property Value in this example Left edge 0 Top edge 140 Width retained 1920 Height retained 800 Rows removed 140 above and 140 below These numbers describe an illustrative source, not a crop preset for every widescreen film. At square pixels the result has an aspect ratio of 2.4:1. Cropping is not resizing Cropping keeps the selected samples and changes the picture boundary. Resizing reconstructs a picture at a new resolution. A workflow can do both, but scaling a 1920 × 1080 frame to 1920 × 800 without a crop squashes the whole image instead of removing its bars. A visible crop can be performed while displaying video, or during conversion to a new encoded stream. Some formats also signal a display crop without deleting coded samples. These approaches can produce the same visible rectangle while leaving different data in the file. For an Emby library, inspect more than one scene before making a cropped copy. Variable-aspect-ratio sequences, end credits, and subtitles can extend into an area that appeared empty earlier. Automatic black-border detection can also mistake a dark scene for a border. Cropping may reduce the work of a later encoder because it has fewer samples to encode. It does not guarantee a particular file-size saving, and changing the rectangle can affect the display aspect ratio . Keep the intended picture shape consistent with the final dimensions and pixel aspect ratio. See Also Letterboxing and Pillarboxing Video Display Aspect Ratio Video Resolution References FFmpeg video filters documentation ITU-T H.264: Advanced video coding

articles/video/geometry/Video-Resolution.title: Video Resolution | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/Video-Resolution.keywords: Video Resolution Video resolution is the number of picture samples across and down a frame. A 1920 × 1080 video has 2,073,600 positions in its main picture grid: a little over two million. A resolution label describes that grid, rather than the amount of visible detail. A sharp 1080p source can look better than a poorly compressed 4K copy. Enlarging an older recording adds output pixels, but cannot recover information that was absent from the recording. Familiar label Common stored dimensions Main-grid samples per frame 720p HD 1280 × 720 921,600 1080p Full HD 1920 × 1080 2,073,600 2160p Ultra HD 3840 × 2160 8,294,400 DCI 4K full container 4096 × 2160 8,847,360 These are common full-frame formats. A cropped film can have a different height, and “4K” alone does not identify one exact width. Count the picture, then interpret its shape The width-to-height ratio of the stored grid is not always the displayed shape. Anamorphic video uses nonsquare pixels, so a 1440 × 1080 grid can represent a 16:9 picture. Rotation metadata can also turn a landscape grid into a portrait presentation. Black bars introduce another distinction. A 1920 × 1080 file can include a film occupying only 1920 × 800 pixels, with the remaining rows storing the bars. The file is still 1920 × 1080; the active image is smaller. For Emby playback, more samples generally mean more scaling and decoding work. Ultra HD contains four times as many main-grid positions as Full HD. That does not guarantee a file four times as large: bitrate, frame rate, compression, and the scene itself also matter. Read the resolution alongside those properties when comparing versions of a film. See Also Video Display Aspect Ratio Anamorphic Video How Digital Video Represents Moving Pictures References ITU-R BT.709: HDTV picture parameters ITU-R BT.601: Standard-definition television parameters ITU-R BT.2020: Ultra-high-definition picture parameters DCI Digital Cinema System Specification 1.4.2: Image containers

articles/video/geometry/Video-Rotation-M.title: Video Rotation Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/video/geometry/Video-Rotation-M.keywords: Video Rotation Metadata A phone can record a portrait clip while storing each frame in a landscape grid. Rotation metadata tells the player how to orient that grid for display, so the stored width and height need not match the picture you see. QuickTime and related media workflows use display transformation matrices, which can describe rotation as well as other transformations. Media inspectors may present the rotation as a simple angle even when it is represented by a matrix in the file. Square-pixel example Stored dimensions Presented dimensions No quarter-turn 1920 × 1080 1920 × 1080 One quarter-turn 1920 × 1080 1080 × 1920 The table assumes a pure 90° rotation and no additional scaling or crop. Rotating the description or the pictures There are two ways to make an upright result. A player can rotate the decoded picture while presenting it, leaving the stored samples unchanged. Alternatively, a conversion can rotate the samples and encode a new stream whose dimensions already match the upright picture. When the samples are physically rotated, the old rotation instruction must also be handled correctly. Applying the same instruction again can rotate the result twice. Simply deleting metadata from an untouched sideways recording causes the opposite problem: the player loses the information it needed. This matters when the same home video looks upright in one Emby playback route and sideways in another. Check the original file's display transformation and the dimensions of any transcoded output. Direct Play and transcoding put the interpretation and processing at different points in the playback path. A correct thumbnail is useful evidence, but it does not prove that every playback component has handled the metadata the same way. Compare the actual video as well as the poster or preview image. See Also Video Resolution Video Display Aspect Ratio References Apple QuickTime File Format: Matrices FFmpeg: Display transformation matrices FFmpeg command-line documentation

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: How Dolby Vision Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: How Dolby Vision Works Dolby Vision carries a picture together with information that helps reproduce it on displays with different capabilities. That information can describe the scene and preserve adjustments made while preparing the release. A useful way to follow the process is: Stage What happens Grading The finished HDR appearance is established Analysis and optional trims Picture characteristics are measured and mapped results can be adjusted Encoding Video and Dolby Vision metadata are packaged for distribution Playback A compatible processing path uses the signal and metadata for the target display The analysis need not involve a colorist manually adjusting every frame. Dolby describes both shot-based analysis, with optional creative trims, and automatic frame-based analysis for appropriate workflows. Dolby Vision is not one interchangeable file format. Its profiles define different ways of delivering the picture. Some have an HDR10 or HLG-compatible base, while others require Dolby Vision-specific interpretation. Some use one video layer; others use two. This matters when two Dolby Vision files behave differently in the same Emby app. The label alone leaves out the profile, codec, container, and the capabilities of the complete playback path. Support for one profile is not proof of support for all of them. Nor does a Dolby Vision indicator reveal every internal processing step. To understand whether a compatible base picture is being used or additional data is involved, start with fallback compatibility and base and enhancement layers . The purpose remains the picture: keep familiar midtones convincing while adapting bright detail and color to the screen available. See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision RPU Metadata Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Metadata levels Dolby Vision: Shot analysis and long-play analysis Dolby Vision: Playback device capabilities

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers The base layer (BL) is the main encoded picture in a Dolby Vision stream. Some profiles also have an enhancement layer (EL) . Dolby Vision metadata accompanies the video but is a different kind of data. Conceptual structure. Packaging and decoder details depend on the profile. An enhancement layer is not simply a second, independently watchable version of the film. In the UHD Blu-ray workflow, it can contain a residual: information used with the base layer to reconstruct the intended signal. The MEL/FEL distinction describes whether that residual contributes additional picture information. The base layer's standalone usefulness depends on the profile. Profile 7 has an HDR10-compatible base. A Profile 5 base requires Dolby Vision-specific interpretation; treating it as ordinary HDR10 is not an equivalent fallback. There is an important packaging trap here: one file or one reported video track does not necessarily mean one coded layer . Container tracks, codec layers, and metadata units describe different levels of the format. For Emby comparisons, a Dolby Vision badge alone is insufficient to establish that enhancement data affected the displayed pixels. Record the source profile and layer information, then identify the player and delivery method. Playback can look plausible when a compatible base is used, even though it is not the complete Dolby Vision reconstruction. See Also Dolby Vision RPU Metadata Dolby Vision MEL and FEL Dolby Vision Profile 7 References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: UHD Blu-ray authoring workflow Dolby: Encoding Dolby Vision mezzanine assets

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision MEL and FEL | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision MEL and FEL MEL means minimum enhancement layer; FEL means full enhancement layer. These terms are especially relevant to Profile 7 UHD Blu-ray content. Enhancement type Picture residual Practical implication MEL Zero residual No additional picture residual needs reconstruction FEL Nonzero residual Full reconstruction needs the enhancement information Both still belong to a Dolby Vision workflow with metadata. MEL therefore does not mean “Dolby Vision without dynamic metadata,” and FEL is not just a larger metadata file. A FEL can carry information needed to reconstruct differences between the encoded base picture and the source prepared for Dolby Vision. Depending on the authoring choices, those differences can involve precision and the brightness range. The visible effect depends on the actual title and processing path; the label alone is not a quality score. This is why a player showing a Dolby Vision indicator does not by itself prove full FEL processing. A useful test needs known content and evidence about the decoder path, not merely the logo appearing on screen. For a file served by Emby, keep three observations separate: the source contains an FEL, the session is using Dolby Vision output, and the additional residual contributes to reconstruction. They are related claims, but one does not establish all three. If an enhancement layer is discarded during a conversion, the resulting file may still produce a valid picture from its compatible base. Calling that operation lossless requires more care than observing that the main video was copied: information present in the original enhancement layer may no longer be available. See Also Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers Dolby Vision Profile 7 Dolby Vision RPU Metadata References Dolby Vision: Distinguishing MEL and non-MEL bitstreams Dolby Vision: UHD Blu-ray authoring workflow

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision RPU Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision RPU Metadata RPU is the name you often see beside Dolby Vision video in media reports. It carries Dolby Vision metadata; it is not an additional movie image or an audio track. The metadata can describe picture characteristics and processing instructions. Depending on the content and metadata version, it can include analysis, target-display trims, and the active picture area. Information in the Dolby Vision workflow Why it matters Scene analysis Describes the picture being adapted Creative trims Adjusts the mapped appearance for a target Active-area information Distinguishes the picture from surrounding letterbox regions The RPU must remain associated with the correct frames. A useful thought experiment is an edit that removes the first second of video but keeps the old metadata timing: the instructions no longer describe the pictures receiving them. Dolby's authoring guide identifies out-of-sync metadata as a possible cause of unexpected brightness changes. In HEVC delivery, the metadata is carried in special units alongside the encoded picture. A media report showing BL+RPU therefore means a base layer plus metadata, not two image layers. BL+EL+RPU adds an enhancement layer . When examining an Emby playback issue, an RPU-present flag establishes that metadata was detected in the source. It does not prove that the player used it, that it is synchronized, or that the full output path supports that Dolby Vision profile. The metadata also cannot simply be borrowed from another release because its title matches. Different edits, frame timing, framing, or grades can break the relationship between the information and the picture. See Also How Dolby Vision Works Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers Dolby Vision MEL and FEL References Dolby: Encoding Dolby Vision mezzanine assets Dolby Vision: Metadata levels Dolby Vision: UHD Blu-ray authoring workflow

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility A Dolby Vision file can sometimes play correctly without Dolby Vision processing by using its compatible base picture . Whether that is possible depends on the stream's profile and base arrangement. Example Compatible base interpretation Profile 5 None as ordinary HDR10 or SDR Profile 7 HDR10 Profile 8.1 HDR10 Profile 8.4 HLG Profile 9 SDR The table describes signal compatibility, not a device-support list. A player still needs to open the container, decode the codec, and deliver a suitable signal. Newer AV1 and multiview profiles introduce their own requirements; see Profile 10 and Profile 20 . There are three distinct outcomes worth separating during Emby playback: The Dolby Vision picture is processed through a supported path. A compatible base is used without the Dolby Vision presentation. The picture is converted into a new output format, for example SDR. The second outcome can avoid video re-encoding, but it does not imply an identical appearance to the first. The third involves a transformation; removing metadata alone does not accomplish it. An SDR television also does not become HDR-capable merely because the source has an HDR10 fallback. It still needs a suitable HDR-to-SDR conversion somewhere in the playback path. For a useful comparison, note both Emby's delivery method and the display's active mode. Direct Play says that the server is delivering the file unchanged. It does not prove which metadata, layers, or fallback the player ultimately uses. See Also Dolby Vision Profile 5 Dolby Vision Profile 7 Dolby Vision Profile 8 How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: Playback device capabilities Dolby: Introduction to Dolby Vision Profile 10 Dolby: Profile 20 FAQ

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 10 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 10 Dolby Vision Profile 10 brings Dolby Vision delivery to AV1 . It uses a single ten-bit picture layer with metadata carried in AV1's metadata structure. Variant Base-picture compatibility 10.0 Dolby Vision-specific interpretation 10.1 HDR10-compatible 10.4 HLG-compatible These are different base arrangements within the profile, not three steps on a quality ladder. Dolby's Profile 10 introduction describes using an existing Dolby Vision master to prepare AV1 delivery; a new profile number does not inherently mean that the film was remastered. For an Emby playback path, there are two separate capability questions: can it decode AV1, and can it use this Dolby Vision profile? Support for HEVC-based Dolby Vision does not answer either question by itself. Likewise, AV1 hardware decoding alone does not establish Dolby Vision Profile 10 support. The fallback picture also depends on the variant. A properly supported HDR10 or HLG base can be useful when Dolby Vision processing is unavailable, while the 10.0 signal needs the appropriate interpretation or conversion. Changing a container or codec label cannot turn HEVC Profile 8 into AV1 Profile 10. The compressed picture format differs, so a real change of codec requires decoding and encoding. Metadata handling must stay consistent with the resulting pictures. When comparing files, retain the codec and base-compatibility details alongside the Dolby Vision label. They explain far more about a playback mismatch than the profile number alone. See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Profile 8 Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby: Introduction to Dolby Vision Profile 10 Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 20 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 20 Dolby Vision Profile 20 extends the delivery system to stereoscopic video: separate views for the left and right eyes. Its 3D form uses Multiview HEVC (MV-HEVC) Main10 , rather than placing two reduced-size views beside each other in one ordinary frame. Structure What the layers represent Profile 20 stereoscopic MV-HEVC Different views of the scene Profile 7 base and enhancement layers Components used to reconstruct a Dolby Vision picture Those are different uses of the word “layer.” A second eye view is not a Profile 7-style enhancement residual. The specification also defines a 2D form using HEVC. Profile 20 therefore does not always mean that a file contains stereo views. The stream and playback capabilities still need inspection; the cited public specification does not make 2D playback a requirement of every approved Profile 20 device. Profile 20 has additional metadata-processing requirements. Existing Dolby Vision support for other profiles is not enough to claim support for it. This is particularly relevant when considering an Emby session on a headset or another multiview display: container handling, view assignment, decoding, and Dolby Vision processing must work together. Current profile definitions list both a Dolby Vision-specific base form and an HLG-compatible form. That signal-level compatibility should not be read as a promise that an ordinary HLG television can play every packaged stereo stream or reproduce both eye views. For a playback report, include whether the content is 2D or stereoscopic, the codec, the base compatibility, and the exact app/device. “Dolby Vision works on this device” leaves the decisive questions unanswered. See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby: Profile 20 FAQ Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 3 (Legacy) | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 3 (Legacy) Dolby Vision Profile 3 is a legacy delivery arrangement. Dolby lists it among profiles not supported for new applications ; it remains useful to recognize when inspecting older material. Property Legacy Profile 3 Codec Eight-bit HEVC Picture structure Base plus enhancement layer Layer resolution relationship Equal resolution Base compatibility No standard HDR10 or SDR fallback It is not a version number for the Dolby Vision grading system, and it does not mean “Profile 8.3.” Profile, metadata version, and base-compatibility identifiers are separate concepts. If an old file appears in an Emby library, current Dolby Vision support on a device is not sufficient evidence of Profile 3 support. Preserve the complete media report when investigating it. The lack of a compatible base is especially important: discarding Dolby Vision information is not equivalent to producing ordinary HDR10. Renaming the profile cannot replace a proper conversion. For comparison, legacy Profile 4 used a different base arrangement with SDR compatibility. See Also Dolby Vision Profile 4 (Legacy) Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Profiles not supported for new applications

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 4 (Legacy) | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 4 (Legacy) Dolby Vision Profile 4 is a legacy dual-layer HEVC arrangement with an SDR-compatible base. Dolby now lists it among profiles not supported for new applications. Property Legacy Profile 4 Codec precision Ten-bit HEVC Picture layers Base and enhancement Enhancement resolution One-quarter of the base picture's pixel count Base fallback SDR-compatible Its ten-bit base is a useful counterexample to the assumption that ten-bit video must be HDR. Precision and the meaning of the signal are different properties. Profile 4 should not be confused with Profile 7 . Both use two layers, but their compatible base pictures differ. A report that mentions only “dual-layer Dolby Vision” omits that important distinction. In an Emby investigation, seeing an SDR output from a compatible Profile 4 base can be a fallback outcome rather than evidence that the entire file was converted. Establish the actual playback method and delivered stream before drawing that conclusion. Legacy status also does not mean that every existing decoder has stopped supporting it. It describes Dolby's direction for new applications, not a universal capability statement about installed devices. See Also Dolby Vision Profile 3 (Legacy) Dolby Vision Profile 7 Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Profiles not supported for new applications Dolby Vision: Distinguishing MEL and non-MEL bitstreams

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 5 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 5 Dolby Vision Profile 5 uses one ten-bit HEVC picture layer with Dolby Vision metadata. Its most important compatibility property is that the base picture is not a standalone HDR10 or SDR picture . Component Profile 5 arrangement Video codec Ten-bit HEVC Picture layers One base layer Dolby Vision metadata Present alongside the video Standard HDR10 or SDR fallback Not provided by the base signal The signal uses Dolby Vision reshaping and the IPT-PQ-C2 color representation. A decoder that understands HEVC compression but then treats the decoded components as ordinary HDR10 can interpret the colors incorrectly. Being able to decompress the frames is only one part of playing them correctly. For an Emby library, this explains why “the device plays HEVC” is not enough evidence that it can display a particular Profile 5 file. The selected player and rendering path must interpret the Dolby Vision signal, or a converter must produce a different correctly encoded output. Removing the Dolby Vision metadata or changing the file's label does not perform that conversion. The underlying sample values still represent the Profile 5 signal. A useful comparison is Profile 8.1 : its compatible base can be used as HDR10 when the rest of the path supports it. Profile 5 makes a different delivery choice. Neither profile number tells you whether one release has a better grade, fewer compression artifacts, or more carefully preserved detail. See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Profile 8 Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 7 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 7 Dolby Vision Profile 7 is the dual-layer format used in the Dolby Vision UHD Blu-ray workflow. It combines an HDR10-compatible base with an enhancement layer and Dolby Vision metadata. Part Purpose Base layer A complete HDR10-compatible picture Enhancement layer Additional reconstruction information, according to the authoring mode RPU metadata Dolby Vision processing information associated with the pictures A non-Dolby Vision HDR10 path can use the base picture, provided the container, codec, and playback path are otherwise supported. That fallback is an intentional property of the format, not a sign that the file has necessarily been damaged. For full Dolby Vision reconstruction, the enhancement details matter. A minimum enhancement layer has no additional picture residual to reconstruct. A full enhancement layer carries a nonzero residual. These can place different demands on a decoder even though both files say Profile 7. When the same movie behaves differently in an Emby app and a disc player, compare the complete delivery path. Moving compressed data into another container does not automatically give the destination player the disc player's Dolby Vision decoding capabilities. A Dolby Vision indicator is useful evidence about the selected output mode, but it is not proof that every original enhancement-layer contribution survived or was used. Conversely, an HDR10 indicator can describe a valid fallback picture. If a tool converts Profile 7 to a single-layer profile, examine what happened to the enhancement layer and metadata. The new label alone does not establish that all the original reconstruction information was retained. See Also Dolby Vision Base and Enhancement Layers Dolby Vision MEL and FEL Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: UHD Blu-ray authoring workflow Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 8 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 8 Dolby Vision Profile 8 uses a single ten-bit HEVC picture layer plus Dolby Vision metadata. The base-layer compatibility identifier matters: the current Dolby specification lists HDR10-compatible and HLG-compatible forms. Common shorthand Base picture Profile 8.1 HDR10-compatible Profile 8.4 HLG-compatible The number after the point in this shorthand identifies base compatibility. It is not the level field of a full codec string . A report containing “Profile 8.1” and “dvhe.08.06” can be perfectly consistent: the latter identifies Profile 8, Level 6. Profile 8.4 is particularly relevant to personal-video libraries. Apple's HDR video documentation describes camera-captured Dolby Vision content using an HLG base and metadata about the intended viewing environment. The base is therefore not ordinary PQ HDR10, even though both can appear under a general HDR label. For an Emby session, fallback must match that base. An HDR10-capable path may be appropriate for 8.1; HLG handling is relevant to 8.4. Neither compatibility identifier promises that every container and player combination will work. There is no Dolby Vision picture enhancement layer in Profile 8. That makes it distinct from Profile 7 , where the enhancement layer may contain reconstruction information. Converting one into the other deserves examination of what was preserved, not just a comparison of the final profile numbers. When troubleshooting, keep the complete profile, compatibility, and level information. Reducing it to “Profile 8” removes one of the most useful clues about how the base picture should look. See Also HDR10 Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) Dolby Vision Profile 5 Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes Apple TN3145: HDR video metadata

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profile 9 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profile 9 Dolby Vision Profile 9 is an unusual reminder that Dolby Vision does not always mean ten-bit HEVC . This profile uses eight-bit AVC, also called H.264, with an SDR-compatible base. Property Profile 9 Compression AVC/H.264 Coded precision Eight bits Dolby Vision picture enhancement layer None Base compatibility SDR The base and Dolby Vision presentation are different interpretations of the delivered system. A compatible ordinary AVC/SDR path can use the SDR base without providing the Dolby Vision result. The eight-bit label describes the coded base signal; it is not a complete description of the Dolby Vision processing or final display signal. Equally, Dolby Vision metadata is not a guarantee that the source contains the same precision or grade as another release. For Emby troubleshooting, a player successfully decoding H.264 establishes only codec compatibility. Using Profile 9 as Dolby Vision also needs support for that profile and its metadata path. A result that appears as SDR may be using the intended fallback. Avoid interpreting “9” as a quality tier above Profile 8 . Profile numbers distinguish delivery arrangements; the film's mastering and compression remain separate questions. See Also Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels Dolby Vision Fallback Compatibility References Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification Dolby Vision: Profile constraints and notes

articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.title: Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/dolby-vision/.keywords: Dolby Vision Profiles and Levels A Dolby Vision profile describes a kind of stream. A level describes limits on the processing required for that stream. Neither is a picture-quality rating. Term Question it answers Profile Which codec, layer structure, and signal arrangement are used? Level What decoded pixel rate, width, and bitrate bounds apply? Base-layer compatibility ID Can the base picture be interpreted by another defined HDR or SDR system? For example, in a codec string such as dvhe.05.06 , the 05 identifies Profile 5 and the 06 identifies Level 6. A higher level does not mean a newer or better Dolby Vision grade; it permits a different processing load. Resolution and frame rate work together. A 3,840 × 2,160 picture at 24 frames per second contains about 199 million pixel samples per second. At 60 frames per second, that becomes about 498 million. Bitrate and width limits also apply, so pixel rate alone is not a complete compatibility test. Be careful with the shorthand 8.1 . It commonly means Profile 8 with an HDR10-compatible base; it is not the same notation as the profile-and-level fields in a complete codec string. Profile 8 explains this distinction. When reporting an Emby playback problem, include the complete media information rather than only “Dolby Vision.” The app version, device, container, profile, and playback method together make the report useful. A device's Dolby Vision capability can cover some profiles and levels without covering every possible stream. The individual profile pages explain the resulting compatibility questions; fallback compatibility explains what happens when the Dolby Vision path is unavailable. See Also How Dolby Vision Works Dolby Vision Profile 5 Dolby Vision Profile 8 References Dolby Vision: Bitstream levels Dolby Vision: Playback device capabilities Dolby Vision: Bitstream profiles specification

articles/video/hdr/formats/HDR10.html.title: HDR10 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/HDR10.html.keywords: HDR10 HDR10 is a widely used HDR delivery format. The 10 refers to ten-bit signal precision; it does not mean a 10,000-nit television or ten times the brightness of SDR. Its core ingredients have separate roles: Ingredient Role Ten-bit values Provide finer gradations than eight-bit values PQ transfer characteristics Relate encoded values to intended light output BT.2020 color signaling Define the color representation Static mastering metadata Describe the mastering display used for the release Content may also carry MaxCLL and MaxFALL . Those are reported content light levels, not television requirements. HDR10 does not specify one universal appearance on every display. A screen that cannot reproduce the source's brightest values still needs to fit the picture to its own range. Static metadata supplies context, while the display or player decides how to use it. What the label does not tell you HDR10 is not a video codec or a filename extension. A file's codec, container, audio, and subtitles remain relevant to Emby playback compatibility . It is also not proof that the content uses the whole BT.2020 gamut or reaches PQ's upper limit. A restrained grade can be fully valid HDR10. If an Emby session produces SDR output, the picture needs HDR-to-SDR conversion . Simply removing the HDR10 metadata leaves the original signal values in place. Conversely, adding HDR10 metadata to an SDR encode does not create new highlight information. HDR10+ builds on this delivery approach by adding information that can vary with the picture. See Also What HDR Video Adds to SDR HDR10+ HDR Metadata References SMPTE ST 2084: PQ reference display transfer function SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata HDR10+ Technologies: System white paper

articles/video/hdr/formats/HDR10-Plus.ht.title: HDR10+ | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/HDR10-Plus.ht.keywords: HDR10+ HDR10+ adds dynamic metadata to an HDR10-compatible picture. This gives a supporting playback system more information about the current scene when fitting it to the display. Consider a film that cuts from a dim candlelit room to a bright snowfield. A single program-wide maximum cannot describe the distribution of brightness in both scenes very well. HDR10+ metadata can provide information specific to each scene or frame. Playback path How the information can be used HDR10+ processing available Dynamic metadata can guide the adaptation HDR10 processing available, HDR10+ ignored The compatible HDR10 picture can still be used SDR output required The picture still needs HDR-to-SDR conversion The dynamic metadata is standardized in SMPTE ST 2094-40 . It describes characteristics and mapping guidance; it is not a second image layer containing extra picture detail. Dynamic metadata cannot recover detail already removed during mastering or compression. It also cannot make two displays with very different brightness and color capabilities look physically identical. Its benefit is better-informed adaptation of the available picture. In Emby, separate the source format from the whole playback path. The file may contain HDR10+ metadata, but retaining and using it depends on the delivered stream, player, output connection, and display. A television showing ordinary HDR rather than HDR10+ can be using the compatible base picture; that is a different outcome from a failed decode. When comparing the two modes, use the same release and scene. A different encode or grade can create a larger difference than the metadata system itself. See Also HDR10 HDR Metadata Why Tone Mapping Is Needed References HDR10+ Technologies: System white paper SMPTE ST 2094-40: Dynamic metadata, Application 4

articles/video/hdr/formats/HLG.html.title: Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/formats/HLG.html.keywords: Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) Hybrid Log-Gamma, usually shortened to HLG , is an HDR system developed by the BBC and NHK. It is useful in television production because its basic HDR presentation does not depend on per-program mastering metadata. The name describes its encoding shape: the lower section uses a gamma-like relationship and the upper section uses a logarithmic one. This allocates signal space to both ordinary scene content and strong highlights.
