Part of the HLG chain Main purpose Camera encoding Represent relative scene light in the video signal Display processing Adapt the relationship between scene light and displayed light Output display Reproduce the result within its brightness capability Unlike PQ's absolute light-output scale, HLG's end-to-end rendering allows adaptation to the display and viewing environment. The same encoded HLG signal therefore does not imply one fixed luminance for every pixel on every screen. HLG is sometimes described as backward compatible with SDR. That needs context: an SDR path may obtain a usable picture under suitable signaling and color handling, but this does not guarantee correct results on every older TV or player. Gamut and transfer-function interpretation still matter. For an Emby library, HLG can appear in broadcast material and camera recordings. Do not assume that an HDR badge always means PQ or HDR10. If the image looks wrong after conversion, identifying the actual source transfer characteristics is more useful than increasing the bitrate. An HLG recording can also form the compatible base of some Dolby Vision Profile 8 content. In that case, HLG and Dolby Vision describe related parts of the same stream rather than two unrelated movies. See Also HDR Capture in Cameras HDR10 What HDR Video Adds to SDR References ARIB STD-B67: Hybrid Log-Gamma system parameters ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television image parameters BBC R&D: HDR television frequently asked questions

articles/video/hdr/HDR-Camera-Capture.ht.title: HDR Capture in Cameras | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Camera-Capture.ht.keywords: HDR Capture in Cameras An HDR picture starts with information the camera actually captured. If a sunlit window has already become a featureless clipped patch in the recording, an HDR export label cannot bring its detail back. Capture dynamic range is often described in stops . Each additional stop represents a doubling of the light ratio. This describes the sensor and recording workflow; it is not a promise about how many nits the finished film will use. A useful distinction for home videos in an Emby library is whether the recording is ready for normal viewing or still needs production work. Recording approach What happens next Log video A deliberately encoded source for grading and conversion into a viewing format Raw capture Sensor-oriented data that needs development and an image-processing pipeline HLG recording Can provide a delivery-ready HDR signal for a compatible viewing path A flat-looking log recording is therefore not necessarily broken HDR. Sony, for example, describes S-Log as intended for subsequent grading, while HLG recordings are intended for compatible HDR displays. Camera preview assistance can show a more normal-looking image without changing the underlying log recording. Exposure still matters. Preserving a bright sky by lowering exposure too far can leave important shadows noisy. HDR can make both clipped highlights and shadow noise more visible, because the final presentation has room to reveal them. For a personal-video library, identify the recording mode before diagnosing playback. Grading and mastering turn captured material into a finished image. HDR-to-SDR tone mapping solves a later display-range problem; it is not a substitute for developing or grading camera originals. See Also HDR Mastering in the Studio Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG) What HDR Video Adds to SDR References ARRI: HDR FAQ Sony: What is S-Log? Sony: Gamma display assist and HDR recording ITU-R BT.2408: HDR television production guidance

articles/video/hdr/HDR-Luminance-Nits.ht.title: Luminance and Nits | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Luminance-Nits.ht.keywords: Luminance and Nits One nit equals one candela per square metre (cd/m²). Both units describe luminance: the light leaving a surface in a particular direction, weighted for human vision. In video discussions, nits help distinguish a small bright reflection from the ordinary white objects around it. They are not a measure of resolution, color saturation, or the electricity a television consumes. Number being discussed What it describes A pixel or patch at 500 nits The intended or measured luminance of that part of the image A 1,000-nit mastering display A capability or configuration of the reference display used during grading A display's advertised peak A measured capability under particular test conditions MaxFALL of 200 nits The highest frame-average content light level reported for the program The same unit does not make these interchangeable. A small patch at 1,000 nits and an entire frame averaging 1,000 nits are very different demands on a display. HDR production guidance uses a reference white of 203 nits in specified reference conditions. This leaves space above ordinary white for highlights; it is not a requirement that every white shirt in every film measure 203 nits. There is another easy trap: twice the nits does not mean twice the perceived brightness . Vision adapts to the scene and surroundings. Nor is twice the video code value necessarily twice the luminance: transfer functions such as PQ are nonlinear. For an Emby playback comparison, keep the distinction between the source's light levels and the screen's actual output. Tone mapping can deliberately make them different. A source metadata number is not a measurement of your television. See Also What HDR Video Adds to SDR MaxCLL and MaxFALL Why Tone Mapping Is Needed References BIPM: Principles governing photometry ITU-R BT.2408-6: HDR production and reference white SMPTE ST 2084: PQ reference display transfer function

articles/video/hdr/HDR-Mastering.html.title: HDR Mastering in the Studio | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Mastering.html.keywords: HDR Mastering in the Studio HDR mastering is where the available camera information becomes a deliberate viewing experience. The colorist decides how bright a window should feel, whether faces remain restrained, and which shadow details should be visible. A camera may capture more information than the finished release uses. Mastering is not an instruction to stretch every shot from black to maximum brightness. Production decision What the viewer may notice Highlight placement A reflection can sparkle without the whole scene becoming bright Shot matching Cuts between cameras keep a coherent look Shadow treatment A night scene can remain dark while important objects remain distinguishable Mapping review The image is checked on targets with less brightness or a different gamut The reference monitor gives those judgments a known basis. Mastering display metadata describes its configured color volume; it does not describe every pixel in the movie or require a home screen with identical capabilities. For Dolby Vision, image analysis can be followed by a trim pass : the colorist reviews a mapped version and, where needed, adjusts its appearance for another target. Those decisions can travel as metadata rather than as a complete second movie. This helps explain a familiar Emby comparison: an HDR release converted to SDR during playback need not look identical to a separately mastered SDR release. The two may incorporate different creative decisions, even if both are technically correct. When judging a tone-mapping result, look for lost detail or unnatural shifts within the same release first. Treat the separate SDR release as another authored version, not a pixel-for-pixel reference that every HDR conversion must reproduce. See Also HDR Capture in Cameras Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 How Dolby Vision Works References Dolby Vision: Color grading best practices SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata Dolby Vision: Shot analysis and long-play analysis

articles/video/hdr/HDR-Video.html.title: What HDR Video Adds to SDR | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/HDR-Video.html.keywords: What HDR Video Adds to SDR A lamp and the wall it illuminates do not look equally bright in real life. HDR video gives a picture more room to preserve that difference: the lamp can stand out while the wall remains at a comfortable level. The improvement is about the range within the image. An HDR film can still contain a dark room, a muted landscape, or an intentionally low-contrast shot. Making every part of the image brighter would change the creative decision rather than demonstrate HDR. Picture characteristic What it tells you Dynamic range How far the picture can extend between dark and bright levels Resolution How many picture samples describe the scene Color gamut Which colors can be represented Bit depth How finely the signal values are divided These characteristics can improve together, but they are separate. A 4K file is not necessarily HDR, and ten-bit encoding alone is not enough to identify HDR. BT.2100 defines HDR image parameters, including the PQ and HLG systems. Why two HDR screens can look different A file describes an image; it cannot guarantee that every display has enough brightness or color capability to reproduce it exactly. Tone mapping adapts the image to those limits. Room lighting and display settings also affect what you see. When comparing playback through Emby, use the same scene and note the playback method . The source's HDR label and the display's active output mode answer different questions. A file can begin as HDR and reach an SDR screen after conversion, or arrive unchanged and be adapted by the player. See Also Why Tone Mapping Is Needed Luminance and Nits HDR10 References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television image parameters SMPTE ST 2084: PQ reference display transfer function BBC R&D: HDR television frequently asked questions

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 SMPTE ST 2086 records the color volume of the mastering display : the display configuration on which the finished picture was judged. It provides context for reproducing the picture elsewhere. Metadata component What it describes Red, green, and blue primaries The display's configured primary colors White point The chromaticity used for neutral white Maximum mastering luminance The top of the configured luminance range Minimum mastering luminance The bottom of that range Suppose a report lists a mastering maximum of 1,000 nits. That does not say that every frame, or even the brightest pixel, reaches 1,000 nits. The display could have been capable of showing a brighter highlight than the filmmaker chose to use. Content light levels are described separately by MaxCLL and MaxFALL . Another apparently contradictory combination is a BT.2020 video signal with P3 mastering primaries. The encoded signal and the mastering display are different things: the wider encoding space can carry colors graded on the narrower display. The two labels do not need to match. ST 2086 also does not specify the complete tone-mapping recipe. It does not contain shot-by-shot creative adjustments or define the mastering display's transfer function. In an Emby media report, read these fields as source context, not as minimum requirements for your television. A display with a different color volume needs adaptation, but that alone does not make the file unsuitable for playback. Tone mapping explains the brightness part of that adaptation. See Also HDR Metadata MaxCLL and MaxFALL HDR Mastering in the Studio References SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: MaxCLL and MaxFALL | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: MaxCLL and MaxFALL MaxCLL and MaxFALL describe different kinds of brightness in a video. Both are expressed in nits, but one concerns the brightest content and the other the brightest frame average. Field Expanded name What it summarizes MaxCLL Maximum Content Light Level The highest content light level across the program MaxFALL Maximum Frame-Average Light Level The largest of the individual frame averages MaxFALL is not the average brightness of the whole film . Imagine a mostly dark movie with one very bright outdoor shot. That shot can determine MaxFALL even though the rest of the movie is much darker. A simplified example shows why the two values differ. If 1% of a frame is at 1,000 nits and the remaining 99% is at 10 nits, its average is 19.9 nits. A bright point can therefore coexist with a low frame average. This arithmetic illustration is not a complete specification of how production tools calculate the metadata. These fields are separate from the mastering display's maximum . One describes the content; the other describes a display configuration. Neither number measures the output of the television currently playing the file. Missing or zero light-level fields should not be read as a black movie. They can indicate unavailable information. Metadata may also be inaccurate, so a converter can need its own image analysis instead of relying only on the reported maximum. When comparing Emby tone-mapping results, record these values alongside the exact source version. Different encodes of the same title can carry different metadata, and that can change an implementation's starting assumptions. See Also HDR Metadata Luminance and Nits Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 References Dolby: Calculating MaxFALL and MaxCLL SMPTE: HDR Imaging Ecosystem report

articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.title: HDR Metadata | Emby Learn
articles/video/hdr/metadata-and-light-le.keywords: HDR Metadata HDR metadata is information that accompanies the picture. It can tell a player what the encoded values mean, describe the display used for mastering, or guide adaptation as the scene changes. These are different jobs. A useful way to read a media-information report is to separate them: Information The question it helps answer Transfer characteristics, primaries, matrix How should the pixel values be interpreted? Mastering display metadata What color volume was used for grading? MaxCLL and MaxFALL What light-level bounds are reported for the content? Dynamic metadata What additional information applies to this shot or frame? The first row is often called color signaling rather than HDR metadata in a narrower sense. It is still essential to correct playback. A ten-bit stream with the wrong transfer-function tag can be interpreted incorrectly even when its video compression is valid. Static metadata applies to the program or sequence; dynamic metadata can change during it. Dynamic does not mean that every pixel carries a separate instruction, nor does a metadata block contain a hidden higher-resolution copy of the movie. For Emby troubleshooting, distinguish the source from the delivered stream. During video transcoding , a new picture stream is encoded. Its signaling must describe that output; copying an HDR label onto tone-mapped SDR would not turn it back into HDR. Metadata also depends on accurate authoring. A plausible-looking number is not proof that it was measured correctly. MaxCLL and MaxFALL are particularly easy to misread as display specifications, while ST 2086 describes the mastering display instead. See Also Mastering Display Metadata: SMPTE ST 2086 MaxCLL and MaxFALL Dolby Vision RPU Metadata References ITU-R BT.2100-3: HDR television image parameters SMPTE ST 2086: Mastering display color volume metadata SMPTE ST 2094-40: Dynamic metadata, Application 4 Dolby Vision: Metadata levels

articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Gamut Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Gamut Mapping A vivid neon sign can fit the brightness range of an SDR picture yet still have a color that the target cannot reproduce. Gamut mapping decides what to do with those out-of-range colors. It complements tone mapping, which handles the brightness range. A color gamut describes a set of reproducible colors. Simply converting the coordinates from one color space to another does not guarantee that every resulting color falls within the target. Some values may still be outside its limits. The tradeoff is visible in saturated detail Treatment What may happen to a colorful highlight Hard clipping Different source colors reach the same boundary; distinctions disappear Gradual compression Colors approach the boundary more gently, but some saturation changes Broad desaturation Everything fits more easily, while colors that already fitted may look unnecessarily muted There is no single adjustment that preserves brightness, saturation, hue, and every color difference when the target cannot contain them all. Different methods choose different compromises. libplacebo's gamut-mapping definitions , for example, distinguish channel clipping, soft compression, and desaturation. This becomes especially relevant during HDR-to-SDR conversion . The source and output may use different color primaries, and tone mapping itself can push colors beyond the permitted output range. Brightness and color handling therefore need to agree. When comparing an Emby playback result, look beyond a white cloud or gray ramp. A red stage light or colorful shop sign can reveal lost color detail even when neutral highlights look good. If the whole picture has the wrong tint, first check that its source and output color information are being interpreted correctly; gamut mapping is not a substitute for correct color signaling. A smaller gamut also does not mean every frame must look less colorful. Colors already comfortably inside the target can often be retained with little or no visible change. See Also Color Gamut Color Volume How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping References libplacebo 7.349.0: gamut mapping functions ITU-R BT.2020: UHDTV image parameters ITU-R BT.709: HDTV image parameters

articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping Highlight roll-off is the gently flattening part of a tone-mapping curve near its bright end. It lets successively brighter source values remain distinguishable while using progressively less of the remaining output range. Think of sunlight on a white shirt. Hard clipping can turn several bright folds into the same flat white. A roll-off can retain those folds, although the differences between them become smaller. Qualitative sketch, not a measured display response or a particular curve implementation. Axis spacing is illustrative. The knee is where the compromise begins The point where the response starts bending is often called the knee . Above it, the slope decreases: a large increase in source brightness produces a smaller increase in output brightness. BT.2390 describes an example that uses a smooth knee to adapt to a display's available luminance range. Starting the bend earlier gives the highlights more room to approach white. It also changes a wider part of the picture. Starting later can leave more ordinary tones alone, but squeezes the brightest details into a narrower output interval. A shoulder that is too compressed can preserve numerical differences that are barely visible to the viewer. The actual shape depends on the curve and its parameters. Mobius , for example, has a lower section that remains unchanged before its transition, while Hable also shapes darker values. Roll-off is a feature of the response, not the name of a single algorithm. For an Emby playback comparison, inspect bright textures alongside faces and ordinary surfaces. Retaining a lamp's filament is less useful if the rest of the scene becomes undesirably dim. Also check saturated lights: preserving highlight brightness detail does not automatically preserve their color, which is part of gamut mapping . See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2390 Gamut Mapping References ITU-R BT.2390-6: HDR television and display adaptation FFmpeg 8.1: tone-mapping implementation

articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping A tone mapper needs some idea of how much brightness it must fit into the output. That information can come from metadata, a configured assumption, or analysis of the decoded picture. Peak detection examines the picture itself. It does not measure the physical brightness of your television. The distinction matters because several different numbers can accompany HDR video: Value What it describes Mastering-display maximum The upper luminance capability reported for the display used in mastering MaxCLL The reported maximum content light level MaxFALL The reported maximum average light level of a frame Detected peak An estimate derived from the pixels currently being analyzed FFmpeg's metadata definitions keep mastering-display information and content light levels separate. None of these values is the target screen's measured peak. One unusually bright pixel can matter Using the brightest pixel is straightforward, but a tiny sparkle may then influence how the whole frame is mapped. Some implementations can instead choose a very high percentile of the brightness distribution. This discounts a small number of extreme values, trading possible loss in tiny highlights for more room elsewhere. libplacebo exposes this distinction . It also smooths measurements over time; without smoothing, small changes between frames could cause distracting brightness fluctuations. The balance between stability and reacting to a new scene is covered in scene-adaptive tone mapping . This explains why selecting the same curve name does not always reproduce the same picture. Two implementations can feed that curve different peak estimates. When comparing an Emby result, include a dim scene with isolated lights as well as a bright outdoor scene. A single paused frame does not reveal whether the estimate remains stable during motion. Peak detection can improve decisions when metadata is absent or unhelpful, but it adds processing work and remains an estimate. It cannot recover detail already clipped in the source. See Also Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls References FFmpeg 8.1: mastering-display and content-light metadata libplacebo 7.349.0: peak-detection parameters

articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.title: Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/color-and-lu.keywords: Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping A dark conversation and a sunlit landscape do not need the same compromise between midtones and highlights. Scene-adaptive tone mapping can adjust to their different brightness distributions instead of using one fixed mapping throughout the film. The information may come from dynamic metadata or from analysis of the picture . Measuring content during playback can make a mapping adaptive even when the file has no scene-by-scene metadata. This does not add an authored creative decision that was absent from the source; it lets the renderer make a more informed estimate. Conceptual processing flow. It does not describe a specific Emby implementation. React quickly, but not to everything Changing the mapping independently for every frame can make an otherwise steady object seem to pulse when a bright object enters the shot. Temporal smoothing reduces that instability. Too much smoothing, however, can make the mapper slow to respond when the film cuts from a dark room to daylight. Scene-change handling helps resolve that tension. For example, libplacebo's peak detector can reduce smoothing when the change in brightness is large enough. This is an implementation example, not a universal rule for detecting an edit or a promise about an Emby setting. Adaptive also does not necessarily mean local: a mapper can change over time while still applying the same curve across the whole frame. Processing different parts of one frame differently is a separate choice. When assessing an Emby playback result, let the scene run. Watch a face as a bright window enters the frame, and watch the first moments after a hard cut. Stable midtones and a clean transition tell you more than a particularly attractive screenshot. A visible brightness change can also come from the source or the display's own processing, so it is useful to establish where tone mapping occurs before attributing it to the server. See Also Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls References libplacebo 7.349.0: peak-detection and scene-change handling FFmpeg 8.1: OpenCL tone-mapping kernels

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Hable | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Hable Hable is the tone mapping curve John Hable developed for Uncharted 2 . Its aim was a film-like response: bright areas approach white gradually, while the darker parts of the image also receive deliberate shaping. Hable describes its origins and publishes the original formula in Filmic Tonemapping Operators . FFmpeg 8.1 Hable curve: source peak 8, output white 1, relative linear-light values for neutral gray. Dashed gray shows clipping. This illustrates the curve, not an Emby preset. The close-up shows that this version already changes lower values; it is not an unchanged section followed only by a highlight knee. That makes it more than a way to squeeze down the brightest pixels. The filmic shape has three parts: Part of the curve What it shapes Toe The transition out of black and the separation of dark tones Middle section The brightness and contrast of ordinary scene content Shoulder The gradual compression of strong highlights toward white The appeal during HDR-to-SDR conversion is that a bright reflection can retain gradations instead of becoming a flat white patch. The tradeoff is that midtones can become darker too. If an Emby playback comparison preserves the sky but makes a person's face noticeably dimmer, the tone curve is one possible contributor; the brightest highlights alone do not tell the whole story. The name does not specify every processing choice. For example, FFmpeg's software implementation uses fixed curve coefficients and normalizes the result against the source peak. Different peak assumptions can therefore change the result even with the same curve selected. Hable is useful to recognize in existing settings and discussions, but it is not a universal quality recommendation: current libplacebo documentation treats it as a legacy option. See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard References John Hable: Filmic Tonemapping Operators John Hable: Filmic Tonemapping with Piecewise Power Curves FFmpeg 8.1: tonemap implementation libplacebo: tone mapping options

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius Mobius asks a practical question: if a darker part of the picture already fits, why compress it? Its curve leaves values below a transition point unchanged, then smoothly bends the higher values into the available output range. The name comes from the mathematical Möbius transformation used for that upper section. libplacebo describes the curve and its relationship to Reinhard . FFmpeg 8.1 Mobius curve: knee 0.3, source peak 8, output white 1, relative linear-light values for neutral gray. Dashed gray shows clipping. This illustrates the curve, not an Emby preset. In the close-up, the lines coincide up to the knee and then separate smoothly. The knee marks the start of compression without introducing a sharp corner. The transition is often called the knee . Moving it changes where the compromise begins: Knee position Effect on the curve Lower Compression begins earlier, spreading it across more of the input range. Higher More values remain unchanged, leaving less output range for the brightest details. For example, FFmpeg's software tonemap filter defaults to a knee of 0.3. At the curve itself, inputs of 0.1 and 0.3 stay at 0.1 and 0.3; higher inputs enter the curved section. These are normalized linear-light values, not a percentage of the film's HDR peak. That makes Mobius interesting when investigating an HDR-to-SDR conversion where ordinary objects look too dim. However, preserving the lower part of the curve does not guarantee an unchanged final pixel: surrounding color conversion and highlight desaturation can also affect it, as the FFmpeg implementation shows. When comparing playback through Emby, look at both familiar midtones and bright textured areas. A higher knee can preserve the former while making the latter harder to distinguish. Mobius explains that tradeoff clearly; its presence in an implementation is not a claim that it is the best current choice. libplacebo classifies it as a legacy option . See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard References FFmpeg: tonemap filter FFmpeg 8.1: tonemap implementation libplacebo: tone mapping options

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard Reinhard gives a simple answer to a difficult problem: progressively compress brighter values so that even an extremely bright input can fit below the output's maximum white. It takes its name from Erik Reinhard, coauthor of the 2002 paper Photographic Tone Reproduction for Digital Images . The simplest version is output = input / (1 + input) . Here, input is an already scaled, linear-light value; output white is 1. These are not video code values or measurements in nits. Input Output, rounded 0.1 0.091 1 0.500 4 0.800 10 0.909 Notice how much less room remains between the last two outputs. Bright details still have different values, but their contrast is reduced. The same compression also reaches into ordinary tones: an input of 1 becomes 0.5. This explains why preserving highlights can come with a flatter or dimmer-looking picture. Those numbers illustrate the basic equation from the paper , not the exact output of an Emby playback session. Video implementations can adjust the curve and normalize it to a finite source peak; FFmpeg's software tonemap filter does both. FFmpeg 8.1 Reinhard curve: parameter 0.5, source peak 8, output white 1, relative linear-light values for neutral gray. Dashed gray shows clipping. At input 1, this peak normalization raises the basic equation's result from 0.5 to 0.5625. The graph represents the stated implementation, not an Emby preset. There is another useful distinction when reading comparisons: the original research also includes exposure scaling and a spatially varying method. FFmpeg's Reinhard option implements a global curve, so a result produced by the full photographic method is not automatically representative of that setting. For the alternative idea of leaving lower values unchanged and compressing only above a chosen transition, see Mobius . See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius References Reinhard, Stark, Shirley and Ferwerda: Photographic Tone Reproduction for Digital Images (2002) Photographic Tone Reproduction for Digital Images: paper PDF FFmpeg 8.1: tonemap implementation

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Clip | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Clip Clipping puts a hard ceiling on a value. Below the ceiling it keeps the value unchanged; above it, every input becomes the same maximum. FFmpeg 8.1 clip mapping with scale parameter 1. Both axes use relative linear light for neutral gray; output white is 1. The flat section is the important part. Three parts of a bright cloud with inputs of 2, 4, and 8 all become 1. The cloud's positions remain, but the brightness differences that made its texture visible disappear. Input Output 0.2 0.2 1 1 2 1 8 1 A highlight roll-off bends toward the limit gradually, leaving output space for some of those differences. It starts changing the values before they reach the ceiling. Clipping preserves the in-range part exactly and spends none of that range on brighter values. See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls Tone Mapping Curve: Linear Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping References FFmpeg 8.1: clipping tonemap implementation libplacebo: clipping function

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Gamma | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Gamma A gamma tone mapper reshapes brightness with a power function. Compared with uniform scaling, this can give lower values more room while still bringing the source peak down to the output limit. FFmpeg 8.1 CPU tone mapper, gamma parameter 1.8, source peak 8 and output white 1. Axes are relative linear light for neutral gray; the very dark region uses FFmpeg's linear extension. For most of this example, the operation is output = (input / 8)^(1 / 1.8) . An input of 4 becomes about 0.68, rather than the 0.5 produced by dividing everything by eight. That raises the mapped brightness of this value without increasing the output ceiling. The near-black detail matters Applying a power function all the way to zero can give the darkest values a very steep response. FFmpeg switches to a small linear section below an input of 0.05. The graph represents that implementation detail as well as the main power curve. Other implementations use the name differently. libplacebo's gamma mapper retains an unchanged section below a knee, then fits a power curve above it. Its knee parameter is not interchangeable with FFmpeg's gamma parameter. Neither setting is simply the display gamma . One is a brightness remapping choice; the other describes a signal/display relationship. For Emby users reading logs or comparing images, the useful question is therefore which implementation and parameters are involved. A bare label of Gamma is insufficient to reproduce a result. Pay particular attention to shadow separation as well as overall brightness: lifting a dark region does not guarantee that it gains useful detail. See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls Video Gamma Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius References FFmpeg 8.1: gamma tonemap implementation libplacebo 7.360.1: gamma mapping

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Linear | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Linear Linear tone mapping applies a proportional range adjustment. If a linear-light input reaches eight times the desired output white, dividing every value by eight makes the brightest value fit. The arithmetic is simple. Its consequence matters more: ordinary objects are darkened along with the brightest highlight. Peak ratio 8:1. Green scales linear light; blue stretches PQ values using libplacebo's convention, with output white at 203 nits. Both are shown on relative linear-light axes. Gain is 1 and black is zero. Linear in which space? A straight line in one signal representation need not be straight in another. The blue line bends here because its proportional operation happens in PQ , not in the linear-light values used by the axes. This distinction appears in real software. FFmpeg's CPU linear tone mapper works on linear-light samples. libplacebo distinguishes linear , a PQ-space stretch, from linearlight . Matching the option name alone does not match their output. Linear-light example Output Input 0.8 0.1 Input 4 0.5 Input 8 1 Unlike clipping , proportional scaling does not flatten all over-range values into the same white. It keeps differences between them, but allocates less brightness to the whole picture. That can make it understandable for a modest range adjustment and disappointing for a large HDR-to-SDR reduction. When an Emby comparison looks dark, check which processing stage and working space produced it before interpreting a setting labeled Linear as one universal curve. See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls Tone Mapping Curve: Clip Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 References FFmpeg 8.1: linear tonemap implementation libplacebo 7.360.1: linear and linearlight functions ITU-R BT.2100: HDR signal representations

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.title: Tone Mapping Curve: Spline | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/gener.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: Spline A spline is built from curve segments that meet smoothly. In libplacebo's tone mapper, two polynomial segments join at one pivot. That gives the mapper a way to shape the darker and brighter parts of the picture while keeping the transition continuous. libplacebo 7.360.1, default constants, zero black levels, 1,000-nit input peak and 100-nit output peak. Scene-average brightness is unspecified. This is the brightness function, not a complete color conversion. The plot is one member of a family, rather than the single shape that the word spline always means. With different source, target, or scene information, the pivot and the resulting curve can change. What the pivot does Think of the pivot as a point the two pieces agree to pass through. Changing its input position affects where the picture starts giving up more brightness separation. Changing its output position changes how bright that part of the scene becomes. The contrast control adjusts the slope around that region. Making a section steeper preserves more contrast there, but leaves less room elsewhere. It cannot create additional output range. This explains why an adaptive spline may behave differently on a dim interior and a bright exterior even when the selected curve name stays the same. Scene-adaptive tone mapping provides the changing information; the spline provides a shape that can respond to it. For an Emby playback comparison, keep the playback path and scene fixed before judging the setting. The Windows app's rendering stage can perform tone mapping independently of server delivery. A server transcode and local player rendering are not automatically using the same spline or parameters. See Also What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2390 References libplacebo 7.360.1: tone-mapping functions libplacebo: curve constants and parameter meanings

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.title: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2390 | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2390 BT.2390 is an ITU-R report about HDR television. The tone-mapping option named after it usually refers to its electrical–electrical transfer function , or EETF: a way of adapting a signal between different display ranges. Its recognizable feature is a smooth roll-off. Lower values can follow an unchanged section before highlights bend toward the destination's limit. libplacebo 7.360.1 brightness mapping, 1,000 → 100 nits, zero black levels. Offset 0.5 follows the report's knee convention; offset 1.0 is libplacebo's default. Calculation happens in PQ; axes show light levels. Why two BT.2390 results can differ The graph's two lines have the same endpoints but do not start reducing brightness at the same place. The earlier bend changes more of the picture to make room for highlights. That is an implementation setting, not a change of video codec. Black-level assumptions also matter: the report's adaptation can account for a destination that cannot reproduce the source black level. This example isolates the highlight behavior by setting both black levels to zero. The EETF should not be confused with an EOTF . An EOTF relates a signal to display light. Here, PQ helps perform a transformation between the source and destination signal ranges. For an Emby playback comparison, record the target brightness and the actual mapper, not just “BT.2390.” The same label can hide a different knee offset. The approach is also relevant to HDR-to-HDR mapping , where both ends are HDR but the display still has a smaller range than the source. See Also Highlight Roll-Off in Tone Mapping Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping References ITU-R Report BT.2390-11 libplacebo 7.360.1: BT.2390 implementation libplacebo: knee-offset definition

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.title: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2446 Method A | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2446 Method A Method A is one of the HDR/SDR conversion methods described in ITU-R Report BT.2446. It is a conversion recipe, rather than a codec or a piece of HDR metadata carried by the film. The report's complete method includes color processing as well as brightness adaptation. A renderer option named BT.2446A may expose its brightness function inside the renderer's own wider pipeline. libplacebo 7.360.1's Method A brightness function, 1,000 → 100 nits, zero black levels. The plot does not represent the method's complete color processing. What the curve shows The calculation passes through a logarithmic representation and a piecewise mapping before producing output light levels. The slope changes across the range rather than applying one constant scale factor. For the plotted example, an input of 100 nits becomes about 23 nits, while 500 nits becomes about 73 nits. Those values describe this configured function. They are not promises about the brightness of an Emby screen: later signal encoding, display behavior, and the chosen target still matter. Name encountered What it tells you BT.2446 The report containing several conversion methods Method A One particular method in that report A renderer's BT.2446A option An implementation that must be understood in its pipeline context This distinction helps when reading tone-mapping comparisons. A screenshot made using a full conversion recipe and one made using only its brightness stage need not match, even when both descriptions say Method A. When interpreting an Emby result, consider gamut mapping alongside the curve. Color handling can change the appearance of bright saturated objects without changing this one-dimensional graph. See Also How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Gamut Mapping Tone Mapping Curve: BT.2390 References ITU-R Report BT.2446-1: HDR and SDR conversion methods libplacebo 7.360.1: Method A brightness function

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.title: Tone Mapping Curve: ST 2094-10 in libplacebo | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: ST 2094-10 in libplacebo SMPTE ST 2094-10 describes dynamic metadata for a color-volume transform. libplacebo's option with this name implements a brightness-mapping function based on the standard's informative Annex B.2. A useful way to picture it is as a curve constrained by three points: the dark end, the bright end, and an adaptation point between them. Moving the middle point changes the treatment of ordinary scene brightness. libplacebo 7.360.1, default constants, 1,000 → 100 nits, zero black levels, no scene-average value. The default adaptation-point selection is used. A family of curves The line shown is not a fixed curve embedded in every ST 2094-10 picture. Source statistics and target assumptions can select a different middle point. The resulting curve may therefore change with the content. That also explains why a maximum-brightness value alone does not fully describe an adaptive mapping. Two scenes with the same brightest reflection can have very different average brightness. There are boundaries to the option's name. The standard contains more than this brightness function, and libplacebo documents that its mapper does not implement the subjective gain, offset, and gamma controls described in Annex B.3. Selecting this curve is consequently not equivalent to decoding and reproducing the complete Dolby Vision processing chain. A curve label cannot establish profile support, enhancement-layer use, or preservation of all metadata. For Emby troubleshooting, separate those format/decoding questions from the mapping applied after decoding. The playback path tells you where that work happens; the mapper's implementation and input information tell you which member of this curve family is used. See Also Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping Tone Mapping Curve: ST 2094-40 in libplacebo How Dolby Vision Works References SMPTE ST 2094-10:2021, Application #1 libplacebo 7.360.1: ST 2094-10 mapping libplacebo: supported mapping controls

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.title: Tone Mapping Curve: ST 2094-40 in libplacebo | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/stand.keywords: Tone Mapping Curve: ST 2094-40 in libplacebo The ST 2094-40 mapping used by libplacebo can take its shape from dynamic metadata. A knee marks a transition, and Bézier control points describe the curved section above it. The mapper can then adapt that shape for a display whose peak differs from the metadata's target. This is more flexible than assigning one permanent curve to an entire film. libplacebo 7.360.1 fallback, 1,000 → 100 nits, zero black levels, default constants, no scene average and no metadata curve anchors. Real metadata can produce a different curve. What happens without the metadata? The graph deliberately shows that case. libplacebo constructs a fallback curve from its brightness-matching rules instead of requiring a complete metadata-defined Bézier curve. The presence of a setting called ST 2094-40 therefore does not prove that a particular film's HDR10+ metadata reached the mapper or was used. It could be operating through this fallback. Available information Consequence Curve anchors and target information A content-provided curve can be adapted Different destination peak The original curve may need adjustment Missing curve metadata The implementation uses a generated fallback For an Emby playback investigation, the important distinction is between the selected mapping method and the information supplied to it . A remux, transcode, decoder, or renderer boundary can be relevant to the second question; the option name answers only the first. Like the other curve plots, this one isolates brightness. It does not demonstrate complete color rendering or certify a playback device's HDR10+ support. Looking at the actual metadata path is more informative than expecting every ST 2094-40 result to resemble one sample graph. See Also Tone Mapping Curve: ST 2094-10 in libplacebo HDR10+ Scene-Adaptive Tone Mapping References SMPTE ST 2094-40:2016, Application #4 libplacebo 7.360.1: ST 2094-40 mapping libplacebo: metadata and fallback behavior

articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/Tone-.title: What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/curves/Tone-.keywords: What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls A tone-mapping curve answers a simple question: for this input brightness, what output brightness should we use? Its shape controls which parts of the picture keep their contrast and which are squeezed together. These are simplified mathematical examples, not Emby presets or a comparison of named curves. Both axes use relative linear-light values. The flat part of the clipping line turns several different inputs into the same output. Detail in those brightness differences is lost. Straight scaling keeps their proportions but reduces the entire range, including the darker values. Smooth compression changes the proportions: brighter inputs receive progressively less space. Reading the shape Part of the curve What it can change in the picture Dark end Separation of near-black details Middle Apparent brightness and contrast of much of the scene Bright end, often called the shoulder How gradually highlights approach the output limit To read a point on the graph, trace upwards from the input axis to the curve, then across to the output axis. Where the curve becomes shallower, equally spaced input levels become closer together at the output: less separation between those brightness levels. A tone-mapping implementation may use linear light, a perceptual signal representation, or another working space. Curves drawn in different spaces cannot be compared just by their shape on a graph. Names such as Hable , Reinhard , and Mobius identify different approaches. The name alone does not specify the whole conversion pipeline , its parameters, or whether a particular Emby playback path uses it. When comparing results, keep the source scene and playback path the same. Look at a face or another ordinary midtone as well as the brightest highlight: preserving one while making the other look wrong is still a compromise. See Also How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Tone Mapping Curve: Hable Tone Mapping Curve: Reinhard Tone Mapping Curve: Mobius References ITU-R BT.2390-11: High dynamic range television

articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: CUDA Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: CUDA Tone Mapping CUDA tone mapping means that an application runs its tone-mapping calculations on an NVIDIA GPU through CUDA. The application supplies a program, called a kernel, that processes many pixels in parallel. CUDA does not prescribe the curve, source-peak estimate, or color handling. Those come from the implementation. Two CUDA tone mappers can therefore produce different pictures, just as a CPU and GPU implementation can aim to produce the same one. CUDA, NVDEC, and NVENC do different jobs Name Job in a possible video-processing path NVDEC Decode compressed video into frames CUDA kernel Perform programmable calculations on those frames, such as tone mapping NVENC Encode processed frames into a compressed video stream NVIDIA documents the video decoder and encoder as hardware engines separate from CUDA cores . Consequently, selecting an NVIDIA decoder or encoder does not by itself prove that tone mapping also runs through CUDA. The useful opportunity is keeping decoded frames accessible to subsequent GPU processing. NVIDIA's NVDEC guide describes decoding into video memory and then processing those frames with CUDA. Avoiding an unnecessary trip through system memory can matter as much as accelerating the curve calculation. For Emby, inspect the actual processing stages when comparing hardware activity. An encoder can be busy while the tone-mapping work runs somewhere else; a single overall GPU percentage can hide that distinction. A supported codec in NVDEC or NVENC also says nothing by itself about the pixel formats accepted by a particular tone-mapping filter. There is no generic CUDA switch that adds this path to every application. The application must include a compatible implementation, and the installed driver and device must satisfy its requirements. The hardware-acceleration documentation describes Emby's platform options; a CUDA-capable graphics card alone is not evidence that every Emby tone-mapping route uses CUDA. See Also CPU Tone Mapping OpenCL Tone Mapping Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session References NVIDIA: CUDA programming model NVIDIA: Video Codec SDK NVIDIA Video Codec SDK 13.0: NVDEC programming guide

articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: OpenCL Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: OpenCL Tone Mapping OpenCL is an interface for running parallel computations on supported devices. An OpenCL tone mapper divides picture processing into many small pieces that can run concurrently, commonly on a GPU. The word OpenCL tells you how the work is submitted, not which tone-mapping curve is used. A filter can offer several curves through the same OpenCL execution path. OpenCL itself also supports device types other than GPUs, so the selected device matters. Three pieces have to fit Piece Its role Application and filter Provide the tone-mapping code and supported input/output formats OpenCL runtime and driver Discover the device, compile or load its program, and submit work Device and frame access Supply the required capabilities and make the decoded pixels accessible A working hardware video decoder does not automatically establish that all three are available. Decoding and OpenCL compute are separate capabilities, even when they use the same physical GPU. FFmpeg 8.1's OpenCL filter provides a concrete example: it accepts specific hardware-frame formats, checks the source transfer characteristics, and launches an OpenCL tone-mapping kernel. Its accepted formats are implementation constraints, not universal limits of the OpenCL standard. That distinction is useful when reading an Emby transcoding log. Successfully selecting a decoder or encoder is only one part of the path. An OpenCL device initialization or filter-format error points to a different stage from a codec error. In a container, the application also needs access to the appropriate runtime and device; success on the host alone does not describe the application's environment. Once it runs, performance depends on more than the curve's arithmetic. Transferring frames between memory domains or incompatible processing stages can add overhead. Whether a particular Emby installation uses this path depends on the platform, bundled implementation, driver, and selected session; OpenCL support on the GPU alone is not a support guarantee. See Also CPU Tone Mapping CUDA Tone Mapping Vulkan Tone Mapping References Khronos: OpenCL specification FFmpeg 8.1: OpenCL tone-mapping filter

articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.title: Vulkan Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/gp.keywords: Vulkan Tone Mapping Vulkan gives applications explicit access to graphics and compute work on a GPU. A renderer can use that access to run shaders that convert color and compress the brightness range of HDR pictures. A shader is a program executed by the GPU. The tone-mapping behavior comes from that program and its parameters; Vulkan supplies the execution interface. Choosing Vulkan does not choose a particular curve or guarantee better highlight detail. The renderer sits above the API libplacebo is an example of a rendering library with a Vulkan backend. It provides picture-processing operations above the lower-level device interface. FFmpeg can use libplacebo as a video filter, showing how the same kind of GPU processing can form part of a conversion rather than only drawing directly to a screen. Layer What it determines Tone-mapping implementation The curve, peak handling, and color decisions Rendering library How the image-processing operations are assembled Vulkan driver and device The available GPU capabilities and execution of the submitted work This separation helps explain why two players can both use Vulkan and still look different. Their processing options, library versions, and assumptions about the display can differ. Vulkan support is also distinct from Vulkan Video codec support. Running tone-mapping shaders does not require that decoding use Vulkan Video; frames can originate from another decoder when the application supports the necessary transfer or sharing. Those connections have their own format and synchronization requirements. In an Emby discussion, first identify whether processing occurs on the server or in the player . A Vulkan-related renderer setting or message concerns that particular application's path. It does not establish that a separate server transcode uses the same API. Availability and performance depend on the complete implementation and driver, not merely a Vulkan version listed for the graphics card. See Also OpenCL Tone Mapping CUDA Tone Mapping What a Tone-Mapping Curve Controls Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session References Khronos: Vulkan specification libplacebo 7.349.0: Vulkan backend interface FFmpeg 8.1: libplacebo filter implementation

articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.title: CPU Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.keywords: CPU Tone Mapping CPU tone mapping carries out the brightness conversion on the computer's general-purpose processor. It is still the same kind of picture operation as GPU tone mapping; the processor doing the calculations does not define the artistic result. For example, FFmpeg's software tonemap filter operates on floating-point RGB values in linear light. Other processing must interpret the incoming HDR signal and prepare the final output format. The tone curve is only one step in that conversion. The work scales with the pictures, not just the bitrate A frame contains pixels to process even when its compressed file is small. These simple counts show why resolution and frame rate matter: Video size and rate Pixels per second, approximately 1920 × 1080 at 24 fps 50 million 3840 × 2160 at 24 fps 199 million 3840 × 2160 at 60 fps 498 million Pixel counts only, not a performance benchmark. Color conversion, decoding, encoding, and memory traffic add their own costs. Four times as many pixels does not guarantee exactly four times the processing time, but it does explain why a comfortable 1080p workload says little about 4K at a higher frame rate. Multiple simultaneous sessions add to the total. In an Emby transcoding session, CPU use may also come from decoding, subtitle rendering, audio conversion, or encoding. A high CPU reading alone does not identify tone mapping as the bottleneck. Likewise, an accelerated encoder does not prove that all preceding filters run on the GPU. Software processing can be useful when the required GPU path is unavailable or when the frames are already in system memory. Moving them to a GPU and back has a cost of its own. The Emby Windows FAQ gives a concrete example of a player combining software decoding with GPU presentation. Compare the whole playback path , including whether it keeps up with the source frame rate. The labels CPU and GPU are execution choices, not quality ratings. See Also Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session OpenCL Tone Mapping CUDA Tone Mapping References FFmpeg 8.1: software tone-mapping implementation FFmpeg 8.1: filter documentation

articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.title: Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/execution/To.keywords: Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session The playback method shown by Emby describes how the server delivers the video. It does not describe every step between the original file and the light coming from the screen. Tone mapping can happen when the server converts HDR video for an SDR playback target. It can also happen after delivery, in a player or in an HDR display adapting the picture to its own brightness limits. Examples of where adaptation can occur. The diagram is not an inventory of supported combinations for every Emby app. Start with the video being delivered With Direct Play , the server does not convert the video. Direct Stream can change the packaging or other tracks while leaving the video intact. In either case, any necessary adaptation of those video pixels takes place downstream. With video transcoding, the server decodes and re-encodes the video and can change its pixels in between. When that includes HDR-to-SDR conversion , the player receives the resulting SDR picture. Transcoding alone does not establish that tone mapping occurred: a conversion may be needed for another reason. Then follow the player and display The Emby Windows FAQ describes tone mapping performed by GPU shaders during presentation. This also shows why software decoding does not necessarily mean software tone mapping: the two stages can use different processors. If HDR reaches the screen, the screen may still need HDR-to-HDR adaptation . An HDR indicator confirms the signal mode, not that every original highlight is reproduced without adjustment. When investigating a difference, record the app, playback method, delivered HDR or SDR format, and display mode. Server tone-mapping settings cannot explain a change in a session whose video the server passed through unchanged. Following the actual path narrows the comparison to the stage that could have changed the picture. See Also How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping CPU Tone Mapping References ITU-R BT.2390-6: HDR television and display adaptation

articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.title: HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: HDR-to-HDR Tone Mapping An HDR screen can still need tone mapping. Accepting an HDR signal tells us which signal formats the screen understands; it does not mean the screen can reproduce every brightness that signal can describe. Consider a film containing highlights at 2,000 nits played on a display that can reach 600 nits under the relevant conditions. Both ends of this example are HDR. The display still needs to fit those highlights into its available range. HDR-to-HDR tone mapping does that without first reducing the picture to SDR. Part of the picture What a suitable mapping aims to do Ordinary midtones Keep their intended appearance where the target permits Bright highlights Compress their range while retaining visible differences Dark detail Account for the target's black level rather than assuming perfect black These are goals, not a guarantee that every mapping leaves midtones unchanged. HDR describes more than one display capability PQ describes absolute display-light levels over a much larger range than a typical consumer screen can reproduce. The BT.2390 report describes adapting those levels to a target with different black and white limits. The output can remain an HDR signal while its useful brightness range changes. The source's mastering-display maximum is not necessarily its brightest actual pixel. Content analysis and metadata help establish what needs fitting. Color volume also matters: retaining HDR does not remove limits on bright, saturated colors. For Emby playback, separate the delivered stream from the screen's final rendering. With Direct Play, the server has not rewritten the video, but the player or display can still adapt it. Two HDR televisions can therefore show the same Emby stream differently. The useful starting point is where the mapping happens , before comparing curves or changing server settings. See Also How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Peak-Luminance Detection for Tone Mapping Where Tone Mapping Happens in an Emby Playback Session Perceptual Quantizer (PQ): SMPTE ST 2084 References ITU-R BT.2390-6: HDR television and display adaptation ITU-R BT.2100: HDR television image parameters

articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.title: How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works | Emby Learn
articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: How HDR-to-SDR Tone Mapping Works Imagine a scene with a person beside a window: the face has ordinary indoor brightness, the outdoor sky is much brighter, and a reflection on glass is brighter still. An HDR picture can keep those regions distinct across a large range of light. An SDR conversion has less brightness range available, yet still needs to show a convincing face, a bright window, and some structure in the reflection. Tone mapping decides how to redistribute that brightness. The complete HDR-to-SDR conversion also has to interpret the original signal, fit its colors into the output color system, and produce correctly encoded SDR samples. Each part affects the result. A well-chosen highlight curve cannot repair incorrectly interpreted input values. For Emby playback, this conversion can happen in a server transcode or during presentation by a playback renderer. Both paths need to solve the same underlying problem, even though their implementations and output targets can differ. These are the jobs in the conversion. An implementation can combine operations or perform parts in different working spaces. Decoding gives samples; their meaning still matters A video decoder reconstructs numerical picture samples from the compressed stream. The converter then needs to know what those numbers represent. Many video sources store luma and color-difference components rather than directly storing red, green, and blue. Their matrix coefficients describe the relationship to color components. Signal range describes how stored code values represent nominal black, white, and color differences. Color primaries establish the meaning of the RGB color coordinates. Transfer characteristics relate nonlinear signal values to light. Those properties work together. If limited-range values are interpreted as full-range values, nominal black and white are assigned the wrong positions. The picture can have raised blacks or altered contrast before tone mapping starts. If the wrong matrix is used, reconstructing the color components can introduce a different error. Changing the tone curve would then adjust an already misinterpreted picture. Bit depth has a separate role. Ten bits provide more possible sample values than eight bits. They do not identify which color system or transfer function those values use. A ten-bit source can be SDR. For a PQ source, the signal has an absolute reference-display light meaning. A normalized PQ value of 0.5 corresponds to approximately 92.2 nits for neutral gray. It does not mean half of a television's peak brightness or half of PQ's 10,000-nit reference range. The nonlinear transfer function is what establishes that relationship. Before applying a curve defined in linear light, the converter must obtain linear-light values. For a neutral PQ gray, applying the PQ electro-optical transfer function gives its reference luminance. In a common linear-RGB processing path, the converter first restores nonlinear RGB from the luma/chroma samples using the appropriate range and matrix. It then applies the PQ transfer interpretation to those components to obtain linear RGB. Encoded luma and linear-light luminance are different quantities, so applying the PQ equation to luma alone would not perform this full color reconstruction. A method designed for a perceptual working space performs a different set of transformations. The conversion of HLG also needs to account for its system relationship to the intended display. Assigning PQ's absolute-light interpretation to HLG samples would skip that relationship. The important question at this stage is which representation the particular mapping expects. For example, FFmpeg's CPU tone-mapping filter expects linear-light input. Decide which brightness range to fit There are two ends to the decision: the useful brightness range in the source and the intended brightness behavior of the destination. A source can provide several kinds of information: Mastering-display metadata describes the display used during mastering, including its luminance capabilities. That is information about the mastering environment. Content-light metadata can summarize properties such as the maximum content light level. That is a description of the content under the metadata's measurement definition. Measured picture statistics come from inspecting the actual decoded pictures. A renderer can use them to adapt its mapping to the material being shown. A mastering display capable of 1,000 nits does not require every picture to contain a 1,000-nit highlight. Similarly, a whole-program maximum describes the brightest relevant content, not the brightness of each scene. These distinctions matter because reserving output range for a peak that is absent from the current scene can change how much brightness is available to its ordinary objects. The mapper may use a fixed source assumption, trustworthy metadata, peak detection , or a combination. If its assumed peak is too low, brighter source values can reach a part of the mapping that was never intended to preserve their distinctions. If the assumed peak is unnecessarily high, more compression may be applied than the scene needs. The destination also needs a defined target. A conventional SDR reference-display example can use 100 nits for white and a specified display transfer function. An actual television may show SDR white more brightly, particularly in a bright room. The largest brightness number on its product sheet does not, by itself, establish the intended SDR rendering. Reference white, black level, and viewing conditions influence the relationship between the converted picture and its appearance. The converter can prepare a conventional SDR signal for later display adjustment, or a renderer can adapt directly to a particular output. Those are different targets for the mapping. For the worked example below, choose an 800-nit source peak and a 100-nit SDR output peak . Use 100 nits as one unit on both sides solely to make the arithmetic easy: input values run from zero to eight, and output values from zero to one. This normalization does not assign a 100-nit reference white to all HDR material. Work through what the brightness curve does Three simple mappings show the tradeoff clearly. Let x be the input light level in the relative units just defined. Straight scaling uses x / 8. It fits the entire range, with the same scaling factor everywhere. An 800-nit highlight becomes 100 nits, but a 100-nit object becomes only 12.5 nits. If most of the scene sits well below its brightest highlight, the picture can become unnecessarily dark. Clipping uses the smaller of x and one. Inputs up to 100 nits retain their light levels in this example; every higher input becomes 100 nits. A 200-nit cloud and an 800-nit reflection then have the same output value. Their original brightness separation has disappeared. A smooth nonlinear mapping can devote more output range to ordinary brightness levels and compress the highlights more strongly. For an easily calculated example, use: T(x) = (9/8) × x / (1 + x) This function maps zero to zero and eight to one. For an input of one, its result is (9/8) × 1/2 = 0.5625. With the chosen output reference, that means 56.25 nits. Illustrative neutral-gray mappings. For this example, multiply either axis by 100 to express its light level in nits. The green curve is T(x) above; these are calculated relationships, not measured Emby presets. Source light level Straight scaling Clipping Smooth mapping T(x) 20 nits 2.5 nits 20 nits 18.75 nits 80 nits 10 nits 80 nits 50 nits 100 nits 12.5 nits 100 nits 56.25 nits 200 nits 25 nits 100 nits 75 nits 400 nits 50 nits 100 nits 90 nits 800 nits 100 nits 100 nits 100 nits All three make the 800-nit peak fit. They produce very different pictures everywhere else. The smooth example keeps substantially more brightness in the 80-nit region than straight scaling does, while retaining some separation among the highlights that clipping merges. That separation is still compressed. Under the smooth curve, a 600-nit region becomes about 96.43 nits, while an 800-nit region becomes 100. A source difference of 200 nits has become about 3.57 nits. The converter has preserved an ordering and a distinction, but has greatly reduced their spacing. Curve slope explains the contrast redistribution The slope of the curve describes how a small change in input light affects the output. A flat segment gives no separation to neighboring inputs. A shallow segment gives little separation; a steeper segment gives more. The green curve gradually becomes shallower toward its top. This is a highlight roll-off : extra source brightness has progressively less effect on output brightness. Fine texture in a very bright region can consequently become difficult to see even while its values remain mathematically distinct. A practical mapper has to choose how much separation to retain in shadows, middle brightness levels, and highlights. Preserving more of one region's brightness differences spends part of the finite output range. A curve's midpoint and any transition into highlight compression matter as much as its endpoint. The example's 100-nit object becomes 56.25 nits. That makes the effect on ordinary objects explicit: mapping is not confined to the few pixels above the SDR ceiling. Other curves can preserve a selected lower interval more closely or place the transition differently. The curve overview links to individual shapes and their behavior. Keep brightness changes from distorting the colors A neutral-gray example has equal RGB components, so a scalar curve is easy to interpret. Color introduces another choice: which quantity drives that curve, and how is the resulting brightness change applied to the components? Consider a linear RGB color with components 2, 1, 0.5 in one fixed set of primaries. Applying the example curve independently to each component gives 0.75, 0.5625, 0.375 . The original red-to-green ratio was 2; it is now about 1.33. The component proportions have changed, so the operation changes the color's chromaticity as well as its brightness. An alternative is to derive a single brightness-related quantity, calculate a scale factor, and apply that same factor to all three components. If the maximum component 2 drives the example curve, it maps to 0.75. The factor is 0.75 / 2 = 0.375 , producing 0.75, 0.375, 0.1875 . The original component ratio of 4:2:1 is retained. This calculation illustrates why a tone mapper needs a color strategy. A luminance-driven method can use a different driving quantity from a maximum-component method. Preserving linear RGB proportions retains chromaticity in that fixed color system, while perceived saturation can still change with brightness and viewing conditions. There is also the question of which colors the destination can represent. HDR material commonly uses a wider color gamut than a BT.709 SDR destination. Conversion between their primaries changes the RGB coordinates needed to describe a color. For a color outside the destination gamut, those coordinates can include a negative component or a component beyond the output range. Scaling the brightness alone does not necessarily bring that color into gamut. Independently clipping offending components changes their proportions and can cause hue shifts or merge distinct colors. Gamut mapping instead provides a strategy for fitting the color—for example, reducing its distance from a neutral color while trying to preserve hue. Brightness and saturation limits interact through the destination's color volume . A strongly saturated color cannot necessarily reach the same luminance as neutral white. A conversion may therefore adjust both brightness and chroma to obtain a useful result. The different methods in ITU-R BT.2446 show why HDR-to-SDR conversion includes color processing alongside tone mapping. A movie also needs stable decisions over time A fixed mapping produces the same output for the same input throughout the program. That consistency can be useful, but a single curve chosen for the brightest scene may use the available range less effectively in a much dimmer scene. Scene-adaptive tone mapping changes parameters based on the content. It can make better use of the output range, but the parameter changes themselves become visible if they are too abrupt. Imagine a stationary face beside a window. A tiny flash in the window raises the measured peak for one picture. If that peak immediately changes the mapping for the whole picture, the face can darken for that instant, although its source values did not change. When the flash ends, it brightens again. The viewer sees pumping caused by the adaptation. A method can moderate that response by considering the distribution of bright samples, smoothing parameter changes over time, or distinguishing a scene cut from a brief highlight. Those choices balance responsiveness against stability. Looking at one still frame will not reveal whether the conversion maintains a consistent appearance through movement, flashes, and cuts. Turn the mapped light back into an SDR signal After brightness and color processing, the converter has to produce samples whose encoding matches the intended SDR interpretation. Linear-light values cannot simply be written into a nonlinear video signal without the appropriate transfer operation. Continue the neutral-gray example. An original 100-nit PQ gray has a normalized PQ signal of about 0.508 . Interpreting PQ recovers 100 nits, which is x = 1 in the chosen working units. Applying T(x) produces y = 0.5625, meaning 56.25 nits in the chosen SDR display model. For an ideal SDR reference display with zero black, 100-nit white, and the BT.1886 exponent of 2.4, the nonlinear signal needed to obtain that light is: signal = 0.5625^(1/2.4) ≈ 0.787 The sequence is therefore: Representation Value for this neutral gray Normalized input PQ signal About 0.508 Interpreted HDR light 100 nits Linear mapping input x 1 Linear mapping output T(x) 0.5625 Intended output light 56.25 nits Normalized SDR signal for the stated ideal display About 0.787 The input and output signal numbers differ because they have different transfer meanings. Writing 0.5625 directly as that nonlinear SDR signal would produce only about 25.14 nits under the same display model. The tone-mapping calculation could be correct while the displayed brightness was wrong because the output encoding step was skipped. The real output process also accounts for black level and the selected conversion method. BT.2446 describes several methods; their processing spaces and transfer operations differ. The calculation above isolates one display-referred example so that the distinction between light values and signal values is visible. For a conventional video output, the converter prepares the required luma/chroma representation, numerical range, bit depth, and matching color signaling. Retagging original HDR samples as SDR performs none of the brightness or color calculations. Correct labels describe the converted values; they do not create those values. Precision matters during this work. Intermediate calculations can retain more precision than the final video format. When values are reduced to the output bit depth, rounding can make smooth gradients form visible steps. Dithering can make those steps less conspicuous by distributing rounding error. It helps represent the converted gradient; it cannot restore highlight differences that the mapping has already merged. Relate the conversion to the playback path During an Emby video transcode , the server decodes the HDR source, processes the pictures for the selected output, and encodes the resulting stream. Tone mapping is a picture-processing operation within that path. It changes the delivered rendition while the library file remains available as the source. During local presentation, a playback renderer can perform adaptation as it prepares pictures for the screen. The Windows app documentation describes tone mapping at this stage. Direct Play therefore identifies the server's delivery behavior; it does not, on its own, describe every color or brightness operation performed by the app, operating system, and display. To investigate an unexpected result, first establish where conversion happens and what output is intended. Then use the appearance to narrow the stage worth examining: Raised black or incorrect contrast throughout the picture: check input and output range interpretation, transfer characteristics, and display mode before adjusting highlight compression. Ordinary objects look sensible but bright texture disappears: examine the assumed source peak and highlight mapping. Check several frames to distinguish strong compression from time-dependent adaptation. Brightness looks plausible but vivid colors shift: examine primary conversion, gamut handling, and chroma processing. A stationary object brightens and darkens when another area flashes: examine how the mapping adapts over time. These observations connect a visible change to the operations that can cause it. Comparing the same scene along known playback paths—using both moving pictures and representative stills—makes that investigation much more informative than judging the brightest highlight alone. articles/video/tone-mapping/fundamentals.keywords: Why Tone Mapping Is Needed An HDR film can contain a bright reflection on a car alongside a face in shadow. An SDR screen cannot reproduce the same range of light. Tone mapping fits that range into the available output , deciding how much room to give the face, the reflection, and everything between them. Simply cutting off everything above the screen's limit loses differences between bright objects. Darkening the entire picture can fit the highlights, but make the rest unnecessarily dim. A tone-mapping curve makes a more selective compromise. For scale, an SDR reference viewing setup uses a peak of 100 nits, while an HDR highlight might reach 1,000 nits. A nit is a unit of luminance (one candela per square metre). Dividing every light level by ten would fit that example, but would also turn a 100-nit object into a 10-nit one. Why changing the playback quality is not enough Change What it changes Does it solve the brightness mismatch? Lower the resolution The number of pixels No Reduce the bitrate The amount of compressed data No Relabel HDR as SDR How a player interprets the signal No; the picture values still need conversion Tone-map the picture The relationship between input and output brightness Yes, as part of a correctly configured conversion Tone mapping is one part of HDR-to-SDR conversion . Color also needs appropriate handling; fixing brightness alone does not guarantee correct color. Where Emby fits The work can happen at different points in a playback session. Emby Server can tone-map during video transcoding. A player can also do it locally: the Emby Windows FAQ describes tone mapping in the app's rendering stage. That is why the server's playback method and the final appearance are separate questions. Direct Play describes delivery from the server; it does not mean the player or display leaves the picture untouched. Different mappings can retain different amounts of highlight contrast or change the apparent brightness of faces. They cannot reproduce all the original HDR brightness on an SDR screen, or guarantee the same result as a separately graded SDR release.
